Stat 2 — The Question Bank

Eight themes, three sets of fifteen · Course 2.1 · Methods & Statistics

How to use this

Pick a theme on the left, then a set, then a question number. Choose an option — you have to commit before anything is explained. Working out which kind of question you are looking at is most of what the exam tests, and you cannot practise that while reading the answer.

Once you answer, the panel opens: what the question is really asking in plain English, which type it is, the procedure, the full working line by line, and why each wrong option was tempting. At the bottom of every panel there are two links — one to that theme on your own study site, one to your dashboard — so you can go straight to the material if a question lands badly.

Three sets per theme. Set A sits where the homework sits — the plain forward question for every topic. Set B goes a step harder: two-step calculations, working backwards from a printed figure to recover a design, telling near-identical procedures apart. Set C deliberately refuses to repeat Set A’s shapes — it runs the rules backwards, hands you a conclusion and asks what produced it, sets two researchers against each other, changes a design and asks what moves, and asks you to find the one wrong entry in a printed table. A quarter of Set C needs no arithmetic at all.

Set C is also weighted like a full mock paper rather than evenly: 15 on correlation and regression and 15 on regression inference, 18 on one-way ANOVA, 15 each on factorial ANOVA and repeated measures, 12 each on proportions and chi-square, and 18 on causality, research design and the ethics of inference, which your eight themes had no home for. It spends nothing on Theme 1 foundations.

Every set is built to mirror your own homework papers and earlier practice papers: the question shapes are the same, the studies and the numbers are all new.

Symptom → diagnosis → treatment

Every question type in this material. Read the left column as “what the question says”, the middle as “what it actually is”, and the right as “what you do about it”.

📶 Measurement levels
“The variable … is measured on which scale?”
Nominal / ordinal / interval / ratio
A factor is allocated, a response is measured. Does 0 mean “none at all”? Then ratio. Numbers used as labels are still nominal.
📐 Spread and the SD
“The standard deviation is…”
SS ⁄ (N − 1), then the square root
Deviations always sum to zero, so square them first. Divide by N − 1, never N. The square root puts you back in the original units.
🔔 z-scores and the Normal table
“What proportion scored more than…”
z, then the Normal table
z = (score − mean) ⁄ SD. The table gives the area to the LEFT; everything else is 1 minus that, or one area minus another. Sketch it before you look it up.
🔀 z or t, and which t
“The test statistic is…” with a spread given
σ given → z; s from the sample → t
Population SD handed to you means z. An SD computed from your own data means t, on N − 1 df, against a higher critical value.
🧭 Causality and research design
A study that only measured both variables
Association, never cause
Cause needs random ASSIGNMENT and a comparison group. Random sampling buys generalisation, not causation — they are different words doing different jobs.
⚖️ Ethics and inference
“The result was significant, so…”
Ask what else was run
One pre-specified test holds α at 5%. Several tests, or a choice made after seeing the data, quietly raise it — and a non-significant result is not evidence of no effect.
✅ Conditions and plus four
“Can we use the Normal approximation?”
Count successes AND failures
At least 10 of each for one proportion, at least 5 in each of four cells for two. A big n does not rescue a lopsided split.
📏 Interval for a proportion
“The margin of error is…”
z* × √(p̂(1 − p̂) ⁄ n)
The margin is only half the interval. An option that gives you two numbers in brackets is the interval, not the margin — read which one is being asked for.
🔔 The sampling distribution of p-hat
“The probability that at least …% of them…”
A Normal calculation on p-hat
Centre on p, spread √(p(1 − p) ⁄ n), then z and the table. This is the one proportions question that is really a z-score question wearing different clothes.
🧮 The statistic and its df
“The degrees of freedom for the chi-square test are…”
(r − 1)(c − 1)
Rows minus one times columns minus one. N never enters it, and neither does the number of cells.
🎯 Expected counts
“The expected count for that cell is…”
row total × column total ⁄ N
Margins and N only — the observed count in that cell never appears in its own expected count. Never round it.
🔗 Chi-square against the z test
A 2 × 2 table, and both a z test and a chi-square mentioned
They are the same test
For a 2 × 2 table χ² = z², so the two give exactly the same two-sided P-value. An option saying one is smaller is wrong.
📈 Reading a correlation
“The correlation is about…”
Sign from the direction, size from the scatter
r = +0.8 and r = −0.8 are equally strong. r has no units and does not change if you swap the axes. Two points always give exactly ±1.
🥧 r-squared
“…% of the variation is explained by…”
r², not r
Square it. A correlation of 0.87 explains 0.76 of the variation, not 0.87 — and “87% of the variation” is the designed trap.
📐 Testing a slope
“The degrees of freedom for the t test for the slope are…”
n − p − 1
One predictor costs two: n − 2. The same df runs the slope test, the intercept test, any interval for either, and the Residual Error row.
🅕 The overall F test
“The value of the F statistic is…”
MS model ⁄ MS error
Both mean squares first. Dividing the sums of squares straight away gives a plausible wrong number that is always one of the options.
🎯 Mean response or one individual
“…for the mean response” against “…for one individual”
Two intervals, same centre
The interval for one individual is always the wider of the two. Both are narrowest at x̄ and widen either side.
🔢 Degrees of freedom
“The degrees of freedom for the F test are…”
A PAIR: (k − 1, N − k)
Groups minus one, then total minus groups. Three groups of ten gives (2, 27) — never (3, 30) and never (2, 10).
✅ The equal-spread condition
“Is the ANOVA appropriate?”
Largest SD against smallest
The rule of thumb is that the largest standard deviation should be no more than about twice the smallest. 2.5 and 6.4 fails it.
⚖️ Hypotheses and conclusions
“The hypotheses tested are…”
H₀ all equal, Hₐ NOT all equal
Never “all the means differ”, and never a directional Hₐ. A small P says some mean differs from the others, not which, and not that they all do.
🔢 Degrees of freedom
“The degrees of freedom for interaction are…”
(a − 1)(b − 1)
Multiply the two main-effect df. The cell count a × b is a different number, and it is always one of the options.
📈 Interaction plots
“This plot indicates / suggests…”
Three readings, in order
PARALLEL? → interaction. APART? → the line factor. TILTED? → the axis factor. Answer all three before looking at the options. Crossing is not required for an interaction.
🔧 Sphericity and the correction
“Mauchly’s test was significant, so…”
Correct the degrees of freedom
A significant Mauchly means sphericity is rejected, so use Greenhouse-Geisser: multiply both df by epsilon. The F does not change, the df and the P-value do.
💪 What the pairing buys you
The same people measured more than once
Pull the person variation out
Each person being consistently high or low goes into its own row instead of the error term, which is why a repeated-measures design finds effects an independent design misses on the same numbers.
⚖️ What it does NOT mean
“We may conclude that…” with two tempting options
Usually the modest one
Read each option as a claim and ask what would have to be true. Causation needs random assignment; a direction needs the means; an F or a χ² on its own gives neither.

Question 1

📶 Measurement levels

Identifying the measurement level

A questionnaire records each respondent’s highest completed qualification as one of “school”, “bachelor’s”, “master’s” or “doctorate”. This variable is measured on which scale?
  • ainterval
  • bratio
  • cordinal
  • dnominal
🔎 What it is really asking

The categories have an order but the gaps between them are not equal amounts.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Measurement level: telling ordinal from nominal.

🛠️ The procedure

Nominal = names with no order. Ordinal = ordered, but the gaps are not known to be equal. Interval = equal gaps, no true zero. Ratio = equal gaps and a true zero.

🧮 The working
The four categories have a clear order — a doctorate is more than a master’s, which is more than a bachelor’s. So it is not merely nominal.

But the step from school to bachelor’s is not the same "amount of qualification" as the step from master’s to doctorate, and there is no way to say by how much. Unequal, undefined gaps.

That is exactly ordinal.

What it permits: counts, the mode, the median and percentiles. Not a mean — "the average qualification is 2.4" has no meaning.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Interval would need the gaps to be equal and measurable, as degrees Celsius are. There is no unit of qualification.
b.Ratio would need both equal gaps and a meaningful zero, so that one value could be "twice" another. A master’s is not twice a bachelor’s.
d.Nominal would mean the four categories had no order at all, like eye colour. These are plainly ranked.
🏷️ Ordered but with undefined gaps = ordinal. Mode and median only.

Question 2

📶 Measurement levels

Spotting a ratio variable

Which of these four variables is measured on a ratio scale?
  • athe number of therapy sessions a client has attended
  • bthe year in which a client first sought treatment
  • ca client’s score on a 7-point satisfaction scale
  • dthe clinic site a client attends
🔎 What it is really asking

Which one has a zero that means "none at all"?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Measurement level: applying the absolute-zero test.

🛠️ The procedure

The test for ratio is: does 0 mean "none at all"? If it does, ratios are meaningful and you may say one value is twice another.

🧮 The working
Zero sessions attended means no sessions at all, so the zero is real and six sessions really is twice three. That is ratio.

Run the test on the others:
• Year of first treatment — year 0 is a calendar convention, not "no time". Interval.
• A 7-point satisfaction scale — ordered, but the gaps are not known to be equal, and there is no zero point on it at all. Ordinal.
• Clinic site — just names. Nominal.

The habit: ask "what would a zero mean here?" before anything else.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Year of first treatment is interval: the zero is a convention, so year 2000 does not stand for twice as much elapsed time as year 1000.
c.A 7-point scale is ordinal — the distance from 3 to 4 is not guaranteed to match the distance from 6 to 7, and there is no true zero.
d.Clinic site is nominal. Numbering the sites 1, 2, 3 in the data file does not change that.
🏷️ Does 0 mean "none at all"? Then ratio.

Question 3

📊 Describing a distribution

Naming the skew from the summary figures

Three wards are compared on the number of nights patients stay after a routine procedure. The summary figures are shown below.

Which ward’s distribution is most clearly right-skewed?
Nights in hospital after a routine procedure · three wards
GroupnmeanmedianSD
Ward A406.26.01.4
Ward B409.87.05.1
Ward C406.16.11.3
  • aWard A
  • bWard C
  • cnone of them — all three look symmetrical
  • dWard B
🔎 What it is really asking

Which ward has its mean pulled well above its median?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Describing a distribution: reading skew from the mean, median and SD.

🛠️ The procedure

In a right skew the mean sits above the median, because the long tail of high values drags the mean and not the median. A much larger SD points the same way.

🧮 The working
Compare each mean with its own median:
  Ward A: 6.2 against 6.0 — almost identical.
  Ward B: 9.8 against 7.0 — the mean is 2.8 nights above the median.
  Ward C: 6.1 against 6.1 — identical.

Ward B also has an SD of 5.1 against 1.4 and 1.3 in the other two.

A mean well above the median plus a much bigger spread is the signature of a right skew — a few patients staying a very long time.

And the consequence: for Ward B the median of 7 nights describes a typical patient; the mean of 9.8 describes nobody.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Ward A has a mean and median within 0.2 of each other and a small SD. That is as close to symmetrical as real data gets.
b.Ward C has its mean and median at the same value, 6.1 — the picture of symmetry.
c.Ward B is clearly not symmetrical: a 2.8-night gap between mean and median and an SD nearly four times the others.
🏷️ Mean above median = right skew. The tail drags the mean, not the median.

Question 4

📊 Describing a distribution

Choosing the honest summary

For the ward with a mean of 9.8 nights and a median of 7.0 nights, the more informative summary of a typical stay is:
Nights in hospital after a routine procedure · three wards
GroupnmeanmedianSD
Ward A406.26.01.4
Ward B409.87.05.1
Ward C406.16.11.3
  • aneither — a skewed distribution has no centre
  • bthe median, because the distribution is skewed
  • cthe mean, because it uses every observation
  • deither one, since both describe the centre
🔎 What it is really asking

Skewed data: which measure of centre should be reported?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Describing a distribution: which centre to report.

🛠️ The procedure

Under skew or outliers, report the median. The mean uses every value, which is exactly why a handful of extreme values drags it away from typical.

🧮 The working
The mean of 9.8 sits 2.8 nights above the median of 7.0, so a few long stays are pulling it upward.

The median asks only who is standing in the middle, so those long stays move it barely at all. It is the better description of a typical patient.

This is why house prices, salaries and hospital stays are reported as medians almost everywhere.

Not an instruction to hide the mean: report both and say the distribution is skewed. The gap between them is itself informative.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.A skewed distribution has a perfectly good centre. It just needs the resistant measure rather than the sensitive one.
c.Using every observation is the mean’s weakness here, not its strength — the extreme stays are observations too, and they drag it.
d.They are not interchangeable when the distribution is skewed: 9.8 and 7.0 tell a reader different things about a typical stay.
🏷️ Skewed or outliers → report the median.

Question 5

📐 Spread and the SD

The sum of squared deviations

Eight students reported how many hours they revised in the week before a test. The figures are shown below.

The sum of the squared deviations from the mean, as a whole number, is:
Hours of revision in the week before a test · 8 students
StudentABCDEFGH
Hours of revision4681010121416
  • a112
  • b80
  • c14
  • d16
🔎 What it is really asking

Find the mean, subtract it from each value, square, and add.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Spread: computing SS from raw data.

🛠️ The procedure

SS = Σ(X − x̄)². Find the mean first, then square each deviation before adding — the deviations themselves always sum to zero.

🧮 The working
Mean = (4 + 6 + 8 + 10 + 10 + 12 + 14 + 16) ⁄ 8 = 80 ⁄ 8 = 10.

Deviations: −6, −4, −2, 0, 0, +2, +4, +6.  They sum to 0, as they always must.

Squares: 36, 16, 4, 0, 0, 4, 16, 36.

SS = 36 + 16 + 4 + 0 + 0 + 4 + 16 + 36 = 112

What comes next: variance = 112 ⁄ 7 = 16, and SD = √16 = 4 hours.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.80 is the sum of the hours themselves, which you use to get the mean and then leave behind.
c.14 is the range, 16 − 4. The range uses only the two extreme values; SS uses all eight.
d.16 is the variance, 112 ⁄ 7 — one step further on than the question asked.
🏷️ SS = Σ(X − x̄)². Square first, then add.

Question 6

📐 Spread and the SD

Variance and SD from SS

For those same eight students the sum of squared deviations is 112. The standard deviation, as a whole number of hours, is:
Hours of revision in the week before a test · 8 students
StudentABCDEFGH
Hours of revision4681010121416
  • a14
  • b3.7
  • c4
  • d16
🔎 What it is really asking

Turn SS into a standard deviation.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Spread: SS → variance → SD.

🛠️ The procedure

Variance = SS ⁄ (N − 1), then SD = √variance. The division is by N − 1 because the data are a sample.

🧮 The working
Variance = 112 ⁄ (8 − 1) = 112 ⁄ 7 = 16 (hours squared).

SD = √16 = 4 hours.

The square root is what puts the answer back into hours — variance is in hours squared, which nobody can picture.

The reading: a typical student is about 4 hours away from the class average of 10.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.14 is the range, 16 − 4 — a different measure of spread altogether, and one that uses only two of the eight values.
b.3.7 is √(112 ⁄ 8) — dividing by N instead of N − 1. With a sample it is always N − 1, here 7.
d.16 is the variance, in hours squared. The SD is its square root.
🏷️ SS ⁄ (N − 1) = variance. √variance = SD, back in the original units.

Question 7

🔔 z-scores and the Normal table

Computing a z-score

Scores on a reading test are approximately Normal with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. A child scores 124. That child’s z-score, to two decimal places, is:
  • a0.24
  • b2.40
  • c1.24
  • d1.60
🔎 What it is really asking

How many standard deviations above the mean is 124?

🧭 Which type of question this is

z-scores: turning a raw score into a position.

🛠️ The procedure

z = (score − mean) ⁄ SD. The sign gives the direction, the number gives the distance in standard deviations.

🧮 The working
z = (124 − 100) ⁄ 15 = 24 ⁄ 15 = 1.60

So the child sits 1.6 standard deviations above average.

What it buys you: because the distribution is Normal, the table turns that 1.60 into a percentage — 94.52% of children score below this child, so 5.48% score above.

The check: the score is above the mean, so z must be positive. A z between 1 and 2 means "unusual but not rare".
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.24 is 24 ⁄ 100 — dividing the difference by the mean instead of by the standard deviation.
b.2.40 is 24 ⁄ 10, as though the SD were 10. Read the SD off the stem.
c.1.24 is 124 ⁄ 100 — the score over the mean, which is not a z-score at all. You must subtract before you divide.
🏷️ z = (score − mean) ⁄ SD. Subtract first, then divide by the SD.

Question 8

🔔 z-scores and the Normal table

A tail area from the Normal table

On that same reading test — mean 100, standard deviation 15 — the proportion of children scoring above 130, to four decimal places, is:
  • a0.1587
  • b0.0228
  • c0.9772
  • d0.0456
🔎 What it is really asking

Convert to z, then take the area in the upper tail.

🧭 Which type of question this is

z-scores: reading an upper-tail area.

🛠️ The procedure

Convert to z, look up the area to the left, then subtract from 1 to get the area to the right.

🧮 The working
z = (130 − 100) ⁄ 15 = 30 ⁄ 15 = +2.00

The table gives the area to the left of 2.00 as 0.9772.

Above 130 is therefore 1 − 0.9772 = 0.0228, about 2.3% of children.

The sanity check that catches most errors here: 130 is well above average, so the proportion above it must be small. Any answer over 0.5 is wrong before you check the arithmetic.

This also matches the 68–95–99.7 rule: about 95% sit within 2 SDs, leaving about 2.5% in each tail.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.1587 is the area above z = +1, which would be a score of 115, not 130.
c.0.9772 is the area to the left of 130 — the proportion scoring less, which is what the table gives you directly. The question asked for above.
d.0.0456 is both tails added, 2 × 0.0228. The question asked about one direction only.
🏷️ The table gives the LEFT area. Right = 1 − left. Sketch it first.

Question 9

🔔 z-scores and the Normal table

The 68–95–99.7 rule

For the same reading test, the proportion of children scoring between 85 and 115 is closest to:
  • a68%
  • b95%
  • c50%
  • d34%
🔎 What it is really asking

85 and 115 are one SD either side of the mean.

🧭 Which type of question this is

z-scores: applying the empirical rule.

🛠️ The procedure

About 68% of a Normal distribution lies within 1 SD of the mean, about 95% within 2 SDs, and about 99.7% within 3.

🧮 The working
85 is (85 − 100) ⁄ 15 = −1.00 and 115 is (115 − 100) ⁄ 15 = +1.00.

So the question is asking for the area between z = −1 and z = +1, which is the first line of the empirical rule: about 68%.

Exactly, from the table: 0.8413 − 0.1587 = 0.6827, so 68.3%.

Worth memorising, because it turns a table lookup into a two-second sanity check — and because exams ask it directly.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.95% is the area within 2 standard deviations, which here would be 70 to 130.
c.50% is the area on one side of the mean. The interval asked about straddles the mean.
d.34% is half of 68% — the area from the mean out to one SD in a single direction, not both.
🏷️ ±1 SD ≈ 68% · ±2 SD ≈ 95% · ±3 SD ≈ 99.7%.

Question 10

⚖️ The logic of a test

Writing the null hypothesis

A clinic’s records show that appointments have historically lasted a mean of 72 minutes. A new booking system is introduced and 36 appointments are timed. For a test of whether the mean has changed, the null hypothesis is:
  • aH₀: µ ≠ 72
  • bH₀: x̄ = 75
  • cH₀: µ = 72
  • dH₀: x̄ = 72
🔎 What it is really asking

Which symbol, and which value, belong in H₀?

🧭 Which type of question this is

The logic of a test: stating the hypotheses.

🛠️ The procedure

H₀ is always about the population parameter and always contains the equals sign. It states the claim you are going to pretend is true.

🧮 The working
The claim being tested concerns the population mean appointment length, so the parameter is µ, and the claimed value is the historical 72.

H₀: µ = 72.  Hₐ: µ ≠ 72, because "has it changed" sets no direction.

Why not x̄. You measured x̄ from the 36 appointments — it is a known number. There is nothing left to hypothesise about it. Hypotheses are always statements about the population you cannot see.

Why the equals sign lives in H₀. It is the specific claim, and a specific claim is what lets you build a distribution and work out a P-value.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The "not equal to" belongs in Hₐ. H₀ must carry the equals sign so that it pins down one distribution.
b.This has both faults at once: the sample symbol, and a value taken from the data rather than from the claim.
d.x̄ is the sample mean — something you measured, not something you hypothesise about. Hypotheses name population parameters.
🏷️ H₀ is about µ, not x̄, and it always holds the equals sign.

Question 11

⚖️ The logic of a test

Interpreting a P-value

A clinic’s appointments have historically lasted a mean of 72 minutes. After a new booking system is introduced, a test of whether the mean has changed returns P = 0.046. The correct interpretation is:
  • athere is a 4.6% probability that the mean is in fact unchanged
  • bthere is a 4.6% probability that this conclusion is the wrong one
  • c4.6% of appointments now run longer than they used to run
  • dif the mean were unchanged, a result this far out would happen 4.6% of the time
🔎 What it is really asking

What exactly is the 0.046 the probability of?

🧭 Which type of question this is

The logic of a test: what a P-value is.

🛠️ The procedure

A P-value is the probability of data at least this extreme, given that H₀ is true. The claim is the assumption, never the conclusion.

🧮 The working
The calculation that produces 0.046 begins by assuming µ = 72 and asks how often a sample mean would land this far from 72 by chance alone. The answer is 4.6% of the time.

Everything in that sentence is conditional on H₀ being true. The P-value cannot be a probability about H₀, because H₀ was treated as certain while computing it.

The phrasing that gives the error away: "the probability that the mean is…". The mean is not random; it is a fixed unknown. Your data were the random thing.

At α = .05 this is significant, but only just — and "just significant" is a reason to report the estimate and its interval too, not to stop.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.This puts the probability on the hypothesis rather than on the data. H₀ is not random, so it has no probability of being true or false.
b.The probability of being wrong depends on whether H₀ is in fact true, which is exactly what you do not know. α is a long-run error rate, not the chance this particular conclusion is mistaken.
c.This describes individual appointments. The test is about the mean of all of them, not about what fraction got longer.
🏷️ P = the chance of DATA this extreme, GIVEN H₀. Never a probability about H₀.

Question 12

🚨 Errors and power

Naming the error

A researcher concludes that a new booking system has changed mean appointment length, when in fact it has not. This is:
  • aa sampling error, but not a Type I or Type II error
  • ba Type I error
  • ca Type II error
  • da loss of power
🔎 What it is really asking

H₀ was true, and it was rejected. Which error is that?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Errors: naming Type I against Type II.

🛠️ The procedure

Type I = rejecting a true H₀ — crying wolf, probability α. Type II = failing to reject a false H₀ — missing it, probability β.

🧮 The working
Nothing really changed, so H₀ was true. The researcher nevertheless rejected it. True H₀ plus a rejection is the top-left cell of the table: a Type I error.

Its probability is α, which the researcher chose — set α = .05 and you accept crying wolf one time in twenty when there is nothing there.

The mirror case: had the system really changed appointment length and the test missed it, that would be a Type II error, with probability β.

A way to keep them straight: Type I comes first and is the one you set first.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.It is precisely a Type I error. The name exists for exactly this case: a true null rejected.
c.A Type II error is the opposite situation — a real effect that the test fails to detect. Here there was no real effect.
d.Power is the chance of catching a real effect, 1 − β. It is not an error, and it is not relevant when H₀ is true.
🏷️ True H₀ rejected = Type I (α). False H₀ kept = Type II (β).

Question 13

🚨 Errors and power

What raises power

A study has low power to detect a difference that really exists. The most effective way to raise its power is to:
  • aincrease the sample size
  • blower α from .05 to .01
  • cuse a two-sided test instead of a one-sided one
  • dreport the result as significant anyway
🔎 What it is really asking

Which change improves the chance of detecting a real effect?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Power: which lever actually works.

🛠️ The procedure

Power is 1 − β. It rises with a bigger n, a bigger real effect, a smaller spread, and a larger α — and n is the one you can change without paying for it somewhere else.

🧮 The working
A bigger n shrinks the standard error, which moves the sampling distributions apart relative to their own spread, so a real difference is easier to detect.

Concretely, for a true shift of 4 with σ = 10 and α = .05 two-sided, power runs .52 at n = 25, .89 at n = 64, and .98 at n = 100.

Why the others make it worse or do nothing. Lowering α to .01 cries wolf less often but misses more — β rises, so power falls. Going two-sided splits the rejection region, which lowers power in the direction you cared about.

What else genuinely helps: cleaner measurement, a more homogeneous sample, or a paired design — all of which shrink the spread.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Lowering α makes the test more conservative, so it rejects less often — including when it should. That lowers power, not raises it.
c.A two-sided test spreads the 5% across both tails, so it needs a more extreme result to reject in either direction. Power goes down.
d.Reporting a result as significant when it is not is not a way of raising power; it is a way of committing a Type I error on purpose.
🏷️ Bigger n raises power. Smaller α lowers it.

Question 14

🔀 z or t, and which t

Choosing between z and t

A researcher tests whether the mean of a sample of 36 differs from a claimed value. The standard deviation is computed from the 36 observations themselves. The appropriate reference distribution is:
  • at with 36 degrees of freedom
  • bthe standard Normal, because n is at least 30
  • ct with 35 degrees of freedom
  • dthe standard Normal
🔎 What it is really asking

Was the spread given to you, or estimated from the data?

🧭 Which type of question this is

The z-against-t fork.

🛠️ The procedure

σ known → z, no degrees of freedom. σ estimated from the sample → t, on N − 1 degrees of freedom.

🧮 The working
The standard deviation came from the 36 observations, so it is s, not σ. Estimating the spread costs you something, and the t distribution is what charges you for it: slightly fatter tails and a higher critical value.

df = N − 1 = 36 − 1 = 35.

How much it matters here. The same statistic of 2.00 gives P = .046 read against the Normal and P = .053 read against t on 35 df — opposite sides of .05. The critical values are 1.96 and 2.030.

In practice σ is almost never known, so t is the usual answer; z turns up in exam questions because σ has been handed to you.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The degrees of freedom are N − 1, not N. Estimating the mean from the same 36 observations costs one.
b."n ≥ 30" is a rule about when the Central Limit Theorem makes the sampling distribution roughly Normal. It is not a licence to use z when σ is unknown — the curves are close at n = 36, but t is still the correct one.
d.The standard Normal is for a known σ. Here the spread was estimated, so the Normal understates how uncertain the answer is.
🏷️ σ given → z. s from your data → t on N − 1.

Question 15

🔀 z or t, and which t

Choosing which t

Twenty students are tested at the start of a course and again at the end, and the researcher wants to know whether scores changed. The appropriate test is:
  • aan independent-samples t test on 38 degrees of freedom
  • ba one-sample t test on 39 degrees of freedom
  • can independent-samples t test on 19 degrees of freedom
  • da paired t test on 19 degrees of freedom
🔎 What it is really asking

Twenty people, two measurements each. Which design is that?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Choosing which t: pairing comes before counting groups.

🛠️ The procedure

If the same people are measured twice, the design is paired: compute each person’s difference, then run a one-sample test on those differences, on N − 1 df where N is the number of people.

🧮 The working
There are twenty people, not forty, and each contributes one difference — their end score minus their start score.

So it is a paired t test, on 20 − 1 = 19 degrees of freedom, testing H₀: the mean difference is zero.

Why not independent. An independent-samples test assumes the two columns come from different people. Running it here throws away the pairing — the fact that a strong student is strong in both columns — which is usually the most useful information in the whole study, and it gets the degrees of freedom wrong as well.

The habit: count the people, not the columns.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.38 df would be right for two independent groups of twenty — forty different people. Here the same twenty appear twice.
b.A one-sample test on 39 df would need forty independent observations. There are twenty people and twenty differences.
c.The df is right for a paired design, but the test named is the wrong one. Independent-samples on 19 df is not a combination that exists.
🏷️ Same people twice → paired t, on (number of PEOPLE − 1) df.

Question 1

📶 Measurement levels

What a numeric code does not change

Sleep researcher Vandermeer asks 120 participants to rate their sleep quality as “poor”, “fair”, “good” or “excellent”, and enters those answers in her data file as 1, 2, 3 and 4. Her results table then reports “mean sleep quality = 2.74”. The objection to that figure is:
  • anothing — the 1 to 4 coding makes it interval
  • bthe median is unavailable for this variable
  • ccoding 1 to 4 does not make the gaps equal
  • da mean needs a true zero, which 1 to 4 lacks
🔎 What it is really asking

The numbers in the file are labels. Does averaging labels mean anything?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Measurement level: what a numeric code buys you, and what it does not.

🛠️ The procedure

Decide the level from the variable, never from how it was typed into the file. Ordered categories with unknown gaps are ordinal, and a mean needs at least interval.

🧮 The working
Step one — the level. Poor → fair → good → excellent is clearly ordered, so it is not nominal. But is the step from poor to fair the same amount of sleep quality as the step from good to excellent? There is no way to say. Unknown gaps, so ordinal.

Step two — what ordinal allows. Counts, the mode, the median, percentiles. Not a mean, because a mean adds the values together, and adding 1 to 3 only makes sense if the distance from 1 to 2 equals the distance from 2 to 3.

Typing 1, 2, 3, 4 into a spreadsheet is a bookkeeping decision. Vandermeer could have used 1, 2, 4, 8 and the data would carry exactly the same information — but the "mean" would come out completely different. That is the giveaway that the mean is not a property of the variable at all.

The habit: before you read a mean, ask what one unit of the variable is. If you cannot name it, the mean is decoration.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Coding changes nothing about the variable. The level is a fact about what was measured, not about which symbols were used to record it.
b.The median is exactly what is available here, along with the mode and the percentages in each category. It is the mean that is not.
d.A true zero is the test for ratio, one level higher. The mean only needs equal gaps, which is the interval level — and this variable fails even that.
🏷️ The level belongs to the variable, not to the numbers you typed in.

Question 2

📶 Measurement levels

Working back from the statistics reported

Sports scientist Thibault reports the median and the interquartile range of one variable and writes that “a mean of this variable would be meaningless”. Both of those decisions are correct. The variable is:
  • athe order in which runners finished a race
  • beach runner’s finishing time in seconds
  • cthe air temperature on race day in °C
  • dthe running club each runner belongs to
🔎 What it is really asking

Which variable allows a median but not a mean? Both halves have to hold.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Measurement level: reasoning backwards from which statistics are legitimate.

🛠️ The procedure

Match the level to the statistics it permits. Nominal → counts and the mode only. Ordinal → median and percentiles, but no mean. Interval and ratio → the mean as well.

🧮 The working
The clue is that two things must be true at once: the median is allowed and the mean is not. Only one level does both, and that is ordinal.

Finishing order is ordinal. First, second, third are ranked, so a middle rank exists and quartiles of rank exist. But the gap between first and second might be a tenth of a second while the gap between second and third is a minute, so "mean finishing position = 7.3" describes nothing.

Run the other three through the same two-part test:
• Finishing time in seconds — ratio. Median allowed, mean allowed. Fails the second half.
• Temperature in °C — interval. Median allowed, mean allowed. Fails the second half.
• Running club — nominal. The mean fails, but so does the median, because the clubs are not in any order. Fails the first half.

The habit: when a question tells you which statistics were used, read it as a clue about the level rather than as background.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Finishing time in seconds is ratio — a mean time is the most natural summary there is, so Thibault’s second statement would be wrong.
c.Degrees Celsius is interval: the gaps are equal even though the zero is a convention, so a mean temperature is perfectly meaningful.
d.Club membership is nominal, so there is no middle club and no interquartile range. Thibault’s first statement would be the wrong one.
🏷️ Median but no mean = ordinal. Nominal loses the median too.

Question 3

📊 Describing a distribution

A mean recomputed after a correction

Health psychologist Rietveld times how long each of 50 patients waits to be seen and finds a mean of 24.0 minutes and a median of 18.0 minutes. She then discovers that one patient’s wait was typed as 310 minutes when it should have been 31. The corrected mean, to two decimal places, is:
  • a18.16
  • b18.00
  • c29.58
  • d18.42
🔎 What it is really asking

Rebuild the total, swap the one value, divide by the same 50.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Describing a distribution: recovering and repairing a total.

🛠️ The procedure

A mean is total ⁄ n, so work with the total. Multiply the mean by n to get it back, take out the wrong value, put in the right one, and divide by the same n.

🧮 The working
Recover the total: 24.0 × 50 = 1200 minutes.

Swap the values: 1200 − 310 + 31 = 921 minutes.

Divide by 50 again — the patient is still in the study, so n has not changed:
921 ⁄ 50 = 18.42 minutes.

One mistyped digit was carrying the mean 5.58 minutes above where it belonged.

And the median? It stays at 18.0. The corrected value, 31, is still above the middle of the distribution, so nobody changes places and the middle patient is the same person. That is resistance in one line: the median noticed nothing.

The habit: any question that changes one value in a known mean is a question about the total. Go to the total first and the arithmetic is trivial.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.18.16 is 890 ⁄ 49 — the bad value deleted rather than corrected. The patient did wait 31 minutes, so there are still 50 waits to average.
b.18.00 is the median, which this correction barely touches. The question asked for the mean, and the two are no longer equal.
c.29.58 is 24.0 + 279 ⁄ 50 — the correction applied in the wrong direction. The typo made the recorded wait too long, so fixing it must pull the mean down.
🏷️ Change one value in a known mean? Go through the TOTAL.

Question 4

📊 Describing a distribution

What a rescaling leaves alone

Lecturer Marchetti marks coursework out of 20 and then rescales every mark to a percentage by multiplying it by 5. Comparing the percentages with the original marks, the quantity that is unchanged is:
Six coursework marks, before and after the rescaling
StudentABCDEF
Mark out of 2011149171215
Rescaled to a percentage557045856075
  • athe mean
  • beach student’s z-score
  • cthe standard deviation
  • dthe variance
🔎 What it is really asking

Which summary survives multiplying every value by the same number?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Describing a distribution: the effect of a linear rescaling.

🛠️ The procedure

Multiplying every value by c multiplies the mean by c and the SD by c, and multiplies the variance by c². A z-score divides one by the other, so the c cancels.

🧮 The working
The six marks are 11, 14, 9, 17, 12, 15.

Mean:      13.000 → 65.000   (× 5)
SD:        2.8983 → 14.4914  (× 5)
Variance:  8.400 → 210.000   (× 25, because the SD was squared)

Now the z-score of student D, who scored 17 out of 20, which is 85%:

before: (17 − 13) ⁄ 2.8983 = 1.3801
after:  (85 − 65) ⁄ 14.4914 = 1.3801

Both the numerator and the denominator were multiplied by 5, so the 5 cancels. Every student’s z-score is identical on the two scales.

And the point of it: a z-score describes a position in the group. Relabelling the scale cannot move anybody relative to anybody else, so no position can change. That is why z-scores let you compare across tests measured in different units at all.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The mean scales with the data as well: 13 out of 20 becomes 65%. Only a ratio of two scaled quantities survives.
c.The standard deviation is in the units of the data, so it scales with them: 2.8983 marks becomes 14.4914 percentage points.
d.The variance scales by the square of the multiplier — 8.400 becomes 210.000, a factor of 25, not 5. It is the most changed of the four.
🏷️ Multiply everything by c: mean ×c, SD ×c, variance ×c², z unchanged.

Question 5

📐 Spread and the SD

Recovering SS from a reported SD

Sports psychologist Olofsdottir reports that the 10 athletes in her sample completed a mean number of press-ups with a standard deviation of 6.00. The sum of the squared deviations from the mean, as a whole number, is:
  • a36
  • b60
  • c324
  • d360
🔎 What it is really asking

Run SS → variance → SD backwards, from the SD to the SS.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Spread: working backwards from a printed standard deviation.

🛠️ The procedure

Forwards it is variance = SS ⁄ (N − 1) and SD = √variance. Backwards, therefore, SS = SD² × (N − 1): square to undo the root, multiply to undo the division.

🧮 The working
Undo the square root first: variance = 6.00² = 36.00.

Then undo the division. It was by N − 1 = 10 − 1 = 9, so multiply by 9:

SS = 36.00 × 9 = 324

Check it by going forwards again: 324 ⁄ 9 = 36, and √36 = 6.00. ✓

The habit: write the forward chain down the margin — SS → ÷(N−1) → variance → √ → SD — and then read it right to left, inverting each arrow. Squaring undoes a root; multiplying undoes a division. You never have to remember a separate backwards formula.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.36 is the variance, one step short of the answer. It is in press-ups squared, while SS is what you divide to get it.
b.60 is 6.00 × 10, the SD multiplied by the sample size. Nothing in the chain multiplies an un-squared SD by anything.
d.360 is 36 × 10 — multiplying by N instead of by N − 1. With a sample the divisor going forwards was 9, so 9 is what you multiply by coming back.
🏷️ SS = SD² × (N − 1). Square to undo the root, multiply to undo the divide.

Question 6

📐 Spread and the SD

A missing value, then the SD

Cognitive researcher Dubois asks five participants to recall words from a 30-word list. One score was lost from her file, but she knows the mean of all five was 18. The standard deviation of the five scores, to two decimal places, is:
Words recalled from a 30-word list · 5 participants, mean 18
Participant12345
Words recalled1215?2124
  • a4.74
  • b4.24
  • c22.50
  • d3.60
🔎 What it is really asking

Recover the missing score from the mean first, then do the SD.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Spread: SD from raw data, with one value to recover first.

🛠️ The procedure

A mean tells you the total: total = mean × n. Subtract the scores you have to get the missing one. Then the usual chain — deviations, squares, SS, ÷(N − 1), √.

🧮 The working
Step one — the missing score.
Total must be 18 × 5 = 90. The four known scores add to 12 + 15 + 21 + 24 = 72.
Missing score = 90 − 72 = 18.

Step two — the spread of 12, 15, 18, 21, 24.
Deviations from 18: −6, −3, 0, +3, +6.  They sum to 0, as they always must.
Squares: 36, 9, 0, 9, 36.
SS = 36 + 9 + 0 + 9 + 36 = 90

variance = 90 ⁄ (5 − 1) = 90 ⁄ 4 = 22.50
SD = √22.50 = 4.74 words

Do not be spooked by the coincidence: the total is 90 and the SS is also 90. They are different quantities that happen to share a number here — one is a sum of scores, the other a sum of squared deviations.

The habit: two-part questions always give you the hinge. Here the hinge was the mean, used once to find the gap and then again as the centre to deviate from.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.4.24 is √(90 ⁄ 5) — divided by N instead of N − 1. These five participants are a sample, so the divisor is 4.
c.22.50 is the variance, in words squared. The square root is what puts the answer back into words, and the question asked for the SD.
d.3.60 is the mean of the unsquared absolute deviations, 18 ⁄ 5. Squaring before averaging is what makes it a standard deviation.
🏷️ Mean × n gives the total. The total gives you any one missing value.

Question 7

🔔 z-scores and the Normal table

A raw score from a percentile

Neuropsychologist Haverkamp uses a working-memory test that is approximately Normal with a mean of 48 and a standard deviation of 7.5. The lowest score that still places a client in the top 10%, to two decimal places, is:
  • a49.28
  • b57.61
  • c38.39
  • d60.34
🔎 What it is really asking

An area is given and a score is wanted — so the table is read the other way.

🧭 Which type of question this is

z-scores: from a percentile back to a raw score.

🛠️ The procedure

Two steps in the reverse direction. Find the z with the right area below it, then undo the z formula: score = mean + z × SD.

🧮 The working
Step one — turn the area into a z. "Top 10%" means 90% of clients score below the cut, so you want the z with 0.9000 to its left. The table gives z = 1.28 (1.281552 exactly).

Step two — turn the z into a score.
score = 48 + 1.281552 × 7.5 = 48 + 9.6116 = 57.61

The direction check that catches almost every slip here: the top 10% must sit above the mean of 48, so the answer has to be bigger than 48. Anything below 48 is wrong before you check a single digit.

And the habit: ordinary z questions go score → z → area. Percentile questions go area → z → score. Same three stations, opposite direction of travel — so read the stem for which end you were handed.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.49.28 is 48 + 1.28, the z added on without being multiplied by the SD. A z is a count of standard deviations, so it has to be scaled by one before it can join a score.
c.38.39 uses z = −1.28, which is the bottom 10% cut-off. The sign of z is the direction, and "top" means positive.
d.60.34 uses z = 1.645, the cut-off for the top 5%. 1.645 and 1.28 are the two most-confused values on the table — 1.645 leaves 5% above, 1.28 leaves 10%.
🏷️ Percentile → score: find z from the area, then mean + z × SD.

Question 8

🔔 z-scores and the Normal table

The area between two scores

On Haverkamp’s working-memory test — mean 48, standard deviation 7.5 — the proportion of clients scoring between 42 and 58, to four decimal places, is:
  • a0.9088
  • b0.3031
  • c0.2119
  • d0.6969
🔎 What it is really asking

Two boundaries, so two lookups and a subtraction.

🧭 Which type of question this is

z-scores: the area between two values.

🛠️ The procedure

Convert both ends to z. The table gives the area to the left of each, so the strip between them is left area of the upper end − left area of the lower end.

🧮 The working
z for 42 = (42 − 48) ⁄ 7.5 = −6 ⁄ 7.5 = −0.80
z for 58 = (58 − 48) ⁄ 7.5 = 10 ⁄ 7.5 = +1.3333

Left of +1.3333:  0.9088
Left of −0.80:    0.2119

Between them: 0.9088 − 0.2119 = 0.6969, about 69.7% of clients.

(Rounding the z to 1.33 before you look it up gives 0.9082 and an answer of 0.6964 — the same to two decimals, which is all any option here asks for.)

Why subtraction and not addition. The table always hands you everything from the far left up to your z. "Everything below 58" already contains "everything below 42", so you take the smaller piece away rather than adding the two together. Adding them would count the whole left tail twice and give 1.12 — over 1, which no proportion can be.

The habit: sketch the curve and shade the strip before touching the table. A thirty-second drawing turns this from a formula into something you can see.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.9088 is everybody scoring below 58, the lower boundary ignored. It is the first of the two lookups, not the answer.
b.0.3031 is the area outside the two scores — the two tails added. It is 1 − 0.6969, so it answers the opposite question.
c.0.2119 is the lower tail on its own, the proportion scoring below 42. That is the piece you subtract, not the piece you keep.
🏷️ Area between = upper left area − lower left area. Sketch it first.

Question 9

🔔 z-scores and the Normal table

One client against a sample mean

Haverkamp now draws a random sample of 25 clients from that same population — mean 48, standard deviation 7.5. The probability that the mean of the 25 scores is above 50, to four decimal places, is:
  • a0.0912
  • b0.3949
  • c0.9088
  • d0.1824
🔎 What it is really asking

The thing that varies here is an average of 25 people, not one person.

🧭 Which type of question this is

z-scores: the sampling distribution of the mean.

🛠️ The procedure

A sample mean varies less than an individual does. Its spread is the standard error, σ ⁄ √n, and once you have that it is an ordinary z question.

🧮 The working
Step one — the right spread. This question is about a mean of 25, so

SE = 7.5 ⁄ √25 = 7.5 ⁄ 5 = 1.5

Step two — the z, using the SE underneath.

z = (50 − 48) ⁄ 1.5 = +1.3333

Step three — the upper tail. 1 − 0.9088 = 0.0912, about a 9% chance.

Compare it with one client. For a single person, z = (50 − 48) ⁄ 7.5 = 0.2667 and the chance of scoring above 50 is 0.3949 — more than four times as likely. Averaging 25 people irons out the extremes, so a mean of 50 is far harder to reach than an individual score of 50.

The one question to ask every time: is the stem talking about one observation or about the mean of several? One → divide by σ. A mean → divide by σ ⁄ √n. Nothing else about the calculation changes.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.0.3949 divides by 7.5 instead of by 1.5, which answers the question for a single client rather than for the mean of 25.
c.0.9088 is the area to the left — the probability the sample mean comes out below 50. The table gives this directly, and the question asked for above.
d.0.1824 is 2 × 0.0912, the tail doubled. Doubling belongs to a two-sided P-value; this question asked about one direction.
🏷️ Mean of n? Divide by σ⁄√n. One observation? Divide by σ.

Question 10

⚖️ The logic of a test

Recovering the statistic from a P-value

A paper by Zielinski reports only “two-sided P = 0.0384” for a z test, without printing the statistic. The value of |z| behind it, to two decimal places, is:
  • a1.96
  • b2.58
  • c2.07
  • d1.77
🔎 What it is really asking

Split the P between the two tails before you look anything up.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The logic of a test: from a P-value back to the statistic.

🛠️ The procedure

A two-sided P is the sum of both tails. So each tail holds P ⁄ 2, and the z you want is the one with P ⁄ 2 above it.

🧮 The working
Halve the P first: 0.0384 ⁄ 2 = 0.0192 in each tail.

So the area to the left of z is 1 − 0.0192 = 0.9808, and the table gives

|z| = 2.07  (2.070559 exactly)

Check it forwards: 2 × (area above 2.0706) = 2 × 0.0192 = 0.0384. ✓

Why the halving is the whole question. Forget it and you look up 0.0384 as a single tail, which gives 1.77 — a statistic that would have produced a two-sided P of 0.077, twice as big. The factor of two between one-sided and two-sided is the single most common slip in this whole topic, in both directions.

And the decision it supports: 2.07 is past 1.96, so this result is significant at the 5% level and not at the 1% level, where the cut-off is 2.576. The P of 0.0384 says the same thing without any table at all.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.1.96 is the 5% two-sided critical value — the fixed number you compare a statistic with, not a statistic recovered from data.
b.2.58 is the 1% two-sided critical value, 2.576. It corresponds to P = 0.01, not to the 0.0384 printed in the paper.
d.1.77 treats 0.0384 as a single tail. That is the z for a one-sided P of 0.0384, whose two-sided P would be 0.0768.
🏷️ Two-sided P → halve it, THEN look up the z.

Question 11

⚖️ The logic of a test

From a P-value to the interval

Lefebvre tests H₀: µ = 100 against a two-sided alternative and obtains P = 0.03. Her 95% confidence interval for µ therefore:
  • aexcludes 100 at every confidence level
  • bcontains 100, since 0.03 is below 0.05
  • ccannot be known from the P-value alone
  • dexcludes 100
🔎 What it is really asking

Does a P of 0.03 tell you whether 100 is inside the 95% interval?

🧭 Which type of question this is

The logic of a test: the interval–test duality.

🛠️ The procedure

A two-sided test at α and a (1 − α) interval always agree. Reject at α = .05 and the 95% interval must exclude the null value; fail to reject and it must contain it.

🧮 The working
P = 0.03 is below α = 0.05, so Lefebvre rejects H₀ at the 5% level. The matching interval is the 95% one, and the two can never contradict each other, so 100 must lie outside it.

The reason they agree is that they are the same arithmetic read two ways. The interval is the set of values that would not be rejected at the 5% level. If 100 is rejected, 100 is not in that set.

Now the part that catches people: the levels have to match. P = 0.03 is above 0.01, so the 99% interval — the partner of a 1% test — does contain 100. One interval excludes the value, the other includes it, and both come from the same data.

Say it to a friend: "a 95% interval and a 5% test are the same answer in different clothes — but only if the 95 and the 5 add up to 100."
✗ Why the others are wrong
a."At every confidence level" is too strong. P = 0.03 sits above 0.01, so the 99% interval does contain 100 — raise the confidence enough and any value gets back in.
b.This gets the comparison the right way round and the conclusion backwards. P below α means reject, which means the interval excludes the null value.
c.It can be known, and exactly: a two-sided P and the matching interval are two readings of the same calculation, so P < .05 settles the 95% interval.
🏷️ P < .05 ⇔ the 95% interval excludes the null value. Match the levels.

Question 12

🚨 Errors and power

Computing the power of a planned test

Caruana will test H₀: µ = 60 against a two-sided alternative at the 5% level, with the population standard deviation known to be 12 and a sample of 36. If the population mean is in fact 65, the probability her test reaches significance, to two decimal places, is:
  • a0.50
  • b0.71
  • c0.95
  • d0.29
🔎 What it is really asking

How likely is a significant result when the effect is real and this big?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Power: computing it from the design.

🛠️ The procedure

Two steps. First find which sample means would reject H₀, using µ₀ and the standard error. Then ask how probable those sample means are when the true mean is 65.

🧮 The working
Step one — the rejection rule, built around H₀.
SE = 12 ⁄ √36 = 12 ⁄ 6 = 2.0
Reject if x̄ is more than 1.96 standard errors from 60, that is below 60 − 3.92 = 56.08 or above 60 + 3.92 = 63.92.

Step two — how often that happens when µ is really 65. Recentre on 65, same SE of 2.0:
z for the upper boundary = (63.92 − 65) ⁄ 2.0 = −0.54
area above −0.54 = 0.7054
The lower boundary is 4.5 standard errors below 65, contributing 0.000004 — negligible.

power = 0.71, and β = 1 − 0.71 = 0.29.

What the picture looks like: two Normal curves of the same width, one centred at 60 and one at 65, with a vertical line at 63.92. Power is the slice of the right-hand curve that falls past the line. Slide the curves apart (a bigger effect) or make them narrower (a bigger n) and that slice grows.

The reading: even with a real five-point effect, Caruana misses it nearly three times in ten. That is the argument for computing power before collecting data rather than after.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.50 is the power you would have if the true mean sat exactly on the boundary of 63.92. The true mean is 65, which is past it.
c.0.95 is 1 − α, the proportion of correct decisions when H₀ is true. Power is about the case where H₀ is false, and the two have no reason to be equal.
d.0.29 is β, the Type II error rate — the chance the test misses this effect. Power is its complement, and the question asked for significance.
🏷️ Power: find the rejection boundary under H₀, then its tail area under the truth.

Question 13

🚨 Errors and power

Turning beta into a count of studies

Grimaldi reviews 200 published studies, every one of them testing an effect that genuinely exists in the population, and every one with a Type II error rate of 0.35 against an effect of that size. The expected number of these studies that reach significance, as a whole number, is:
  • a130
  • b70
  • c190
  • d10
🔎 What it is really asking

Each study is one chance to detect a real effect. What is that chance?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Power: applying 1 − β to a set of studies.

🛠️ The procedure

Power = 1 − β is the probability that one study detects a real effect of that size. Multiply it by the number of studies to get how many are expected to succeed.

🧮 The working
Step one — turn β into power.
power = 1 − 0.35 = 0.65

Step two — apply it to the 200 studies.
expected successes = 0.65 × 200 = 130
expected misses    = 0.35 × 200 = 70

Notice which error rate is relevant. Every one of these 200 studies is looking at a real effect, so H₀ is false every time. A Type I error is impossible here — you cannot wrongly reject a null that was false to begin with. α never enters the calculation.

Why this matters outside the exam: 70 perfectly well-conducted studies of a real effect come back non-significant. If only the 130 get published, the literature will look far more certain than the evidence actually is. Under-powered research is how that happens.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.70 is 0.35 × 200, the number expected to miss the effect. It is the mirror of the answer — β applied instead of 1 − β.
c.190 is 0.95 × 200, using 1 − α. α is the false-alarm rate when H₀ is true, and here H₀ is false in all 200 studies.
d.10 is 0.05 × 200, the Type I error rate applied to studies where no Type I error is possible. Only β and power apply when the effect is real.
🏷️ Power = 1 − β, and it is the chance ONE study detects a real effect.

Question 14

🔀 z or t, and which t

Which statistic, and against which curve

Pedersen uses a standardised anxiety scale whose population standard deviation is published as 15. She tests 25 clients, finds a sample mean of 108, and compares it with the published population mean of 100. To two decimal places, the statistic and the distribution she should read it against are:
  • az = 0.53, the standard Normal
  • bt = 2.67 on 25 df
  • cz = 2.67, the standard Normal
  • dt = 2.67 on 24 df
🔎 What it is really asking

Was the spread published, or computed from these 25 clients?

🧭 Which type of question this is

The z-against-t fork, with the statistic computed.

🛠️ The procedure

The statistic is always (x̄ − µ₀) ⁄ (spread ⁄ √n). What the fork decides is which curve you read it against: a published σ → the standard Normal, no df; an s from your own data → t on N − 1.

🧮 The working
Step one — the fork. The 15 is published for the scale, not calculated from Pedersen’s 25 clients. So it is σ, and the reference curve is the standard Normal. There are no degrees of freedom to quote, because nothing was estimated.

Step two — the statistic. The denominator is the standard error of the mean, never σ itself:
SE = 15 ⁄ √25 = 15 ⁄ 5 = 3.0
z = (108 − 100) ⁄ 3.0 = 8 ⁄ 3 = 2.67

Two-sided P = 0.0077, so this is significant at both the 5% and the 1% level.

The two separate decisions: √n belongs to the arithmetic and is needed whichever curve you use. z-or-t belongs to where the spread came from. Students who merge the two questions get one of them wrong.

Worth knowing: had the 15 come from the 25 clients, t = 2.67 on 24 df gives P = 0.013 — the same statistic, a slightly larger P, because estimating the spread costs you something.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.53 is 8 ⁄ 15 — divided by σ rather than by the standard error of 3.0. A sample mean of 25 varies five times less than one client does.
b.This gets both halves wrong: t when σ is published, and N rather than N − 1 for the degrees of freedom.
d.t on 24 df would be exactly right had the 15 been calculated from these 25 clients. It was published for the scale instead, so nothing was estimated and no df are owed.
🏷️ √n is arithmetic; z-or-t is about where the spread came from. Decide separately.

Question 15

🔀 z or t, and which t

Recovering a design from printed degrees of freedom

A results table in Wojcik’s paper reads “t = 2.14, df = 34, P = .040” for a comparison of two independent groups of equal size. The number of participants in each group, as a whole number, was:
  • a17
  • b36
  • c35
  • d18
🔎 What it is really asking

Work the df rule backwards, then remember the groups were equal.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Choosing which t: reading a design out of the degrees of freedom.

🛠️ The procedure

For two independent groups df = n₁ + n₂ − 2. So add the 2 back to recover the total, then halve it because the two groups were the same size.

🧮 The working
Step one — undo the "− 2".
n₁ + n₂ = 34 + 2 = 36 participants altogether.

Step two — split them.
36 ⁄ 2 = 18 in each group.

Check it forwards: 18 + 18 − 2 = 34. ✓

Why 2 and not 1. An independent-samples test estimates two means, one per group, and each estimate costs one degree of freedom. A one-sample or paired test estimates a single mean and costs one, which is the N − 1 rule.

Keep the three rules side by side:
• one-sample t → df = N − 1
• paired t → df = (number of people) − 1
• independent t → df = n₁ + n₂ − 2

And why this is worth practising: a printed df is often the only clue to what design a paper actually ran. 34 on a two-group comparison means 36 people; 34 on a paired comparison would mean 35.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.17 halves the df without adding the 2 back first. The subtraction has to be undone before the splitting, not after.
b.36 is the total across both groups. The question asked how many were in each, and the stem says the groups were equal.
c.35 is df + 1, the one-sample rule of N − 1 run backwards. That rule costs one degree of freedom; a two-group comparison costs two.
🏷️ Independent groups: df = n₁ + n₂ − 2. Add 2 back, then split.

Question 1

🧭 Causality and research design

The flaw behind a reported finding

Aarsland reports that the 140 patients who joined a voluntary evening walking group lost more weight over six months than the 160 patients who did not join. The same nurse weighed everybody, at the same two time points. The flaw that best explains her result is:
  • asix months is too short for weight to change
  • bthe two groups were not of exactly equal size
  • cthe patients chose which group they were in
  • dthe nurse knew which patients had joined the group
🔎 What it is really asking

Who decided which patients ended up in the walking group?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Causality: self-selection into the groups.

🛠️ The procedure

Ask who did the sorting. When participants put themselves into the groups, the two groups differ before the study starts, and anything that made someone join can also move the outcome.

🧮 The working
The two groups were not built by Aarsland. They built themselves.

Think about who joins an evening walking group: people who already have the time, the energy, the health to walk for an hour, and the intention to lose weight. Every one of those also predicts weight loss without any walking. So the comparison is not "walking against not walking"; it is "people who were ready to change against people who were not".

Now check the three rival answers against the design.

The nurse knowing. This is a real worry in general — but weight is read off a set of scales, and a nurse’s expectations do not move a number she is reading. Blinding matters most for outcomes that have to be judged.

Six months. If the window were too short, nobody would have changed and there would be no gap to explain. The gap is there; the question is what produced it.

Unequal groups. 140 against 160 costs a little precision and nothing else. Groups do not have to match in size to be compared.

The habit: on the first read of any stem, find the verb that put people into groups. Joined · chose · signed up · volunteered — the groups differ to start with. Assigned · allocated · randomised — the causal door opens.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.If six months were too short nothing would have moved, and there would be no difference to account for. A gap did appear; the question is what made it.
b.Groups of 140 and 160 are compared perfectly happily. Unequal sizes cost a little precision; they do not make one group unlike the other.
d.Weight comes off a set of scales, so the nurse’s expectations have little room to act on it. Blinding bites hardest on outcomes somebody has to judge.
🏷️ Participants sorted themselves → the groups differed before the study began.

Question 2

⚖️ Ethics and inference

The cost of testing many outcomes

Granholm’s protocol lists 12 outcome measures. It states that each will be tested at the 5% level and that any significant result will be written up. The objection to that plan is:
  • aacross twelve tests the false-alarm risk is about 46%
  • bthe twelve tests have to be reported in separate papers
  • ctwelve outcomes are too many to measure in one study
  • dthe 5% level is too strict to use twelve times over
🔎 What it is really asking

α = 5% is a promise about one test. What is it worth across twelve?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Ethics of inference: multiple testing.

🛠️ The procedure

Each test run on a true null has a 5% chance of a false alarm. Across k independent tests the chance that at least one fires is 1 − 0.95ᵏ, which climbs fast.

🧮 The working
Suppose none of the twelve outcomes is really affected — twelve true nulls.

P(one test stays quiet) = 0.95
P(all twelve stay quiet) = 0.95¹² = 0.3596
P(at least one fires) = 1 − 0.3596 = 0.4596, about 46%

The expected number of false alarms is 12 × 0.05 = 0.60 — better than one free discovery per study, with nothing whatever going on.

That calculation assumes the twelve tests are independent. Real outcome measures overlap, so the true risk is somewhat below 46% — and it is nowhere near the 5% the protocol implies, and it cannot be read off the paper by a reader.

What the plan is missing, not what it did wrong. No individual P-value will be miscalculated. The problem is the sentence "any significant result will be written up": it makes the study a search rather than a test.

Three honest repairs: name one primary outcome in advance and treat the other eleven as exploratory; report all twelve results whatever they say; or tighten the threshold so that the whole family keeps its 5%.

The habit: ask of every significant finding you read, "how many tests were behind this one?" The printed 5% means 5% when the answer is one.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Separate papers would make it worse, not better — a reader of one paper would have no way of knowing that eleven other tests existed.
c.Measuring twelve things is sensible and cheap. It is testing all twelve at 5% and reporting the winners that breaks the error rate.
d.The 5% level is not too strict; across twelve tests it is far too loose. Tightening the threshold is one of the repairs, not the complaint.
🏷️ k tests at α: the family risk is 1 − (1 − α)ᵏ. Count the tests.

Question 3

🧭 Causality and research design

How far a causal claim reaches

Cavalcanti randomly assigns 80 undergraduate volunteers to a new revision technique or to their usual method, and the new technique wins. A reviewer objects to her sentence “this technique improves revision for students”. The objection is sound because:
  • arandom assignment leaves a confounder alive in her data
  • bone study on its own cannot support a causal claim
  • cthe usual method was not itself assigned at random
  • d80 volunteers are not a sample of students in general
🔎 What it is really asking

Her causal claim is sound. Which population is it sound about?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Causality: what random assignment buys, and what it does not.

🛠️ The procedure

Two different randomisations do two different jobs. Random assignment buys a causal reading inside the study. Random sampling buys the right to carry the finding out to a population. She did the first and not the second.

🧮 The working
Take the sentence apart. "This technique improves revision" is the causal half; "for students" is the scope half.

The causal half is earned. A coin decided who got the new technique, so the two groups started out alike on average on everything — the variables she thought of and the ones she did not. A difference at the end has two candidates left, the technique or chance, and the test deals with chance.

The scope half is not. Her 80 people are undergraduates who volunteered. Volunteers differ from non-volunteers in motivation and in free time, and undergraduates differ from school pupils and from adult learners. Nothing in the design connects those 80 to any wider group.

So the sentence she can defend is: the technique improved revision for people like these volunteers. Carrying it further is a separate argument, usually made by repeating the study somewhere else.

Why the other three fail. Random assignment is precisely what removes systematic confounding, so that objection attacks the one part of her design that is sound. One study can license a causal claim — a randomised trial does exactly that. And both arms came out of the same coin toss, so asking for the usual method to be "assigned too" misreads how a randomisation works.

The habit: when a stem says "random", ask random what. Random into groups → cause. Random from a population → generalisation.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Random assignment is what removes systematic differences between the groups. This objection aims at the strongest part of her design.
b.A single randomised trial does license a causal claim for the people in it. Replication strengthens it; its absence does not void it.
c.Both arms came out of the same randomisation — that is what assigning 80 people to two conditions means. There is no second coin to toss.
🏷️ Random assignment → cause. Random sampling → scope. Check which one you have.

Question 4

🧭 Causality and research design

Checking a suspected confounder

Hemelrijk finds that pupils who eat a hot school lunch score higher on a concentration test than pupils who bring sandwiches. She suspects family income accounts for the whole gap. The measurement that would let her examine that suspicion is:
  • athe school’s mean concentration score last year
  • beach pupil’s family income, recorded before testing
  • ceach pupil’s concentration score measured twice over
  • dthe number of pupils in each of the two lunch groups
🔎 What it is really asking

To investigate a third variable, you first have to have measured it.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Causality: confounding and lurking variables.

🛠️ The procedure

A confounder is a third variable linked to both the grouping and the outcome. You can only examine, adjust for or rule out a confounder you have actually recorded.

🧮 The working
Draw the two arrows income would need. Does income reach the lunch? Yes — families on lower incomes are likelier to qualify for a free hot meal, or likelier to send sandwiches, depending on the school. Does income reach concentration? Yes, through housing, sleep, stress and much else. Both arrows draw, so income is a candidate confounder.

And now the point of the question: a candidate you have not measured can only be speculated about. With income on the file she can compare hot-lunch and sandwich pupils within income bands, or adjust for it, and see whether the gap survives.

Be clear about what that buys and what it does not. Adjusting for income handles income — measured as well as her data allow. It does nothing about the variables she never recorded. Random assignment is the one move that handles the unmeasured ones too, and here nobody can be assigned a family.

The other three measurements are not third variables at all. A second concentration score improves the reliability of the outcome. The group sizes affect precision. Last year’s school mean is a fact about the school, identical for both groups, so it cannot explain a difference between them.

The habit: for every candidate confounder, draw two arrows and then ask whether the variable is in the data file. No arrows, no confounder; no column, no answer.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Last year’s school mean is one number shared by both groups, so it cannot account for a difference between them this year.
c.Measuring the outcome twice makes the outcome more reliable. It says nothing about why the two lunch groups differ.
d.Group sizes govern how precisely the gap is estimated. A third variable has to vary between the groups, and a count does not.
🏷️ A confounder needs two arrows — and a column in your data file.

Question 5

⚖️ Ethics and inference

Two readings of a non-significant result

Iversen compares two therapy formats with 22 clients in each group and obtains P = 0.19. She writes that the two formats are equally effective. Her co-author writes that the study cannot tell them apart. The defensible sentence is:
  • aIversen’s — 44 clients is enough to settle this
  • bneither — a P-value above α cannot be interpreted
  • cthe co-author’s — the study is simply inconclusive
  • dIversen’s — P = 0.19 is a long way above 0.05
🔎 What it is really asking

The test found nothing. Does "found nothing" mean "there is nothing"?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Ethics of inference: a non-significant result is not evidence of no effect.

🛠️ The procedure

Failing to reject H₀ is a statement about the evidence, not about the world. A small study fails to reject whether the true difference is zero or whether it is substantial, so the result cannot tell those two apart.

🧮 The working
What P = 0.19 says: if the two formats were identical, 22 clients per group would produce a gap this large or larger about one time in five. Unremarkable, so there is no evidence of a difference.

Now ask what else produces P = 0.19. A real and useful difference, measured on 44 clients, very often does. Two groups of 22 facing a true standardised difference of 0.5 — a difference most supervisors would want to know about — reach significance only about 37% of the time at the 5% level. Nearly two misses in three.

So her data are compatible with no difference and with a difference worth having. A result that cannot separate those two is inconclusive, which is exactly the co-author’s sentence.

The fourth option overcorrects. A large P-value is perfectly interpretable: it says the data are consistent with H₀. What it cannot do is establish H₀.

What would have let Iversen claim equivalence: a confidence interval narrow enough to exclude every difference big enough to matter. With 22 per group the interval is far too wide for that, which is why printing it beside the P-value is the honest move.

Say it to a friend: "we didn’t find a difference" is not "there isn’t one" — it can just mean we didn’t look hard enough.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Forty-four clients give this comparison about a 37% chance of catching a difference of real size. That is a study too small to settle anything, not one large enough.
b.A P-value above α is perfectly interpretable — it says the data are consistent with H₀. What it cannot do is establish H₀, which is the error being made.
d.How far above 0.05 the P-value sits measures how unsurprising the data are under H₀, not how certain it is that H₀ holds. A big P is weak evidence, not strong evidence.
🏷️ Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Print the interval too.

Question 6

🧭 Causality and research design

Whether the comparison group is a fair one

Jurado compares the 60 students who completed a six-week mindfulness course with the 40 who dropped out of it, and finds the completers less stressed at week six. The change that would make this a fair comparison is:
  • akeeping a randomly chosen half off the course from the start
  • basking the 40 dropouts why they left the course
  • ccomparing week-six scores with each student’s week-one score
  • dcounting how many sessions each completer attended
🔎 What it is really asking

Are the students who dropped out a fair stand-in for "no course"?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Causality: what a comparison group has to be.

🛠️ The procedure

A comparison group has to differ from the treated group in the treatment and in nothing systematic besides. Dropouts fail that: dropping out is a choice, and whatever drove it may also drive the outcome.

🧮 The working
Jurado does have two groups, so this is not the "no control group at all" problem. His problem is worse disguised: the control group is made of people who left.

Why that breaks the comparison. Students drop out of a stress course because they are too stressed and busy to keep attending, or because they were not getting on with it. Either way, the act of dropping out is tangled up with the outcome being measured. Comparing the stayers with the leavers compares stressed students with less stressed students, whatever the course does.

Note that it can bite in either direction, which is why it is not a bias you can mentally correct for.

What the fix does. Toss a coin at the start, put half the willing students on a waiting list, and compare everyone who started in the group they were put in. Both arms then contain their own dropouts, their own busy weeks and their own natural recovery, so those cancel in the comparison.

The other three repairs leave the comparison untouched. Asking the dropouts their reasons is useful background and changes no number. A week-one to week-six comparison inside the completers is a before-and-after study with no control at all — a step backwards. Counting sessions attended tells him about dose among the completers and still has no untreated group to measure against.

The habit: find the comparison group and ask how people ended up in it. A group defined by something that happened during the study is not a control group.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Their reasons are worth knowing and change nothing about the arithmetic. The 40 would still be a group defined by having left.
c.That is a before-and-after comparison inside the completers, with no untreated group at all — time and natural recovery walk straight back in.
d.Sessions attended describes the dose among completers. It still leaves him with no group that did not take the course.
🏷️ A group defined by what happened during the study is not a control group.
