Question 7

🧭 Causality and research design

Regression to the mean

Lindeboom picks out the 30 pupils with the lowest scores on a reading screen, gives them a term of extra help, and screens them again. Their mean score rises by 7 points. The explanation his design cannot rule out is:
  • athirty pupils are too few to detect a 7-point rise
  • blow scores drift back towards the average on retesting
  • cthe extra help was delivered by trained specialists
  • dreading scores are measured on an ordinal scale
🔎 What it is really asking

The pupils were chosen for being extreme. What happens to extreme scores next time?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Causality: regression to the mean and natural recovery.

🛠️ The procedure

Any single score is partly the pupil and partly the day — a bad night, a misread question, a lucky guess. Select the lowest scores and you select pupils who had a bad day as well as pupils who struggle, and the bad days do not repeat.

🧮 The working
Lindeboom chose his 30 pupils because their scores were extreme. That choice is what creates the problem.

Split a screen score into two parts: the pupil’s real reading level, and the wobble of that particular morning. The lowest 30 scores are the pupils whose real level is low and whose wobble happened to be downward. On the second screen the real level is still there; the downward wobble is replaced by a fresh one, as likely up as down. The group mean therefore rises — with no teaching at all. That is regression to the mean.

Alongside it sit two more explanations he cannot separate: pupils get better at reading over a term anyway, and they get better at the screen itself the second time.

What would settle it. Keep the 30 lowest scorers as one pool and toss a coin: half get the extra help, half carry on as usual. Both halves regress by the same amount, both mature over the term, both meet the test twice — so the difference between the halves is the help.

The other options do not compete. Specialist teaching is part of the treatment, not a rival to it. Reading scores on a screen are routinely treated as interval and averaged, and even if they were not, that would not explain a rise. Too few pupils makes a rise hard to detect, and here a rise was detected.

The habit: whenever people are selected for being extreme — the worst sleepers, the highest scorers, the clinic’s sickest patients — expect the next measurement to be less extreme, and insist on a control group before believing anything else.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Too small a sample makes a real rise hard to detect. Here a rise was detected; the question is what produced it.
c.Specialist teaching is part of what he is testing, not a rival explanation for the rise. It is the treatment, described.
d.Screen totals are routinely treated as interval and averaged. Even on an ordinal reading, that would not manufacture a 7-point rise.
🏷️ Selected for being extreme → expect a less extreme score next time, free.

Question 8

⚖️ Ethics and inference

Choosing the analysis after seeing the data

Mazurek collects her data, then tries three different definitions of “improved”, and reports the one that reaches P = 0.03. The three definitions overlap heavily. What the printed 0.03 no longer describes is:
  • athe arithmetic of the analysis she chose to report
  • bthe number of participants who improved at all
  • cthe direction in which the improvement ran
  • dthe error rate of the procedure she actually followed
🔎 What it is really asking

A P-value describes a procedure. Which procedure did she really run?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Ethics of inference: the analysis chosen after the data.

🛠️ The procedure

A P-value is the probability of a result this extreme if H₀ is true, for one pre-specified analysis. Choose the analysis after seeing which one wins and the printed number stops describing what you did.

🧮 The working
Separate two things that are easy to run together.

Her arithmetic is right. Given the third definition of "improved", 0.03 is the correct P-value. Nothing in her paper is miscalculated.

Her procedure is not what the 0.03 describes. The procedure was: try three definitions, report the best. If the three were independent tests of a true null, that procedure fires at least once with probability 1 − 0.95³ = 0.1426. Because the three definitions of "improved" overlap heavily, the real rate is lower than 0.1426 — and higher than the 0.05 the paper implies. A reader cannot work out where in that range it falls, because the other two analyses are not in the paper.

That is the precise damage: not a wrong number, but a number that no longer measures anybody’s error rate.

The other three options are untouched by any of this. The count who improved, and the direction they moved in, are facts about her data and are unaffected by when she chose her definition.

The two repairs: fix the definition of "improved" before the data arrive, or report all three analyses and let the reader see the spread. Three analyses honestly reported is a finding; one silently chosen is not.

The habit: ask whether the analysis was decided before or after the data. A P-value earns its meaning from being specified in advance.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The arithmetic of the reported analysis is correct — that is what makes this hard to spot. The flaw is in which analysis reached the page.
b.How many participants improved is a fact about her data. When she settled on a definition does not change the count.
c.The direction of the improvement is also a fact about her data, and it is reported correctly. The damage is to the error rate, not to the description.
🏷️ Decide the analysis before the data, or report every analysis you ran.

Question 9

🧭 Causality and research design

Deciding which variable came first

Oleszko finds that adults who sleep under six hours report more symptoms of low mood. Two readings fit: short sleep worsens mood, or low mood shortens sleep. The finding that would help decide between them is:
  • asleep measured now and mood measured two years later
  • ba larger sample from the same adult population
  • cmood and sleep both measured again the same evening
  • dthe association recomputed with income held constant
🔎 What it is really asking

Both readings fit the same correlation. What would tell them apart?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Causality: reverse causation.

🛠️ The procedure

A correlation carries no arrow. To work out which variable moves first you need time order — one variable measured before the other — and to settle it properly you need the first variable assigned.

🧮 The working
Her data were collected at one moment, so short sleep and low mood arrive together and the arrow could point either way. Both stories are consistent with every number she has.

A prospective measurement breaks the symmetry: measure sleep now, come back in two years and measure mood. If sleep today predicts mood in two years’ time while mood today does not predict sleep, the arrow has a direction. Time order is a real piece of evidence, and it is the one piece she is missing.

Be precise about what it still leaves open. Time order rules out the reverse arrow. It does not rule out a third variable sitting behind both — shift work, chronic pain, a new baby — which can raise sleep loss first and low mood later. The design that closes that too is a randomised sleep-restriction experiment, where a coin shortens people’s sleep.

Why the others cannot help. A larger sample makes the same ambiguous correlation more precise. Measuring both again on one evening adds a second simultaneous snapshot, which is the same problem twice. Holding income constant addresses a confounder, which is a different worry altogether — it does not tell you which of two variables moved first.

The habit: when two readings of a correlation are equally plausible, look for a clock in the design. No clock and no coin, no direction.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.A bigger sample pins the same correlation down more tightly. Precision is not direction; the arrow is just as ambiguous at n = 10,000.
c.A second simultaneous snapshot repeats the problem rather than solving it. Both variables still arrive at the same moment.
d.Holding income constant tackles a third variable. That is confounding, a different worry, and it leaves the direction of the arrow exactly where it was.
🏷️ No clock and no coin in the design → no direction in the finding.

Question 10

🧭 Causality and research design

What blinding protects

Peeters randomly assigns 90 patients to a new painkiller or to an identical-looking dummy tablet. The nurse who later rates each patient’s pain, however, knows which tablet they received. The part of Peeters’s conclusion this puts at risk is:
  • athe generalisation of her result to other patients
  • bthe degrees of freedom she uses for her test
  • cthe size of the difference she reports between the arms
  • dthe claim that the two arms started out comparable
🔎 What it is really asking

The randomisation held and the tablets matched. What is still unblinded?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Causality: placebo, blinding and expectancy.

🛠️ The procedure

A dummy tablet blinds the patient, so their expectations act equally in both arms. Blinding the person who rates the outcome is a separate protection, and it guards the measurement rather than the groups.

🧮 The working
Go through her design piece by piece and see what each part is still doing.

The coin. Intact. The two arms are alike on average on everything at the start, so "the groups were not comparable" is not available as a criticism.

The dummy tablet. Intact. Patients in both arms believe they may be on the drug, so hope, attention and the ritual of taking a tablet are present in both and cancel.

The nurse. Not blinded, and pain is a judged outcome. A nurse who expects the new drug to work can read a wince as a 3 in one arm and a 4 in the other without any dishonesty at all. Those small shifts all point the same way, so they land in the difference between the arms — the very quantity she is reporting.

So the damage is to the measured effect size and to the P-value that follows from it. Comparability is untouched, the scope of the result is a question about who was recruited, and the degrees of freedom come from the sample sizes.

The fix is cheap: have the ratings made by somebody who does not know the allocation, or have patients rate their own pain on a scale, or both. That is what "double blind" means — neither the patient nor the assessor knows.

The habit: ask who knows what. Patient blinding handles the patient’s expectations; assessor blinding handles the rater’s. A judged outcome needs the second one.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.How widely the result travels depends on who was recruited. An unblinded rater distorts the measurement inside the study, not its reach.
b.The degrees of freedom are fixed by the sample sizes. What the nurse knew cannot change how many patients there were.
d.Comparability came from the coin, and the coin was not affected by what the nurse knew later. That part of the design still holds.
🏷️ A judged outcome needs the assessor blinded, not only the patient.

Question 11

⚖️ Ethics and inference

What a significant result lets you say in public

Quaranta’s randomised trial of a study-skills workshop gives a mean gain of 1.4 marks out of 50, with a 95% interval from 0.3 to 2.5 and P = 0.013. The sentence she can defend in public is:
  • athe workshop raises marks substantially for most students
  • bthe workshop raises every student’s marks by 1.4 marks
  • cthe workshop is proven to raise marks by 0.3 to 2.5
  • dthe workshop raises marks, by something like one mark
🔎 What it is really asking

The effect is real. Now: how big is it, and whose marks is it about?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Ethics of inference: what a significant result does and does not entitle you to claim.

🛠️ The procedure

A P-value answers “is there an effect?”. How big comes from the estimate and its interval, and the estimate is about a mean, not about any one student.

🧮 The working
Take the three numbers in turn.

P = 0.013. A gain this large would turn up about one time in eighty if the workshop did nothing. With random assignment behind it, that licenses "the workshop raises marks".

1.4 marks out of 50. That is the size. Just under three percentage points on the paper.

0.3 to 2.5. That is the honesty. The data are consistent with a gain too small for anyone to notice and with one of about two and a half marks. Both ends belong in any public sentence.

Now the three overreaches. "Substantially, for most students" turns a small P-value into a large effect — P measures how surprising, not how big. "Every student’s marks by 1.4" reads a mean as a promise to each individual; plenty of students in the workshop arm will have gone down. "Proven to raise marks by 0.3 to 2.5" misstates the interval as a proved range rather than as the values the data are compatible with, and "proven" is a word no single trial earns.

The habit: after every significant result, say the effect size out loud, with both ends of its interval. If you cannot, you have reported half a finding.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a."Substantially, for most students" reads a small P-value as a large effect. The interval tops out at two and a half marks out of fifty.
b.A mean gain of 1.4 is an average over the arm. Individual students in it will have gone up more, gone up less, and gone down.
c."Proven" is a word no single trial earns, and an interval is the set of values the data are compatible with rather than a proved range.
🏷️ P says whether. The interval says how big. The mean is not a promise to anybody.

Question 12

🧭 Causality and research design

What a matched design buys

Stavrakis forms 40 pairs of pupils matched on last term’s reading score, then tosses a coin inside each pair to decide which pupil gets a new reading scheme. Set against assigning all 80 pupils at random in one go, the matching mainly buys her:
  • aprotection against a Type I error at the 5% level
  • ba smaller standard error from the same 80 pupils
  • cthe licence to say the scheme caused the change
  • da sample that represents the school as a whole
🔎 What it is really asking

Both designs randomise. What does pairing them up add on top?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Causality: matched and blocked designs.

🛠️ The procedure

Matching puts similar pupils together and randomises within each pair. The comparison is then made between pupils who already resembled each other, which strips prior reading ability out of the noise.

🧮 The working
Start with what the two designs share. In both, a coin decides who gets the scheme, so both license the causal claim. Matching is not what buys that.

What matching changes is the noise. Pupils differ enormously in reading ability, and in a single big randomisation all of that variation sits inside the error term. Pair pupils on last term’s score first, and the comparison inside each pair is between two pupils who started level. The between-pupil variation is taken out of the error and put into the pairing, so the same 80 pupils give a smaller standard error and a better chance of detecting a real effect.

What it does not buy. It does not improve the causal claim, which the coin already supplied. It does not make the 80 pupils representative of the school — that depends on how they were recruited, not on how they were split. And it does not touch the Type I error rate, which is whatever α she chose.

The cost side, so you can state the trade: the analysis works on 40 differences rather than 80 scores, so there are fewer degrees of freedom. When the matching variable predicts the outcome well, as last term’s reading score does, the drop in noise is worth far more than the lost df.

The habit: randomisation buys validity, blocking buys precision. Ask which of the two a design feature is for.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The Type I error rate is set by the α she chooses. Pairing pupils does not alter how often a true null is rejected.
c.The causal licence came from the coin, and both designs toss one. Matching adds precision on top of a claim she already had.
d.Whether the 80 pupils stand for the school depends on how they were recruited. How they were split into two groups cannot change that.
🏷️ Randomising buys validity. Matching and blocking buy precision.

Question 13

🧭 Causality and research design

What a licensed causal claim covers

Tiedemann randomly assigns 200 patients at one city hospital to a new discharge plan or to the standard one, and readmissions fall under the new plan. The claim his design supports is that:
  • athe plan lowered readmissions in patients like these
  • bthe plan would lower readmissions in any hospital
  • cthe plan lowers readmissions because patients feel supported
  • dthe plan is associated with fewer readmissions, and no more
🔎 What it is really asking

A clean randomised trial. State the claim at exactly the right strength.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Causality: when a causal claim is licensed.

🛠️ The procedure

Random assignment plus a comparison group licenses the word "lowered". The population it is licensed for is the one the patients came from, and the mechanism is a separate claim needing separate evidence.

🧮 The working
Three dials to set: cause, scope and mechanism.

Cause — yes. A coin decided which plan each patient got, so the two arms started out alike on average on age, diagnosis, severity, home circumstances and everything else. The drop in readmissions has two candidate explanations left, the plan or chance, and the significance test handles chance.

Scope — these patients. Two hundred patients at one city hospital. The claim holds for patients like them in a hospital like that. Carrying it to a rural hospital with different staffing is an extra argument, not a reading of his data.

Mechanism — not tested. "Because patients feel supported" is a second, separate causal claim. He measured readmissions, not feelings, so the mechanism is a hypothesis he could test next.

And the fourth option is the mirror-image error: retreating to "associated" throws away what the randomisation paid for. Under-claiming is also getting the answer wrong.

The habit: read each option as a claim and ask what would have to be true for it. Random assignment buys cause; sampling buys scope; only a study of the mechanism buys the mechanism.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b."Any hospital" stretches 200 patients at one city hospital to every setting. Scope comes from who was sampled, not from how well the trial was run.
c.The mechanism is a second causal claim. He measured readmissions, not how supported patients felt, so this is untested.
d.Retreating to "associated" gives away what the randomisation paid for. Under-claiming a randomised trial is as wrong as over-claiming a survey.
🏷️ Random assignment buys cause, sampling buys scope, neither buys the mechanism.

Question 14

⚖️ Ethics and inference

What publication bias does to a literature

Ullmann finds 15 published studies of one effect, 14 of them significant, and works out that each had about a 40% chance of detecting the effect if it is real. The reading best supported by that pattern is:
  • athe 15 studies together prove the effect is real
  • bthe published studies must have been badly analysed
  • cstudies that found nothing were mostly never published
  • dthe effect is larger than any single study suggests
🔎 What it is really asking

At 40% power, how many of 15 honest studies should have come out significant?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Ethics of inference: publication bias and selective reporting.

🛠️ The procedure

Power is the chance that one study detects a real effect. Across many studies of the same real effect, the share that come out significant should sit near the power — so a literature that is nearly all significant has studies missing from it.

🧮 The working
Do the bookkeeping that power makes possible.

If 15 studies each had a 40% chance of detecting the effect, the expected number significant is 15 × 0.40 = 6. Ullmann is looking at 14. The chance of 14 or more out of 15 at 40% power is about 0.000025 — so this is not a run of luck.

Turn it round instead. If 14 significant results were produced by studies with 40% power, roughly 14 ⁄ 0.40 = 35 studies must have been completed, of which about 20 never reached a journal. They are not missing because they were bad; they are missing because they found nothing, which is harder to publish. That is the file drawer.

What it does to the record. A study only gets published if it happened to land in the significant tail, so published estimates are selected for being large. The average published effect is therefore bigger than the real one, and replications disappoint — which is why option two has it exactly backwards.

The third option treats a count of significant results as proof. A pile of selected studies is not stronger evidence than one unselected study; it may be weaker, because you cannot tell how large the pile really was.

The repairs: registering studies before they run, so the unpublished ones are countable; journals that accept null results; and pre-registration, which fixes the analysis as well as the existence of the study.

The habit: ask of any literature, "how many studies would I expect to be significant at this power?" If the answer is far below what you see, look for the missing ones.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.A count of significant results is not proof when the count was filtered. You cannot tell how large the original pile of studies was.
b.Nothing here points at bad analysis. The 14 published P-values can each be computed correctly; the problem is which studies reached print.
d.Selection pushes the other way. A study reaches print by landing in the significant tail, so published effects run larger than the real one.
🏷️ Compare the share significant with the power. The gap is the file drawer.

Question 15

🧭 Causality and research design

What random assignment guarantees

Waelkens randomly assigns 60 participants to two groups, then compares the groups on 8 background variables. One of the eight differs significantly at the 5% level. The right reading of that is:
  • athe randomisation has failed and should be redone
  • brandom assignment makes groups identical, so this is an error
  • cthe significant variable should be used as the outcome
  • done in eight is about what chance alone produces
🔎 What it is really asking

Random assignment balances groups on average. Does it balance them exactly?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Causality: what random assignment does, in expectation.

🛠️ The procedure

Random assignment makes the groups alike in expectation — on average over all the ways the coin could have fallen — not exactly in any one study. Each baseline test also carries its own 5% false-alarm rate.

🧮 The working
Two reasons to expect exactly what Waelkens saw.

First, balance is an average property. A coin spreads age, prior scores and everything else evenly across the two groups on average over all possible randomisations. In the one randomisation she actually performed the groups will differ a little on every variable. What random assignment removes is any systematic difference — a reason for one group to be older — not the chance ones.

Second, she ran eight tests. Each has a 5% chance of firing when the groups really do match, so the expected number of significant baseline differences is 8 × 0.05 = 0.40, and the chance of at least one is 1 − 0.95⁸ = 0.3366. One in eight is an ordinary outcome, not a symptom.

Why re-randomising is the wrong response. Tossing again until the baseline tables look tidy is a decision made after seeing the data, and it quietly stops the allocation being random. The usual options are to pre-specify adjustment for a few important background variables, or to block on them before assigning — both decided in advance.

And the fourth option inverts the design: a background variable measured before the treatment cannot be the outcome of it.

The habit: "balanced in expectation" is the exact phrase. Expect small chance differences, and expect about α of your baseline tests to fire.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Re-tossing until the baseline table looks tidy is a choice made after seeing the data, and it is what stops an allocation being random.
b.Random assignment balances the groups in expectation, not exactly. Identical groups were never what it promised, so nothing has gone wrong.
c.A background variable was measured before the treatment was given, so it cannot be an outcome of the treatment.
🏷️ Random assignment balances groups in expectation, not exactly.

Question 16

🧭 Causality and research design

Two designs, one conclusion

Zubkov reviews the two studies below. Both report that children who are read to at bedtime read better at seven. The causal claim “being read to improves reading” is licensed by:
Two studies of bedtime reading and reading at seven · Zubkov’s review
Study 1Study 2
Families1,200 drawn at random from the register160 who answered an advert
Who decided which children were read tothe families themselvesa coin, inside the study
Reading measuredonce, at age sevenat age five and again at seven
  • aneither study, since reading cannot be assigned
  • bStudy 2 only — a coin decided who was read to
  • cStudy 1 only — its sample is the representative one
  • dboth studies, since both found the same pattern
🔎 What it is really asking

One study picked its families at random; the other assigned the reading at random.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Causality: observational study against experiment.

🛠️ The procedure

Read one line of the design: who decided which children were read to? If the families decided, the finding is an association. If the study decided, by a coin, the causal door opens.

🧮 The working
Study 1. A beautiful sample — 1,200 families drawn at random from the register, so whatever it measures describes the register’s families. But the families chose bedtime reading for themselves, and reading at bedtime travels with books in the house, parents’ own reading, time, and quiet. Any of those could raise reading at seven on its own. Association, measured well, in a known population.

Study 2. An unlovely sample — 160 families who answered an advert, representing nobody in particular. But a coin decided which of them ran the nightly reading programme, so the two arms started out alike on average, and the arm that read aloud read better at seven. Cause, in these families.

The two studies have opposite strengths, which is why Zubkov wants both. Study 1 tells him the pattern exists across the population; Study 2 tells him that bedtime reading is part of what produces it.

The two remaining options go wrong in opposite directions. "Both studies" treats agreement between designs as evidence about mechanism — but a confounded finding repeated in a larger sample is still confounded. "Neither" is simply false: Study 2 assigned bedtime reading, so it plainly can be assigned.

The habit: put every study through one question before you read its results — who set the value of the explanatory variable? Everything else follows from the answer.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Study 2 assigned a nightly reading programme at random, so bedtime reading plainly can be assigned. It was, in 160 families.
c.Study 1’s sample is the better one, and its families chose bedtime reading for themselves. A representative sample buys scope, not cause.
d.Two studies agreeing is reassuring about the pattern. It does not repair the design of the one in which the families chose for themselves.
🏷️ Who set the explanatory variable? That one line decides what the study can claim.

Question 17

⚖️ Ethics and inference

What a failed replication shows

Bastiaanse publishes a significant effect from two groups of 30. An independent team repeats the study with the same design, three times the sample and a pre-registered analysis, and finds nothing. The reading best supported is:
  • athe effect is real but confined to the first team’s setting
  • bthe two results average out to a half-sized effect
  • cthe original result may well have been a false positive
  • dthe second team must have made a procedural error
🔎 What it is really asking

Which of the two studies was better placed to detect a real effect?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Ethics of inference: replication and pre-registration.

🛠️ The procedure

A null result is informative in proportion to the study’s power. A pre-registered replication three times the size has a much better chance of catching a real effect, so its failure to find one carries real weight.

🧮 The working
Put numbers on the two studies. Against a true standardised difference of 0.5:

Two groups of 30 — power 0.478. A coin flip.
Two groups of 90 — power 0.916.

So if the effect were real and that big, the replication would have found it about nine times in ten. It did not. Together with a pre-registered analysis, which removes the freedom to search for a significant version, that is genuine evidence against the original — and the likeliest single explanation is that the first significant result was a false positive, which happens at rate α to every honest researcher.

Keep the claim at the right strength. "May well have been" is as far as it goes. One failed replication does not prove absence either; a smaller real effect would be missed by both studies, and genuine differences in setting do exist. The next step is to report both results and pool them, not to pick a winner.

The other options each dodge the evidence. Assuming the second team erred is the file drawer in miniature — the result is discounted because of what it found. Confining the effect to the first setting is a post-hoc rescue that explains any failure whatsoever. And averaging a positive and a null into "half-sized" is not how evidence combines: a pooled analysis weights studies by their precision, and the larger study carries most of the weight.

The habit: before reading a null result, ask what power the study had. A well-powered null says something; an under-powered null says very little.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Restricting the effect to the original setting after the fact is a rescue that would explain away any failed replication whatsoever.
b.Evidence does not combine by averaging two conclusions. A pooled analysis weights by precision, so the larger study carries most of the weight.
d.Discounting a result because of what it found is the file drawer in miniature. Nothing in the stem points at an error by the second team.
🏷️ A null from a well-powered, pre-registered study is evidence. A small null is not.

Question 18

🧭 Causality and research design

What statistical control can and cannot do

Cerutti finds that adults who attend a gym report better mood, and writes that “once income and age are held constant statistically, the relationship is causal”. The flaw in that sentence is:
  • aholding two variables constant leaves all the others alive
  • bincome and age cannot be held constant in any analysis
  • cmood is ordinal, so it cannot be adjusted for at all
  • da causal claim needs a sample of at least 1,000 adults
🔎 What it is really asking

Adjustment handles the variables you measured. What about the rest?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Causality: statistical control against random assignment.

🛠️ The procedure

Adjusting for a variable removes the part of the association that that variable explains, as well as it was measured. Random assignment balances the variables you thought of and the ones you did not.

🧮 The working
Adjustment is a real tool, and Cerutti has used it correctly. What he has over-claimed is its reach.

List what else differs between gym-goers and non-gym-goers, beyond income and age: existing health, chronic pain, free time, how sociable they are, whether a friend already goes, how they slept last week. Every one of those can raise mood on its own, and none of them is in his model. Two columns of adjustment leave all of them untouched.

There is a second, quieter limit: a variable adjusted for is only handled as well as it was measured. "Income" as a banded self-report is a rough stand-in for the thing that actually matters, so even the adjustment he did make is partial.

Why random assignment is different in kind, not in degree. A coin does not need to know what the confounders are. Assigning a random half of willing adults to a subsidised gym membership balances sociability and chronic pain and sleep without anyone naming them.

And note what his analysis does deliver: an association between gym attendance and mood that is not explained by income or age. That is a genuine and publishable finding. The only faulty word in his sentence is "causal".

The habit: for any adjusted association, ask which confounders are in the model and which are merely unmentioned. Adjustment handles a list; randomisation handles the unknown.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Income and age are routinely held constant, either by adjustment or by comparing within bands. That part of his analysis is ordinary and sound.
c.Mood questionnaire totals are routinely treated as interval and adjusted. Even on an ordinal reading, that is not what makes his sentence wrong.
d.Sample size governs precision, not causality. A million self-selected gym-goers would leave the same confounders in place.
🏷️ Adjustment handles the confounders you measured. A coin handles the rest.

Question 1

📏 Interval for a proportion

Margin of error for one proportion

School psychologist Marta screens 87 primary-school pupils for a reading difficulty and 44 of them screen positive. She wants a 95% confidence interval for the proportion in the population. The margin of error, to three decimal places, is:
  • a0.003
  • b0.105
  • c0.054
  • d0.211
🔎 What it is really asking

Compute z* × SE, not the interval itself.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Interval for one proportion: the margin only.

🛠️ The procedure

margin = z* √(p̂(1 − p̂) ⁄ n). The margin is half the width of the interval, not the interval.

🧮 The working
p̂ = 44 ⁄ 87 = 0.5057

SE = √(0.5057 × 0.4943 ⁄ 87) = √0.0028729 = 0.05360

margin = 1.96 × 0.05360 = 0.105

The interval, if it had been asked for, is 0.506 ± 0.105 = 0.401 to 0.611.

Read which one the question wants. "Margin of error" is one number. "Confidence interval" is two. Exams put both on the option list.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.003 is the variance p̂(1 − p̂) ⁄ n, before the square root. Easy to stop one step early on a calculator.
c.0.054 is the standard error, before multiplying by 1.96. The SE is the building block; the margin is z* times it.
d.0.211 is the full width of the interval, 2 × 0.105. The margin is the distance from the centre to one end.
🏷️ Margin = z* × SE. Half the interval, not the whole of it.

Question 2

🔔 The sampling distribution of p-hat

Probability from the sampling distribution of p-hat

It is known that 12% of all students taking a particular course are awarded a distinction. In one section there are 155 students. The probability that at least 14% of them are awarded a distinction is closest to:
  • a0.77
  • b0.06
  • c0.50
  • d0.22
🔎 What it is really asking

A Normal calculation on p-hat, not on one student.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The sampling distribution of p-hat.

🛠️ The procedure

Centre on p, spread √(p(1 − p) ⁄ n), then turn the threshold into a z and read the tail. This is a z-score question wearing proportions clothing.

🧮 The working
Centre: p = 0.12. Spread: SE = √(0.12 × 0.88 ⁄ 155) = √0.0006813 = 0.02610.

z = (0.14 − 0.12) ⁄ 0.02610 = +0.77

P(p̂ ≥ 0.14) = P(z ≥ 0.77) = 1 − 0.7794 = 0.2206, about 0.22.

Check the counts first: 155 × 0.12 = 18.6 successes and 155 × 0.88 = 136.4 failures, both well over 10, so the Normal approximation is justified.

Note which p goes in the SE. Here the population value 0.12 is known, so it is the one used — not the 0.14 from the question.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.77 is the area to the left of z = 0.77 — the probability of fewer than 14%. The question said "at least".
b.0.06 would come from an SE that is too small; it is the tail beyond about z = 1.55, which is what you get using n alone rather than p(1 − p) ⁄ n.
c.0.50 is what you would get if 14% were the centre of the distribution. It is not — 12% is.
🏷️ Centre on p, spread √(p(1−p)⁄n), then it is just a z-score.

Question 3

✅ Conditions and plus four

Is the Normal approximation justified?

A researcher wants a confidence interval for the proportion of a population with a rare trait. In a sample of 400 people, 6 have the trait. Using the large-sample interval here is:
  • anot justified, because there are fewer than 10 successes
  • bjustified, because n is well over 30
  • cjustified, because n × p̂ × (1 − p̂) is greater than 10
  • dnot justified, because the sample is less than 10% of the population
🔎 What it is really asking

Check successes and failures separately, not n.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conditions: the counts check.

🛠️ The procedure

For a one-proportion interval you need at least 10 successes and 10 failures in the sample. A large n does not rescue a lopsided split.

🧮 The working
Successes = 6. Failures = 394.

6 is below 10, so the condition fails — even though n = 400 looks generous.

What to do instead: the plus-four interval, which adds two successes and two failures: p̃ = 8 ⁄ 404 = 0.0198.

Why it matters. With only 6 successes the sampling distribution of p̂ is skewed, not Normal, and the ordinary interval can run below zero — which is impossible for a proportion.

The habit: count both categories before you reach for any formula.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b."n ≥ 30" is a rule of thumb for means. For proportions the condition is on the counts, and this sample fails it.
c.n × p̂ × (1 − p̂) is not the condition. The two separate counts — np̂ and n(1 − p̂) — are, and the second of those is fine while the first is not.
d.The 10% condition is about sampling without replacement from a finite population, and a sample smaller than 10% of the population satisfies it. It is not the problem here.
🏷️ Ten successes AND ten failures. Count both, never just n.

Question 4

⚖️ Test for a proportion

A one-proportion z test on the boundary

A university claims that half of its psychology students attend every seminar. A survey of 150 students finds 63 who do. For a two-sided test of the claim at the 5% level, the conclusion is:
  • areject the claim — 63 is far below the expected 75
  • bno conclusion is possible without the population standard deviation
  • creject the claim — the result falls exactly on the 5% boundary
  • dfail to reject the claim — 42% is close enough to 50%
🔎 What it is really asking

Compute z against p₀ = 0.50 and compare with 1.96.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Test for one proportion.

🛠️ The procedure

SE is built from p₀, not from p̂: SE = √(p₀(1 − p₀) ⁄ n). Then z = (p̂ − p₀) ⁄ SE, and compare |z| with 1.96.

🧮 The working
p̂ = 63 ⁄ 150 = 0.4200.

SE = √(0.50 × 0.50 ⁄ 150) = √0.0016667 = 0.04082

z = (0.4200 − 0.5000) ⁄ 0.04082 = −1.96

Two-sided P = 0.0500 — exactly on the line. With the convention P ≤ α, this rejects at the 5% level, but only by a hair.

Why this is worth meeting once. A result sitting on the boundary is the clearest possible demonstration that .05 is a convention, not a fact about the world. The honest report gives z, P and the interval together, and says it is marginal.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The conclusion happens to be to reject, but the reason is wrong: how far 63 is from 75 in raw counts says nothing until it is divided by a standard error.
b.A proportion has no separate standard deviation to supply — p₀ determines the spread. This is the confusion with testing a mean.
d.42% against 50% is an eight-point gap on 150 students, which is exactly what the test evaluates — and it reaches the boundary. "Close enough" is not a test.
🏷️ Test → SE from p₀. Interval → SE from p̂.

Question 5

⚔️ Two proportions

The pooled z test for two proportions

Two tutorial formats are compared. 78 of 120 students pass under the flipped format and 90 of 180 under the standard one. For a test of whether the pass rates differ, the pooled estimate of the common proportion is:
  • a0.150
  • b0.560
  • c0.575
  • d0.650
🔎 What it is really asking

Pool the counts, not the two proportions.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Two proportions: the pooled estimate.

🛠️ The procedure

Pooled p̂ = (X₁ + X₂) ⁄ (n₁ + n₂). Add the successes and add the sample sizes — never average the two proportions.

🧮 The working
Pooled p̂ = (78 + 90) ⁄ (120 + 180) = 168 ⁄ 300 = 0.560

Why pooling at all. H₀ says the two groups share one proportion, so under H₀ the best estimate of it uses every observation in the study.

Where it goes next: SE = √(0.56 × 0.44 × (1⁄120 + 1⁄180)) = 0.05850, so z = 0.15 ⁄ 0.0585 = 2.56 and P = .010.

And where it does NOT go: the confidence interval for the difference keeps each group’s own p̂, giving SE = 0.0573 and an interval of 3.8 to 26.2 points.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.150 is the difference between the two proportions, which is the numerator of z, not the pooled estimate underneath it.
c.0.575 is the average of 0.65 and 0.50. That ignores the fact that one group is half again as large as the other — pooling adds counts, not proportions.
d.0.650 is the flipped group’s own proportion, 78 ⁄ 120, not a pooled estimate.
🏷️ Pool the COUNTS: (X₁+X₂) ⁄ (n₁+n₂). Never the average of two proportions.

Question 6

⚔️ Two proportions

Reading an interval for a difference

Researchers compare two schools on the percentage of pupils who read for pleasure. The 95% confidence interval for the difference in proportions (school B − school A) runs from 0.04 to 0.22. A head teacher claims there is no real difference between the schools. The head teacher is:
  • acorrect — the interval is too narrow to show anything
  • bcorrect — values near zero are still plausible
  • cneither, because a P-value is needed to decide
  • dincorrect — the whole interval lies above zero
🔎 What it is really asking

Does the interval contain zero?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Two proportions: turning an interval into a verdict.

🛠️ The procedure

An interval for a difference is a test of "no difference" if you ask one question: does it contain zero?

🧮 The working
The interval runs from 0.04 to 0.22. Zero is not in it — the lowest plausible difference is still 4 percentage points in school B’s favour.

So "no real difference" is not among the values the data support, and the head teacher is incorrect.

The equivalence worth knowing: a 95% interval that excludes zero corresponds to a two-sided test significant at the 5% level. You do not need the P-value separately — the interval already answered it, and it tells you the size of the gap as well.

What the interval does not say: which school is better for any individual pupil, or why the gap exists.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.04 to 0.22 is a perfectly usable interval. A narrow interval is a precise one — it is good news, not a reason to withhold a conclusion.
b.Values near zero are exactly what the interval rules out. Its lower end is 0.04, so zero sits outside it.
c.The interval is sufficient. An interval excluding zero at 95% already corresponds to P < .05 two-sided.
🏷️ Interval for a difference: does it contain 0? That is the test.

Question 7

🧮 Margin of error and sample size

Planning the sample size

A polling organisation wants a 95% confidence interval for a proportion with a margin of error no larger than 4 percentage points, and has no prior estimate of the proportion. The number of people needed is:
  • a601
  • b385
  • c550
  • d2401
🔎 What it is really asking

n = (z*⁄m)² p*(1 − p*), with the worst-case p*.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Sample size planning.

🛠️ The procedure

n = (z* ⁄ m)² × p*(1 − p*), rounded up. With no prior estimate use p* = 0.5, which maximises p*(1 − p*) and so gives the safe answer.

🧮 The working
z* = 1.96, m = 0.04, p* = 0.5.

n = (1.96 ⁄ 0.04)² × 0.25 = 49² × 0.25 = 2401 × 0.25 = 600.25

Round up: 601 people.

Rounding down is the one direction that is actually wrong — 600 would leave the margin a shade above 4 points.

The scaling to remember: m is squared and on the bottom, so halving the margin quadruples n. A 2-point margin would need 2401.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.385 is the answer for a 5-point margin, (1.96⁄0.05)² × 0.25 = 384.16 → 385.
c.550 does not come out of the formula at any sensible p*; it is the kind of round number that looks like a sample size.
d.2401 is (1.96 ⁄ 0.04)² without multiplying by p*(1 − p*) — the factor of 0.25 was dropped.
🏷️ n = (z*⁄m)²p*(1−p*). No guess → p* = 0.5. Always round UP.

Question 8

📏 Interval for a proportion

Which interval for a small lopsided sample

In a sample of 20 items a researcher finds 6 defective. For a confidence interval for the proportion defective she should use:
  • aneither method
  • bthe large-sample interval with a wider z*
  • cthe plus-four interval
  • dthe large-sample interval
🔎 What it is really asking

Do the counts clear 10 each?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conditions: choosing between the two intervals.

🛠️ The procedure

Large-sample interval needs 10 successes and 10 failures. When they are not there but n is at least about 10, use plus four.

🧮 The working
Successes = 6, failures = 14. Six is below ten, so the large-sample interval is not justified.

n = 20 is enough for the plus-four repair: p̃ = (6 + 2) ⁄ (20 + 4) = 8 ⁄ 24 = 0.3333, and the SE uses the same p̃ and n + 4 = 24.

Both parts change. Substituting p̃ but dividing by 20 is a common slip and gives the wrong interval.

Why not "neither". Plus four exists precisely for this case, and is recommended down to about n = 10.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a."Neither" would leave you with no interval at all, when plus four is designed for exactly this situation.
b.Widening z* does not fix a skewed sampling distribution. The problem is the shape, not the confidence level.
d.The large-sample interval needs at least 10 of each. With 6 defectives it is the method being ruled out.
🏷️ Counts under 10 but n at least ~10 → plus four, with n + 4 in the SE too.

Question 9

📏 Interval for a proportion

Reading a confidence interval correctly

A 95% confidence interval for the proportion of adults who have used a mental-health app is 0.338 to 0.462. Which statement is correct?
  • aif the sample were larger, 95% of the sample would fall in this range
  • b95% of intervals built this way contain the true proportion
  • cthere is a 95% probability that the true proportion lies in this interval
  • d95% of adults have used an app between 33.8% and 46.2% of the time
🔎 What it is really asking

What does the 95% actually describe?

🧭 Which type of question this is

What a confidence level means.

🛠️ The procedure

The 95% is a property of the method, not of your one interval. p is not random; the interval was.

🧮 The working
The sampling already happened. This particular interval either contains the true proportion or it does not — there is no probability left in it.

What is true is that the procedure catches p in 95% of all the samples it could have been applied to. That is what the 95% describes.

The accepted shorthand. "We are 95% confident that p is between 0.338 and 0.462" is fine to write — it is understood as shorthand for the sentence above. What is not fine is converting it into a probability about p.

The tell: any option beginning "there is a 95% probability that the proportion…" is putting the randomness in the wrong place.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.A confidence interval is not a prediction about where future sample values will fall. That is a different interval entirely.
c.This puts the probability on p, which is a fixed unknown rather than a random quantity. Your interval was the random thing.
d.This describes individual adults and a fraction of their time. The interval is about one population proportion, not about how often anyone does anything.
🏷️ 95% describes the recipe, not the one interval it produced.

Question 10

⚖️ Test for a proportion

One-sided against two-sided

A researcher believed before collecting data that a new information leaflet would raise the proportion of patients attending follow-up above the historical 45%. For this test the alternative hypothesis should be:
  • aHₐ: p ≠ 0.45
  • bHₐ: p̂ > 0.45
  • cHₐ: p < 0.45
  • dHₐ: p > 0.45
🔎 What it is really asking

A direction was committed to in advance.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The logic of a test: one-sided against two-sided.

🛠️ The procedure

A one-sided alternative is legitimate only if the direction was fixed before seeing the data. It puts all of α in one tail, so the cut-off is 1.645 rather than 1.96.

🧮 The working
The direction was committed to in advance and it was "raise", so Hₐ: p > 0.45, with H₀: p = 0.45.

All 5% sits in the upper tail, so the critical value is +1.645.

The honest cost. A one-sided test has more power in the direction you chose and no power at all in the other — if the leaflet made attendance worse, this test cannot detect it, however badly.

And the cheat it must not become. Looking at your result first and then picking the tail it fell in doubles your real Type I error rate from 5% to 10%.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Two-sided is the honest default, but the stem says the direction was fixed in advance — which is exactly the condition that licenses a one-sided test.
b.Hypotheses are statements about the population parameter p, never about the sample statistic p̂.
c.The direction is the wrong way round. The researcher predicted an increase.
🏷️ One-sided only if the direction was fixed BEFORE the data. Cut-off 1.645.

Question 11

📏 Interval for a proportion

What changes the width of an interval

A 95% confidence interval for a proportion is recomputed as a 99% interval from the same sample. The new interval will be:
  • awider, because z* is larger
  • bnarrower, because the confidence is higher
  • cthe same width, because the data have not changed
  • dwider, because the standard error is larger
🔎 What it is really asking

Which part of the formula does the confidence level change?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Interval for one proportion: what the confidence level does.

🛠️ The procedure

The confidence level enters only through z*. More confidence means a bigger z*, and a bigger multiplier means a wider interval.

🧮 The working
z* goes from 1.96 at 95% to 2.576 at 99%.

p̂ and n are unchanged, so SE is unchanged. Only the multiplier grows, so the margin grows by a factor of 2.576 ⁄ 1.96 = 1.31 — the interval is 31% wider.

The trade-off in one line. You cannot have more confidence and more precision from the same data. Being surer means saying less.

The only way to buy both is a bigger n, which shrinks the SE itself.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Higher confidence gives a wider interval, not a narrower one. Being more certain of catching p means casting a bigger net.
c.The data are unchanged, but the multiplier is not — the confidence level changes z*, which changes the width.
d.The standard error depends only on p̂ and n, both unchanged. It is z*, not the SE, that the confidence level moves.
🏷️ Confidence level changes z* only. Higher confidence → wider.

Question 12

🔔 The sampling distribution of p-hat

The effect of n on the standard error

The standard error of p̂ for a sample of 100 is 0.048. For a sample of 400 drawn from the same population, the standard error will be about:
  • a0.096
  • b0.048
  • c0.024
  • d0.012
🔎 What it is really asking

n goes up by a factor of four. What happens to the SE?

🧭 Which type of question this is

The sampling distribution of p-hat: the √n effect.

🛠️ The procedure

SE = √(p(1 − p) ⁄ n), so n sits under a square root. Multiplying n by four divides the SE by √4 = 2.

🧮 The working
n goes from 100 to 400, a factor of 4.

The SE divides by √4 = 2: 0.048 ⁄ 2 = 0.024.

The rule to carry: quadruple the n, halve the SE. Precision is expensive — halving your error again would need 1 600.

What does not matter: how big the population is. Population size does not appear in the formula, provided the sample is a small slice of it.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.096 is the SE doubled. A bigger sample makes the estimate more precise, so the SE must fall.
b.0.048 is the original SE, unchanged — which would be true only if n had not changed.
d.0.012 would need n × 16, not n × 4. That is the SE at n = 1 600.
🏷️ Quadruple n → halve the SE. n is under a square root.

Question 13

⚔️ Two proportions

Difference against relative risk

In a study of dropout, 4% of students on one programme withdraw against 2% on another. A report states that the first programme "doubles the risk of withdrawal". This statement is:
  • acorrect, and the better way to report the finding
  • bcorrect, but it conceals that the difference is 2 percentage points
  • cincorrect, because the difference is only 2 percentage points
  • dincorrect, because relative risk cannot be computed from percentages
🔎 What it is really asking

Is the ratio right, and is it the whole story?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Two proportions: difference against ratio.

🛠️ The procedure

The relative risk is 0.04 ⁄ 0.02 = 2.00, so "doubles" is arithmetically correct. The difference is 2 percentage points — also correct, and much less dramatic.

🧮 The working
Both statements describe the same two numbers:
  ratio = 0.04 ⁄ 0.02 = 2.00 — "twice the risk"
  difference = 0.04 − 0.02 = 0.02 — two percentage points

So "doubles the risk" is true. It is also, on its own, misleading: it sounds like a large effect when it means 4 students in a hundred instead of 2.

Why ratios inflate for rare outcomes. With a small baseline there is no ceiling on the ratio — 2% against 0.2% is a relative risk of 10. With a 50% baseline the ratio can never exceed 2 at all.

The standard: report both, and always print the two raw percentages beside them.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.It is correct but it is not the better way to report it on its own — a ratio without its baseline hides how big the thing being doubled actually is.
c.The difference being small does not make the ratio wrong. Both numbers are correct descriptions of the same comparison.
d.Relative risk is a ratio of two proportions and percentages are proportions. It computes perfectly well.
🏷️ Ratio and difference are both honest. A ratio without its baseline is not.

Question 14

✅ Conditions and plus four

Which condition has failed

A researcher surveys 60 members of one university sports club and uses the result to build a confidence interval for the proportion of all students at the university who exercise weekly. The most serious problem with this interval is:
  • athe sample size of 60 is too small for a proportion
  • bthe counts of successes and failures will be too small
  • cthe 10% condition is violated
  • dthe sample is not random, so it need not represent the population
🔎 What it is really asking

Which assumption does the sampling method break?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conditions: random sampling before anything else.

🛠️ The procedure

Every interval and test in this theme assumes a random sample from the population of interest. No formula repairs a biased sampling method.

🧮 The working
Members of a sports club exercise far more than students in general, so the sample is systematically unlike the population the interval is supposed to describe.

The arithmetic will still produce a tidy interval. It will simply be an interval for the wrong population — and a bigger sample from the same club would make it narrower and no less wrong.

This is the condition that cannot be checked from the data. Counts you can count; Normality you can look at; randomness you can only know from how the sample was taken.

The phrase for the exam: this is selection bias, and it limits what the result can be generalised to.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.60 is a perfectly workable sample size for a proportion, provided the counts clear 10 each. Size is not the problem here.
b.With 60 club members the counts of weekly exercisers and non-exercisers would very likely both exceed 10. The counts condition is probably satisfied.
c.The 10% condition concerns sampling without replacement from a finite population; 60 out of a whole university satisfies it comfortably.
🏷️ No formula fixes a biased sample. Random sampling comes first.

Question 15

⚖️ Test for a proportion

What a non-significant result means

A test of whether a proportion differs from 0.45 returns z = −1.56, P = 0.120. The correct conclusion at the 5% level is:
  • athere is not enough evidence of a difference from 0.45
  • bthe proportion is equal to 0.45 in the population
  • cthe proportion differs from 0.45, but only slightly
  • dthe test should be rerun one-sided to reach 0.05
🔎 What it is really asking

How should a P of 0.120 be written up?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conclusions: failing to reject.

🛠️ The procedure

P > α means fail to reject H₀. That is a statement about the strength of the evidence, not about the world.

🧮 The working
P = 0.120 is well above 0.05, so H₀ is not rejected.

The honest sentence: there is not enough evidence to conclude that the proportion differs from 0.45.

Never "we accept H₀", and never "the proportion equals 0.45". Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence — the study may simply have been too small to detect a real difference.

What would strengthen the report: a confidence interval. It would show which values are plausible, and whether the study could have detected a difference worth caring about at all.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Failing to reject never establishes H₀. The data are consistent with 0.45, and also with a range of other values.
c.The test did not find a difference, so claiming one — even a slight one — is exactly what P = 0.120 does not license.
d.Switching to a one-sided test after seeing the result is the cheat that doubles the real Type I error rate. The alternative is fixed before the data.
🏷️ P > α → "not enough evidence". Never "accept H₀".

Question 1

📏 Interval for a proportion

A full interval for one proportion

Nutrition researcher Delacroix asks 264 first-year students whether they skipped breakfast on the morning of the survey, and 99 say they did. Her 95% confidence interval for the proportion in the whole first year, to three decimal places, runs from:
  • a0.258 to 0.492
  • b0.298 to 0.452
  • c0.317 to 0.433
  • d0.345 to 0.405
🔎 What it is really asking

Three steps: the proportion, its standard error, then both ends.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Interval for one proportion: the whole interval.

🛠️ The procedure

p̂ ± z* √(p̂(1 − p̂) ⁄ n), with z* = 1.96 at 95%. Build it in order — p̂, then SE, then the margin, then the two ends.

🧮 The working
p̂ = 99 ⁄ 264 = 0.3750

SE = √(0.3750 × 0.6250 ⁄ 264) = √0.00088778 = 0.029796

margin = 1.96 × 0.029796 = 0.058399

0.3750 − 0.0584 = 0.317   and   0.3750 + 0.0584 = 0.433

Check the counts before you trust it: 99 skipped and 264 − 99 = 165 did not. Both are comfortably over 10, so the Normal-based interval is justified.

Reading it out loud: somewhere between about 32% and about 43% of the first year skip breakfast. Six percentage points of uncertainty either side of 37.5% — which is what 264 students buys you, and why nobody should quote the 37.5% on its own.

The habit: write SE and margin on separate lines. Every wrong option on this question comes from stopping on the wrong line.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.258 to 0.492 uses the full width, 2 × 0.0584, on each side. The margin is the distance from the centre to one end.
b.0.298 to 0.452 uses z* = 2.576, which is the 99% multiplier. At 95% the multiplier is 1.96.
d.0.345 to 0.405 uses the SE of 0.0298 as the margin, with the 1.96 never applied. That would be about a 68% interval, not a 95% one.
🏷️ p̂, then SE, then × 1.96, then ±. Four lines, in that order.

Question 2

📏 Interval for a proportion

Recovering the confidence level

A report by Borkowski gives a sample of 300 adults, a sample proportion of 0.40, and an interval of 0.3271 to 0.4729, but never says what confidence level was used. It was:
  • a99%
  • b95%
  • c90%
  • d98%
🔎 What it is really asking

Which multiplier would stretch this SE into this margin?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Interval for one proportion: working backwards to z*.

🛠️ The procedure

The confidence level enters the interval only through z*. Recover the margin from the printed ends, compute the SE yourself from p̂ and n, and z* = margin ⁄ SE.

🧮 The working
The SE you can compute from the stem alone:
SE = √(0.40 × 0.60 ⁄ 300) = √0.0008 = 0.028284

The margin comes from the printed ends — half the width:
margin = (0.4729 − 0.3271) ⁄ 2 = 0.1458 ⁄ 2 = 0.0729

So the multiplier used was
z* = 0.0729 ⁄ 0.028284 = 2.577, which is the familiar 2.576 — the 99% value.

Confirm it by building the other three and seeing which fits:
• 90%: 1.645 × 0.028284 = 0.0465 → 0.354 to 0.446
• 95%: 1.960 × 0.028284 = 0.0554 → 0.345 to 0.455
• 98%: 2.326 × 0.028284 = 0.0658 → 0.334 to 0.466
• 99%: 2.576 × 0.028284 = 0.0729 → 0.327 to 0.473 ✓

The four multipliers worth having by heart: 1.645, 1.960, 2.326, 2.576 for 90%, 95%, 98% and 99%. Two of them appear on nearly every proportions question.

And the sanity check: a wide interval means a big z*. This one is ±0.073 on an SE of 0.028 — nearly two and a half SEs, so it had to be one of the high-confidence levels before you divided anything.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.95% would use z* = 1.96 and give a margin of 0.0554, an interval of 0.345 to 0.455. That is visibly narrower than the one printed.
c.90% would use z* = 1.645, the narrowest of the four, giving 0.354 to 0.446. Lower confidence always means a shorter interval.
d.98% would use z* = 2.326 and give 0.334 to 0.466 — close, but the recovered multiplier is 2.577, not 2.326.
🏷️ z* = margin ⁄ SE. Recover the margin as half the printed width.

Question 3

⚖️ Test for a proportion

The P-value of a one-proportion test

A health authority claims that 30% of adolescents meet the national activity guideline. Steenkamp surveys 320 adolescents and finds 112 who do. The two-sided P-value for a test of the authority’s claim, to four decimal places, is:
  • a0.0255
  • b0.0608
  • c0.9745
  • d0.0510
🔎 What it is really asking

A test, so the standard error is built on the claimed value.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Test for one proportion: computing the P-value.

🛠️ The procedure

In a test the spread comes from p₀, because you are assuming H₀ while you compute: SE = √(p₀(1 − p₀) ⁄ n). Then z = (p̂ − p₀) ⁄ SE, and a two-sided P doubles the tail.

🧮 The working
p̂ = 112 ⁄ 320 = 0.3500

SE = √(0.30 × 0.70 ⁄ 320) = √0.000656 = 0.025617

z = (0.3500 − 0.3000) ⁄ 0.025617 = 0.05 ⁄ 0.025617 = 1.9518

One tail above 1.9518 is 0.0255, so the two-sided P is
2 × 0.0255 = 0.0510

And the decision: 0.0510 is above 0.05, so at the 5% level Steenkamp does not reject the claim — by a margin of one thousandth. The matching 95% interval would contain 0.30, just barely.

Do not round early. Round z to 1.95 and the doubled tail comes out 0.0512; round it to 2.00 and you get 0.0455, which lands on the other side of 0.05 and reverses the conclusion. Carry four decimals through the whole calculation and round only at the end.

The honest write-up: z = 1.95, P = .051, not significant at the 5% level — and say plainly that it is marginal rather than pretending the line means something exact.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.0255 is one tail only. The claim was "30%", which sets no direction, so both tails count and the tail must be doubled.
b.0.0608 builds the SE from p̂ instead of p₀: √(0.35 × 0.65 ⁄ 320) = 0.026663 gives z = 1.8752. That SE belongs to an interval, not to a test.
c.0.9745 is the area to the left of z — what the table hands you directly. A P-value is always a tail, so it can never be anywhere near 1.
🏷️ Test → SE from p₀. Interval → SE from p̂. Different questions, different SE.

Question 4

🔔 The sampling distribution of p-hat

A count turned into a proportion first

It is established that 22% of referrals to a clinic are closed within a month. Moravec takes a random batch of 250 referrals. The probability that at least 66 of them are closed within a month, to four decimal places, is closest to:
  • a0.5000
  • b0.0465
  • c0.9535
  • d0.0931
🔎 What it is really asking

The threshold is a count, but the distribution you know is one of proportions.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The sampling distribution of p-hat: a count as the threshold.

🛠️ The procedure

Turn the count into a proportion first — 66 ⁄ 250. Then centre on p, spread √(p(1 − p) ⁄ n), and read the upper tail.

🧮 The working
Convert the threshold: 66 ⁄ 250 = 0.2640.

Centre: p = 0.22. Spread:
SE = √(0.22 × 0.78 ⁄ 250) = √0.0006864 = 0.026199

z = (0.2640 − 0.2200) ⁄ 0.026199 = 0.044 ⁄ 0.026199 = +1.6794

P(p̂ ≥ 0.264) = 1 − 0.9535 = 0.0465, about one batch in twenty.

Check the condition: 250 × 0.22 = 55 closures expected and 250 × 0.78 = 195 not, both far above 10, so the Normal model is safe to use.

Which p goes into the SE. The population value, 0.22 — the one you are assuming. The 0.264 is the threshold being tested against that assumption, not an estimate of anything. Using 0.264 in the SE is the single commonest error on this type.

The habit: underline whether the stem gives you a count or a proportion. If it is a count, your first line of working is always the division.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.5000 is what you get by centring the distribution on 0.264. The centre is the population value 0.22; 0.264 is the threshold.
c.0.9535 is the area to the left — the probability that fewer than 66 are closed. The question said "at least".
d.0.0931 is 2 × 0.0465, the tail doubled. Doubling belongs to a two-sided P-value; this is a probability in one direction.
🏷️ Count threshold? Divide by n first. The SE always uses the population p.

Question 5

⚔️ Two proportions

The test statistic for two proportions

Castellano compares relapse within a year under two aftercare plans. 51 of 150 clients relapse on plan A and 36 of 180 on plan B. For a two-sided test of whether the two relapse rates differ, the value of the test statistic, to two decimal places, is:
  • a3.62
  • b0.14
  • c2.87
  • d5.77
🔎 What it is really asking

One standard error for the gap, built on the assumption that the rates are equal.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Two proportions: computing the test statistic.

🛠️ The procedure

H₀ says the two groups share one proportion, so estimate that one proportion from all the data: p̂ = (X₁ + X₂) ⁄ (n₁ + n₂). Then SE = √(p̂(1 − p̂)(1⁄n₁ + 1⁄n₂)) and z = (p̂₁ − p̂₂) ⁄ SE.

🧮 The working
The two rates and the gap between them:
p̂₁ = 51 ⁄ 150 = 0.3400   p̂₂ = 36 ⁄ 180 = 0.2000   difference = 0.1400

Pool the counts, not the proportions:
p̂ = (51 + 36) ⁄ (150 + 180) = 87 ⁄ 330 = 0.263636

The standard error of the difference carries one term per group:
1⁄150 + 1⁄180 = 0.0066667 + 0.0055556 = 0.0122222
SE = √(0.263636 × 0.736364 × 0.0122222) = √0.0023728 = 0.048711

z = 0.1400 ⁄ 0.048711 = 2.87, so the two-sided P is 0.0041.

Why 1⁄n₁ + 1⁄n₂ and not 1⁄(n₁ + n₂). You are measuring the uncertainty of a difference, and each group contributes its own wobble. Two sources of noise add, they do not merge into one big sample. Putting 330 under a single root would shrink the SE to 0.024 and double the statistic.

And the verdict: P = .004, so the relapse rates differ — 34% against 20%, a gap of 14 percentage points.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.3.62 uses only plan A’s own standard error, √(0.34 × 0.66 ⁄ 150) = 0.0387. Plan B is half of the comparison and its uncertainty counts too.
b.0.14 is the raw difference in the two rates, never divided by anything. A difference only becomes a statistic once it is measured in standard errors.
d.5.77 puts a single combined n of 330 under the root, SE = √(0.2636 × 0.7364 ⁄ 330) = 0.0243. A difference needs one term per group, not one pooled sample.
🏷️ Pool the counts, then 1⁄n₁ + 1⁄n₂ inside the root. Each group brings its own noise.

Question 6

✅ Conditions and plus four

Which sample clears the counts

Fontaine has three independent samples, shown below, and wants a confidence interval for a proportion from each of them. The ordinary large-sample interval is justified for:
Three independent samples · size and number of successes
SamplenSuccesses
A409
B2512
C300291
  • asample B only
  • bsamples A and B
  • call three samples
  • dsample C only
🔎 What it is really asking

Write down both counts for all three samples before you decide anything.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conditions: the counts rule applied to several samples at once.

🛠️ The procedure

You need at least 10 successes and at least 10 failures. The failures are n − successes, so compute them — they are where the rule usually breaks.

🧮 The working
Fill in the missing column first.

Sample A: 9 successes, 40 − 9 = 31 failures. 9 is below 10 → fails.
Sample B: 12 successes, 25 − 12 = 13 failures. Both clear 10 → passes.
Sample C: 291 successes, 300 − 291 = 9 failures. 9 is below 10 → fails.

So only sample B qualifies — and it is the smallest of the three.

That is the whole lesson. The condition is about the two counts, never about n. Sample C has 300 people and still fails, because the trait is so common that almost nobody lacks it. Sample B has 25 people and passes, because the split is near even.

Why the rule has two halves. A proportion is squeezed between 0 and 1. When p̂ is near either wall, the sampling distribution is skewed rather than Normal and a symmetric ± margin can run past 0 or past 1 — impossible values. Ten of each is the course’s rough guarantee that there is room on both sides.

What to do with A and C: the plus-four interval, which adds two successes and two failures and so pulls p̂ away from the wall.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Sample A has only 9 successes, one short of ten. Its 40 participants cannot make up for the missing success — the rule counts categories, not people.
c.Sample C fails for exactly the same reason as A, at the other end: only 9 failures among 300. A huge n is no protection against a lopsided split.
d.Sample C is the one with the largest n and also the one with only 9 failures. Picking it means using size as the condition instead of the two counts.
🏷️ Compute n − successes every time. The failures are where the rule breaks.

Question 7

🧮 Margin of error and sample size

Sample size with a prior estimate

Rasmussen is planning a survey, and a pilot study puts the proportion near 0.20. She wants a 95% confidence interval with a margin of error no larger than 0.03. The smallest number of people that will do, as a whole number, is:
  • a682
  • b683
  • c1068
  • d4269
🔎 What it is really asking

The margin formula solved for n, with the pilot value as p*.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Sample size planning: with an estimate in hand.

🛠️ The procedure

n = (z* ⁄ m)² × p*(1 − p*), then round up. When a pilot gives you an estimate, use it as p*; the fallback of 0.5 is only for when you have nothing.

🧮 The working
z* = 1.96, m = 0.03, p* = 0.20.

(1.96 ⁄ 0.03)² = 65.3333² = 4268.29

p*(1 − p*) = 0.20 × 0.80 = 0.16

n = 4268.29 × 0.16 = 682.93 → round up to 683

Why up and never down. Check both candidates against what she asked for:
at n = 683, margin = 1.96 √(0.16 ⁄ 683) = 0.02999 ✓ inside 0.03
at n = 682, margin = 1.96 √(0.16 ⁄ 682) = 0.03002 ✗ outside 0.03
One person is the difference between meeting the specification and missing it, which is why rounding up is a rule and not a preference.

What the pilot saved her. With no estimate she would have to use p* = 0.5 and recruit 1 068 people. Knowing the proportion is near 0.20 cuts that by 385 people, because p*(1 − p*) falls from 0.25 to 0.16.

The risk of using a pilot: if the true proportion turns out nearer 0.5, the finished margin will be wider than 0.03. That is the price of the smaller sample.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.682 is 682.93 rounded down. It leaves the margin at 0.0300 2, which is outside the limit she set.
c.1068 uses p* = 0.5, which is the fallback for when nothing is known. The pilot estimate of 0.20 is exactly the information that lets you do better.
d.4269 is (1.96 ⁄ 0.03)² with the p*(1 − p*) factor left off altogether — the formula stopped one multiplication early.
🏷️ Pilot estimate? Use it as p*. Still round UP, always.

Question 8

⚖️ Test for a proportion

Recovering the count from a printed z

Bauwens reports a test of H₀: p = 0.60 on a sample of 400 and prints only “z = −2.45”. The number of successes in her sample, as a whole number, was:
  • a240
  • b184
  • c221
  • d216
🔎 What it is really asking

Everything in the standard error is in the stem, so the z can be undone.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Test for one proportion: working backwards to the data.

🛠️ The procedure

The SE of a test needs only p₀ and n, both given. So rearrange z = (p̂ − p₀) ⁄ SE into p̂ = p₀ + z × SE, and the count is n × p̂.

🧮 The working
Step one — the standard error, which needs no data at all:
SE = √(0.60 × 0.40 ⁄ 400) = √0.0006 = 0.024495

Step two — undo the z. It is negative, so p̂ sits below 0.60:
p̂ = 0.60 + (−2.45 × 0.024495) = 0.60 − 0.060012 = 0.5400

Step three — turn the proportion back into a count:
400 × 0.5400 = 216 successes

Check it forwards: (216⁄400 − 0.60) ⁄ 0.024495 = (0.54 − 0.60) ⁄ 0.024495 = −2.449. ✓

Why this works for a test and not for an interval. A test’s SE is built from p₀, which the hypothesis hands you. An interval’s SE is built from p̂ — the very thing you would be trying to find — so the same trick would go round in a circle.

Mind the sign. A negative z means the sample fell short of the claim, so you subtract. Adding gives 264 successes, a result just as far out in the other direction and the wrong answer to this question.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.240 is 400 × 0.60, the count H₀ predicts. That is the number the data are being compared with, not the number observed.
b.184 is 400 − 216, the failures rather than the successes. The question asked for the category that p refers to.
c.221 uses z = −1.96, the 5% critical value, in place of the −2.45 actually printed. The reported statistic is the one carrying the information.
🏷️ A test’s SE needs only p₀ and n — so a printed z can always be undone.

Question 9

📏 Interval for a proportion

The interval a lopsided sample needs

Developmental researcher Mikkelsen screens 30 toddlers for a speech delay and 4 screen positive. The 95% confidence interval she is entitled to report, to three decimal places, runs from:
  • a0.048 to 0.305
  • b0.012 to 0.255
  • c0.040 to 0.313
  • d0.019 to 0.248
🔎 What it is really asking

Check the counts first — they decide which interval you are allowed.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Interval for one proportion: the plus-four repair.

🛠️ The procedure

With fewer than 10 successes the ordinary interval is out. Add two successes and two failures: p̃ = (X + 2) ⁄ (n + 4) — and use n + 4 in the standard error too.

🧮 The working
Counts first: 4 positive and 30 − 4 = 26 negative. Four is below ten, so the ordinary interval is not justified.

The repair adds two of each:
p̃ = (4 + 2) ⁄ (30 + 4) = 6 ⁄ 34 = 0.176471

SE = √(0.176471 × 0.823529 ⁄ 34) = √0.0042744 = 0.065379

margin = 1.96 × 0.065379 = 0.128140

0.176471 ± 0.128140 = 0.048 to 0.305

Both parts change, and that is the whole trick. The 2 goes into the numerator twice over — once as +2 successes, once as +4 in the denominator — and the same n + 4 goes under the root. Substituting p̃ but leaving 30 in the SE is the commonest slip and gives 0.040 to 0.313.

What the repair is doing. With 4 successes out of 30, p̂ = 0.133 is close to the wall at zero, and the ordinary interval reaches down to 0.012 — far too confident about how low the rate could be. Nudging the estimate toward 0.5 widens the interval and keeps it honest.

Say it to a friend: "pretend you saw two more of each, then do the ordinary thing."
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.0.012 to 0.255 is the ordinary interval on p̂ = 4 ⁄ 30. That is precisely the interval the counts rule out, and its lower end is implausibly close to zero.
c.0.040 to 0.313 uses p̃ = 0.1765 in the numerator but leaves n = 30 under the root. The n + 4 belongs in the standard error as well.
d.0.019 to 0.248 puts n + 4 = 34 under the root but keeps p̂ = 0.1333 on top. The proportion has to be the adjusted one too.
🏷️ Plus four changes BOTH: p̃ = (X+2)⁄(n+4), and n + 4 under the root.

Question 10

⚔️ Two proportions

The interval for a difference in proportions

For Castellano’s two aftercare plans — 51 of 150 clients relapsing on plan A and 36 of 180 on plan B — the 95% confidence interval for the difference in relapse rates (plan A − plan B), to three decimal places, runs from:
  • a0.064 to 0.216
  • b−0.236 to −0.044
  • c0.044 to 0.236
  • d0.091 to 0.189
🔎 What it is really asking

An interval, not a test — so nothing gets pooled.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Two proportions: the interval for the difference.

🛠️ The procedure

An interval keeps each group’s own proportion: SE = √(p̂₁(1 − p̂₁)⁄n₁ + p̂₂(1 − p̂₂)⁄n₂). Then (p̂₁ − p̂₂) ± 1.96 × SE.

🧮 The working
p̂₁ = 0.3400, p̂₂ = 0.2000, so the estimate at the centre is 0.1400.

Each group contributes its own term:
0.3400 × 0.6600 ⁄ 150 = 0.2244 ⁄ 150 = 0.00149600
0.2000 × 0.8000 ⁄ 180 = 0.1600 ⁄ 180 = 0.00088889
SE = √0.00238489 = 0.048835

margin = 1.96 × 0.048835 = 0.095715

0.1400 ± 0.0957 = 0.044 to 0.236

Why no pooling here. Pooling assumes the two rates are equal — that is H₀, and it belongs to the test. An interval is not assuming anything; it is estimating how big the gap is, so each group speaks with its own proportion.

And the decision, free of charge: zero is not in the interval, so the two rates differ at the 5% level. That agrees with the test’s P of 0.0041, as it must.

What the interval adds that the P-value cannot: a size. Plan A’s relapse rate is somewhere between 4 and 24 percentage points higher. The lower end is what anyone deciding whether to fund plan B will want to see.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.064 to 0.216 uses only plan A’s standard error, √(0.34 × 0.66 ⁄ 150) = 0.0387. Both groups contribute uncertainty to a difference.
b.−0.236 to −0.044 is the interval for plan B − plan A. The stem fixed the order as plan A first, and the sign is the whole meaning of a difference.
d.0.091 to 0.189 uses the SE of 0.0488 as the margin, with 1.96 never applied. That builds roughly a 68% interval instead of a 95% one.
🏷️ Interval → each group’s own p̂. Pooling belongs to the test, nowhere else.
