Question 11

🔔 The sampling distribution of p-hat

The n behind a target standard error

Tancredi wants the standard error of a sample proportion to be 0.020 in a population where the proportion is 0.40. The sample size she needs, as a whole number, is:
  • a625
  • b1000
  • c12
  • d600
🔎 What it is really asking

Solve the standard-error formula for n instead of for the SE.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The sampling distribution of p-hat: rearranging for n.

🛠️ The procedure

Start from SE = √(p(1 − p) ⁄ n). Square both sides to kill the root, then rearrange: n = p(1 − p) ⁄ SE².

🧮 The working
p(1 − p) = 0.40 × 0.60 = 0.24

SE² = 0.020² = 0.0004  ← squaring the SE is the step everything turns on

n = 0.24 ⁄ 0.0004 = 600

Check it forwards: √(0.24 ⁄ 600) = √0.0004 = 0.020. ✓

Why the squaring matters so much. n sits under a square root in the forward formula, so coming back it has to be squared out. Skip it and you get 12 instead of 600 — wrong by a factor of fifty, and the kind of answer worth noticing is absurd before you check the algebra.

The scaling to carry into the exam: because SE² is on the bottom, halving the standard error costs four times the sample. Tancredi would need 2 400 people for an SE of 0.010.

And a sanity check: an SE of 0.02 is small, so n should be large. Any answer in the tens or hundreds is suspicious before you look at it twice.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.625 uses p* = 0.5 — the worst-case value for planning when nothing is known. Here the proportion is given as 0.40, so use it.
b.1000 is 0.40 ⁄ 0.0004 — p on top instead of p(1 − p). The numerator of the variance is always the product of the two.
c.12 is 0.24 ⁄ 0.020 — divided by the standard error rather than by its square. Squaring is what undoes the root.
🏷️ n = p(1 − p) ⁄ SE². Square the SE, every time.

Question 12

🧮 Margin of error and sample size

The margin a fixed budget buys

Rasmussen is told instead that her budget allows exactly 500 respondents, and this time she has no prior estimate of the proportion. The largest margin of error her 95% interval could end up with, to three decimal places, is:
  • a0.037
  • b0.044
  • c0.022
  • d0.088
🔎 What it is really asking

The planning formula run forwards — n is fixed, the margin is the unknown.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Sample size planning: the margin from a fixed n.

🛠️ The procedure

Same formula, different unknown: m = z* √(p*(1 − p*) ⁄ n). With no estimate, p* = 0.5 is the worst case, because p*(1 − p*) is largest there — so it gives the biggest the margin could be.

🧮 The working
p*(1 − p*) = 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25

SE = √(0.25 ⁄ 500) = √0.0005 = 0.022361

m = 1.96 × 0.022361 = 0.0438 → 0.044, about 4.4 percentage points

Why p* = 0.5 is the worst case. Run p*(1 − p*) along the range: 0.25 at p* = 0.5, 0.24 at 0.4, 0.21 at 0.3, 0.16 at 0.2, 0.09 at 0.1. It peaks dead centre, so using 0.5 guarantees the finished margin is no wider than what you quoted. Every other value would be a promise you might not keep.

The same formula, both directions. Given a margin, solve for n (Rasmussen’s 683). Given an n, solve for the margin (this 0.044). Exams ask it both ways round, so read which quantity the stem has fixed before you start.

And the trade-off in one line: 500 people buys ±4.4 points. Getting to ±2.2 points would take 2 000.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.037 uses z* = 1.645, the 90% multiplier. At 95% the multiplier is 1.96, and a lower confidence level would quietly promise more precision than was asked for.
c.0.022 is the standard error, before multiplying by 1.96. The margin is z* times the SE, and the question asked for the margin.
d.0.088 is 2 × 0.044, the full width of the interval. The margin is the distance from the centre to one end.
🏷️ Same formula both ways: m from n, or n from m. Read which one is fixed.

Question 13

⚔️ Two proportions

Reading a difference interval backwards

Weisskopf prints a 95% confidence interval for the difference between two proportions as −0.012 to 0.148, and reports nothing else. The margin of error behind it, to three decimal places, is:
  • a0.080
  • b0.068
  • c0.160
  • d0.148
🔎 What it is really asking

An interval is estimate ± margin, so both pieces can be read off the ends.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Two proportions: recovering the estimate and the margin.

🛠️ The procedure

Every interval is estimate ± margin. So the estimate is the midpoint of the two ends, and the margin is half the width.

🧮 The working
Half the width is the margin:
margin = (0.148 − (−0.012)) ⁄ 2 = 0.160 ⁄ 2 = 0.080

And while you are here, the midpoint is the estimate:
estimate = (−0.012 + 0.148) ⁄ 2 = 0.136 ⁄ 2 = 0.068

So Weisskopf observed a gap of 6.8 percentage points, give or take 8.0 — which is to say, 0.068 ± 0.080.

Watch the minus sign. Subtracting a negative lower end adds: 0.148 − (−0.012) = 0.160, not 0.136. Getting this wrong is the usual reason a recovered margin comes out as 0.068.

And the verdict the interval already contains: zero lies inside it, so a two-sided test at the 5% level would not reject equal proportions. The data are consistent with no difference — and also with a difference as large as 15 points, which is the honest way to describe a study this imprecise.

The habit: given any printed interval, write its midpoint and its half-width underneath it. Those two numbers are the whole result.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.0.068 is the point estimate — the midpoint rather than the half-width. It is the centre of the interval, not its reach.
c.0.160 is the full width of the interval, end to end. The margin is half of it, the distance from the centre to one end.
d.0.148 is the upper end, which measures from zero rather than from the estimate. A margin is always measured from the centre.
🏷️ Midpoint = the estimate. Half the width = the margin. Mind the minus sign.

Question 14

✅ Conditions and plus four

Which proportion the counts check uses

Jablonski tests whether a side effect occurs in more than 4% of patients. Among the 180 patients in her trial, 10 report it. On the counts condition for this test:
  • ait holds: n = 180 is far above 30
  • bit fails: 10 ⁄ 180 is below 0.10
  • cit fails: 180 × 0.04 is only 7.2
  • dit holds: 10 patients reported the effect
🔎 What it is really asking

For a test, which proportion do the expected counts come from?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conditions: p₀ for a test, p̂ for an interval.

🛠️ The procedure

A test works under H₀, so its counts are the ones H₀ expects: np₀ and n(1 − p₀), both at least 10. An interval assumes nothing, so it uses the observed np̂ and n(1 − p̂).

🧮 The working
The hypothesised value is p₀ = 0.04, so:

np₀ = 180 × 0.04 = 7.2
n(1 − p₀) = 180 × 0.96 = 172.8

7.2 is below 10, so the condition fails.

The trap, spelled out. The observed counts are 10 and 170, and 10 does clear the bar. If Jablonski wanted an interval for the rate, she would be fine. She wants a test, and a test asks how the statistic behaves when H₀ is true — a world in which only 7.2 cases are expected. That world is where the Normal approximation has to hold, and it does not.

The one-line rule for the exam: whichever p you put in the standard error is the same p you put in the counts check. Test → p₀ in both. Interval → p̂ in both. They never mix.

What to do instead: an exact binomial test, which needs no approximation at all.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a."n ≥ 30" is a rule of thumb for means. Proportions are checked on the two counts, and 180 patients is no help when the hypothesised rate is 4%.
b.Nothing in the condition compares a proportion with 0.10. The rule is about counts of at least 10, and 10 ⁄ 180 = 0.056 is a rate, not a count.
d.The observed 10 is the count an interval would check. A test checks the counts H₀ expects, and H₀ here expects only 7.2.
🏷️ Whichever p is in your SE is the p in your counts check. Test → p₀.

Question 15

⚖️ Test for a proportion

A one-sided decision that just misses

Before collecting any data, Eriksen predicted that adding a practical component to a training course would raise the proportion of trainees passing the final assessment above the historical 35%. Of the 240 trainees on the revised course, 96 passed. At the 5% level she should:
  • areject the claim — 40% is well above 35%
  • breject the claim — z = 1.62 is past 1.282
  • cnot reject — the counts are too small to test
  • dnot reject the claim — z = 1.62 is short of 1.645
🔎 What it is really asking

One tail, so the cut-off is not 1.96. Compute z and compare.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Test for one proportion: a one-sided decision.

🛠️ The procedure

The direction was fixed in advance, so all 5% sits in the upper tail and the cut-off is 1.645, not 1.96. The SE still comes from p₀.

🧮 The working
p̂ = 96 ⁄ 240 = 0.4000

SE = √(0.35 × 0.65 ⁄ 240) = √0.00094792 = 0.030788

z = (0.4000 − 0.3500) ⁄ 0.030788 = 0.05 ⁄ 0.030788 = 1.6240

The one-sided cut-off at 5% is 1.645. Since 1.624 < 1.645, Eriksen does not reject. The one-sided P is 0.0522, just above 0.05.

Check the condition while you are here: np₀ = 84 and n(1 − p₀) = 156, both well over 10. The test is legitimate; it simply did not reach the line.

And the temptation to name. One extra pass would have done it — 97 of 240 gives z = 1.76, just past the 1.645 cut-off. It is very tempting to call 0.052 "marginally significant" or to recruit a few more trainees and look again. Both convert a fixed 5% error rate into something larger and unstated, which is how a finding that does not exist gets published.

The honest write-up: the pass rate rose from 35% to 40%, z = 1.62, one-sided P = .052; the evidence falls just short at the 5% level, and the study was too small to settle it either way.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.40% against 35% is the gap the test is evaluating, and on 240 clients it does not reach the cut-off. "Well above" is an impression, not a decision rule.
b.1.282 is the cut-off that leaves 10% in one tail, not 5%. The one-sided 5% value is 1.645.
c.The counts are fine: np₀ = 84 and n(1 − p₀) = 156, both far above 10. The test is valid — it just misses.
🏷️ One-sided at 5% → compare with 1.645. Two-sided → 1.96.

Question 1

📏 Interval for a proportion

Working back from a printed interval to the sample

Kleinschmidt’s report prints a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of staff who use the staff canteen as 0.287 to 0.413. The appendix giving the sample has been lost. The sample was:
  • a220 staff, 88 of whom use it
  • b100 staff, 35 of whom use it
  • c220 staff, 77 of whom use it
  • d440 staff, 154 of whom use it
🔎 What it is really asking

Read p̂ and the margin off the printed ends, then see which sample delivers them.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Interval for one proportion: recovering the sample behind it.

🛠️ The procedure

Every interval is estimate ± margin. The midpoint of the printed ends is p̂ and half the width is the margin, so take those two numbers first and only then start testing candidates.

🧮 The working
Midpoint: (0.287 + 0.413) ⁄ 2 = 0.350, so p̂ = 0.35.

Half-width: (0.413 − 0.287) ⁄ 2 = 0.063, so the margin is 0.063.

The midpoint already kills one candidate: 88 ⁄ 220 = 0.40, which would centre the interval on 0.40 and not on 0.35.

Three candidates survive with p̂ = 0.35, so the margin has to choose between them. Since margin = 1.96 √(0.35 × 0.65 ⁄ n), only n is still free:

n = 100: 1.96 × √(0.2275 ⁄ 100) = 1.96 × 0.047697 = 0.0935 → 0.257 to 0.443
n = 220: 1.96 × √(0.2275 ⁄ 220) = 1.96 × 0.032157 = 0.0630 → 0.287 to 0.413 ✓
n = 440: 1.96 × √(0.2275 ⁄ 440) = 1.96 × 0.022739 = 0.0446 → 0.305 to 0.395

The habit: there is no need to test four candidates blind. The midpoint settles p̂ in one subtraction, and the width then leaves you at most one forward calculation to make.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.220 staff with 88 users gives p̂ = 88 ⁄ 220 = 0.40. That interval would be centred on 0.40, and the printed one is centred on 0.35.
b.100 staff with 35 users also gives p̂ = 0.35, but on a fifth of the data: its interval runs 0.257 to 0.443, far wider than the one printed.
d.440 staff with 154 users has the right p̂ of 0.35 and twice the data, so its interval is 0.305 to 0.395 — visibly narrower than the one printed.
🏷️ Midpoint gives p̂, half the width gives the margin. Then n is the only unknown.

Question 2

⚖️ Test for a proportion

Which proportion belongs in a test’s standard error

Opdahl tests whether her clinic closes referrals within a month at the regional rate of 40%: of 90 referrals, 27 were closed in time. She gets P = 0.053 and does not reject. Her co-author Verbeke, from the same 90 referrals, gets P = 0.038 and rejects. The defensible analysis is:
  • aOpdahl’s — a test builds its SE from p₀
  • bVerbeke’s — an SE must come from the data
  • cboth — either standard error is acceptable
  • dneither — 90 referrals are too few to test
🔎 What it is really asking

Two P-values from one data set. Which spread does a test use?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Test for one proportion: the standard error under H₀.

🛠️ The procedure

A test is carried out inside the null world: you assume p = p₀ for the length of the calculation, so the spread is √(p₀(1 − p₀) ⁄ n). The sample’s own p̂ belongs in the standard error of an interval, where nothing is being assumed.

🧮 The working
p̂ = 27 ⁄ 90 = 0.300, and p₀ = 0.40.

Opdahl’s route — the spread H₀ predicts:
SE = √(0.40 × 0.60 ⁄ 90) = √0.0026667 = 0.051640
z = (0.300 − 0.400) ⁄ 0.051640 = −1.94, two-sided P = 0.0528

Verbeke’s route — the spread the sample shows:
SE = √(0.300 × 0.700 ⁄ 90) = √0.0023333 = 0.048305
z = −0.100 ⁄ 0.048305 = −2.07, two-sided P = 0.0384

Verbeke’s SE is smaller because 0.30 sits further from a half than 0.40 does, and p(1 − p) is largest at a half. A smaller denominator makes a bigger statistic, and here the two land on opposite sides of 0.05 — so the choice decides the conclusion.

Why p₀ wins for a test. The P-value answers "how often would a sample of 90 land this far from 0.40 if the regional rate held here?" In that world the spread is the one 0.40 implies. Verbeke’s SE answers a different question and is the right one for an interval, where no value of p is being assumed.

Check the condition while you are here: under H₀ the expected counts are 90 × 0.40 = 36 and 90 × 0.60 = 54, both comfortably over 10, so the test is legitimate.

Worth knowing, because it looks like a contradiction: the 95% interval from Verbeke’s SE is 0.300 ± 1.96 × 0.048305 = 0.205 to 0.395, which excludes 0.40 while the test fails to reject it. For proportions the two procedures use different standard errors, so in a borderline case they can disagree. When they do, report both.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.The data’s own p̂ gives the standard error of an interval, where nothing is assumed. A test assumes H₀ while it computes, so it uses p₀.
c.They are not interchangeable here: 0.0528 and 0.0384 fall on opposite sides of 0.05, so one of them has to be the reported analysis.
d.The counts under H₀ are 36 and 54, both well over 10, so the test is perfectly legitimate. The dispute is about which standard error, not about whether to test.
🏷️ Test → p₀ in the standard error. Interval → p̂. Two questions, two spreads.

Question 3

🔔 The sampling distribution of p-hat

From the spread of p-hat back to a range of counts

Dobrescu knows that 30% of the children referred to her service have a speech difficulty, and she will see 400 referrals this year. The central 95% of the distribution of the number with a speech difficulty runs, to the nearest whole number, from:
  • a111 to 129
  • b105 to 135
  • c116 to 124
  • d102 to 138
🔎 What it is really asking

A range of counts — so work in proportions and convert back only at the end.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The sampling distribution of p-hat: turning its spread into counts.

🛠️ The procedure

p̂ is centred on p with spread √(p(1 − p) ⁄ n), and the central 95% of a Normal distribution is the centre ± 1.96 standard errors. Multiply both ends by n to turn proportions back into children.

🧮 The working
Centre p = 0.30. Spread:

SE = √(0.30 × 0.70 ⁄ 400) = √0.000525 = 0.022913

1.96 × 0.022913 = 0.044908, so p̂ runs from 0.255092 to 0.344908.

Back to counts, by multiplying both ends by 400:
400 × 0.255092 = 102.0   and   400 × 0.344908 = 138.0

So 95% of years like this produce between 102 and 138 children with a speech difficulty, around a centre of 120.

Check the condition first, as always: 400 × 0.30 = 120 and 400 × 0.70 = 280, both far above 10, so the Normal model is safe.

The habit: the formula only works in proportions, so convert the question into proportions, do the work there, and multiply by n on the last line. Converting in the middle is where the 4.49 percentage points turn into 4.49 children.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.111 to 129 is the centre ± one standard error, which covers about 68% of years rather than 95%. The 1.96 was never applied.
b.105 to 135 uses z* = 1.645, the 90% multiplier. The question asked for the central 95%, where the multiplier is 1.96.
c.116 to 124 is 120 ± 4.49, reading the margin of 4.49 percentage points as 4.49 children. The margin has to be multiplied by n as well.
🏷️ Do the work in proportions. Multiply by n on the last line only.

Question 4

✅ Conditions and plus four

The counts rule when it is the failures that are scarce

Fimreite asks 180 randomly chosen hospital staff whether they have had the seasonal vaccination, and all but seven say they have. The obstacle to the ordinary large-sample interval here is:
  • athe margin of error will exceed 0.05
  • bonly seven of the 180 said otherwise
  • ca sample of 180 is too small to use it
  • dthe 10% condition fails for 180 staff
🔎 What it is really asking

Count both categories. The stem only gives you one of them directly.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conditions: the counts rule, read from the smaller category.

🛠️ The procedure

The ordinary interval needs at least 10 successes and at least 10 failures. The stem will usually hand you the big number, so your first line of working is the subtraction that produces the small one.

🧮 The working
Vaccinated: 180 − 7 = 173. Not vaccinated: 7.

173 clears 10 easily. Seven does not, so the condition fails.

And the arithmetic still runs, which is the danger. p̂ = 173 ⁄ 180 = 0.9611, SE = 0.014410, margin = 0.0282, giving 0.933 to 0.989 — a tidy-looking interval you are not entitled to.

Why not. p̂ sits very close to the wall at 1. The sampling distribution of a proportion that near a boundary is skewed rather than Normal, so a symmetric ± margin is the wrong shape for it, whichever way the ends happen to fall.

The repair: plus four. Add two of each category — p̃ = 175 ⁄ 184 = 0.9511, with n + 4 = 184 under the root as well — giving 0.920 to 0.982. Pulled away from the wall, and wider, which is the honest direction.

The habit: the rule counts categories, never people. A sample of 180 can fail it and a sample of 25 split evenly can pass it.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The margin is only 0.028, and in any case no condition sets a limit on how wide a margin may be. A wide interval is imprecise, not invalid.
c.Size is not the rule. 180 staff split anywhere near evenly would clear both counts with room to spare; it is the lopsided split that fails.
d.The 10% condition is about what share of the population was sampled, and nothing here suggests 180 is a large slice of a hospital’s staff.
🏷️ Ten successes AND ten failures. Compute n − X on your first line.

Question 5

⚔️ Two proportions

What sample size does to a two-proportion test

Jaskiewicz compares two recruitment leaflets; her counts are below. Her two-sided test of the two application rates gives P = 0.36. Of the changes below, the one that would have made the same two rates significant at the 5% level is:
Applications after two recruitment leaflets · 80 recipients
LeafletAppliedDid not applyTotal
Leaflet A182240
Leaflet B142640
Total324880
  • a80 recipients in each group
  • ba one-sided test in the predicted direction
  • c360 recipients in each group
  • d160 recipients in each group
🔎 What it is really asking

The gap stays at 10 points whatever she does. What has to shrink?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Two proportions: the sample size behind a test.

🛠️ The procedure

The gap p̂₁ − p̂₂ does not move when n changes; the standard error does, and n sits under a square root inside it. Four times the data buys twice the statistic, not four times.

🧮 The working
Her rates: 18 ⁄ 40 = 0.45 and 14 ⁄ 40 = 0.35, a gap of 0.10. Pooled p̂ = 32 ⁄ 80 = 0.40.

As it stands: SE = √(0.40 × 0.60 × (1⁄40 + 1⁄40)) = √0.012 = 0.1095, z = 0.10 ⁄ 0.1095 = 0.91, P = 0.36.

She needs z past 1.96, so the statistic has to grow by a factor of 1.96 ⁄ 0.91 = 2.15. Because the statistic grows with √n, the sample has to grow by 2.15² ≈ 4.6 — roughly 185 per group just to reach the line.

Check the candidates at the same two rates:
 80 per group: SE = 0.0775, z = 1.29, P = 0.197
160 per group: SE = 0.0548, z = 1.83, P = 0.068 — close, and still short
360 per group: SE = 0.0365, z = 2.74, P = 0.006 ✓

And the change that is not a change. One-sided, at the 40 she actually has, the P-value is 0.181 — nowhere near 0.05. Even when halving a tail would help, a direction chosen after seeing which way the data fell is not a repair; it is a 10% test reported as a 5% one.

The habit: when a result just misses, work out the factor the statistic needs and square it. That is the sample size question answered in one line.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.80 per group doubles the data, which multiplies the statistic by √2 to 1.29 and leaves P at 0.197. Doubling n is the smallest of the three changes.
b.One-sided at her actual 40 per group gives P = 0.181, still far from 0.05 — and a tail chosen after seeing the data would not have been hers to halve.
d.160 per group quadruples the data and doubles the statistic to 1.83, giving P = 0.068. A near miss is still a miss, and 185 per group is the break-even point.
🏷️ Gap fixed, SE shrinking with √n. Need z × k? Multiply n by k².

Question 6

📏 Interval for a proportion

Using an interval to answer a threshold question

Linnankoski surveys 320 parents about a later school start, and three in every eight of them support it. The council will adopt the change only if more than 40% of parents support it. On that criterion her 95% interval:
  • acannot settle it — 0.40 falls inside 0.322 to 0.428
  • bsettles it against — p̂ = 0.375 is below 0.40
  • csettles it for — the interval reaches above 0.40
  • dcannot settle it — 320 parents are too few to ask
🔎 What it is really asking

Turn the wording into a count, build the interval, then locate the council’s 40%.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Interval for one proportion: deciding a threshold question.

🛠️ The procedure

Build p̂ ± 1.96 √(p̂(1 − p̂) ⁄ n), then ask where the threshold sits. A threshold inside the interval is one the data are compatible with meeting and with missing — so it is not settled.

🧮 The working
First the count the stem buried: three in every eight of 320 = 120 parents.

p̂ = 120 ⁄ 320 = 0.375

SE = √(0.375 × 0.625 ⁄ 320) = √0.00073242 = 0.027063

margin = 1.96 × 0.027063 = 0.053043

0.375 ± 0.0530 = 0.322 to 0.428

The council’s 0.40 lies inside that. Her 320 parents are consistent with support running at 32% — comfortably short — and with it running at 42.8% — comfortably past. The survey does not decide the question.

Why the point estimate is not enough. 0.375 is below 0.40, which makes the second option tempting, but a single number carries no statement about how far it could be from the truth. The margin is 5.3 points and the shortfall is 2.5 — smaller than her own uncertainty.

What would settle it: a margin small enough that 0.40 falls outside. Getting to ±0.02 at this p̂ needs (1.96 ⁄ 0.02)² × 0.234375 = 2,251 parents — seven times the survey she has.

The habit: when a stem names a threshold, the answer is almost never the point estimate. Build the interval and say which side of it the threshold is on.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.p̂ = 0.375 is below 0.40 by 2.5 points, which is less than the interval’s own margin of 5.3 points. A point estimate on its own settles nothing.
c.The interval reaching above 0.40 is not evidence that the threshold is met either. Both readings fail for the same reason: 0.40 is inside.
d.320 parents are plenty to survey — the counts are 120 and 200. The sample is valid; it is simply not precise enough for this particular threshold.
🏷️ Threshold inside the interval → the data cannot decide. Say so plainly.

Question 7

⚖️ Test for a proportion

Matching a confidence level to a P-value

Montagne tests H₀: p = 0.50 on 400 patients, 176 of whom recovered, and reports a two-sided P = 0.016. Her 99% confidence interval for p therefore:
  • acannot be decided until it is computed in full
  • bcontains 0.50 — 0.016 is above 0.01
  • cexcludes 0.50 — 0.016 is below 0.05
  • dexcludes 0.50, as any interval from these data does
🔎 What it is really asking

A P-value settles one interval: the one whose level matches its α.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Test and interval: matching the levels.

🛠️ The procedure

A two-sided test at α and a (1 − α) interval are the same arithmetic read from opposite ends. So compare P with 0.05 to settle the 95% interval and with 0.01 to settle the 99% one.

🧮 The working
Confirm the P-value first. p̂ = 176 ⁄ 400 = 0.44, and under H₀

SE = √(0.50 × 0.50 ⁄ 400) = 0.025,  z = (0.44 − 0.50) ⁄ 0.025 = −2.40, two-sided P = 0.0164 ✓

Now match the levels. 0.0164 is below 0.05, so a 5% test rejects and the 95% interval excludes 0.50. But 0.0164 is above 0.01, so a 1% test does not reject and the 99% interval contains 0.50.

Build them and see: SE from p̂ = √(0.44 × 0.56 ⁄ 400) = 0.024819.
95%: 0.44 ± 1.96 × 0.024819 = 0.391 to 0.489 — 0.50 outside
99%: 0.44 ± 2.576 × 0.024819 = 0.376 to 0.504 — 0.50 inside

So "significant" is a statement about a level. The same data exclude 0.50 at 95% and include it at 99%. Raise the confidence far enough and any value gets back in.

One caveat specific to proportions: the test’s standard error uses p₀ and the interval’s uses p̂, so the two agree very closely rather than exactly. Here both readings land the same way, as they usually do.

Say it to a friend: "a 99% interval is the partner of a 1% test — so check the P-value against 0.01, not against 0.05."
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Everything needed is already in the stem: a two-sided P-value settles the matching interval without any further arithmetic.
c.0.05 is the partner of the 95% interval, which does exclude 0.50. The question asked about the 99% one, whose partner is 0.01.
d.The 95% interval does exclude 0.50 and the 99% interval contains it, so "any interval from these data" is false in both directions.
🏷️ 99% interval ↔ 1% test. Compare P with 0.01, not with 0.05.

Question 8

🧮 Margin of error and sample size

Checking a planned sample against a budget

Nijboer needs a 95% margin of error no wider than 4 percentage points, and a pilot puts the proportion near 0.35. Her budget covers 500 respondents. Whether that is enough:
  • ano — she needs 2,401 respondents
  • byes — 500 gives a 4.2-point margin
  • cyes — 500 clears the 4-point target
  • dno — she needs 547 respondents
🔎 What it is really asking

Work out the n the specification demands, then compare it with what she can afford.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Margin of error and sample size: the planning figure as an input.

🛠️ The procedure

n = (z* ⁄ m)² × p*(1 − p*), rounded up. The pilot supplies p*; the fallback of 0.5 is for when there is no estimate at all.

🧮 The working
z* = 1.96, m = 0.04, p* = 0.35.

(1.96 ⁄ 0.04)² = 49² = 2401

p*(1 − p*) = 0.35 × 0.65 = 0.2275

n = 2401 × 0.2275 = 546.2 → round up to 547

Why up, in one line each way:
at n = 547, margin = 1.96 √(0.2275 ⁄ 547) = 0.03997 ✓ inside 0.04
at n = 546, margin = 1.96 √(0.2275 ⁄ 546) = 0.04001 ✗ outside 0.04

Now the question actually asked. Her budget is 500, and 500 < 547, so it is not enough. Spelled out: at n = 500 the margin is 1.96 √(0.2275 ⁄ 500) = 0.0418, which is 4.2 percentage points — wider than the 4.0 she specified.

The step that is easy to skip. The computed 547 is not the answer; it is the input to the answer. Read the last sentence of the stem again before you choose an option — the exam likes to put the intermediate figure on the list.

And what her options now are: find 47 more respondents, accept a margin of 4.2 points and say so, or drop to 90% confidence, where 500 respondents give 1.645 √(0.2275 ⁄ 500) = 0.035, that is 3.5 points.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.2,401 is (z* ⁄ m)² with the p*(1 − p*) factor never applied — the formula stopped one multiplication early.
b.The 4.2 points is correctly computed and 4.2 is wider than the 4.0 she specified, so it is the reason the answer is no.
c.500 respondents give a margin of 4.2 points, which misses the target rather than clearing it. She needs 547.
🏷️ Round the planning n up — then answer the question the stem actually asked.

Question 9

✅ Conditions and plus four

Diagnosing an impossible interval

Zandvliet records a serious reaction in 3 of 75 patients and reports a 95% confidence interval of −0.004 to 0.084. The feature of her sample that produced a negative lower end is:
  • aonly three patients had a reaction
  • bthe 75 patients were not randomly chosen
  • cshe used z* = 1.96 rather than 2.576
  • dthe 75 are more than a tenth of the ward
🔎 What it is really asking

A proportion cannot be negative. What let the formula produce one?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conditions: what the counts rule is protecting you from.

🛠️ The procedure

The ordinary interval is p̂ ± a symmetric margin, which assumes the sampling distribution of p̂ is Normal. Close to the wall at 0 that distribution is skewed, and a symmetric margin can reach past 0 into values a proportion cannot take.

🧮 The working
The arithmetic is hers and it is correct:

p̂ = 3 ⁄ 75 = 0.04,  SE = √(0.04 × 0.96 ⁄ 75) = 0.022627,
margin = 1.96 × 0.022627 = 0.044349  →  −0.004 to 0.084

Now the counts: 3 reactions and 72 non-reactions. Three is below ten, so the condition fails — and the impossible lower end is that failure announcing itself out loud. With p̂ this close to zero, a margin as wide as 0.044 has further to travel downward than there is room for.

The repair: plus four. p̃ = (3 + 2) ⁄ (75 + 4) = 5 ⁄ 79 = 0.0633, with n + 4 = 79 under the root too, giving 0.010 to 0.117. Both ends possible, and wider, because her data really are compatible with a rate several times the 4% she observed.

Why a bigger z* makes it worse, not better: at 99% the margin becomes 2.576 × 0.022627 = 0.0583, so the interval runs −0.018 to 0.098. More confidence pushes the lower end further below zero.

The habit: glance at both ends of every interval you compute for a proportion. An end below 0 or above 1 means the method was not licensed here, not that the population is unusual.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.A non-random sample would give an interval for the wrong population, and it would still land between 0 and 1. Bias does not make an end impossible.
c.A larger z* widens the interval, so at 99% the lower end falls to −0.018. The multiplier is making the symptom worse, not causing it.
d.Breaking the 10% condition makes an interval too cautious — wider than it needs to be. It cannot push an end past zero.
🏷️ An impossible end is the counts condition announcing itself.

Question 10

⚔️ Two proportions

When two samples are not independent

Pirovano has the four comparisons of two proportions below to analyse. The one for which the two-sample z procedure is not valid is:
  • a200 volunteers split at random into two arms
  • b140 men and 160 women from one register
  • c90 sibling pairs, one sibling in each condition
  • dtwo clinics, 120 patients surveyed at each
🔎 What it is really asking

The two-sample standard error adds two variances. When is that addition earned?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Two proportions: the independence condition.

🛠️ The procedure

The procedure uses SE = √(var₁ + var₂), and variances add like that only when the two estimates wobble independently. Observations linked in pairs — matched, paired, or the same people twice — break the addition.

🧮 The working
Go through them asking one question: could a result in the first group tell you anything about the matching result in the second?

90 sibling pairs. Yes. The two children in a pair share a home, parents and schooling, so their outcomes move together. The two proportions are not independent, the addition of variances is not earned, and √(var₁ + var₂) overstates how much the difference wobbles — throwing away the precision the pairing was meant to buy. The analysis belongs on the pairs: classify each pair by which sibling had the outcome, and base the test on the pairs where the two differ.

Two clinics. No link — two separate sets of patients, so the procedure is valid as a test. The clinics differ in staff and catchment as well as in whatever is being compared, so a causal reading is off the table. That is a separate objection, and not what the question asked.

200 volunteers randomised. Independent by construction, and the textbook case.

140 men and 160 women. Two disjoint sets of people, so independent. Unequal group sizes are fine — they only change the standard error.

The habit: count the people, not the columns, and ask whether any observation on one side has a partner on the other. Matched data in two columns look exactly like two independent samples until you ask.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Splitting 200 volunteers at random is the textbook two-sample design: the two arms are independent by the way they were formed.
b.140 men and 160 women are disjoint sets of people, so independent. Unequal group sizes only change the standard error, not its validity.
d.Two clinics give two separate sets of patients, so the test is valid. What they do not give is a causal reading, which is a different objection altogether.
🏷️ Matched or paired observations are not two independent samples. Count the people.

Question 11

📏 Interval for a proportion

Reading a sample size off the width of an interval

Rantala and Nordhagen survey the same population and report the 95% intervals below. Neither prints a sample size. It follows that:
Two 95% intervals for the same proportion · neither sample size reported
SurveySample proportion95% interval
Rantala0.460.411 to 0.509
Nordhagen0.460.380 to 0.540
  • aNordhagen surveyed more people than Rantala
  • bNordhagen must have used a higher confidence level
  • cRantala’s sample proportion was nearer to a half
  • dRantala surveyed more people than Nordhagen
🔎 What it is really asking

Same centre, same confidence level. What is left that can change the width?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Interval for one proportion: what sets its width.

🛠️ The procedure

The width of an interval is 2 × z* × √(p̂(1 − p̂) ⁄ n). Fix the confidence level and fix p̂, and n is the only ingredient left — and a bigger n makes a narrower interval.

🧮 The working
Read both intervals properly first.

Rantala:   midpoint 0.46, half-width (0.509 − 0.411) ⁄ 2 = 0.049
Nordhagen: midpoint 0.46, half-width (0.540 − 0.380) ⁄ 2 = 0.080

Same midpoint, as the table says, and the same 95% level — so z* and p̂ are identical in the two calculations. The only ingredient left is n, and Rantala’s interval is the narrower, so Rantala’s sample is the larger.

How much larger, since the width can be read backwards: the margins stand in the ratio 0.080 ⁄ 0.049 = 1.63, and margins go as 1 ⁄ √n, so the samples stand in the ratio 1.63² ≈ 2.7 the other way round.

Recover them outright if you like. SE = margin ⁄ 1.96, then n = p̂(1 − p̂) ⁄ SE²:
Rantala:   SE = 0.049 ⁄ 1.96 = 0.0250, n = 0.2484 ⁄ 0.000625 = 397
Nordhagen: SE = 0.080 ⁄ 1.96 = 0.0408, n = 0.2484 ⁄ 0.001666 = 149

The real samples were 400 and 150. The recovery lands a per cent out because the printed ends are rounded to three decimals, which is as close as a reader can get.

The habit: a printed interval carries its own design inside it. Midpoint → p̂, half-width → margin, and with the level known the margin gives you n.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Nordhagen has the wider interval, which goes with the smaller sample. More data buys precision, so it narrows an interval.
b.The table says both intervals are 95% ones. A higher level would widen Nordhagen’s interval, but it is not what happened here.
c.The table gives both researchers the same sample proportion of 0.46. In any case a p̂ nearer a half makes an interval wider, not narrower.
🏷️ Same level, same p̂ → the narrower interval came from the bigger sample.

Question 12

🔔 The sampling distribution of p-hat

Recovering p from the spread of p-hat

Schellekens draws many random batches of 150 referrals and finds that the proportion self-referred varies from batch to batch with a standard deviation of 0.040. The population proportion is closest to:
  • a0.50 — the only p that fits
  • b0.40 — or equally 0.60
  • c0.24 — the value of p(1 − p)
  • d0.04 — the spread itself
🔎 What it is really asking

You are given the spread of p̂ and asked for its centre — so run the formula backwards.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The sampling distribution of p-hat: working back to p.

🛠️ The procedure

The batch-to-batch spread of p̂ is √(p(1 − p) ⁄ n). Square it to kill the root and multiply by n, and what is left is p(1 − p) — then find the p that gives that product.

🧮 The working
Square the spread: 0.040² = 0.0016.

Multiply by n: 0.0016 × 150 = 0.24, and that is p(1 − p).

Solve it: p − p² = 0.24, so p² − p + 0.24 = 0 and
p = (1 ± √(1 − 0.96)) ⁄ 2 = (1 ± 0.2) ⁄ 2 = 0.40 or 0.60

Check forwards: √(0.40 × 0.60 ⁄ 150) = √0.0016 = 0.040 ✓ — and 0.60 gives exactly the same, because 0.6 × 0.4 is the same product.

Two answers is the result, not a mistake. p(1 − p) is symmetric about a half, so a spread on its own cannot tell 0.40 from 0.60. Only the centre of her batches could, and the question did not give it.

Why 0.50 is tempting: at p = 0.50 the spread would be √(0.25 ⁄ 150) = 0.0408, which rounds to 0.041 — close to 0.040 without being it. p(1 − p) changes slowly near a half, which is exactly why 0.5 is the safe planning value elsewhere.

The habit: the standard-error formula has four symbols in it, SE, p, n and the root. Three given, solve for the fourth — and square the SE whenever you are coming backwards.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.50 would give a spread of 0.0408, not 0.040 — and no p fits uniquely, since 0.40 and 0.60 both give exactly 0.040.
c.0.24 is p(1 − p), the product you reach after squaring and multiplying by n. One step short: it still has to be turned into p.
d.0.04 reads the spread of p̂ as the proportion itself. A population proportion of 0.04 would give a batch-to-batch spread of √(0.0384 ⁄ 150) = 0.016.
🏷️ Square the spread, multiply by n, solve p(1 − p). Two answers, either side of a half.

Question 1

▦ Reading a two-way table

A conditional percentage from a two-way table

Clinical psychologist Veenstra assigns 200 adults on a waiting list to either group or individual coaching and records who finishes the 8-week programme. Of the clients who received individual coaching, the percentage who completed the programme is:
Completion of an 8-week online wellbeing programme · 200 adults
Coaching formatCompletedDropped outTotal
Group3862100
Individual5743100
Total95105200
  • a60.0%
  • b43%
  • c57%
  • d28.5%
🔎 What it is really asking

Of the individual-coaching clients only — so divide by that row’s total.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading a two-way table: a conditional (row) percentage.

🛠️ The procedure

A conditional percentage needs you to decide what the "of" is. "Of the individual-coaching clients" means the denominator is that row’s total, not the whole table and not the column.

🧮 The working
The individual-coaching row is 57 completed and 43 dropped out, total 100.

57 ⁄ 100 = 57%

The comparison that matters is with the other row: 38 ⁄ 100 = 38% in group coaching. A gap of 19 percentage points.

The habit: underline the words after "of" in the stem, then find that total in the table before you divide anything.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.60.0% is 57 ⁄ 95, the share of all completers who had individual coaching. That is the column percentage, and it answers a different question.
b.43% is the percentage of that row who dropped out. It is the right denominator and the wrong column.
d.28.5% is 57 ⁄ 200 — the 57 clients as a share of everybody, which mixes the two formats back together.
🏷️ Find the words after “of”. That total is your denominator.

Question 2

▦ Reading a two-way table

A marginal proportion

In Veenstra’s study, the proportion of all 200 clients who dropped out, to three decimal places, is:
Completion of an 8-week online wellbeing programme · 200 adults
Coaching formatCompletedDropped outTotal
Group3862100
Individual5743100
Total95105200
  • a0.525
  • b0.475
  • c0.620
  • d0.430
🔎 What it is really asking

One number for the whole table — a margin, not a comparison.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading a two-way table: the marginal distribution.

🛠️ The procedure

A marginal proportion ignores the other variable completely: take the column total and divide by N.

🧮 The working
The "dropped out" column totals 62 + 43 = 105.

105 ⁄ 200 = 0.525

Check it against its partner: 95 ⁄ 200 = 0.475, and 0.525 + 0.475 = 1.000.

What a margin cannot do: it describes the 200 clients as one pool, so it tells you nothing at all about whether format matters. For that you need the two row percentages, 62% against 43%.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.0.475 is the proportion who completed, 95 ⁄ 200 — the other margin.
c.0.620 is the dropout rate in group coaching only, 62 ⁄ 100. That is a conditional proportion, not a marginal one.
d.0.430 is the dropout rate in individual coaching only, 43 ⁄ 100.
🏷️ Marginal = one column total over N. It cannot show an association.

Question 3

🎯 Expected counts

An expected count in a 2 × 2 table

Veenstra now tests whether format and completion are related. The expected count for group-coaching clients who completed the programme is:
Completion of an 8-week online wellbeing programme · 200 adults
Coaching formatCompletedDropped outTotal
Group3862100
Individual5743100
Total95105200
  • a38
  • b52.5
  • c50
  • d47.5
🔎 What it is really asking

Row total times column total over N — not the count that is sitting there.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Expected counts: one cell of a two-way table.

🛠️ The procedure

expected = (row total × column total) ⁄ N. Nothing else enters it, and you never round it.

🧮 The working
That cell’s row total is 100 (all group-coaching clients) and its column total is 95 (all completers). N = 200.

expected = (100 × 95) ⁄ 200 = 9500 ⁄ 200 = 47.5

Do the whole table once and it becomes obvious what the formula is doing:
Expected counts if format and completion were unrelated
Coaching formatCompletedDropped outTotal
Group47.552.5100
Individual47.552.5100
Total95105200
Both rows get the same expected counts here, because the two rows have the same total of 100. The expected table always keeps the real margins — 47.5 + 47.5 = 95, 52.5 + 52.5 = 105.

Read what the 47.5 means: if format made no difference at all, the overall completion rate of 47.5% would apply to both formats. The observed 38 is 9.5 below that, and the observed 57 is 9.5 above it.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.38 is the observed count in that cell. A cell’s own observed count never appears in its expected count — that is the whole point of the comparison.
b.52.5 is the expected count for the cell next door, group coaching and dropped out. Right row, wrong column total.
c.50 is half of the 100 group-coaching clients. That would be the expected count only if completion ran at exactly 50%, and here it runs at 47.5%.
🏷️ Expected = row × column ⁄ N. Margins only, never rounded.

Every row of the expected table splits in the same 120 : 130 ratio as the whole sample — 48% late, 52% not — because that is exactly what "no association" means.

Compare it with the observed table and the cyclists stand out: 60 observed against 48.0 expected, twelve more late pupils than no-association would predict.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.33.6 is the expected count for bus users who were late, (70 × 120) ⁄ 250. Right column, wrong row.
c.52.0 is the expected count for cyclists who were never late. Right row, wrong column.
d.60.0 is the observed count for cyclists who were late. That is the number you will compare 48.0 against, not the expected count itself.
🏷️ Row × column ⁄ N, whatever the size of the table.

Question 5

🎯 Expected counts

What expected counts are built from

In any chi-square test of a two-way table, the expected counts are worked out:
  • aby splitting N equally between the cells
  • bfrom the row and column totals, assuming the association found
  • cfrom the row and column totals, assuming no association
  • dfrom each cell’s own observed count and its row total
🔎 What it is really asking

Which numbers go in, and under which hypothesis.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Expected counts: what they represent.

🛠️ The procedure

The expected counts are the table you would see if the null hypothesis were true — no association — while the row and column totals stayed exactly as observed.

🧮 The working
Two things go into every expected count and nothing else does: the margins, and H₀.

The margins are kept because they are not what is in question. Veenstra assigned 100 clients to each format, and 95 of the 200 completed; those facts are not in dispute. What is in dispute is whether the 95 completers are spread evenly across the two formats.

H₀ supplies the spreading rule: apply the overall column split to every row. That is why the formula is row × column ⁄ N and why each expected row ends up in the same ratio as the table as a whole.

Why this matters for the test: χ² measures how far the observed table has drifted from a table built on H₀. If the expected counts were built from the association you found, there would be nothing left to measure.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Splitting N equally between the cells ignores the margins. It would put 50 in each of Veenstra’s four cells, when 105 of her 200 clients dropped out.
b.Assuming the association found is backwards. Expected counts describe the world under H₀; the test asks how far the data are from that world.
d.A cell’s own observed count is deliberately excluded. If it went in, the expected count would chase the observed one and the difference would shrink to nothing.
🏷️ Expected counts = your real margins, plus H₀’s spreading rule.

Question 6

🧮 The statistic and its df

One cell’s contribution to chi-square

In Veenstra’s table the observed count for group coaching and completion is 38 and the expected count is 47.5. That cell’s contribution to the chi-square statistic, to two decimal places, is:
Completion of an 8-week online wellbeing programme · 200 adults
Coaching formatCompletedDropped outTotal
Group3862100
Individual5743100
Total95105200
  • a1.90
  • b1.72
  • c9.50
  • d0.20
🔎 What it is really asking

One term of the sum, not the whole statistic.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The chi-square statistic: a single cell’s term.

🛠️ The procedure

Each cell contributes (O − E)² ⁄ E. Square the difference before dividing, and divide by the expected count, never the observed one.

🧮 The working
O − E = 38 − 47.5 = −9.5

(O − E)² = (−9.5)² = 90.25

90.25 ⁄ 47.5 = 1.90

The squaring is what makes the sign stop mattering: the cell below it is 9.5 above its expected count and contributes the same 1.90.

The four contributions in full: 1.90, 1.72, 1.90, 1.72 — adding to 7.24, which is χ². The two dropout cells contribute less because they are divided by a larger expected count of 52.5.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.1.72 is the contribution of the two dropout cells, 90.25 ⁄ 52.5. Same difference of 9.5, bigger expected count underneath.
c.9.50 is |O − E| itself, before squaring and dividing. It is the raw gap, not a contribution.
d.0.20 is 9.5 ⁄ 47.5 — the gap divided by E but never squared. Squaring is what stops the positive and negative gaps cancelling out.
🏷️ (O − E)² ⁄ E. Square first, and always divide by E.

Question 7

🧮 The statistic and its df

Degrees of freedom for a two-way table

The degrees of freedom for Okonkwo’s chi-square test of travel against lateness are:
Lateness over one term by how pupils travel to school · 250 pupils
How they travelLate at least onceNever lateTotal
Walk305080
Cycle6040100
Bus304070
Total120130250
  • a249
  • b2
  • c1
  • d5
🔎 What it is really asking

Count rows and columns of the table, and nothing else.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The chi-square statistic: degrees of freedom for a two-way table.

🛠️ The procedure

df = (r − 1)(c − 1), where r and c are the numbers of rows and columns of categories. The sample size never enters it.

🧮 The working
The table has 3 travel categories and 2 lateness categories — the Total row and column are not categories.

df = (3 − 1)(2 − 1) = 2 × 1 = 2

What the 2 counts: once you know the margins, you can fill in two cells freely and the other four are then forced. Try it — fix the walk/late and cycle/late cells and every remaining cell follows from the totals.

Why it matters: df picks the critical value. On 2 df the 5% cut-off is 5.991; on 1 df it would be 3.841 and on 5 df 11.070. Getting df wrong moves the goalposts, not just the label.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.249 is N − 1. Chi-square df never involve the sample size — a 3 × 2 table has 2 df whether 250 pupils or 25,000 are in it.
c.1 is the df for a 2 × 2 table. It would be right for Veenstra’s table and not for this one.
d.5 is the number of cells minus one, 6 − 1. That is the goodness-of-fit rule applied to a two-way table, where it does not belong.
🏷️ (rows − 1)(columns − 1). Never the cells, never N.

Question 8

🧮 The statistic and its df

Computing chi-square for a 2 × 2 table

For Veenstra’s 2 × 2 table, the value of the chi-square statistic, to two decimal places, is:
Completion of an 8-week online wellbeing programme · 200 adults
Coaching formatCompletedDropped outTotal
Group3862100
Individual5743100
Total95105200
  • a3.84
  • b1.90
  • c3.62
  • d7.24
🔎 What it is really asking

Add a (O − E)² ⁄ E term for every cell — all four of them.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The chi-square statistic: computing it from a full table.

🛠️ The procedure

χ² = Σ (O − E)² ⁄ E, summed over every cell. Get the expected table first, then work across it cell by cell.

🧮 The working
Expected counts: 47.5 and 52.5 in each row, since both rows total 100 and the columns split 95 : 105.

Completed, group:      (38 − 47.5)² ⁄ 47.5 = 90.25 ⁄ 47.5 = 1.900
Dropped out, group:    (62 − 52.5)² ⁄ 52.5 = 90.25 ⁄ 52.5 = 1.719
Completed, individual: (57 − 47.5)² ⁄ 47.5 = 90.25 ⁄ 47.5 = 1.900
Dropped out, individ.: (43 − 52.5)² ⁄ 52.5 = 90.25 ⁄ 52.5 = 1.719

χ² = 1.900 + 1.719 + 1.900 + 1.719 = 7.238, so 7.24.

Then the decision: on 1 df the 5% critical value is 3.841 and the 1% value is 6.635. 7.24 is past both, and the exact P-value is .007. Format and completion are associated.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.3.84 is the critical value on 1 df at α = .05, not a statistic computed from these data. It is the number you compare 7.24 against.
b.1.90 is one cell’s contribution. There are four cells and all four count.
c.3.62 is what you get by adding one row only, 1.900 + 1.719. Every cell in the table contributes, not just the row you are looking at.
🏷️ Every cell contributes. Four cells in a 2 × 2, so four terms.

Question 9

🥧 Goodness of fit

Expected counts for a goodness-of-fit test

A university states that its intake splits 50% science, 30% humanities and 20% arts. Student-affairs researcher Hallström takes one year’s 300 students and counts 138, 102 and 60. The expected counts under the university’s claim are:
A university’s claimed intake split against one year’s 300 students
Programme trackShare the university claimsStudents observed
Science50%138
Humanities30%102
Arts20%60
Total100%300
  • a150, 90 and 60
  • b100, 100 and 100
  • c138, 102 and 60
  • d50, 30 and 20
🔎 What it is really asking

Turn the claimed percentages into counts out of 300.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Goodness of fit: expected counts from a claimed distribution.

🛠️ The procedure

For goodness of fit, expected = n × the proportion the claim gives that category. The claim supplies the proportions; your sample supplies only n.

🧮 The working
n = 300, and the claim gives .50, .30 and .20.

Science:    300 × .50 = 150
Humanities: 300 × .30 = 90
Arts:       300 × .20 = 60

Check: 150 + 90 + 60 = 300, which the expected counts must always do.

How this differs from a two-way table: there the expected counts came out of the margins, because the null hypothesis only said "no association". Here H₀ names the actual proportions, so they come straight out of the claim.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.100, 100 and 100 would be the expected counts if the claim were that the three tracks are equally popular. This claim says 50 ⁄ 30 ⁄ 20.
c.138, 102 and 60 are the observed counts. Setting expected equal to observed would make χ² zero by construction.
d.50, 30 and 20 are the claimed percentages, not counts. They add to 100, not to the 300 students in the sample.
🏷️ Goodness of fit: expected = n × the claimed proportion.

Question 10

🥧 Goodness of fit

Computing a goodness-of-fit chi-square

Examinations officer Maassen offers four exam slots and asks 200 students which they prefer, expecting the four to be equally popular. The counts are 42, 58, 51 and 49. The value of the chi-square statistic, to two decimal places, is:
Preferred exam slot · 200 students, four slots offered
Exam slotMorningMiddayAfternoonEveningTotal
Students choosing it42585149200
  • a1.28
  • b0.01
  • c2.60
  • d7.81
🔎 What it is really asking

The same Σ (O − E)² ⁄ E, with one term per category.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Goodness of fit: computing the statistic.

🛠️ The procedure

Expected counts first — n ⁄ k when the claim is "equally popular" — then Σ (O − E)² ⁄ E across the categories.

🧮 The working
Equally popular over four slots means expected = 200 ⁄ 4 = 50 for each.

Morning:   (42 − 50)² ⁄ 50 = 64 ⁄ 50 = 1.28
Midday:    (58 − 50)² ⁄ 50 = 64 ⁄ 50 = 1.28
Afternoon: (51 − 50)² ⁄ 50 =  1 ⁄ 50 = 0.02
Evening:   (49 − 50)² ⁄ 50 =  1 ⁄ 50 = 0.02

χ² = 1.28 + 1.28 + 0.02 + 0.02 = 2.60

And the verdict: df = 4 − 1 = 3, where the 5% critical value is 7.815. 2.60 is nowhere near it — P = .46. These counts are an ordinary amount of wobble around 50 apiece, and Maassen has no evidence against equal popularity.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.1.28 is the contribution of the morning slot alone. All four categories contribute.
b.0.01 is 2.60 ⁄ 200 — dividing the finished statistic by n. χ² is already scaled by the expected counts; nothing further is divided by n.
d.7.81 is the critical value on 3 df at α = .05. It is what you compare your statistic with, not the statistic.
🏷️ Expected = n ⁄ k when the claim is “equal”. Then one term per category.

Question 11

🥧 Goodness of fit

Degrees of freedom for goodness of fit

The degrees of freedom for Hallström’s test of the university’s 50 ⁄ 30 ⁄ 20 claim against her 300 students are:
A university’s claimed intake split against one year’s 300 students
Programme trackShare the university claimsStudents observed
Science50%138
Humanities30%102
Arts20%60
Total100%300
  • a3
  • b1
  • c299
  • d2
🔎 What it is really asking

Count the categories, then subtract one.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Goodness of fit: degrees of freedom.

🛠️ The procedure

df = k − 1, where k is the number of categories. There is no second factor to multiply by, and N still never enters it.

🧮 The working
There are k = 3 tracks.

df = 3 − 1 = 2

What the 2 counts: the three observed counts have to add to 300, so once two of them are fixed the third is forced. Two free choices, two degrees of freedom. (The expected counts have no freedom at all — H₀ fixes them.)

Finish the test while you are here: χ² = (138 − 150)² ⁄ 150 + (102 − 90)² ⁄ 90 + (60 − 60)² ⁄ 60 = 0.96 + 1.60 + 0.00 = 2.56. On 2 df the 5% critical value is 5.991, so P = .28 and the year’s intake is consistent with the claim.

Keep the two df rules apart: one row of categories → k − 1. A table of rows against columns → (r − 1)(c − 1).
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.3 is the number of categories, before subtracting one. The subtraction is what the "− 1" in every df rule is for.
b.1 would be right for a 2 × 2 two-way table. This is one row of three categories, not a 2 × 2.
c.299 is n − 1, the df for a one-sample t test. Chi-square df count categories, never people.
🏷️ Goodness of fit: df = categories − 1. Nothing to do with n.

Question 12

🔍 Conditions and wording

Checking the condition for a chi-square test

Health psychologist Baptista compares relapse within six months under two programmes, 20 participants in each: Programme A has 1 relapse, Programme B has 6. A chi-square test here is not appropriate because:
Relapse within six months · 40 participants, 20 per programme
ProgrammeRelapsedDid not relapseTotal
Programme A11920
Programme B61420
Total73340
  • athe two groups are the same size
  • btwo expected counts are below 5
  • cone observed count is below 5
  • da sample of 40 is too small for any test
🔎 What it is really asking

Which counts does the condition apply to — the ones you see, or the ones H₀ predicts?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conditions: the expected-count rule.

🛠️ The procedure

The chi-square condition is about expected counts, not observed ones. For a 2 × 2 table the usual course rule is that all four expected counts should be at least 5.

🧮 The working
Margins: 20 and 20 across the rows, 7 relapses and 33 non-relapses down the columns, N = 40.

Relapsed, A:  (20 × 7) ⁄ 40 = 3.5
Relapsed, B:  (20 × 7) ⁄ 40 = 3.5
Not relapsed: (20 × 33) ⁄ 40 = 16.5 in each row

Two of the four expected counts are 3.5, below 5. The condition fails.

Why you must check first: the arithmetic still runs. It gives χ² = 4.33 and P = .038, which looks like a result — and it is not one, because with expected counts that small the chi-square distribution is a poor approximation to the real sampling distribution of the statistic. Report that the condition fails; Fisher’s exact test is the usual alternative.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Equal group sizes are a feature of a good design, not a problem. They have nothing to do with the chi-square condition.
c.One observed count is below 5 — the single relapse in Programme A — but the condition is not about observed counts. A table can have an observed 0 and still satisfy it.
d.Sample size is not the rule, and 40 is not automatically too small. A 2 × 2 with 40 participants split evenly across the columns would pass easily.
🏷️ The condition is on EXPECTED counts: all four ≥ 5 in a 2 × 2.

Question 13

🔍 Conditions and wording

Wording the conclusion of a chi-square test

Okonkwo’s test of travel against lateness gives χ² = 10.04 on 2 df, P = .007. Using α = .05, the conclusion she may draw is:
Lateness over one term by how pupils travel to school · 250 pupils
How they travelLate at least onceNever lateTotal
Walk305080
Cycle6040100
Bus304070
Total120130250
  • atravel and lateness are associated
  • bhow pupils travel causes them to be late
  • cbus users are late more often than the rest
  • dthe association between them is strong
🔎 What it is really asking

What a significant chi-square licenses you to say — and what it does not.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conditions and wording: interpreting a significant chi-square.

🛠️ The procedure

A chi-square test answers exactly one question: is there an association? It does not say which cells drove it, how big the association is, or which variable caused which.

🧮 The working
P = .007 is below α = .05, so reject H₀. H₀ was "travel and lateness are not associated", so you conclude that they are associated in the population. Stop there.

The three things the test cannot tell you:
• Cause. Pupils were not assigned a way of getting to school — those who live furthest away take the bus, and distance could drive both.
• Where. χ² adds all six cells together. Cyclists contributed the most (3.00 and 2.77 of the 10.04), but the test itself never names a cell.
• How much. A P-value responds to sample size as well as to effect size. With 2,500 pupils instead of 250, the same percentages would give P < .0001 and the association would be no stronger.

Say it to a friend: "something is going on between these two variables" — and nothing more specific than that.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Causation needs random assignment, and nobody was assigned a commute. This is an observational table.
c.Naming bus users goes beyond the test. χ² is a single number for the whole table; looking at the contributions afterwards is a separate step, and here it points at cyclists, not bus users.
d."Strong" is a statement about size, and a P-value is not a measure of size. A tiny association in a huge sample gives a tiny P.
🏷️ Significant χ² = there is an association. Not where, not how big, not why.

Question 14

🔗 Chi-square against the z test

Chi-square against the two-proportion z test

On the same 2 × 2 table, Veenstra also runs a two-sided two-proportion z test and gets z = −2.69, while her chi-square statistic was 7.24. The two P-values will be:
Completion of an 8-week online wellbeing programme · 200 adults
Coaching formatCompletedDropped outTotal
Group3862100
Individual5743100
Total95105200
  • adifferent, with the chi-square P-value the smaller
  • bidentical only because n here is large
  • cidentical, because χ² = z²
  • ddifferent, because they test different hypotheses
🔎 What it is really asking

Are these two tests related, or merely similar?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Chi-square against the z test: the exact equivalence.

🛠️ The procedure

For a 2 × 2 table the two tests are algebraically the same test: χ² = z², and the chi-square P-value equals the two-sided z P-value.

🧮 The working
Square the z: (−2.6904)² = 7.2381.

Chi-square: 7.2381.

Not approximately — exactly, to every decimal place, because the two formulas rearrange into one another. Both give P = .0071.

The critical values match in the same way: 1.96² = 3.8416, and the 5% critical value of χ² on 1 df is 3.8415 — the same number, give or take the rounding in 1.96. Pass one threshold and you pass the other.

So why have both? The z test gives you a direction and a confidence interval for the difference in proportions, which the chi-square test cannot. Chi-square earns its place on tables bigger than 2 × 2, where there is no single difference to put an interval around.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Neither P-value is smaller — they are the same number, .0071. The chi-square P matches the two-sided z P, not a one-sided one.
b.The identity is algebra, not an approximation, so n does not come into it. It holds for any 2 × 2 table, though both tests need the expected counts to be big enough to be trusted.
d.They test the same hypothesis in two notations: "the two proportions are equal" and "the two variables are not associated" are the same claim about a 2 × 2 table.
🏷️ 2 × 2: χ² = z², same two-sided P. Exactly, not roughly.

Question 15

🔗 Chi-square against the z test

Choosing between chi-square and the z test

Veenstra wants to test specifically whether completion is higher under individual coaching than under group coaching. She should:
Completion of an 8-week online wellbeing programme · 200 adults
Coaching formatCompletedDropped outTotal
Group3862100
Individual5743100
Total95105200
  • ause the chi-square test and report its P-value as one-sided
  • buse the chi-square test, since it is the same test
  • crun a separate chi-square test within each format
  • duse the z test, which can be made one-sided
🔎 What it is really asking

A directional hypothesis — which of the two equivalent tests can carry one?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Chi-square against the z test: choosing between them.

🛠️ The procedure

Chi-square is always two-sided: squaring the differences throws the direction away. A directional question needs the z test, whose statistic keeps its sign.

🧮 The working
Her hypotheses are directional: H₀: p_individual = p_group against Hₐ: p_individual > p_group.

The z test can express that. z = +2.69 for the difference in her direction, and the one-sided P is .0036.

Chi-square cannot. Every term is squared, so a table tilted the other way — 57 completing under group coaching and 38 under individual — gives the identical χ² of 7.24. A statistic that cannot tell the two tables apart cannot answer a question about which way round they are.

The sign is the whole point: z = +2.69 and z = −2.69 are different results and both square to 7.24. That is what gets lost.

And one more reason to prefer z here: it gives her an interval for the difference in completion rates, which is what anyone funding the programme will actually ask for.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.A chi-square P-value is two-sided by construction. Relabelling it one-sided does not make it directional, because the statistic never recorded a direction to begin with.
b.The two tests are the same on a 2 × 2 only for a two-sided question. The moment the hypothesis has a direction, the equivalence stops being useful.
c.Testing within each format separately has no comparison left in it — a single row of one format’s own clients cannot say anything about the other format.
🏷️ Directional question → z test. χ² squares the direction away.

Question 1

▦ Reading a two-way table

A column percentage from a two-way table

Occupational psychologist Dekkers records, for 320 call-centre employees, which shift pattern they work and whether they report burnout. Of the employees who report burnout, the percentage who work nights, to one decimal place, is:
Burnout by shift pattern · 320 call-centre employees
Shift patternReports burnoutNo burnoutTotal
Fixed days2496120
Rotating4872120
Nights324880
Total104216320
  • a10.0%
  • b25.0%
  • c30.8%
  • d40.0%
🔎 What it is really asking

Of the burnout group only — so the denominator is that column’s total.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading a two-way table: a conditional (column) percentage.

🛠️ The procedure

Decide what the "of" is before you divide. "Of the employees who report burnout" points at the burnout column, so its total goes underneath.

🧮 The working
The burnout column totals 24 + 48 + 32 = 104.

Night-shift employees who report burnout: 32.

32 ⁄ 104 = 0.30769 = 30.8%

Do the other two while you are there: 24 ⁄ 104 = 23.1% on fixed days and 48 ⁄ 104 = 46.2% on rotating shifts. Those three add to 100% — 100.1% as printed, which is only the rounding — and that is the check that you used a column denominator throughout.

The habit: a row percentage and a column percentage answer different questions from the same cell. Here the question is about the make-up of the burnout group, not about the burnout rate of night staff.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.10.0% is 32 ⁄ 320, the 32 employees as a share of the whole workforce. That mixes the burnout group back in with everybody else.
b.25.0% is 80 ⁄ 320, the share of the workforce who work nights. It never looks at burnout at all.
d.40.0% is 32 ⁄ 80 — of the night staff, the share reporting burnout. Right cell, row denominator instead of column.
🏷️ Underline the words after “of”. That total is the denominator.

Question 2

▦ Reading a two-way table

Comparing two conditional percentages

Dekkers wants to report how much more common burnout is on rotating shifts than on fixed days. The gap between those two groups, in percentage points to one decimal place, is:
Burnout by shift pattern · 320 call-centre employees
Shift patternReports burnoutNo burnoutTotal
Fixed days2496120
Rotating4872120
Nights324880
Total104216320
  • a20.0 percentage points
  • b24.0 percentage points
  • c7.5 percentage points
  • d100.0 percentage points
🔎 What it is really asking

Two row percentages first, then subtract one from the other.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading a two-way table: comparing conditional percentages.

🛠️ The procedure

Work out the burnout rate within each shift pattern — each divided by its own row total — and only then subtract. A gap in percentage points is a difference between two percentages.

🧮 The working
Rotating: 48 ⁄ 120 = 40.0%
Fixed days: 24 ⁄ 120 = 20.0%

40.0 − 20.0 = 20.0 percentage points

Here the two rows happen to have the same total of 120, so the counts could be compared directly. That is luck, not method — the night row totals 80, and comparing its 32 with the other rows’ counts would be meaningless.

And the distinction to keep: 40% is twice 20%, so the burnout rate is 100% higher in relative terms. "Twenty percentage points" and "one hundred per cent higher" describe the same two numbers. Say which one you mean.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.24.0 is 48 − 24, the difference between the two counts. Counts are not percentages, and this one only looks percentage-like because both rows total 120.
c.7.5 comes from dividing both cells by N: 15.0% − 7.5%. Those are shares of the whole workforce, not burnout rates within a shift pattern.
d.100.0 is the percentage change — 40% is 100% higher than 20%. That is a relative comparison, not a gap in percentage points.
🏷️ Percentage points = subtract two percentages that share no denominator.

Question 3

🎯 Expected counts

Recovering a margin from expected counts

Social psychologist Pavlidis tests whether a bystander is more likely to step in when alone than in a group. Her report prints only the expected counts, below, and not her observed table. The number of her participants who did intervene, as a whole number, is:
Pavlidis’s expected counts · her observed table is not printed
The bystander wasIntervenedDid not intervene
Alone36.054.0
In a group44.066.0
  • a90
  • b120
  • c200
  • d80
🔎 What it is really asking

Work backwards: the expected table keeps the real margins.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Expected counts: recovering a margin from them.

🛠️ The procedure

Expected counts are built as row × column ⁄ N, which leaves every margin exactly as it was observed. So adding a column of the expected table gives you back that column’s real total.

🧮 The working
Add the "intervened" column: 36.0 + 44.0 = 80.

The rest of the design falls out the same way. Rows: 36.0 + 54.0 = 90 were alone, 44.0 + 66.0 = 110 were in a group. Grand total: 200 participants.

Check the formula from the other direction: (90 × 80) ⁄ 200 = 36.0. ✓

Why this works at all: the margins are the part of the table the null hypothesis does not question. H₀ redistributes the counts inside the table; it never moves a total. That is also why you can never tell from an expected table alone what the observed counts were.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.90 is the number who were alone, found by adding across a row instead of down the column. That is the other variable’s margin.
b.120 is the number who did not intervene, 54.0 + 66.0. Right method, wrong column.
c.200 is N, the total of the whole expected table. It answers "how many took part", not "how many intervened".
🏷️ Expected counts keep the real margins — so you can read a margin back off them.

One cell of Dekkers’s table was lost in printing and is shown as ? below. The expected count for night-shift employees who report burnout, to one decimal place, is:

🔎 What it is really asking

Decide first which numbers an expected count actually needs.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Expected counts: deciding what the formula needs.

🛠️ The procedure

expected = (row total × column total) ⁄ N. Only margins go in — so a missing cell in the middle of the table does not stand in your way at all.

🧮 The working
The night row totals 80 and the burnout column totals 104, and both are printed. N = 320.

expected = (80 × 104) ⁄ 320 = 8320 ⁄ 320 = 26.0

The missing count was never needed. (If you want it: 104 − 24 − 48 = 32, because the column has to reach its own total.)

And the decision this teaches: look at what the formula asks for before you start repairing the table. You would need that recovered 32 for the cell’s contribution, (32 − 26.0)² ⁄ 26.0 = 1.38, and for nothing else here.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.39.0 is the expected burnout count for the fixed-days and rotating rows, which total 120 rather than 80. Right column, wrong row.
c.32.0 is the missing observed count, recovered from the column total. It is real, and it is not what was asked for.
d.54.0 is the expected count for night staff with no burnout, (80 × 216) ⁄ 320. Right row, wrong column.
🏷️ Expected counts need margins only. A hole in the middle cannot block you.

Turn the percentage into a column total first, then apply the usual rule.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Expected counts: building one when a margin is given as a percentage.

🛠️ The procedure

The formula needs counts, not percentages. Convert the 30% into a column total, then use expected = (row total × column total) ⁄ N.

🧮 The working
Step one — the column totals: 0.30 × 400 = 120 used the service, so 400 − 120 = 280 did not.

Step two — the cell: expected = (160 × 120) ⁄ 400 = 19 200 ⁄ 400 = 48.0

a.112.0 is the expected number of first-years who did not use the service, (160 × 280) ⁄ 400. Right row, wrong column.

d.120.0 is 30% of all 400 students — the column total, not the cell. It is the first step, stopped one step early.

Question 6

🧮 The statistic and its df

A cell’s contribution with the expected count unknown

In Dekkers’s table, 24 of the 120 fixed-days employees report burnout. That cell’s contribution to the chi-square statistic, to two decimal places, is:
Burnout by shift pattern · 320 call-centre employees
Shift patternReports burnoutNo burnoutTotal
Fixed days2496120
Rotating4872120
Nights324880
Total104216320
  • a5.77
  • b2.78
  • c9.38
  • d0.38
🔎 What it is really asking

Two steps: the expected count first, then (O − E)² ⁄ E.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The chi-square statistic: a single cell’s term.

🛠️ The procedure

Nothing is handed to you here, so build the expected count yourself: (row × column) ⁄ N. Then the cell contributes (O − E)² ⁄ E.

🧮 The working
Expected: (120 × 104) ⁄ 320 = 12 480 ⁄ 320 = 39.0

O − E = 24 − 39.0 = −15.0

(−15.0)² = 225 and 225 ⁄ 39.0 = 5.7692, so 5.77.

This is the largest of the six contributions — fixed-days staff are 15 employees short of the burnout count that no-association would predict, and 15 is a big gap against an expected 39.

The habit: write the expected count down before you touch the subtraction. Most lost marks on this topic are a correct (O − E)² sitting over the wrong denominator.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.2.78 is the cell next door, (96 − 81)² ⁄ 81. The same gap of 15, divided by a larger expected count of 81.
c.9.38 is 225 ⁄ 24 — divided by the observed count. The denominator is always the expected count.
d.0.38 is 15 ⁄ 39, the gap over E without being squared. Squaring is what stops the positive and negative gaps cancelling.
🏷️ Expected count first, then (O − E)² ⁄ E. Never divide by O.

Question 7

🧮 The statistic and its df

Recovering a table’s shape from its degrees of freedom

A chi-square test of the association between two categorical variables is reported with 6 degrees of freedom. Of the designs below, the one that gives that df is:
  • a7 categories in one row
  • b4 rows and 3 columns
  • c3 rows and 3 columns
  • d6 rows and 2 columns
🔎 What it is really asking

Run df = (r − 1)(c − 1) backwards: which shapes multiply out to 6?

🧭 Which type of question this is

The chi-square statistic: degrees of freedom, worked backwards.

🛠️ The procedure

df = (r − 1)(c − 1). Going backwards means factorising: ask which pairs of whole numbers multiply to 6, then add one to each.

🧮 The working
6 factorises as 6 × 1, 3 × 2, 2 × 3 and 1 × 6. Adding one to each side gives the tables that work: 7 × 2, 4 × 3, 3 × 4 and 2 × 7.

Only one of those is on the list: 4 rows and 3 columns, since (4 − 1)(3 − 1) = 3 × 2 = 6. ✓

Check the others: 3 × 3 gives (2)(2) = 4, and 6 × 2 gives (5)(1) = 5.

And the decision: df is not a label you attach afterwards, it is what picks the critical value — 12.592 at 5% on 6 df, against 9.488 on 4 df and 11.070 on 5 df. Reading a reported df backwards is a quick way to check you have understood somebody else’s table before you trust their P-value.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.7 categories in one row does give 7 − 1 = 6, but that is the goodness-of-fit rule for a single variable. With one variable there is no association to test.
c.3 rows and 3 columns gives (3 − 1)(3 − 1) = 4 df, not 6. Nine cells, but df counts the free choices, not the cells.
d.6 rows and 2 columns gives (6 − 1)(2 − 1) = 5 df. The 6 in "6 rows" is not the df — every row and column loses one.
🏷️ Factorise the df: (r − 1)(c − 1) = 6 means a 4 × 3, 3 × 4, 7 × 2 or 2 × 7 table.

Computing chi-square for a 3 × 2 table

The value of the chi-square statistic for the whole of Dekkers’s table, to two decimal places, is:
Burnout by shift pattern · 320 call-centre employees
Shift patternReports burnoutNo burnoutTotal
Fixed days2496120
Rotating4872120
Nights324880
Total104216320

  • b5.99
  • c4.56
  • d13.68
🔎 What it is really asking

One (O − E)² ⁄ E term for each of the six cells, then add them all.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The chi-square statistic: computing it from a full table.

🛠️ The procedure

χ² = Σ (O − E)² ⁄ E over every cell. Build the whole expected table first; trying to hold six expected counts in your head is where this goes wrong.

🧮 The working
Expected counts, each (row × column) ⁄ 320:
Expected counts if shift pattern and burnout were unrelated
Shift patternReports burnoutNo burnoutTotal
Fixed days39.081.0120
Rotating39.081.0120
Nights26.054.080
Total104216320
Now one term per cell:

Fixed, burnout:    (24 − 39.0)² ⁄ 39.0 = 225 ⁄ 39.0 = 5.7692
Fixed, none:       (96 − 81.0)² ⁄ 81.0 = 225 ⁄ 81.0 = 2.7778
Rotating, burnout: (48 − 39.0)² ⁄ 39.0 =  81 ⁄ 39.0 = 2.0769
Rotating, none:    (72 − 81.0)² ⁄ 81.0 =  81 ⁄ 81.0 = 1.0000
Nights, burnout:   (32 − 26.0)² ⁄ 26.0 =  36 ⁄ 26.0 = 1.3846
Nights, none:      (48 − 54.0)² ⁄ 54.0 =  36 ⁄ 54.0 = 0.6667

χ² = 13.6752, so 13.68.

And the decision: df = (3 − 1)(2 − 1) = 2, where the 5% critical value is 5.991 and the 1% value is 9.210. 13.68 is past both, and P = .001. Shift pattern and burnout are associated.

Worth noticing: the fixed-days row contributes 8.55 of the 13.68 on its own. The test does not say that, but a glance at the contributions tells you where to look afterwards.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.9.23 is the burnout column alone, 5.7692 + 2.0769 + 1.3846. The "no burnout" column is half the table and contributes too.
b.5.99 is the critical value on 2 df at α = .05. It is what you compare the statistic with, not the statistic.
c.4.56 is 13.6752 ⁄ 3 — averaging over the three shift patterns. The terms are added, never averaged.
🏷️ Six cells, six terms, one sum. Expected table on paper first.
