Question 9

🥧 Goodness of fit

Expected counts from a claimed ratio

Developmental researcher Weisz classifies the attachment style of 240 children. A textbook claims the four styles occur in the ratio 6 : 2 : 1 : 1. The expected counts under that claim are:
A textbook’s claimed 6 : 2 : 1 : 1 split against 240 children
Attachment styleRatio the textbook claimsChildren observed
Secure6132
Avoidant254
Ambivalent130
Disorganised124
Total10 parts240
  • a144, 48, 24 and 24
  • b60, 20, 10 and 10
  • c60, 60, 60 and 60
  • d132, 54, 30 and 24
🔎 What it is really asking

Turn the ratio into proportions of n, in two steps.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Goodness of fit: expected counts from a claimed ratio.

🛠️ The procedure

A ratio is not a set of proportions until you divide by its total. Add the parts, find what one part is worth, then multiply each category by its own number of parts.

🧮 The working
The parts add to 6 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 10.

One part is therefore 240 ⁄ 10 = 24 children.

Secure:       6 × 24 = 144
Avoidant:     2 × 24 = 48
Ambivalent:   1 × 24 = 24
Disorganised: 1 × 24 = 24

Check: 144 + 48 + 24 + 24 = 240. Expected counts must always add back to n.

The same thing in proportions: 6 ⁄ 10 = .60, 2 ⁄ 10 = .20, .10 and .10, then expected = n × proportion. Ratios and percentages are two notations for one claim; the formula only ever wants n × proportion.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.60, 20, 10 and 10 reads the ratio as percentages and applies them to 100 rather than to the 240 children actually classified.
c.60, 60, 60 and 60 is n ⁄ 4 — the expected counts if the four styles were equally common. The textbook claims nothing of the kind.
d.132, 54, 30 and 24 are the observed counts. Setting expected equal to observed would force χ² to zero.
🏷️ Add the parts, divide n by that, then scale each category up.

Question 10

🥧 Goodness of fit

Computing a goodness-of-fit chi-square

The value of the chi-square statistic for Weisz’s 240 children against the 6 : 2 : 1 : 1 claim, to two decimal places, is:
A textbook’s claimed 6 : 2 : 1 : 1 split against 240 children
Attachment styleRatio the textbook claimsChildren observed
Secure6132
Avoidant254
Ambivalent130
Disorganised124
Total10 parts240
  • a7.81
  • b0.46
  • c3.25
  • d2.96
🔎 What it is really asking

Expected counts from the ratio first, then one term per category.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Goodness of fit: computing the statistic.

🛠️ The procedure

Two steps again: expected = n × the claimed proportion, then Σ (O − E)² ⁄ E across the four categories.

🧮 The working
Expected, from the ten parts: 144, 48, 24, 24.

Secure:       (132 − 144)² ⁄ 144 = 144 ⁄ 144 = 1.00
Avoidant:     ( 54 −  48)² ⁄  48 =  36 ⁄  48 = 0.75
Ambivalent:   ( 30 −  24)² ⁄  24 =  36 ⁄  24 = 1.50
Disorganised: ( 24 −  24)² ⁄  24 =   0 ⁄  24 = 0.00

χ² = 1.00 + 0.75 + 1.50 + 0.00 = 3.25

Notice the ambivalent category: a gap of only 6 children contributes more (1.50) than the secure category’s gap of 12 (1.00), because it is divided by a much smaller expected count. Small expected counts magnify small gaps — which is exactly why the condition insists they are not too small.

And the verdict: df = 4 − 1 = 3, where the 5% critical value is 7.815. 3.25 is well short of it and P = .35. These 240 children are consistent with the claim.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.7.81 is the critical value on 3 df at α = .05 — the threshold, not the statistic.
b.0.46 is Σ |O − E| ⁄ E, with the squaring left out. Without squaring, the gaps partly cancel and the statistic loses its meaning.
d.2.96 comes from dividing each squared gap by the observed count instead of the expected one. The denominator is always E.
🏷️ Expected from the claim, then one squared-gap term per category.

Question 11

🥧 Goodness of fit

Telling the two degrees-of-freedom rules apart

Tornquist cross-classifies 300 therapy clients by diagnosis (4 categories) and by outcome (3 categories). A colleague uses the same 300 clients to test whether the 4 diagnoses occur in the proportions a national register claims. The degrees of freedom for the two tests, in that order, are:
  • a3 and 6
  • b6 and 4
  • c11 and 3
  • d6 and 3
🔎 What it is really asking

Which test is which? One cross-classifies, the other compares to a claim.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Goodness of fit against a two-way table: choosing the df rule.

🛠️ The procedure

Count the classifications, not the categories. Two variables crossed → (r − 1)(c − 1). One variable against a claimed distribution → k − 1.

🧮 The working
Tornquist has two variables crossed in a 4 × 3 table:
df = (4 − 1)(3 − 1) = 3 × 2 = 6

Her colleague has one variable, the 4 diagnoses, tested against a distribution the register supplies:
df = 4 − 1 = 3

The same 300 clients, the same four diagnoses, two different tests — because the questions differ. Tornquist asks whether diagnosis and outcome go together; the colleague asks whether the diagnoses are spread as claimed.

How to tell them apart in one glance: does the stem hand you a distribution (percentages, a ratio, "equally likely")? Then it is goodness of fit, with k − 1. Does it hand you a second variable? Then it is a two-way table, with (r − 1)(c − 1), and the expected counts come out of the margins.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.3 and 6 is the right pair of numbers with the two rules swapped. The cross-classified table is the one with 6.
b.6 and 4 gets the table right but leaves the goodness-of-fit test without its "− 1". Four categories give 3 df, not 4.
c.11 and 3 uses cells − 1 for the table, 12 − 1. That is the goodness-of-fit rule applied to a two-way table, where it does not belong.
🏷️ One classification → k − 1. Two classifications crossed → (r − 1)(c − 1).

Question 12

🔍 Conditions and wording

Finding the smallest expected count from the margins

Clinical researcher Nieminen records, for 60 clients, their referral route (four categories) and whether they completed therapy. Only her margins are printed below. The smallest expected count in her table, to two decimal places, is:
Nieminen’s margins only · referral route by outcome, 60 clients
OutcomeSelf-referredGPSchoolCourtTotal
Completed therapy????30
Left early????30
Total242010660
  • a0.05
  • b3.00
  • c6.00
  • d7.50
🔎 What it is really asking

You can check the condition from the margins alone — no cell counts needed.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conditions: locating the smallest expected count.

🛠️ The procedure

The smallest expected count sits where the smallest row total meets the smallest column total, because expected = (row × column) ⁄ N rises and falls with both.

🧮 The working
The row totals are 30 and 30; the column totals are 24, 20, 10 and 6.

Smallest expected = (30 × 6) ⁄ 60 = 180 ⁄ 60 = 3.00

The full expected row, for either outcome: 12.0, 10.0, 5.0, 3.0.

And the decision: the usual course rule is that the expected counts should all be at least 5. Two of the eight are 3.0, so it fails on that rule — and on the more permissive version taught in some texts (none below 1, no more than a fifth below 5) two of eight is a quarter, so it fails there too. The P-value from this table should not be trusted. Nieminen’s options are to combine the court-referred clients with another route into a sensible larger category, or to collect more data.

The habit: check the condition before you compute anything. It costs one multiplication, and it is decided entirely by the margins — so a table printed with its cells missing can still be screened.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.05 is (30 ⁄ 60) × (6 ⁄ 60), the expected proportion for that cell. Multiply it by N = 60 and you have the 3.00.
c.6.00 is the smallest column total. It is an observed margin, not an expected count, and the condition is about expected counts.
d.7.50 is 60 ⁄ 8, splitting N equally between the eight cells. That ignores the margins, which are exactly what expected counts are built from.
🏷️ Smallest row × smallest column ⁄ N. Screen the condition from the margins.

Question 13

🔍 Conditions and wording

Wording a non-significant conclusion

Weisz’s test of the 6 : 2 : 1 : 1 claim gives χ² = 3.25 on 3 df, P = .35. Using α = .05, the conclusion she may draw is that:
A textbook’s claimed 6 : 2 : 1 : 1 split against 240 children
Attachment styleRatio the textbook claimsChildren observed
Secure6132
Avoidant254
Ambivalent130
Disorganised124
Total10 parts240
  • athe data are consistent with the claimed ratio
  • bthe claimed ratio is now proven to be correct
  • cthe four attachment styles are equally common
  • dthe sample of 240 children is far too small
🔎 What it is really asking

What a non-significant chi-square licenses you to say.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conditions and wording: interpreting a non-significant result.

🛠️ The procedure

P = .35 is above α, so you fail to reject H₀. That is a statement about evidence, not about truth: "these data do not contradict the claim".

🧮 The working
H₀ was that the styles occur in the 6 : 2 : 1 : 1 ratio. The observed counts 132, 54, 30, 24 against the expected 144, 48, 24, 24 are close enough that a sample of 240 would differ this much, or more, about 35% of the time even if the claim were exactly right.

So the ratio survives. It is not confirmed — a ratio of 5.5 : 2.2 : 1.1 : 1.2 would also have survived this test, and so would several others.

Say it to a friend: "the numbers are close to what the textbook predicts, so there is nothing here to argue with" — not "the textbook is right".

And the asymmetry worth remembering: a significant result rules something out; a non-significant result rules nothing in. Failing to find evidence against a claim is not evidence for it.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b."Proven correct" treats failing to reject H₀ as accepting it. A test can only fail to find evidence against a claim; it can never establish it.
c.Equal commonness is a different claim altogether, and the observed 132, 54, 30, 24 are nowhere near the 60 each it would predict.
d.The sample is not the problem: every expected count is 24 or more, so the condition is comfortably met and the test is valid. A large P is a result, not a failure.
🏷️ Non-significant = “consistent with”, never “proven”.

Question 14

🔗 Chi-square against the z test

Getting chi-square from a reported z

Health researcher Rasmussen compares the proportion of participants completing a mindfulness course in two conditions and reports a two-sided two-proportion z test: z = 2.40, P = .016. For that same 2 × 2 table, the chi-square statistic, to two decimal places, is:
  • a4.80
  • b1.55
  • c5.76
  • d2.40
🔎 What it is really asking

Work the equivalence forwards: you have z and you want χ².

🧭 Which type of question this is

Chi-square against the z test: converting between them.

🛠️ The procedure

On a 2 × 2 table the two tests are the same test written twice: χ² = z², with the chi-square P-value equal to the two-sided z P-value.

🧮 The working
χ² = z² = 2.40² = 5.7600

Check it against the P-value he printed: on 1 df, χ² = 5.76 gives P = .0164, and the two-sided z P-value for z = 2.40 is also .0164. The same number, as it must be.

The critical values convert too: 1.96² = 3.8416, and the 5% critical value of χ² on 1 df is 3.8415. Pass one threshold and you pass the other.

And the use of it: this is your free check when a report gives one statistic and you want the other, or when two analyses of the same table seem to disagree. On a 2 × 2 they cannot disagree — if they do, one of them has been computed wrongly.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.4.80 is 2 × 2.40, doubling instead of squaring. The relationship is χ² = z², and doubling only happens to be close when z is near 2.
b.1.55 is √2.40, the conversion run the wrong way. Squaring takes you from z to χ²; the square root takes you back.
d.2.40 is z itself. The two statistics are on different scales: z is a distance in standard errors, χ² is that distance squared.
🏷️ 2 × 2: χ² = z². Square to go one way, square-root to come back.

Question 15

🔗 Chi-square against the z test

When the two-proportion z test is unavailable

Dekkers would like to compare burnout across her three shift patterns using a two-proportion z test. She cannot, because:
Burnout by shift pattern · 320 call-centre employees
Shift patternReports burnoutNo burnoutTotal
Fixed days2496120
Rotating4872120
Nights324880
Total104216320
  • athe z test requires equal group sizes
  • bthe z test cannot be made two-sided
  • cher expected counts are below 5
  • dthree proportions leave no single difference
🔎 What it is really asking

What is the z test actually built to compare?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Chi-square against the z test: choosing the right one.

🛠️ The procedure

The two-proportion z test is built on p₁ − p₂: one difference, one standard error, one statistic. With three groups there is no single difference for it to be about.

🧮 The working
Her three burnout rates are 20.0%, 40.0% and 40.0%. There are three pairwise differences hiding in that — rotating against fixed, nights against fixed, nights against rotating — and the z test has room for exactly one.

So the test for "is burnout related to shift pattern at all?" is the chi-square test on the whole 3 × 2 table: χ² = 13.68 on 2 df, P = .001. One test, one question, all three groups at once.

If she then wants to know which patterns differ, she can compare pairs — but each extra test is another chance of a false positive, so the comparisons have to be planned and the threshold adjusted rather than run freely after the fact.

The decision rule to carry: two groups and a directional question → z. Two groups, no direction → either, since χ² = z². Three or more groups → chi-square on the whole table.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Equal group sizes are not required by the z test, and hers are 120, 120 and 80 in any case. Unequal groups only change the standard error.
b.The z test is routinely two-sided — that is precisely the version that equals chi-square on a 2 × 2. Its special ability is being made one-sided.
c.Her expected counts are 26.0 at the smallest, comfortably above 5. The condition is met; the problem is the number of groups, not their size.
🏷️ z compares two proportions. Three or more groups → chi-square on the table.

Question 1

▦ Reading a two-way table

A comparison that reverses when the groups are split

Clinical director Heslinga audits 200 clients at a service offering therapy online or in person. Overall, 72% of the online clients recovered against 58% of the in-person clients — yet among mild cases, and again among severe cases, the in-person clients did better. The single feature of her data that explains this is:
Recovery by therapy format, split by severity · Heslinga’s 200 clients
ClientsOnline: recoveredOnline: seenIn person: recoveredIn person: seen
Mild cases64801820
Severe cases8204080
All clients7210058100
  • aone of the four recovery counts must have been entered wrongly
  • bthe overall percentages, built on all 200 clients, are the honest ones
  • csevere cases were mostly seen in person, and recover less often
  • dthe online group is the larger of the two, so 72% outweighs 58%
🔎 What it is really asking

Why a comparison can flip when you stop splitting the clients by severity.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading a two-way table: a lurking variable behind the margins.

🛠️ The procedure

Overall percentages compare the two mixtures of client as well as the two formats. When the formats were given to different mixtures, split by the third variable and compare like with like.

🧮 The working
The four honest comparisons:

Mild:   online 64 ⁄ 80 = 80.0% against in person 18 ⁄ 20 = 90.0%
Severe: online 8 ⁄ 20 = 40.0% against in person 40 ⁄ 80 = 50.0%

In person wins by ten points in both. Now look at who was in each group: the online clients were 80% mild cases (80 of 100), the in-person clients 80% severe (80 of 100).

So the overall 72% is mostly a mild-case recovery rate and the overall 58% is mostly a severe-case one. The formats never had a fair race.

The habit: before you trust a percentage from a two-way table, ask what third variable the two rows might differ on. If they differ on something that affects the outcome, the overall figures compare the wrong things.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Nothing is mistyped: 64 + 8 = 72 and 18 + 40 = 58, and every row and column adds to its printed total. The reversal is real arithmetic, not an error.
b.The overall figures are the misleading ones here, because they compare two different mixtures of case. The severity-by-severity figures are the fair ones.
d.Both groups contain exactly 100 clients, so neither percentage outweighs the other. Equal group sizes do not protect you from a lurking variable.
🏷️ Overall percentages compare the groups AND their make-up. Split first.

Question 2

▦ Reading a two-way table

Which percentage answers the question asked

Marcoux and Oksanen read the same table of 200 insomnia clients, below. Marcoux points out that 75% of the clients now in remission had attended the sleep-hygiene workshop, and reports that the workshop helps. Oksanen replies that the table shows nothing of the kind. The reading that survives is:
Insomnia remission after a sleep-hygiene workshop · 200 clients
Attended the workshopIn remissionNot in remissionTotal
Yes6090150
No203050
Total80120200
  • aOksanen’s — remission runs at 40% whether they attended or not
  • bMarcoux’s — 75% of the clients in remission did attend it
  • cMarcoux’s, since three times as many attenders are in remission
  • dneither — a table of 200 clients cannot settle the question
🔎 What it is really asking

Whether a percentage of the remission column can show that attending mattered.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading a two-way table: column percentages against row percentages.

🛠️ The procedure

To ask whether attending mattered you need the remission rate within each group — the row percentages. A percentage taken down the remission column answers a different question: who the remitters happen to be.

🧮 The working
Marcoux’s figure is right and useless. 60 of the 80 clients in remission attended, and 60 ⁄ 80 = 75%. But 150 of the 200 clients attended in the first place, so attenders were always going to fill most of any column.

The comparison that answers his question:

Attended:     60 ⁄ 150 = 40.0% in remission
Did not:      20 ⁄ 50  = 40.0% in remission

Identical. The expected counts come out at 60, 90, 20 and 30 — the observed table exactly — so χ² = 0.000. There is no association here at all.

The habit: a conditional percentage only compares groups if the groups are the denominators. Divide by the row totals, then compare the rows.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.The 75% is a percentage of the remission column. It is large because 150 of the 200 clients attended, not because attending worked.
c.Three times as many attenders are in remission because there are three times as many attenders. The rate is the same 40% in both groups.
d.Two hundred clients are plenty to see a difference of this size — and the table is not silent. It gives a clear answer: the rates are equal.
🏷️ Compare rates WITHIN the groups. A column percentage describes the column.

Question 3

🎯 Expected counts

Finding the mistake in an expected count

Tulloch has 300 students, 90 of them first-generation, and 120 of the 300 have used the writing centre. She writes: “The expected number of first-generation students who used the centre is (90 × 120) ⁄ 120 = 90.” Her mistake is that:
  • ashe used the wrong row total for that cell
  • bshe needed the observed count in the cell as well
  • cshe should have added the two margins, not multiplied them
  • dshe divided by a margin instead of by N
🔎 What it is really asking

Which part of row × column ⁄ N has gone wrong.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Expected counts: diagnosing a stated error.

🛠️ The procedure

expected = (row total × column total) ⁄ N. The denominator is always the sample size. Dividing by one of the margins cancels it and hands the other margin straight back.

🧮 The working
Her two margins are right: 90 first-generation students and 120 users of the centre. Her denominator is not — she has put 120 there instead of 300.

expected = (90 × 120) ⁄ 300 = 10800 ⁄ 300 = 36.0

Notice what her version did: dividing by the column total cancelled it, leaving 90, which is the row total back again.

The check that would have caught it: an expected count is always smaller than each of its own margins, unless a margin is the whole sample — because you are taking a fraction of one margin. A cell of 90 first-generation students cannot have 90 of them expected in one column when 120 of the 300 used the centre.

The habit: say the formula out loud with the numbers in it, including the N. The N is the step people drop.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The row total of 90 is the right one: the cell is about first-generation students, and 90 of the 300 are first-generation.
b.A cell’s own observed count is deliberately kept out of its expected count. That is what makes the comparison between them worth anything.
c.Multiplying is correct. Adding the margins would give 210, a number larger than either margin and larger than the cell could ever hold.
🏷️ Row × column ⁄ N. The denominator is N — never a margin.

Question 4

🎯 Expected counts

How far an observed count falls below its expected one

Youth-services researcher Oyelaran follows 240 adolescents, 40% of them in a mentoring condition, and 25% of the 240 drop out. For the mentored adolescents who dropped out, the amount by which the observed count falls short of the expected count, to one decimal place, is:
Drop-out from a youth programme · 240 adolescents
ConditionDropped outStayedTotal
Mentored187896
Not mentored42102144
Total60180240
  • a42.0
  • b6.0
  • c24.0
  • d1.5
🔎 What it is really asking

Work out the expected count, then use it — the gap is what is wanted.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Expected counts: using one as an input rather than an answer.

🛠️ The procedure

Get the expected count from row × column ⁄ N, then subtract the observed count from it. The expected count is the step on the way, not the destination.

🧮 The working
The mentored row totals 96 (that is the 40%), and the drop-out column totals 60 (the 25%). N = 240.

expected = (96 × 60) ⁄ 240 = 5760 ⁄ 240 = 24.0

observed = 18, so the shortfall is 24.0 − 18 = 6.0

In words: six fewer mentored adolescents dropped out than you would see if mentoring made no difference. The matching cell beside it is six above its expected count — in a 2 × 2 table the four gaps are always the same size, two up and two down, because the margins are fixed.

The habit: read the last line of the stem twice. When it asks for a gap, a share or a contribution, the expected count is an ingredient and the question wants something built out of it.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.42.0 is the number of unmentored adolescents who dropped out. It is the rest of the drop-out column, not a distance from an expected count.
c.24.0 is the expected count itself — the ingredient, not the gap between it and the 18 adolescents actually observed in that cell.
d.1.5 is that cell’s contribution to chi-square, (18 − 24)² ⁄ 24. It is a later step, and it is no longer measured in adolescents.
🏷️ Expected first, then answer the question actually asked.

Question 5

🧮 The statistic and its df

How much of chi-square comes from one cell

For Oyelaran’s table, the percentage of the whole chi-square statistic that comes from the mentored drop-out cell, to one decimal place, is:
Drop-out from a youth programme · 240 adolescents
ConditionDropped outStayedTotal
Mentored187896
Not mentored42102144
Total60180240
  • a15.0%
  • b25.0%
  • c45.0%
  • d30.0%
🔎 What it is really asking

One cell’s term as a share of the total — so you need all four terms.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The chi-square statistic: one term against the whole sum.

🛠️ The procedure

Work out (O − E)² ⁄ E for every cell, add them for χ², then divide the cell you were asked about by that total.

🧮 The working
Expected counts: 24.0 and 72.0 in the mentored row, 36.0 and 108.0 in the other. Every gap is 6.

Mentored, dropped out:   36 ⁄ 24  = 1.5000
Mentored, stayed:        36 ⁄ 72  = 0.5000
Not mentored, dropped:   36 ⁄ 36  = 1.0000
Not mentored, stayed:    36 ⁄ 108 = 0.3333

χ² = 3.3333, and 1.5000 ⁄ 3.3333 = 0.450 = 45.0%

Why that cell dominates: all four gaps are 6, so the only thing separating the terms is the expected count underneath. The smallest expected count, 24, produces the largest term.

The habit: the statistic you compute is sometimes only the denominator of the answer. Finish χ², then go back to the question.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.15.0% is the share from the mentored stayed cell, 0.5000 ⁄ 3.3333 — the cell next door in the same row.
b.25.0% treats the four cells as contributing equally. They cannot: the same gap of 6 is divided by expected counts of 24, 72, 36 and 108.
d.30.0% is the share from the unmentored drop-out cell, 1.0000 ⁄ 3.3333. Right arithmetic, wrong cell.
🏷️ A share needs the whole total. Compute every term, then divide.

Question 6

🧮 The statistic and its df

Working back from chi-square to the counts

Educational psychologist Vigneault tests 120 pupils in a 2 × 2 table of seating arrangement against finishing a task. Every expected count in her table is 30.0 and her chi-square statistic is 4.80. The distance between the observed and the expected count in each cell, as a whole number of pupils, is:
  • a6
  • b12
  • c36
  • d3
🔎 What it is really asking

Run (O − E)² ⁄ E backwards, from the finished statistic to the gap.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The chi-square statistic: recovering an input from the statistic.

🛠️ The procedure

Each cell contributes (O − E)² ⁄ E. With all four expected counts equal, all four terms are equal, so divide χ² by 4, multiply by E, and take the square root.

🧮 The working
In a 2 × 2 table the margins are fixed, so if one cell is 6 above its expected count the cell beside it is 6 below: all four gaps have the same size. With all four expected counts equal to 30 as well, the four terms must be equal.

Each term: 4.80 ⁄ 4 = 1.2000
(O − E)² = 1.2000 × 30 = 36
|O − E| = √36 = 6 pupils

So her table is 36 and 24 in one row, 24 and 36 in the other — margins of 60 and 60 both ways, N = 120. Check forwards: 36 ⁄ 30 four times over = 4.80. ✓

On 1 df that gives P = .029, just significant at α = .05.

The habit: every formula runs both ways. Write it down, mark what you were given, and undo the steps in reverse order — divide, multiply, then square-root.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.12 is the distance between the two observed counts in a row, 36 − 24. Each one is only 6 from the expected count sitting between them.
c.36 is (O − E)², the squared gap, one step before the square root. It is also an observed count in this table, which makes it tempting.
d.3 halves the gap, on the thought that two cells are above and two below. The gap is measured per cell, and each cell is a full 6 away.
🏷️ Given χ², undo it: divide by the number of terms, times E, then square-root.

Question 7

🧮 The statistic and its df

Finding the mistake in a reported test

Fennema cross-classifies 400 clients by referral route (3 categories) and by outcome (4 categories), and writes: “χ² = 18.4, df = 11, P = .07, so referral route and outcome are not associated.” The mistake in her write-up is that:
  • aa statistic of 18.4 is impossible on a 3 × 4 table
  • bshe used the number of cells − 1 for her df
  • cshe should have used N − 1 = 399 for her df
  • dshe reported P when she needed a critical value
🔎 What it is really asking

Check the df against the shape of the table, and see what it does to the verdict.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Degrees of freedom: diagnosing a stated error.

🛠️ The procedure

For a two-way table df = (r − 1)(c − 1). Counting cells and subtracting one is the goodness-of-fit rule, and it does not belong on a table of two variables.

🧮 The working
Her table has 3 × 4 = 12 cells, and 12 − 1 = 11 — which is where her df came from.

The right df: (3 − 1)(4 − 1) = 2 × 3 = 6

Now watch the verdict move. On 11 df the 5% critical value is 19.675, so 18.4 falls short and P = .073. On 6 df the 5% critical value is 12.592, 18.4 is well past it, and P = .0053.

Her statistic was fine. Her df was wrong, so her P was wrong, so her sentence was the opposite of what her data say: referral route and outcome are associated.

The habit: df before P, and P before words. An error in the first step is invisible by the third — the write-up reads perfectly well and is still wrong.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.18.4 is a perfectly possible statistic on a 3 × 4 table. There is no ceiling on χ² — it grows with the sample size and with the size of the gaps.
c.N − 1 is the df of a one-sample t test. Chi-square df count categories, so 400 clients and 4,000 clients give a 3 × 4 table the same 6 df.
d.Reporting an exact P-value is standard, and a critical value would have led to the same reversed conclusion while her df stayed wrong.
🏷️ Two variables → (r − 1)(c − 1). Cells − 1 belongs to goodness of fit.

Question 8

🥧 Goodness of fit

When counts cannot be tested against a claim

Survey researcher Yilmaz wants to compare each of four sets of counts with a published distribution. The survey whose counts cannot be used for that comparison is:
  • apreferred study spot, one choice each from four options
  • bhandedness, recorded once per child, against a 90 : 10 claim
  • cfirst-choice therapy format, one choice each from three
  • dcoping strategies, where students ticked every one they use
🔎 What it is really asking

Which set of counts breaks the one-person-one-category requirement.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Goodness of fit: when the test does not apply.

🛠️ The procedure

The categories must be mutually exclusive and exhaustive: every person lands in exactly one of them, so the counts add up to the number of people. A survey where one person can appear in several categories breaks that.

🧮 The working
Count the people. With 300 students ticking every strategy they use, the counts might add to 700 — the same student is in the “exercise” count and the “talking to friends” count and two others.

That wrecks the test twice over. There is no n to turn the claimed percentages into expected counts, and the cases are not independent of one another, because one student’s four ticks move four categories together.

The other three all put each person in exactly one box, so their counts add to the sample size and the claimed proportions can be multiplied by it.

The habit: add the counts up first. If they do not come to the number of people surveyed, stop — you are not looking at a distribution.

What Yilmaz can do instead: treat each strategy as its own yes-or-no question and report the four percentages separately.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.One choice from four options puts every student in exactly one category, and the four counts add to the sample. That is exactly what the comparison needs.
b.Handedness recorded once per child gives counts that add to the sample, and the 90 : 10 claim supplies the proportions to multiply by it.
c.One first choice from three formats again puts each client in a single category, so the three counts add to the number of clients.
🏷️ One person, one category, counts adding to n. Otherwise it is not a distribution.

Question 9

🥧 Goodness of fit

What happens to chi-square when the sample shrinks

A publisher claims students split equally across four revision formats. Gallardo’s 4,000 students give χ² = 20.00 against that claim, with P < .001. A colleague repeats the survey on 400 students and finds percentages identical to Gallardo’s. His chi-square statistic, to two decimal places, is:
A publisher’s equal-split claim against 4,000 students
Revision formatShare the publisher claimsStudents observed
Flashcards25%1080
Summaries25%1060
Diagrams25%940
Recordings25%920
Total100%4000
  • a2.00
  • b20.00
  • c5.00
  • d0.20
🔎 What it is really asking

Same percentages, a tenth of the people — what does χ² do?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Goodness of fit: how the statistic depends on the sample size.

🛠️ The procedure

χ² is built from counts, not percentages. Scale a sample down by a factor of ten with the percentages unchanged and every term, and so the whole statistic, scales down by ten as well.

🧮 The working
Gallardo’s percentages are 27.0, 26.5, 23.5 and 23.0. On 400 students those give counts of 108, 106, 94 and 92, against 100 expected in each category.

(108 − 100)² ⁄ 100 = 0.64
(106 − 100)² ⁄ 100 = 0.36
(94 − 100)² ⁄ 100 = 0.36
(92 − 100)² ⁄ 100 = 0.64

χ² = 2.00, where Gallardo had 20.00.

Why exactly a tenth: each gap shrank by a factor of 10, so each squared gap shrank by 100, while each expected count shrank by only 10. 100 ⁄ 10 = 10.

And the verdict flips. On 3 df the 5% critical value is 7.815. Gallardo’s 20.00 gives P = .0002; his colleague’s 2.00 gives P = .57. Same percentages, opposite conclusions.

The habit: a very small P on a very large sample is partly a statement about the sample size. Look at how far the percentages actually are from the claim — here, about two points — before you call it important.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.20.00 is Gallardo’s own statistic. The percentages carry over to the smaller survey but the statistic cannot, because χ² counts people.
c.5.00 is 20.00 ⁄ 4, dividing by the number of categories. The categories are already accounted for, in the 3 degrees of freedom.
d.0.20 is 20.00 ⁄ 100, as though χ² scaled with the square of the sample size. It scales in direct proportion to it.
🏷️ χ² grows with n at fixed percentages. Judge size from the percentages.

Question 10

🔍 Conditions and wording

How far a significant result can be pushed

An audit of 300 clients compares the format in which sleep advice was given (three formats) with whether insomnia remitted, and gives χ² = 11.20 on 2 df, P = .004. Mwangi writes that format and remission are associated. Kovalenko writes that the written format produced the best remission rate. At α = .05 the test supports:
  • aboth, since a significant test licenses either
  • bneither, because nobody was assigned a format
  • cMwangi only — the test never names a format
  • dKovalenko only — P = .004 points to one format
🔎 What it is really asking

Which of two readings a single significant chi-square can carry.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conditions and wording: what a significant result does and does not say.

🛠️ The procedure

A significant χ² says one thing: the two variables are associated. It is one number for the whole table, so it cannot name the cell that drove it, and it makes no claim about cause.

🧮 The working
P = .004 is below α = .05, so reject H₀. H₀ was “format and remission are not associated”, and rejecting it gives you Mwangi’s sentence exactly.

Kovalenko has gone one step too far. χ² adds all six cells into a single total; which format did best is a separate question, answered by looking at the three remission rates and the individual contributions — and anything found that way is a follow-up, not part of this test.

Note which objection does not apply. Nobody was assigned a format, so no causal claim is available — but Mwangi did not make one. “Associated” is exactly what an audit can support.

Say it to a friend: “the three formats do not have the same remission rate” — and stop before naming one.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.A significant test licenses one sentence, not any sentence that sounds compatible with it. The extra detail in Kovalenko’s version is not tested.
b.Random assignment is needed for a causal claim. Mwangi only claims an association, which is what a significant χ² on an audit delivers.
d.A P-value has no address in it. It cannot point at the written format, or at any other single cell of the table.
🏷️ Significant χ² = associated. Not which cell, not how big, not why.

Question 11

🔍 Conditions and wording

What must have held for a test to be acceptable

Caprioli reports a chi-square test of a 2 × 5 table of 120 clients, and the referee accepts it without asking for an exact test instead. For that to be reasonable, it must have been true that:
  • aall ten observed counts were at least 5
  • beach of the ten cells held at least 12 clients
  • cthe ten cells held roughly equal numbers of clients
  • dall ten expected counts were at least 5
🔎 What it is really asking

Which counts the usual condition applies to, and how many of them.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conditions: what the expected-count rule requires.

🛠️ The procedure

The convention used on this course is that the expected counts should be at least 5 — all of them, not most of them. It is a rule of thumb about when the chi-square distribution is a good approximation, not a theorem.

🧮 The working
120 clients over 10 cells averages 12 per cell, which sounds safe. It is not a guarantee, because expected counts come from the margins, not from the average.

One rare category is enough to break it. If only 6 of her 120 clients fall in one of the five columns, that column’s expected counts are (60 × 6) ⁄ 120 = 3.0 — below 5, in a sample of 120.

And the observed counts are beside the point. A cell can hold 0 clients and the condition can still be satisfied, because the condition is about the table H₀ predicts, not the table you collected.

The habit: find the smallest row total and the smallest column total, multiply them, divide by N. If that one is at least 5, all of them are.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The rule is about expected counts, not observed ones. An observed count below 5, or even 0, does not by itself break anything.
b.Twelve per cell is the average, 120 ⁄ 10. The condition applies cell by cell to the expected counts, and margins can leave one of them far below the average.
c.Equal cell sizes would mean no association at all, which is not a condition for running the test — it is one of the possible results of it.
🏷️ All expected counts ≥ 5 — a convention, about expected and not observed.

Question 12

🔗 Chi-square against the z test

Whether the two tests can ever disagree

Szymanska has a 2 × 2 table of 200 clients. A colleague tells her that on this table the chi-square test is significant at α = .05 while a two-sided two-proportion z test on the same two percentages is not. Szymanska can answer at once that:
  • ait can when the expected counts are below 5
  • bthat cannot happen — the two P-values are equal
  • cit can, because chi-square uses all four cells
  • dit can, because the z test is the more powerful
🔎 What it is really asking

Are these two tests related, or are they the same test twice?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Chi-square against the z test: what the equivalence rules out.

🛠️ The procedure

On a 2 × 2 table χ² = z², and the chi-square P-value is the two-sided z P-value. Two equal numbers cannot land on opposite sides of α.

🧮 The working
Take any 2 × 2 table. Say the z comes out at 2.50: then z² = 6.25, which is exactly the chi-square statistic, and both P-values are .0124.

The thresholds match too: 1.96² = 3.8416, and the 5% critical value of χ² on 1 df is 3.8415. Pass one and you pass the other.

So what did the colleague see? Almost certainly a one-sided z P-value, which is half the two-sided one — and half of a P just above .05 lands just below it. That is a different question being answered, not a different answer to the same one.

Where the two tests really differ: the z test keeps a sign, so it can be made one-sided and can carry a confidence interval for the difference in proportions. Chi-square squares the direction away, and earns its keep on tables bigger than 2 × 2.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Small expected counts make both results untrustworthy together. They cannot pull the two P-values apart, because the identity χ² = z² is algebra.
c.Chi-square does use all four cells, and on a 2 × 2 that is algebraically identical to comparing the two proportions. Same hypothesis, same arithmetic, same P.
d.Neither test is more powerful than the other, because on a 2 × 2 they are one test. A difference in power would require them to be two.
🏷️ 2 × 2: χ² = z², same two-sided P. A P half the size is a one-sided z.

Question 1

🧩 Explanatory and response

Identifying the explanatory variable

Health researcher Ferreira wants to know whether adults who exercise more have better sleep. For 60 adults she records weekly exercise hours and a sleep-quality score out of 100. In her analysis:
  • aboth are response variables, since neither was manipulated
  • beither may be explanatory, since correlation is symmetric
  • cexercise hours is explanatory and sleep quality is the response
  • dsleep quality is explanatory and exercise hours is the response
🔎 What it is really asking

Which variable is being used to explain the other?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Roles: explanatory against response.

🛠️ The procedure

The explanatory variable is the one you are using to account for the other. Read the research question: whatever sits after "does … affect" or "predicts" is the response.

🧮 The working
Her question is whether exercising more goes with sleeping better. So exercise is doing the explaining and sleep quality is what is being explained.

Exercise hours → explanatory, on the horizontal axis, the x in the regression.
Sleep quality → response, on the vertical axis, the y.

Why it matters here and not for r: the correlation is the same number either way round — swap the axes and r is still 0.56. The regression line is not. Predicting sleep from exercise gives a slope of 2.24; predicting exercise from sleep gives 0.14. Choosing the roles is a decision about the line, not about r.

And note what this design is not: nobody was assigned an amount of exercise, so "explanatory" here means "used to predict", not "shown to cause".
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The absence of manipulation makes this observational; it does not stop one variable being used to explain the other. "Explanatory" is about the analysis, not the design.
b.Correlation is symmetric, but regression is not — and the question is about her analysis, which has a direction built into it.
d.Reversing them would mean using sleep quality to predict how much people exercise — a sensible study, but not the one she described.
🏷️ Explanatory = the predictor, on the x-axis. r ignores the roles; the line does not.

Question 2

🧩 Explanatory and response

What the roles do and do not change

Ferreira’s colleague re-draws the scatterplot with sleep quality on the horizontal axis and exercise hours on the vertical. Compared with the original analysis:
Summary statistics for 60 adults · Ferreira’s study
Exercise (hours per week)Sleep-quality score
mean4.062.0
standard deviation2.510.0
correlationr = 0.56
  • ar is unchanged, but the regression line changes
  • bboth r and the regression line are unchanged
  • cr changes sign, and the line is unchanged
  • dboth r and the regression line change
🔎 What it is really asking

Which of the two is symmetric in x and y, and which is not?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Roles: what swapping the axes does.

🛠️ The procedure

r is symmetric — it is built from the two sets of z-scores multiplied together, and multiplication does not care which is which. The line is not symmetric, because least squares minimises the sum of the squared vertical distances to whichever variable is on the y-axis.

🧮 The working
r stays at 0.56. Same sign, same size.

The line does not. Sleep predicted from exercise:
  b = r s_y ⁄ s_x = 0.56 × 10 ⁄ 2.5 = 2.24 points per hour

Exercise predicted from sleep:
  b = r s_x ⁄ s_y = 0.56 × 2.5 ⁄ 10 = 0.14 hours per point

Two different lines through the same cloud of points. Note that 2.24 × 0.14 = 0.3136, which is r² — the two slopes multiply to r² always.

The practical warning: this is the mistake that turns a correct r into a wrong slope. Work out which SD belongs on top before you divide.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.The line does change, and by a lot — 2.24 against 0.14. Only r survives the swap untouched.
c.r keeps its sign. Nothing about the relationship reversed; only the axes were relabelled.
d.r does not change at all. It has no units and no direction of prediction built into it.
🏷️ Swap the axes: r survives, the line does not.

Question 3

📈 Reading a correlation

Interpreting the size and sign of r

Ferreira finds r = 0.56 between exercise hours and sleep quality. The correct reading of this number is:
Summary statistics for 60 adults · Ferreira’s study
Exercise (hours per week)Sleep-quality score
mean4.062.0
standard deviation2.510.0
correlationr = 0.56
  • aa strong positive linear relationship
  • b56% of sleep quality is explained by exercise
  • cadults exercise 0.56 hours more for each point of sleep quality
  • da moderate positive linear relationship
🔎 What it is really asking

Describe r in words — direction first, then strength.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading a correlation: direction and strength.

🛠️ The procedure

Sign gives the direction; size gives the strength. As a rough guide 0.1–0.3 is weak, 0.3–0.7 moderate and above 0.7 strong. And r measures linear association only.

🧮 The working
The sign is positive, so more exercise goes with better sleep.

0.56 sits in the middle band: a moderate positive linear relationship. The points slope upward but with real scatter around the line.

Three things r = 0.56 does not say:
• Not 56% of anything. That would be r², which is 0.56² = 0.3136, so 31.4%.
• Not a rate of change. The slope is 2.24 points per hour; r carries no units at all.
• Not causation — this is an observational study.

Say it to a friend: "adults who exercise more tend to sleep better, with plenty of exceptions."
✗ Why the others are wrong
a."Strong" is usually reserved for r above about 0.7. At 0.56 the scatter around the line is still substantial.
b.56% is r read as a percentage. The share of variation explained is r², 31.4% — this is the single most common slip on this topic.
c.0.56 is not a slope and has no units. The slope for predicting exercise from sleep happens to be 0.14 hours per point.
🏷️ r: sign = direction, size = strength. Never a percentage, never a rate.

Question 4

📈 Reading a correlation

What r is unaffected by

Ferreira re-expresses exercise in minutes per week instead of hours, and adds 5 points to every sleep-quality score. The correlation is now:
Summary statistics for 60 adults · Ferreira’s study
Exercise (hours per week)Sleep-quality score
mean4.062.0
standard deviation2.510.0
correlationr = 0.56
  • aimpossible to say without the raw data
  • b0.56
  • c33.6
  • d0.61
🔎 What it is really asking

Does r care about units, or about adding a constant?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading a correlation: invariance.

🛠️ The procedure

r is computed from z-scores, so it is unaffected by any change of units or any constant added to either variable. It is a pure, unitless number between −1 and +1.

🧮 The working
Multiplying every x by 60 changes the mean and the SD by the same factor of 60, so every z-score is untouched.

Adding 5 to every y shifts the mean by 5 and changes the SD not at all, so again every z-score is untouched.

r = 0.56, exactly as before.

What does change: the regression line. In minutes the slope becomes 2.24 ⁄ 60 = 0.0373 points per minute, and the +5 lifts the intercept to 58.04. The line is in units; r is not.

The useful consequence: you can compare r across studies that measured things on completely different scales. You cannot compare slopes that way.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The raw data are not needed. Linear rescaling provably leaves r alone, which is one of the reasons r is used at all.
c.33.6 is 0.56 × 60, treating r as though it carried the units of x. r has no units to rescale.
d.0.61 suggests that rescaling strengthens the relationship. No change of units can move r — the points keep exactly the same pattern, only the axis labels change.
🏷️ r is unitless: rescale or shift all you like, r does not move.

Question 5

📈 Reading a correlation

Comparing two correlations

In two separate samples, researcher Kowal finds r = −0.74 between screen time and sleep quality, and r = +0.41 between reading time and sleep quality. Which statement is correct?
  • athey are equally strong, in opposite directions
  • ba negative r is always weaker than a positive one
  • cthe screen-time relationship is the stronger of the two
  • dthe reading-time relationship is the stronger of the two
🔎 What it is really asking

Strength lives in the size of r, not in its sign.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading a correlation: comparing two of them.

🛠️ The procedure

Compare |r|. The sign only tells you which way the cloud of points tilts; it says nothing whatever about how tightly they cluster.

🧮 The working
|−0.74| = 0.74 against |+0.41| = 0.41.

0.74 > 0.41, so the screen-time relationship is stronger — its points sit closer to a straight line.

In shares of variation: screen time accounts for 0.74² = 54.8% of the variation in sleep quality, reading time for 0.41² = 16.8%. More than three times as much.

The negative sign means only that more screen time goes with worse sleep. r = −0.74 and r = +0.74 are mirror images of equal strength.

The mental picture: |r| is how thin the cloud is; the sign is which way it leans.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.They are not equally strong — 0.74 and 0.41 are very different sizes. Equal strength in opposite directions would be −0.74 against +0.74.
b.Nothing about a negative sign weakens a correlation. r = −0.98 is nearly a perfect straight line.
d.0.41 is the weaker of the two. Its points scatter much more widely around their line.
🏷️ Strength = |r|. The sign is direction only.

Question 6

📐 The least-squares line

The slope from summary statistics

Using Ferreira’s summary statistics, the slope of the least-squares line for predicting sleep quality from exercise hours is:
Summary statistics for 60 adults · Ferreira’s study
Exercise (hours per week)Sleep-quality score
mean4.062.0
standard deviation2.510.0
correlationr = 0.56
  • a2.24
  • b0.14
  • c0.56
  • d5.60
🔎 What it is really asking

Build the slope out of r and the two standard deviations.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The least-squares line: the slope.

🛠️ The procedure

b = r × (s_y ⁄ s_x) — the SD of the response on top, the SD of the explanatory variable underneath.

🧮 The working
r = 0.56, s_y = 10.0 (sleep-quality points), s_x = 2.5 (hours).

b = 0.56 × (10.0 ⁄ 2.5) = 0.56 × 4 = 2.24

Check the units, always. The slope must come out in "response units per explanatory unit": points per hour. 10 points ⁄ 2.5 hours gives points per hour. Flip the ratio and you get hours per point, which answers a different question.

What it means: two adults one hour apart in weekly exercise differ, on average, by 2.24 points of sleep quality.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.0.14 is r × (s_x ⁄ s_y) — the ratio upside down. It is the slope for predicting exercise from sleep, in hours per point.
c.0.56 is r itself. r and the slope coincide only when both SDs are equal, which they are not here.
d.5.60 is r × s_y, forgetting to divide by s_x at all.
🏷️ b = r · s_y ⁄ s_x. Response SD on top. Check the units.

Question 7

📐 The least-squares line

The intercept from summary statistics

For Ferreira’s data the intercept of the least-squares line for predicting sleep quality from exercise hours, to two decimal places, is:
Summary statistics for 60 adults · Ferreira’s study
Exercise (hours per week)Sleep-quality score
mean4.062.0
standard deviation2.510.0
correlationr = 0.56
  • a8.96
  • b53.04
  • c62.00
  • d58.00
🔎 What it is really asking

Use the fact that the line passes through the point of means.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The least-squares line: the intercept.

🛠️ The procedure

a = ȳ − b x̄. It falls straight out of the fact that every least-squares line passes through (x̄, ȳ).

🧮 The working
Slope first: b = 2.24 (from r s_y ⁄ s_x).

a = 62.0 − 2.24 × 4.0 = 62.0 − 8.96 = 53.04

The line is ŷ = 53.04 + 2.24x.

Check it on the means: 53.04 + 2.24 × 4.0 = 62.00 = ȳ. Every least-squares line does this, which makes it a free check on your arithmetic.

Does the intercept mean anything here? It is the predicted sleep quality at zero hours of exercise. x = 0 is inside the plausible range for exercise, so 53.04 is interpretable — but it would be meaningless in a study where x never goes near zero.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.8.96 is b x̄, the quantity you subtract from ȳ. One step short of the answer.
c.62.00 is ȳ, the mean of the response. That is the predicted value at x = x̄ = 4, not at x = 0.
d.58.00 is 62 − 4, subtracting x̄ without multiplying by the slope first.
🏷️ a = ȳ − b x̄. The line always goes through (x̄, ȳ) — use it as a check.

Question 8

📐 The least-squares line

Using the line to predict

An adult in Ferreira’s population exercises 8 hours a week. Using ŷ = 53.04 + 2.24x, their predicted sleep-quality score, to two decimal places, is:
Summary statistics for 60 adults · Ferreira’s study
Exercise (hours per week)Sleep-quality score
mean4.062.0
standard deviation2.510.0
correlationr = 0.56
  • a17.92
  • b62.00
  • c79.92
  • d70.96
🔎 What it is really asking

Substitute into the line — intercept plus slope times x.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The least-squares line: prediction.

🛠️ The procedure

Put the x into the equation: ŷ = a + bx. Both terms, every time.

🧮 The working
ŷ = 53.04 + 2.24 × 8 = 53.04 + 17.92 = 70.96

Sense-check it against the means: 8 hours is 4 above the mean of 4, so the prediction should sit 4 × 2.24 = 8.96 above ȳ = 62. And 62 + 8.96 = 70.96. ✓

What a prediction is: the average sleep quality of all adults who exercise 8 hours a week. Individuals scatter around it — with r = 0.56 there is a great deal of scatter, so 70.96 is a centre, not a forecast for one person.

Where to stop: this line was fitted on adults averaging 4 hours with an SD of 2.5. Feeding in 30 hours would be extrapolation, and the line carries no evidence out there.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.17.92 is 2.24 × 8, the slope term on its own. The intercept has been dropped.
b.62.00 is ȳ — the prediction at the mean level of exercise, not at 8 hours.
c.79.92 is 62 + 17.92, adding the slope term to the mean of y instead of to the intercept. It double-counts the 4 hours already inside ȳ.
🏷️ ŷ = a + bx. Both terms, then sense-check against (x̄, ȳ).

Question 9

🥧 r-squared

The share of variation explained

In Ferreira’s study the percentage of the variation in sleep quality that is explained by exercise hours is:
Summary statistics for 60 adults · Ferreira’s study
Exercise (hours per week)Sleep-quality score
mean4.062.0
standard deviation2.510.0
correlationr = 0.56
  • a31.4%
  • b56.0%
  • c74.8%
  • d68.6%
🔎 What it is really asking

Square the correlation, then read it as a percentage.

🧭 Which type of question this is

r-squared: the share of variation explained.

🛠️ The procedure

r² = r × r, reported as a percentage. It is the share of the variation in the response that the line accounts for.

🧮 The working
r² = 0.56² = 0.3136, so 31.4%.

In plain words: exercise accounts for about 31% of the variation in sleep scores. Nearly 69% of that variation is still unaccounted for — age, stress, caffeine, shift work, everything else.

Why squaring is not a technicality: r = 0.56 sounds like "about half the story". r² = 31% says it is under a third. The squaring is what turns a vague feeling of association into an honest accounting of variation.

Symmetric too: r² is 31.4% whichever variable you call the response, because r is the same either way.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.56.0% is r read directly as a percentage — the designed trap on this question, and the one most people fall into.
c.74.8% is √0.56, moving in the wrong direction entirely. Squaring makes a number below 1 smaller, not bigger.
d.68.6% is 1 − r², the share left unexplained. Right arithmetic, wrong half.
🏷️ Square it. r = 0.56 explains 31%, not 56%.

Question 10

🥧 r-squared

What r-squared does not tell you

A second study of 400 adults reports r² = 0.81 between hours of screen use and a sleep score. Which conclusion is justified?
  • ascreen use is responsible for 81% of poor sleep
  • bthe line predicts 81% of individual scores correctly
  • cthe line accounts for 81% of the variation in the sleep score
  • dthe correlation between the two variables is 0.81
🔎 What it is really asking

Variation explained by the line — nothing more than that.

🧭 Which type of question this is

r-squared: reading it correctly.

🛠️ The procedure

r² is the share of the variation in the response that the fitted line accounts for. It is not r, it is not a claim about cause, and it is not a hit rate.

🧮 The working
r² = 0.81 means the line accounts for 81% of the variation in sleep scores — the remaining 19% is scatter around it.

Work out r if you want it: r = ±√0.81 = ±0.90. The sign is not recoverable from r² alone; you need the scatterplot or the slope. Here it would be negative.

Three readings to refuse:
• Cause. Observational data. Shift work could drive both.
• A hit rate. r² says nothing about how many individuals land near their prediction; 19% unexplained variation still leaves real misses.
• The percentage of poor sleep. r² is about variation, not about counting people.

Keep the pair straight: r describes the points, r² accounts for the variation.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Cause needs a design that rules out alternatives. A share of explained variation, however large, cannot supply one.
b."81% of individual scores correct" is not what variation explained means — and a prediction from a line is rarely exactly right for anybody.
d.0.81 is r², so r is ±0.90. Reading r² as r is the same confusion as the previous question running backwards.
🏷️ r² = variation explained by the line. Not r, not cause, not a hit rate.

Question 11

🔍 Residuals, outliers and influence

Computing a residual

One of Ferreira’s adults exercises 6 hours a week and scores 71 on sleep quality. Using ŷ = 53.04 + 2.24x, that adult’s residual, to two decimal places, is:
Summary statistics for 60 adults · Ferreira’s study
Exercise (hours per week)Sleep-quality score
mean4.062.0
standard deviation2.510.0
correlationr = 0.56
  • a−4.52
  • b+66.48
  • c+9.00
  • d+4.52
🔎 What it is really asking

Observed minus predicted, with the sign kept.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Residuals: computing one.

🛠️ The procedure

residual = observed y − predicted ŷ. Observed first, always — the sign is part of the answer.

🧮 The working
Predicted: ŷ = 53.04 + 2.24 × 6 = 53.04 + 13.44 = 66.48.

Residual = 71 − 66.48 = +4.52

The sign carries the meaning: positive means this adult sleeps better than the line predicted for someone who exercises 6 hours. They sit above the line.

And residuals are the whole point of least squares: the line is chosen to make the sum of the squared residuals as small as it can possibly be. No other straight line through this cloud has a smaller total.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.−4.52 is predicted minus observed, the subtraction the wrong way round. It would put this adult below the line when they are above it.
b.+66.48 is the predicted value, not the residual. The residual is what is left over after you subtract it.
c.+9.00 is 71 − 62, measuring from the mean of y instead of from the line. That ignores everything the line knows about this adult.
🏷️ Residual = observed − predicted. Keep the sign; it says above or below.

Question 12

🔍 Residuals, outliers and influence

What the residuals must do

Researcher Nowicki fits ŷ = 9.70 + 2.05x to five participants’ practice sessions and recall scores, and lists the residuals. Which statement about them is always true of a least-squares fit?
The five residuals from ŷ = 9.70 + 2.05x
Practice sessions246810
Observed score1417232630
Predicted by the line13.8017.9022.0026.1030.20
Residual+0.20−0.90+1.00−0.10−0.20
  • athe largest one marks an error in the data
  • bthey add up to zero
  • cthey are all positive or all negative
  • dthey add up to r²
🔎 What it is really asking

A property of every least-squares line, not of this particular dataset.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Residuals: their guaranteed properties.

🛠️ The procedure

For any least-squares line the residuals sum to zero (so their mean is zero) and their squares add to the smallest total any straight line could achieve.

🧮 The working
Add them: +0.20 − 0.90 + 1.00 − 0.10 − 0.20 = 0.00, exactly.

This is not luck. The least-squares line passes through (x̄, ȳ) = (6, 22), and that forces the positive and negative residuals into balance. It is the same reason deviations from a mean always sum to zero.

So the sum is useless as a measure of fit — it is zero for a good line and a terrible one alike. What measures fit is the sum of the squares, 0.04 + 0.81 + 1.00 + 0.01 + 0.04 = 1.90, and no other straight line beats 1.90 here.

How residuals are actually used: plot them against x. A shapeless band means the line fits; a curve or a widening fan means it does not.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.A large residual marks a point far from the line. It may be an error, or a real and interesting case — the residual itself cannot tell you which.
c.Residuals come in both signs by construction — if they were all positive they could not sum to zero.
d.r² is a share of variation between 0 and 1 and has nothing to do with the total of the residuals, which is always zero.
🏷️ Residuals always sum to zero. Fit is judged on their squares, and by the plot.

Question 13

🔍 Residuals, outliers and influence

Outliers against influential points

In a scatterplot of 40 points, one point sits at a very high x value, far to the right of all the others, and close to the line’s current path. Removing it would most likely:
  • achange the slope noticeably, because it has high leverage
  • bleave the slope unchanged, because it lies near the line
  • cchange r but not the slope, since r ignores position
  • dhave no effect, as one point in 40 cannot matter
🔎 What it is really asking

Extreme in x, not extreme in residual — which word applies?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Residuals, outliers and influence: telling the two apart.

🛠️ The procedure

A point extreme in x has high leverage and is potentially influential: it can swing the line. A point with a large residual is an outlier in the y direction and may barely move the line at all.

🧮 The working
Picture the line as a plank balanced at (x̄, ȳ). A point far out in x acts on a long lever arm, so even a small vertical tug there rotates the whole plank.

Being near the line now is not reassurance. It means this point is holding the line where it is. Take it away and the slope is decided entirely by the remaining cluster, which can tilt it a long way.

The two words, kept apart:
• Outlier — big residual, far from the line vertically. Often obvious, often not influential.
• Influential — extreme in x. Often sits close to the line and is easy to miss.

The practical test: fit the line twice, with and without the point, and report both. That is the only way to see influence rather than guess at it.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Lying near the line shows that the point agrees with the current fit, not that the fit would survive without it. High-leverage points usually look well behaved.
c.r and the slope are tied together by b = r s_y ⁄ s_x, so a point that moves one generally moves the other. Position in x matters to both.
d.One point in 40 can matter enormously if it sits far out in x. Leverage, not count, decides.
🏷️ Extreme in x = high leverage = potentially influential. Big residual = outlier.

Question 14

⚖️ What it does NOT mean

What a correlation does not establish

A newspaper reports Ferreira’s r = 0.56 under the headline “Exercise improves sleep”. The headline is unjustified because:
Summary statistics for 60 adults · Ferreira’s study
Exercise (hours per week)Sleep-quality score
mean4.062.0
standard deviation2.510.0
correlationr = 0.56
  • athe sample of 60 adults is too small
  • br measures only linear association
  • cnobody was assigned an amount of exercise
  • dr = 0.56 is too small to support any claim
🔎 What it is really asking

Which feature of the study blocks a causal claim?

🧭 Which type of question this is

What it does NOT mean: correlation and causation.

🛠️ The procedure

A causal claim needs a design that rules out the alternatives — ideally random assignment. In an observational study the two variables may be linked by something else entirely, or run in the other direction.

🧮 The working
Ferreira measured how much people already exercise. She did not allocate it. So at least three explanations survive her data equally well:

• Exercise → sleep, the headline’s reading.
• Sleep → exercise: people who sleep well have the energy to train. The arrow runs backwards and r is identical.
• A third variable: chronic pain, shift work or depression would push exercise down and sleep quality down together, with no direct link between the two at all. This is confounding.

r cannot distinguish between the three. No correlation can.

What would justify the headline: randomly assigning adults to an exercise programme or a control condition. Then the groups differ only by chance in everything else, and the arrow is pinned down by the design.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.60 adults is a workable sample, and sample size is an issue of precision, not of causal direction. Six thousand adults would not fix this headline.
b.True, and irrelevant here — a linear association is exactly what she found. The problem is the causal arrow, not the shape.
d.The size of r is not the objection. Even r = 0.95 from an observational study would not establish cause.
🏷️ No random assignment, no causal claim — however big r is.

Question 15

⚖️ What it does NOT mean

When r near zero is misleading

Researcher Adeyemi plots anxiety against performance for 80 students and finds r = 0.04. The scatterplot shows performance rising to a peak at moderate anxiety and falling again at high anxiety. The correct conclusion is:
  • athere is no relationship between the two variables
  • br should be recomputed with the axes swapped
  • cthe relationship is real but too weak to matter
  • dthere is a relationship, but it is not linear
🔎 What it is really asking

What does r actually measure, and what can hide from it?

🧭 Which type of question this is

What it does NOT mean: r near zero.

🛠️ The procedure

r measures linear association only. A strong but curved relationship can give r close to zero, which is why you plot the data before you trust r.

🧮 The working
The pattern described is an inverted U — the classic anxiety-performance curve.

The rising half contributes positive products of z-scores and the falling half contributes negative ones. They cancel, and r lands near zero.

So r = 0.04 means "no straight-line trend", which is true. It does not mean "no relationship", which is false — anxiety predicts performance rather well here, just not with a line.

The rule this is here to teach: r and the least-squares line are summaries of a linear pattern, and a summary of the wrong shape is worthless. Look at the scatterplot first, every time. A number cannot tell you what shape it came from.

What to do instead: describe the curve, or fit a model with a squared term.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a."No relationship" is exactly the inference the scatterplot forbids. The curve is there in plain sight.
b.Swapping the axes leaves r unchanged at 0.04 — it is symmetric. The problem is the shape, not the orientation.
c.The relationship is far from too weak to matter; it is strong and curved. r = 0.04 is measuring the wrong thing, not measuring a weak thing.
🏷️ r = 0 means no LINE. Plot it before you believe it.

Question 1

🧩 Explanatory and response

Matching a slope to its direction of prediction

Language researcher Moreau measures, for 85 adults, weekly hours of practice on a language app and a vocabulary score, and finds r = 0.64. Her output lists two slopes, 4.80 and 0.0853. The slope for predicting the vocabulary score from practice hours is:
Summary statistics for 85 adults · Moreau’s study
Practice (hours per week)Vocabulary score
mean3.054.0
standard deviation1.29.0
  • aeither, since r is 0.64 both ways
  • b2.44, the average of the two
  • c4.80, in test points per hour
  • d0.0853, in hours per test point
🔎 What it is really asking

Which of the two lines is being asked for — and what units must its slope have?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Roles: matching a slope to the direction of prediction.

🛠️ The procedure

Let the units decide. A slope is always in response units per explanatory unit. Predicting a score from hours means points per hour.

🧮 The working
Vocabulary score is the response, practice hours the explanatory variable. So the slope must be in points per hour.

b = r × (s_y ⁄ s_x) = 0.64 × (9.0 ⁄ 1.2) = 0.64 × 7.5 = 4.80 points per hour.

The other number is the other line: 0.64 × (1.2 ⁄ 9.0) = 0.0853 hours per point, for predicting practice from vocabulary.

A neat check that they are a matched pair: 4.80 × 0.08533 = 0.4096 = r². The two slopes of the two lines always multiply to r².

The habit: before you pick a slope off a page, say out loud what it is "per" — per hour or per point. The units identify the line far faster than the arithmetic does.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.r is the same both ways, but the two lines are not — 4.80 against 0.0853. Correlation is symmetric; regression is not.
b.2.44 averages the two slopes. There is no sense in which the average of two different lines is a line.
d.0.0853 is the slope of the other line, in hours per point. It answers "how much more practice goes with one extra vocabulary point".
🏷️ A slope is response units per explanatory unit. The units name the line.

Question 2

🧩 Explanatory and response

Assigning the roles from a research aim

Psychologist Rinaldi wants to work out how many therapy sessions a client is likely to attend from the score the client gives on a motivation questionnaire at intake. The least-squares line she needs is the one with:
  • asessions attended as the response
  • bmotivation score as the response
  • cwhichever pairing makes r² larger
  • deither pairing, since r is symmetric
🔎 What it is really asking

Which quantity is she trying to produce a value for?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Roles: reading the roles off the research aim.

🛠️ The procedure

Whatever is being predicted is the response, y. Whatever the prediction is made from is explanatory, x. The sentence "predict A from B" hands you both.

🧮 The working
She wants a number of sessions out of the analysis, and she has a motivation score to put into it.

Sessions attended → response, on the vertical axis, the y.
Motivation score → explanatory, on the horizontal axis, the x.

Her line is ŷ = a + b × motivation, with b in sessions per questionnaire point. Fitting it the other way round would give a line that predicts motivation from attendance — perfectly respectable arithmetic, and no use to her at all, because at intake she has the motivation score and not the attendance.

Say it to a friend: "the thing I have goes on the bottom; the thing I want goes up the side."
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Putting motivation on the vertical axis builds a line that predicts motivation from sessions attended, which reverses what she has and what she wants.
c.r² is identical whichever way round you fit the line, so it cannot choose the roles for you. The research question chooses them.
d.r is symmetric, but the least-squares line is not: it minimises vertical distances to whichever variable sits on the y-axis.
🏷️ “Predict A from B” → A is y, B is x. The aim decides, not the arithmetic.

Question 3

📈 Reading a correlation

Recovering r from the slope

Moreau’s least-squares line for predicting vocabulary score from practice hours has a slope of 4.80. Using her summary statistics below, the correlation between the two variables, to two decimal places, is:
Summary statistics for 85 adults · Moreau’s study
Practice (hours per week)Vocabulary score
mean3.054.0
standard deviation1.29.0
  • a4.80
  • b36.00
  • c0.41
  • d0.64
🔎 What it is really asking

Run b = r s_y ⁄ s_x backwards to get r out of it.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading a correlation: recovering it from the fitted slope.

🛠️ The procedure

Rearrange b = r × (s_y ⁄ s_x) into r = b × (s_x ⁄ s_y). The ratio turns over when you move it across.

🧮 The working
r = 4.80 × (1.2 ⁄ 9.0) = 4.80 × 0.13333 = 0.64

Check it forwards: 0.64 × (9.0 ⁄ 1.2) = 0.64 × 7.5 = 4.80. ✓

The safety net you always have here: r must lie between −1 and +1. If your rearrangement produces 36, you have divided where you should have multiplied — no further checking needed, the answer is impossible on its face.

Why this is worth being able to do: output often prints a slope and not an r, or the other way round. With the two standard deviations you can always move between them, and they describe different things — 4.80 is a rate of change, 0.64 is how tightly the points hug the line.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.4.80 is the slope itself. It is in points per hour, and a correlation has no units — nor can it exceed 1.
b.36.00 is 4.80 × (9.0 ⁄ 1.2), the ratio left the wrong way up. A "correlation" of 36 is impossible, which is the clue.
c.0.41 is r², the share of variation the line explains. It is a correct quantity answering a different question.
🏷️ r = b · s_x ⁄ s_y. If |r| comes out above 1, you flipped the ratio.

Question 4

📈 Reading a correlation

Why r changes between samples

Czarnecki repeats Moreau’s study but recruits only adults who practise between 2 and 4 hours a week, and finds r = 0.28 where Moreau found 0.64. The most likely reason is:
  • athe relationship is not linear there
  • bthe restricted range of practice hours
  • ca mistake, since r cannot change
  • dthe smaller sample shrinks r
🔎 What it is really asking

What did Czarnecki change about the sample — and how does that reach r?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading a correlation: what the sample’s spread does to it.

🛠️ The procedure

r measures how much of the scatter in y lines up with x. Narrow the range of x and you remove the part of the pattern that was easiest to see, so r falls even though the underlying relationship is unchanged.

🧮 The working
Moreau’s adults practised anywhere from about 1 to 6 hours — plenty of spread for a trend to show itself in. Czarnecki keeps only a narrow band, 2 to 4 hours.

Inside that band, the predicted vocabulary scores run only from 49.2 to 58.8 — a spread of 9.6 points — while individuals still scatter about 6.9 points around the line, exactly as they did before. The signal has shrunk and the noise has not, so the points look far more like a shapeless cloud: r = 0.28, and r² falls from 41.0% to 7.8%.

The slope, by contrast, is barely affected — the relationship itself did not change, only the slice of it being looked at.

This is called restriction of range, and it is why a selection test can look useless when it is evaluated only on the people who were already selected.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Nothing here suggests a curve, and a curve would not explain the drop: cutting the range of x is sufficient on its own.
c.r is a property of the sample in front of you, not a constant of nature. Change who is in the sample and r changes with it.
d.Sample size affects how precisely r is estimated, not how large it tends to be. A smaller sample is as likely to overstate r as to understate it.
🏷️ Narrow the x range and r falls, even with the relationship untouched.

Question 5

📈 Reading a correlation

Recovering r from r-squared and the slope’s sign

Media psychologist Vidal reports r² = 0.49 between daily social-media hours and a loneliness score for 120 adults, and notes that her fitted line slopes downwards. The correlation, to two decimal places, is:
  • a−0.49
  • b−0.24
  • c−0.70
  • d+0.70
🔎 What it is really asking

Two steps: the size from r², then the sign from somewhere else.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading a correlation: recovering it from r-squared.

🛠️ The procedure

|r| = √r² gives the size. r² is always positive, so it cannot give you the sign — that has to come from the slope or the scatterplot.

🧮 The working
Size: √0.49 = 0.70.

Sign: the line slopes downwards, so r and the slope share that negative sign.

r = −0.70

In words: more social-media hours go with lower loneliness scores — the line slopes down — moderately to strongly, with 49% of the variation in loneliness accounted for by the line.

The step people forget: squaring destroys the sign, so no amount of arithmetic on r² alone can recover it. r = +0.70 and r = −0.70 give exactly the same r² = 0.49. Always fetch the direction from the slope, the scatterplot or the description of the relationship.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.−0.49 is r² wearing a minus sign. The square root has not been taken, so the size is wrong as well as unnecessary.
b.−0.24 is 0.49², squaring again instead of taking the root. That moves away from r, not towards it.
d.+0.70 has the right size and the wrong sign. A downward-sloping line cannot have a positive correlation.
🏷️ |r| = √r². The sign comes from the slope, never from r² itself.

Question 6

📐 The least-squares line

Recovering a standard deviation from the line

Moreau’s least-squares line for predicting vocabulary score from weekly practice hours is ŷ = 39.60 + 4.80x. Her correlation is r = 0.64 and the standard deviation of practice hours is 1.2 hours. The standard deviation of the vocabulary scores, to two decimal places, is:
  • a9.00
  • b5.76
  • c7.50
  • d0.16
🔎 What it is really asking

The slope formula has four quantities in it; three are given, so solve for the fourth.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The least-squares line: solving the slope formula for an input.

🛠️ The procedure

Start from b = r × (s_y ⁄ s_x) and rearrange for the unknown: s_y = b × s_x ⁄ r.

🧮 The working
s_y = (4.80 × 1.2) ⁄ 0.64 = 5.76 ⁄ 0.64 = 9.00

Check it forwards: 0.64 × (9.00 ⁄ 1.2) = 0.64 × 7.5 = 4.80. ✓

A sense-check on the size, too. The slope says one extra hour of practice goes with 4.80 more points, and an hour is well inside one SD of practice (1.2 h). So the vocabulary scores must spread over quite a few points — 9 is believable; 0.16 could not possibly support a slope of 4.80.

The habit worth building: write the formula out, mark which letters you have, and rearrange on paper before you reach for the calculator. Every "work backwards" question on this topic is the same formula read in a different direction.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.5.76 is 4.80 × 1.2, the numerator on its own. Dividing by r is the step that is missing.
c.7.50 is 4.80 ⁄ 0.64, where s_x has been left out. That is the ratio s_y ⁄ s_x, one multiplication short of s_y.
d.0.16 is (0.64 × 1.2) ⁄ 4.80 — the rearrangement upside down, with b and r swapped over.
🏷️ b = r · s_y ⁄ s_x has four slots. Know three and you can always find the fourth.
