Question 7

📐 The least-squares line

Working back from a prediction to its x

Using Moreau’s line ŷ = 39.60 + 4.80x for predicting vocabulary score from weekly practice hours, the number of practice hours whose predicted score is 58.80, to two decimal places, is:
  • a0.25
  • b4.00
  • c12.25
  • d4.80
🔎 What it is really asking

The prediction is given and x is missing — so solve the equation, do not evaluate it.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The least-squares line: inverting a prediction.

🛠️ The procedure

Undo the two operations in the order they were done to x: take the intercept off first, then divide by the slope.

🧮 The working
58.80 = 39.60 + 4.80x

58.80 − 39.60 = 4.80x, so 19.20 = 4.80x

x = 19.20 ⁄ 4.80 = 4.00 hours

Check it forwards: 39.60 + 4.80 × 4 = 39.60 + 19.20 = 58.80. ✓

The whole line, hour by hour:
ŷ = 39.60 + 4.80x · vocabulary score predicted from practice hours
Practice hours12345
Predicted vocabulary score44.4049.2054.0058.8063.60
A second way to see it: 58.80 is 4.80 above ȳ = 54.00, and one hour is worth 4.80 points, so the answer is one hour above x̄ = 3.0. Every least-squares line passes through (x̄, ȳ), which makes the means a useful place to count from.

And one warning about inverting a line: this is arithmetic on the fitted equation, not a prediction of practice hours. If Moreau genuinely wanted to predict hours from scores, she would have to fit the other line, whose slope is 0.0853.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.25 is 4.80 ⁄ 19.20, the final division turned over. Hours should come out of points divided by points-per-hour.
c.12.25 is 58.80 ⁄ 4.80, dividing before the intercept has been removed. The 39.60 is not part of what the slope multiplies.
d.4.80 is the slope. It is the number you divide by, not the answer.
🏷️ Subtract the intercept, then divide by the slope. Check it forwards.

Question 8

📐 The least-squares line

The slope of the line fitted the other way round

Moreau now wants a line for predicting weekly practice hours from the vocabulary score, still with r = 0.64. The slope of that line, to four decimal places, is:
Summary statistics for 85 adults · Moreau’s study
Practice (hours per week)Vocabulary score
mean3.054.0
standard deviation1.29.0
  • a4.8000
  • b0.6400
  • c0.2083
  • d0.0853
🔎 What it is really asking

Which variable is the response now — and which SD therefore goes on top?

🧭 Which type of question this is

The least-squares line: refitting with the roles swapped.

🛠️ The procedure

b = r × (s_y ⁄ s_x) with y meaning the response of this line. Practice hours are now the response, so the hours SD goes on top.

🧮 The working
Response: practice hours, SD 1.2. Explanatory: vocabulary score, SD 9.0.

b = 0.64 × (1.2 ⁄ 9.0) = 0.64 × 0.13333 = 0.0853 hours per point.

Check the units: hours per vocabulary point, which is what a line predicting hours must give. And a sense-check on the size — one extra vocabulary point is a small thing, so a twelfth of an hour is about right.

Why you cannot just rearrange the old line: turning ŷ = 39.60 + 4.80x inside out gives a slope of 1 ⁄ 4.80 = 0.2083, and that is a different number. Least squares minimises vertical distances to the response, so swapping the roles changes what is being minimised and the line has to be fitted again.

The relationship between the two slopes: 4.80 × 0.08533 = 0.4096 = r² (the identity is exact on the unrounded slope). The two lines coincide only when r² = 1, which is also the only time inverting the equation would have worked.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.4.8000 is the slope of the first line, in points per hour. It has the two standard deviations the wrong way up for this question.
b.0.6400 is r itself. r equals the slope only when the two standard deviations are equal, and 1.2 against 9.0 they are not.
c.0.2083 is 1 ⁄ 4.80, obtained by rearranging the first equation rather than refitting. The two regression lines are not inverses of one another.
🏷️ Swap the roles, refit. Response SD on top — never invert the old equation.

Question 9

🥧 r-squared

r-squared when only the slope is given

Moreau’s line for predicting vocabulary score from practice hours has a slope of 4.80. Using the summary statistics below, the percentage of the variation in vocabulary scores that the line accounts for, to one decimal place, is:
Summary statistics for 85 adults · Moreau’s study
Practice (hours per week)Vocabulary score
mean3.054.0
standard deviation1.29.0
  • a41.0%
  • b64.0%
  • c80.0%
  • d59.0%
🔎 What it is really asking

r is not printed, so recover it first — then square it.

🧭 Which type of question this is

r-squared: two steps, with r recovered on the way.

🛠️ The procedure

Get r out of the slope with r = b × (s_x ⁄ s_y), then square it and read it as a percentage.

🧮 The working
Step one: r = 4.80 × (1.2 ⁄ 9.0) = 0.64

Step two: r² = 0.64² = 0.4096, so 41.0%

In plain words: practice hours account for about 41% of the differences in vocabulary scores among these 85 adults. The other 59% belongs to everything else — schooling, reading habits, how long they have been learning.

Why the two-step shape matters: a stem will often hand you a slope and the two standard deviations and ask for a share of variation. Nothing in that sentence mentions r, and r is the only route from one to the other. Recognising the missing middle step is most of the work.

And the usual trap, once more: 0.64 is not 64%.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.64.0% is r read straight off as a percentage. r is recovered correctly and then never squared — the most common slip on this topic.
c.80.0% is √0.64. Taking the root instead of the square moves a number below 1 in the wrong direction.
d.59.0% is 1 − r², the share of the variation left unexplained. Right arithmetic, wrong half of it.
🏷️ Slope → r → r². Two steps, and the squaring is the second one.

Question 10

🥧 r-squared

r-squared against the size of the slope

Two studies of the same two variables are reported below. Vidal finds r² = 0.49 with a slope of −2.50 loneliness points per hour; Mertens finds r² = 0.25 with a slope of −6.00. Which statement is correct?
Two studies of daily social-media hours against a loneliness score
Studyr²Slope (loneliness points per hour)
Vidal · 120 adults0.49−2.50
Mertens · 140 adults0.25−6.00
  • aMertens’s relationship is stronger
  • bthe two studies cannot be compared
  • cVidal’s points cluster more tightly
  • dVidal’s change per hour is larger
🔎 What it is really asking

Which number measures tightness, and which measures steepness?

🧭 Which type of question this is

r-squared: telling it apart from the slope.

🛠️ The procedure

r² is about scatter — how closely the points sit to the line. The slope is about rate — how much y moves per unit of x. A study can be high on one and low on the other.

🧮 The working
Vidal: r² = 0.49, so 49% of the variation in loneliness is accounted for. Her points hug the line more closely.

Mertens: r² = 0.25, so 25%. His points scatter more widely — but each extra hour is worth 6.00 points on his line against 2.50 on hers.

So the correct reading is: Vidal’s relationship is the tighter one, Mertens’s is the steeper one. There is no contradiction in that. Steepness and tightness are different properties of a cloud of points.

The picture to hold: a steep line through a wide smear of points, against a gentle line through a narrow ribbon. The second has the larger r²; the first has the larger slope.

And why it matters practically: the slope tells you how much difference an hour makes, which is what an intervention cares about. r² tells you how well you can predict one person, which is what a screening tool cares about. Reporting one and calling it the other is a real error, not a quibble.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Strength of association is measured by r², and Mertens’s is the lower of the two. A steeper slope is not a stronger relationship.
b.They are directly comparable: r² is unitless, and here both slopes are in the same units, loneliness points per hour.
d.Vidal’s change per hour is the smaller one, 2.50 against 6.00. r² says nothing about the size of the slope.
🏷️ r² = tightness, slope = steepness. A study can be high on one, low on the other.

Question 11

🔍 Residuals, outliers and influence

A residual with the line not yet built

One adult in Moreau’s study practises 5 hours a week and scores 58 on the vocabulary test. Taking r = 0.64 with the summary statistics below, and predicting vocabulary score from practice hours, that adult’s residual, to two decimal places, is:
Summary statistics for 85 adults · Moreau’s study
Practice (hours per week)Vocabulary score
mean3.054.0
standard deviation1.29.0
  • a+5.60
  • b63.60
  • c+4.00
  • d−5.60
🔎 What it is really asking

Three steps: slope, then prediction, then observed minus predicted.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Residuals: computing one from summary statistics.

🛠️ The procedure

Build the line, use it, then subtract: b = r s_y ⁄ s_x, a = ȳ − b x̄, residual = y − ŷ.

🧮 The working
Slope: b = 0.64 × (9.0 ⁄ 1.2) = 4.80

Intercept: a = 54.0 − 4.80 × 3.0 = 54.0 − 14.4 = 39.60

Prediction at x = 5: ŷ = 39.60 + 4.80 × 5 = 39.60 + 24.00 = 63.60

Residual: 58 − 63.60 = −5.60

The sign is the message: this adult scores 5.60 points below what the line predicts for someone practising 5 hours a week. They sit under the line.

And the aside worth carrying: a negative residual is not a bad result or an error. With r = 0.64 there is a great deal of scatter, and residuals of five or six points are entirely ordinary. The line predicts the average score at 5 hours, not this person’s score.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.+5.60 is predicted minus observed, the subtraction the wrong way round. It would place this adult above the line when they are below it.
b.63.60 is the predicted value. It is the number you subtract from, and the residual is what is left after you do.
c.+4.00 is 58 − 54, measuring from the mean of y instead of from the line. That throws away everything the line knows about this adult’s 5 hours.
🏷️ Residual = observed − predicted. Build the line first; keep the sign.

Question 12

🔍 Residuals, outliers and influence

Recovering an observed value from a residual

Moreau reports that one adult who practises 2 hours a week has a residual of −3.20 from the line ŷ = 39.60 + 4.80x, which predicts vocabulary score from practice hours. That adult’s observed vocabulary score, to two decimal places, is:
  • a50.80
  • b46.00
  • c52.40
  • d49.20
🔎 What it is really asking

The residual is given and the observed value is missing — rearrange, do not subtract.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Residuals: working backwards to the observed value.

🛠️ The procedure

residual = y − ŷ, so y = ŷ + residual. Predict first, then add the residual with its own sign.

🧮 The working
Prediction at x = 2: ŷ = 39.60 + 4.80 × 2 = 39.60 + 9.60 = 49.20

y = 49.20 + (−3.20) = 46.00

Check it forwards: 46.00 − 49.20 = −3.20. ✓

The negative residual had to pull the score down from the prediction, and 46.00 < 49.20. If your answer came out above the line, you added where you should have subtracted.
ŷ = 39.60 + 4.80x · vocabulary score predicted from practice hours
Practice hours12345
Predicted vocabulary score44.4049.2054.0058.8063.60
The habit: write the defining equation down, substitute what you know, and solve for the letter that is missing. "Observed minus predicted" is not a rule to be applied in one direction only — it is an equation with three slots, and any two of them give you the third.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.50.80 is 54.0 − 3.20, taking the residual off the mean of y instead of off the prediction. Residuals are measured from the line.
c.52.40 is 49.20 + 3.20, adding the residual as though it were positive. The minus sign is part of the number.
d.49.20 is the predicted value, with the residual ignored altogether. It is where the line sits, not where this adult sits.
🏷️ y = ŷ + residual, sign included. Predict first, then add.

Question 13

🔍 Residuals, outliers and influence

Reading a residual plot

Moreau’s colleague Boström plots the residuals from the vocabulary-on-practice line against practice hours. The band of points is narrow on the left and widens steadily towards the right. This tells her that:
  • athe scatter about the line grows with x
  • bthe line should have a steeper slope
  • cthe relationship is curved, not linear
  • dthe residuals no longer sum to zero
🔎 What it is really asking

What shape is in the residual plot, and which defect makes that shape?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Residuals: diagnosing from the plot’s shape.

🛠️ The procedure

A residual plot should look like a shapeless horizontal band. Each kind of departure has its own signature: a fan means unequal spread, a bend means the wrong shape, a tilt means the line was not least-squares.

🧮 The working
A fan opening to the right says the residuals are small when practice is low and large when practice is high. The line is still the right shape — the points are centred on it all the way along — but its predictions are much more reliable at the left-hand end than at the right.

Three signatures, kept apart:
• Fan or wedge → the spread of y changes with x. Predictions are uneven in precision; a transformation of y often helps.
• Curve or bend → the straight line is the wrong model. r and b are summarising a shape the data do not have.
• Tilt → it is not a least-squares line at all, because its residuals should have no trend in x by construction.

Why anyone bothers plotting residuals: the fan is almost invisible in the original scatterplot, where the upward trend dominates everything. Flattening the trend away is exactly what the residual plot is for.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.A slope that is too steep or too shallow shows up as a tilt in the residual plot, not as a fan — and least squares rules a tilt out anyway.
c.A curved relationship shows up as a bend, with the residuals negative at both ends and positive in the middle. A fan has no bend in it.
d.The residuals of a least-squares line always sum to zero, whatever shape the plot takes. A fan is symmetric about zero and sums to zero just the same.
🏷️ Fan = unequal spread. Bend = wrong shape. Tilt = not least squares.

Question 14

⚖️ What it does NOT mean

Spotting extrapolation

A magazine uses Moreau’s line ŷ = 39.60 + 4.80x to announce a predicted vocabulary score of 135.60 for someone who practises 20 hours a week. Her 85 adults practised between 1 and 6 hours. The objection to that prediction is that:
  • athe prediction ignores the residual
  • bthe line only predicts at the mean
  • c20 hours is far outside the data
  • dr = 0.64 is too small to predict with
🔎 What it is really asking

Is the arithmetic wrong, or is the x being fed in illegitimate?

🧭 Which type of question this is

What it does NOT mean: extrapolation.

🛠️ The procedure

A fitted line carries evidence only over the range of x it was fitted on. Outside that range the arithmetic still works and the evidence has run out — that is extrapolation.

🧮 The working
The arithmetic is impeccable: 39.60 + 4.80 × 20 = 135.60.

The trouble is the 20. Moreau’s adults practised 1 to 6 hours, so her data say nothing at all about 20 hours — more than three times the largest value she observed.

And there is no reason to expect the straight line to continue. Vocabulary learning almost certainly flattens off: the twentieth hour of a week cannot plausibly add the same 4.80 points as the second. A line fitted over 1–6 hours cannot detect that flattening, because none of its data are out there.

The habit: before you substitute an x, check it against the range the line was built from. If it is outside, say so and stop — do not quote the number with a caveat.

Say it to a friend: "that line was drawn through people who practise a few hours a week; it has nothing to say about someone who practises twenty."
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.A prediction is a predicted average and never includes a residual — individual residuals are unknown in advance for everybody, inside the range as well as outside.
b.A line predicts perfectly well across the whole range of x it was fitted on, not only at x̄. The range is the limit, not the mean.
d.The size of r is not the objection. Even r = 0.95 would not license a prediction at an x value the study never observed.
🏷️ Check the x against the range the line was fitted on, before you substitute.

Question 15

⚖️ What it does NOT mean

Correlations computed on group averages

Education researcher Lagerlöf has reading hours and vocabulary scores for 1,800 pupils across 12 schools. Among individual pupils r = 0.41. When she replaces each school by its two averages and correlates those 12 pairs, r = 0.88. The reason for the difference is that:
  • atwelve schools is too few to trust r
  • bthe link really is stronger in schools
  • cr rises whenever the sample shrinks
  • daveraging over schools removes scatter
🔎 What it is really asking

What happened to the individual differences when each school became one point?

🧭 Which type of question this is

What it does NOT mean: correlations on averages.

🛠️ The procedure

Averaging cancels individual variation. The 12 points are means of about 150 pupils each, so most of the person-to-person scatter has been averaged away before r is computed — and r measures scatter.

🧮 The working
Each school’s point is the average of roughly 1,800 ⁄ 12 = 150 pupils. Individual pupils vary enormously; school averages barely vary at all by comparison, because the ups and downs inside a school cancel out.

What is left is the part of the pattern that schools share, and that part lines up neatly. So r climbs from 0.41 to 0.88, and r² from 16.8% to 77.4% — without a single pupil’s relationship having changed.

The error to refuse: quoting 0.88 as the strength of the relationship for a pupil. It is not. It describes schools. A correlation computed on group averages is called an ecological correlation, and it is almost always larger than the individual one.

Say it to a friend: "schools that read more do better as schools — but knowing how much one child reads still tells you much less than 0.88 suggests."

The general lesson: always ask what one point on the scatterplot is. A person, a school, a country and a year are four different questions.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Twelve points give an imprecise r, but imprecision does not push a correlation reliably upwards. The systematic rise comes from the averaging.
b.Nothing here says the relationship is stronger inside schools — the pupil-level r of 0.41 is the figure that describes pupils, and it is the smaller one.
c.Shrinking a sample does not raise r. Picking 12 pupils at random would give an r scattered around 0.41, not around 0.88.
🏷️ Ask what one point is. Correlations on averages run high — ecological correlation.

Question 1

🧩 Explanatory and response

When a least-squares line cannot be fitted at all

Psychometrician Vikander plans four analyses, each using one measured variable to predict another. The one a least-squares line cannot be fitted for is:
  • aa sleep-quality score, from nightly screen-time minutes
  • ba reaction time in milliseconds, from hours spent awake
  • cwhether a client drops out or stays, from their intake score
  • da final exam mark, from the number of seminars attended
🔎 What it is really asking

Which of the four has a response that is not a quantity.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Roles: what kind of variables a line needs.

🛠️ The procedure

A least-squares line predicts a quantity from a quantity. Ask one question of the response: could you take its mean? If not, there is nothing for a line to aim at.

🧮 The working
“Drops out or stays” is a category, not a number. There is no mean drop-out to predict, and a line fitted to it would return values like 0.63 of a client, which is not an answer to anything.

The other three all pair a number with a number: marks with seminars, a sleep score with minutes, milliseconds with hours. Every one of them has a mean you could aim at.

Two warnings that go with this:
• A category is not rescued by coding it 0 and 1. The coding is arithmetic; the variable is still two boxes.
• It is the response that must be a quantity here. Later courses do put a 0 ⁄ 1 variable on the explanatory side, and they handle a 0 ⁄ 1 response with a different model altogether.

The habit: name the response out loud, then ask “can I average it?” before you write down a single formula.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.A sleep-quality score and a number of minutes are both quantities. This is the ordinary case a least-squares line is built for.
b.Milliseconds and hours awake are both measurements. The units are different, which matters for reading the slope and not at all for fitting it.
d.Marks and seminars attended are both counts you can average, so the line is available and its slope is in marks per seminar.
🏷️ Response must be a quantity you could average. Categories need another model.

Question 2

🧩 Explanatory and response

Spotting a line fitted the wrong way round

Pehrsson wants to predict exam marks out of 100 from nightly hours of sleep for 140 students. Her output reads ŷ = 5.80 + 0.02x, and she reports that an extra hour of sleep is worth 0.02 marks. The mistake is that:
  • athe line predicts sleep hours from marks, not marks from hours
  • bthe intercept and the slope have been printed in reverse
  • cthe slope should have been reported as a percentage
  • dthe slope is too small to report without its P-value
🔎 What it is really asking

Check the numbers against the units the response is measured in.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Roles: reading which variable a printed line predicts.

🛠️ The procedure

A slope carries units: response units per explanatory unit. Put a sensible x into the line and see whether what comes out could be a value of the response you wanted.

🧮 The working
Feed in a student who sleeps 8 hours:

ŷ = 5.80 + 0.02 × 8 = 5.96

As a mark out of 100 that is absurd, and every x between 5 and 9 hours gives the same nonsense — the line has nowhere near enough range in it to be producing marks.

Now read it the other way. Feed in a mark of 60:

5.80 + 0.02 × 60 = 7.00 hours of sleep — a thoroughly sensible average.

So the output is the other line: hours of sleep from marks, whose slope of 0.02 means about 1.2 minutes of extra sleep per extra mark. Her own line, marks from hours, is a different line with a different slope, and she has to refit it rather than rearrange this one.

The habit: read every slope aloud with its units — “marks per hour” — and check the intercept is a believable value of the response. Two numbers, two seconds, and this error cannot survive.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Nothing is printed in reverse: 5.80 behaves exactly like an intercept and 0.02 exactly like a slope. The trouble is which variable is on the vertical axis.
c.A slope is not a percentage. It is a rate of change, in response units per unit of the explanatory variable, and reporting it as a percentage would hide the units that give the error away.
d.The size of a slope is not a reason to withhold it, and no P-value would help here. A perfectly significant slope can still be the slope of the wrong line.
🏷️ Put an x in and check the output could be a value of your response.

Question 3

📈 Reading a correlation

A correlation that reverses when two groups are pooled

Bertolini records weekly revision hours and exam marks for 60 first-year and 60 final-year students, below. Inside each year group the two are positively correlated, yet across all 120 students the correlation is negative. The single feature of her data that produces the negative figure is:
Revision hours and exam marks in two year groups · 120 students
Year groupMean revision hoursMean exam markr within the group
First years (60)11.054.0+0.55
Final years (60)6.069.0+0.55
All 120 students8.561.5−0.34
  • athe two year groups are the same size, which cancels the trend
  • bthe within-group figures of +0.55 must be arithmetic slips
  • cr cannot be computed on two groups that were measured separately
  • dfinal years revise fewer hours and still score higher
🔎 What it is really asking

Why a correlation can change sign when two different groups are poured together.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading a correlation: pooling two groups.

🛠️ The procedure

A correlation computed over two groups carries two ingredients: the trend inside each group, and the trend between the two groups’ means. When the group means run the other way, the between part can swamp the within part.

🧮 The working
Inside each group the points slope upward: r = +0.55 in both, with a slope of about +1.9 marks per hour of revision.

Now step from one group to the other. First years average 11.0 hours and 54.0 marks; final years average 6.0 hours and 69.0 marks. Hours go down by 5 while marks go up by 15 — two group means that sit on a steeply downward line.

Pour all 120 students into one cloud and that downward step between the groups dominates: r = −0.34, and the pooled line slopes at −1.1 marks per hour, the opposite sign from both of the lines inside it.

Nothing here is wrong with the data. Final-year students are simply better at the exam and need less revision, and lumping two such groups together measures the gap between them rather than the effect of revising.

The habit: plot the groups in different colours before you compute anything. Two separate clouds with their own trends are not one cloud.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Equal group sizes do not cancel anything — they make the between-group step count for as much as it possibly can. The reversal would survive unequal groups too.
b.The +0.55 figures are correct and so is the −0.34. All three can be true at once, because they are computed on different sets of points.
c.r is perfectly computable on 120 students, and on each group of 60. The question is which of those three numbers answers which question.
🏷️ Two groups in one cloud: r mixes the trend within and the gap between.

Question 4

📈 Reading a correlation

What reversing a scale does to r

Rydberg reports r = +0.48 between weekly hours of sport and a social-connectedness score for 95 teenagers. The questionnaire is then re-scored so that a high score means more isolated, each score replaced by 100 minus itself. The correlation is now, to two decimal places:
  • a+0.23
  • b−0.48
  • c+0.48
  • d−0.52
🔎 What it is really asking

Does reversing the direction of a scale change the sign, the strength, or both?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading a correlation: what leaves r alone and what does not.

🛠️ The procedure

r is built from the two sets of z-scores multiplied together. Adding a constant or multiplying by a positive number leaves every z-score alone. Multiplying by a negative number turns every z-score into its own negative.

🧮 The working
Each score y becomes 100 − y. The mean does the same thing, so every deviation from the mean flips sign, and the standard deviation is unchanged — a mirror image is just as spread out as the original.

So every z-score of the connectedness variable becomes its negative, every product of z-scores flips sign, and r flips with them:

r = −0.48

In words: teenagers who do more sport feel more connected, which is the same as saying they feel less isolated. Nothing about the teenagers changed — only which end of the scale is called “high”.

The habit: before you read any sign, check which way the scale runs. Questionnaires full of reverse-scored items are where this bites.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.+0.23 is 0.48², the share of variation explained. Squaring is not what reversing a scale does, and the result is not a correlation.
c.+0.48 is the figure before the re-scoring. Reversing the scale reverses the direction of the relationship, and the sign of r goes with it.
d.−0.52 gets the sign right and moves the strength. Subtracting every score from 100 leaves the spacing between teenagers untouched, so the strength cannot move.
🏷️ Reverse a scale: r flips sign, keeps its size. Positive rescaling: nothing.

Question 5

📈 Reading a correlation

What a perfect correlation does and does not fix

Zarkova reports r = −1.00 between two measures taken from 30 participants. It follows that:
  • athe least-squares slope is exactly −1.00
  • bthe two measures are on the same scale
  • call 30 points lie on one downward-sloping line
  • done measure falls by a point as the other rises
🔎 What it is really asking

What |r| = 1 pins down, and what it leaves completely open.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading a correlation: the limits of the scale.

🛠️ The procedure

|r| = 1 means every point sits exactly on one straight line, and the sign says which way that line tilts. It says nothing about how steep the line is, because r has no units.

🧮 The working
r = −1.00 is the strongest possible negative result: no scatter at all. As one measure rises the other falls, without a single exception among the 30 participants, and the least-squares line passes through every point.

Steepness is a separate matter, and the slope formula shows why:

b = r s_y ⁄ s_x = −s_y ⁄ s_x

That equals −1.00 only if the two standard deviations happen to be equal. If one measure has an SD of 2 and the other an SD of 10, the slope is −5.00 and r is still −1.00.

Say it to a friend: “the points are on a line that goes down” — that is the whole content of r = −1.00.

The habit: r for the shape, the slope for the size. They answer different questions and only r is unitless.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The slope is −s_y ⁄ s_x, so it is −1.00 only in the special case of equal standard deviations. Any downward slope at all is compatible with r = −1.00.
b.Nothing about r requires a common scale. One measure could be in seconds and the other in points out of 50, and a perfect correlation is still possible.
d.A one-for-one trade would mean a slope of exactly −1, which r cannot tell you. r = −1.00 holds whatever the two scales are.
🏷️ |r| = 1 fixes the shape, never the steepness.

Question 6

📐 The least-squares line

Getting one prediction from another

Occupational psychologist Nordahl fits a line predicting a job-satisfaction score from the daily commute in minutes for 150 employees, below. Her line predicts 56.60 for a 60-minute commute. For a 20-minute commute it predicts, to two decimal places:
Summary statistics for 150 employees · Nordahl’s study
Commute (minutes each way)Job-satisfaction score
mean40.062.0
standard deviation15.09.0
correlationr = −0.45
  • a67.40
  • b45.80
  • c62.00
  • d56.87
🔎 What it is really asking

Move 40 minutes along the line — no intercept needed.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The least-squares line: comparing two predictions.

🛠️ The procedure

The slope is a rate of change: b = r s_y ⁄ s_x, with the SD of the response on top. Two predictions then differ by b × the gap in x, so one prediction plus the slope gets you to any other.

🧮 The working
The slope first, because every step needs it:

b = −0.45 × (9.0 ⁄ 15.0) = −0.27 satisfaction points per minute of commute

20 minutes is 40 minutes less than 60, and the slope is negative, so the prediction goes up:

56.60 + 40 × 0.27 = 56.60 + 10.80 = 67.40

Check it against the full line. a = 62.0 − (−0.27 × 40.0) = 72.80, so ŷ = 72.80 − 0.27x, and 72.80 − 0.27 × 20 = 67.40. ✓ Same answer, more work.

What the prediction is: the average satisfaction of all employees with a 20-minute commute. With r = −0.45 there is a great deal of scatter around it.

The habit: to compare two predictions you never need the intercept. Multiply the slope by the gap in x, and check the direction against the sign of the slope.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.45.80 is 56.60 − 10.80, stepping the 40 minutes the wrong way. The slope is negative, so a shorter commute predicts a higher score, not a lower one.
c.62.00 is the mean satisfaction score, which is the prediction at the mean commute of 40 minutes — not at 20 minutes.
d.56.87 is 56.60 + 0.27, one slope’s worth. That would be the step from 60 minutes to 59, and the two commutes here are 40 minutes apart.
🏷️ Predictions differ by slope × gap in x. Check the sign gives the right direction.

Question 7

📐 The least-squares line

What a line with one prediction tells you

Pulkkinen fits a least-squares line predicting a recall score from hours of revision for 70 students, and it returns the same prediction, 48.0, for every student. It follows that:
  • arevision and recall are unrelated in every sense
  • bhis slope is zero and 48.0 is the mean recall score
  • chis recall scores do not vary from student to student
  • dr = 1.00, since the predictions agree perfectly
🔎 What it is really asking

A flat line — what does it fix about the slope, about r, and about ȳ?

🧭 Which type of question this is

The least-squares line: the flat line and what it means.

🛠️ The procedure

A prediction that never changes means the slope is zero. Since b = r s_y ⁄ s_x, a zero slope means r = 0, and with b = 0 the intercept is a = ȳ, so the line is the horizontal line through the mean response.

🧮 The working
Work through the three consequences in order.

The slope. Identical predictions at different x means b = 0.

The correlation. b = r s_y ⁄ s_x, and s_y and s_x are not zero, so r = 0.

The height. a = ȳ − b x̄ = ȳ − 0 = 48.0. The flat line sits at the mean recall score, which is exactly right: if revision carries no linear information, your best single guess for anyone is the overall mean.

What this does not say: recall scores certainly do vary between his 70 students — the line simply cannot track that variation. And r = 0 rules out a straight-line trend only. Revision and recall could rise and then fall in a clean curve and still give a flat least-squares line.

The habit: a flat line is a statement about the line, not a statement that nothing is happening. Plot the points before you conclude anything.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.“Unrelated in every sense” goes too far. r = 0 rules out a linear trend, and a strong curved relationship would give a flat line too.
c.The scores almost certainly do vary; s_y is what the line is failing to explain. A flat line reports that x cannot track that variation, not that it is absent.
d.r = 1.00 would mean every point sitting exactly on a sloping line. Identical predictions mean the opposite: r = 0.
🏷️ Flat line → b = 0 → r = 0, and the line sits at ȳ. A curve can still be there.

Question 8

📐 The least-squares line

Which of four lines can be the least-squares line

Braithwaite fits a line predicting a wellbeing score from the number of therapy sessions attended. His clients average 20 sessions and a wellbeing score of 55. Only one of these can be his line:
  • aŷ = 55.0 + 1.00x
  • bŷ = 15.0 + 1.25x
  • cŷ = 70.0 − 1.00x
  • dŷ = 35.0 + 1.00x
🔎 What it is really asking

Which candidate passes through the point of means.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The least-squares line: identifying one instead of computing it.

🛠️ The procedure

Every least-squares line passes through (x̄, ȳ). Put x̄ into each candidate and keep the one that returns ȳ.

🧮 The working
x̄ = 20 sessions and ȳ = 55 points, so a + 20b must come to 55.

35.0 + 1.00 × 20 = 55.0 ✓
55.0 + 1.00 × 20 = 75.0 ✗
15.0 + 1.25 × 20 = 40.0 ✗
70.0 − 1.00 × 20 = 50.0 ✗

One candidate survives, and no slope formula was needed.

Why the property holds: the intercept is defined as a = ȳ − b x̄, which rearranges to ȳ = a + b x̄. The means are built into the line, whatever the data.

The habit: use (x̄, ȳ) as a free check on every line you compute as well as on every line you are handed. If your own line misses the point of means, you have made an arithmetic slip.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.ŷ = 55.0 + 1.00x puts the mean response into the intercept. At 20 sessions it predicts 75.0, twenty points above the mean it has to pass through.
b.ŷ = 15.0 + 1.25x predicts 40.0 at 20 sessions, fifteen points below the point of means. Its intercept and slope do not fit together.
c.ŷ = 70.0 − 1.00x predicts 50.0 at 20 sessions, and it slopes downwards, which would say that more sessions go with lower wellbeing.
🏷️ Every least-squares line goes through (x̄, ȳ). Test candidates with it.

Question 9

🥧 r-squared

Reading r and the unexplained share off r-squared

Kolodziej fits a line predicting a parenting-stress score from weekly hours of childcare and reports r² = 0.25. The correlation and the share of the variation his line leaves unexplained are:
  • ar = ±0.50 and 75% unexplained
  • br = 0.25 and 75% unexplained
  • cr = ±0.50 and 50% unexplained
  • dr = ±0.06 and 94% unexplained
🔎 What it is really asking

Two figures, each one step away from r² — and in opposite directions.

🧭 Which type of question this is

r-squared: moving between r² and r, explained and unexplained.

🛠️ The procedure

r = ±√r², and the sign cannot be recovered from r² alone. The explained and unexplained shares add to 100%, so the unexplained share is 1 − r².

🧮 The working
The correlation. √0.25 = 0.50, and r is +0.50 or −0.50. r² throws the sign away by squaring; only the scatterplot or the sign of the slope brings it back. (Here you would expect negative, but r² does not say so.)

The unexplained share. 1 − 0.25 = 0.75 = 75%.

In plain English: a quarter of the differences between parents in stress scores is tracked by how many hours of childcare they do; three quarters of those differences is everything else — sleep, income, support, the children themselves.

Keep the pair apart: r describes the points, r² accounts for the variation. They sit one square apart, and r² never carries a sign.

The habit: when a question asks for two figures, do them separately and write both down. Half-answers are where the marks go.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.r = 0.25 reads r² as though it were r. The correlation is the square root of 0.25; 0.25 is what you get after squaring it.
c.50% unexplained would need r² = 0.50. The two shares add to 100%, so 25% explained leaves 75% unexplained.
d.r = ±0.06 comes from squaring 0.25 a second time, giving 0.0625. Squaring a number below 1 makes it smaller, so the correlation has to be the square root instead.
🏷️ r = ±√r², and unexplained = 1 − r². Two steps, opposite directions.

Question 10

🥧 r-squared

Why a figure from a pilot study moves

Mihailova’s pilot of 10 participants gives r² = 0.49 for a line predicting a mood score from daily step count. Repeating the study with 200 participants gives r² = 0.09. The feature of the pilot that best explains the drop is:
  • athe two studies must have measured different things
  • br² always falls as more participants are added
  • cwith 10 points, one or two unusual pairs can carry the fit
  • dthe pilot’s r² was larger, so its line fitted better
🔎 What it is really asking

Why a number from ten people is not evidence about two hundred.

🧭 Which type of question this is

r-squared: how much a small sample can be trusted.

🛠️ The procedure

r² from a small sample is unstable. It jumps about from sample to sample, and a single unusual pair of points can lift it a long way. A large sample pins it down.

🧮 The working
Take the 200-participant figure as the truth: r² = 0.09, so r = 0.30.

Now ask what samples of 10 from that population look like. In 40,000 simulated samples the average r² was 0.18, the top 5% reached 0.55, and r² came out at 0.49 or more about 8 times in 100. So the pilot is ordinary bad luck, not a contradiction.

And one point can do it single-handed. Nine points scattered with r² = 0.15, plus one participant far out in both step count and mood, gives r² = 0.94 — a tight line through a cloud that has no trend in it.

Neither of those can happen with 200 participants: the sample is too big for one pair to steer, and the estimate settles down near the truth.

The habit: ask how many points a correlation rests on before you react to its size. A pilot is for checking that the measures work, not for estimating how strong a relationship is.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Nothing suggests different measures: it is the same line on the same two variables. Sampling variability alone accounts for the gap.
b.r² does not fall as a matter of course when the sample grows. It settles towards the population value, which may be above the pilot figure as easily as below it.
d.A larger r² in a smaller sample is not a better fit, only a fit to fewer points. The 200-participant figure is the more trustworthy of the two.
🏷️ Small n, unstable r². Ask how many points before you believe a correlation.

Question 11

🔍 Residuals, outliers and influence

Getting back to observed values through residuals

Two of Nordahl’s employees commute 25 and 55 minutes. Against her line ŷ = 72.80 − 0.27x, which predicts job satisfaction from commuting minutes, the first sits 2.50 points above the line and the second 1.50 points below it. The gap between their two observed satisfaction scores, to two decimal places, is:
Summary statistics for 150 employees · Nordahl’s study
Commute (minutes each way)Job-satisfaction score
mean40.062.0
standard deviation15.09.0
correlationr = −0.45
  • a8.10
  • b4.10
  • c1.00
  • d12.10
🔎 What it is really asking

Predictions first, then put each residual back on.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Residuals: rebuilding observed values from the line.

🛠️ The procedure

observed = predicted + residual, with the sign kept. Predict each employee, add or subtract their residual, then subtract the two observed values.

🧮 The working
Predictions from the line:

25 minutes: 72.80 − 0.27 × 25 = 66.05
55 minutes: 72.80 − 0.27 × 55 = 57.95

Put the residuals back on:

first employee:  66.05 + 2.50 = 68.55
second employee: 57.95 − 1.50 = 56.45

Gap = 68.55 − 56.45 = 12.10

The same answer in one line, which is worth seeing: the line alone puts them 30 × 0.27 = 8.10 apart, and the two residuals pull them a further 2.50 + 1.50 = 4.00 apart, because one sits above the line and the other below it. 8.10 + 4.00 = 12.10.

The habit: write observed = predicted + residual at the top of the page. Every question of this shape is that one sentence, rearranged.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.8.10 is the gap between the two predictions, 30 × 0.27. It ignores both residuals, and here they pull the two employees further apart.
b.4.10 subtracts the 4.00 points of residual from the 8.10 instead of adding it. One employee is above her line and the other below, so both offsets widen the gap.
c.1.00 is 2.50 − 1.50, the two residuals on their own. The 30-minute difference in commuting time is still there underneath them.
🏷️ observed = predicted + residual. Keep every sign.

Question 12

🔍 Residuals, outliers and influence

Which points can actually move the slope

In a scatterplot of 50 points, one point sits far above the line but at the middle of the x range. Tsalikis says it is influential and the slope cannot be trusted; Larrieu says it is an outlier that barely touches the slope. The reading that survives is:
  • aneither, since one point among 50 changes nothing
  • bLarrieu’s — a point at the centre of x has no leverage
  • cTsalikis’s — any point far from the line moves the slope
  • dboth, because an outlier is influential by definition
🔎 What it is really asking

For the slope, does it matter how far a point is from the line, or where it is in x?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Residuals, outliers and influence: which one this point is.

🛠️ The procedure

Leverage comes from distance from x̄, not from distance from the line. A big residual at the middle of the x range lifts the intercept and lowers r, while leaving the slope almost exactly where it was.

🧮 The working
Picture the line as a plank balanced at (x̄, ȳ). A tug applied at the balance point lifts the whole plank without rotating it. A tug out at the end rotates it.

The arithmetic is exact. Fit 50 points and the slope comes out at 1.3959. Now add one point at exactly x̄, 25 points above the line:

• slope: 1.3959 — unchanged to every decimal place
• intercept: 10.67 → 11.16, the whole line lifted
• r: 0.93 → 0.84, and r² 0.87 → 0.70

The slope cannot move, because a point at x̄ contributes (x − x̄) = 0 to it. For contrast, one point far out at x = 30 sitting right on the trend moves the slope from 1.3959 to 1.4279 — well behaved, and influential.

The two words, kept apart: an outlier has a big residual and may move nothing. An influential point is extreme in x and often sits close to the line.

The habit: for the slope, ask where the point is in x. For r and the intercept, ask how far it is from the line.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.One point among 50 can matter enormously — if it sits far out in x. Leverage decides, not the head count.
c.Distance from the line is what makes a point an outlier, and an outlier at the centre of x moves the intercept and r rather than the slope.
d.The two words are not synonyms. An outlier with no leverage changes the slope hardly at all, and a high-leverage point often has a small residual.
🏷️ Leverage = far from x̄. Big residual = outlier. Only one swings the slope.

Question 13

🔍 Residuals, outliers and influence

Judging a line by the right quantity

Berendsen fits a line predicting a reading score from weekly reading minutes for 48 children, adds up his 48 residuals, gets zero, and writes that the line fits the data perfectly. The mistake is that:
  • aevery least-squares line gives residuals summing to zero
  • bhe should have divided the total by 48 to get a mean
  • cresiduals cannot be added, since they carry units
  • da total of zero shows the line is too flat
🔎 What it is really asking

Is a zero total evidence about this line, or true of every line?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Residuals: what does and does not measure fit.

🛠️ The procedure

The residuals of any least-squares line add to zero. It follows from the line passing through (x̄, ȳ), so it is true of a line that fits beautifully and of a line that fits dreadfully. A quantity that is always zero carries no information.

🧮 The working
His arithmetic is right and his conclusion is empty. Positive and negative residuals balance by construction: the least-squares line is placed so that they do.

It is the same reason deviations from a mean always add to zero. You would not judge a mean by adding up the deviations from it.

What does measure fit:
• the sum of the squares of the residuals — the line is chosen to make it as small as any straight line can;
• r², the share of the variation in reading scores the line accounts for;
• the residual plot, which shows whether a straight line was the right shape at all. A shapeless band means yes; a curve or a widening fan means no.

Say it to a friend: “the residuals cancelling out is the line’s definition, not its report card.”
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Dividing zero by 48 gives zero. The mean residual is as uninformative as the total, and for exactly the same reason.
c.Residuals can be added: they are all in the units of the response, reading-score points. The trouble is that their total is fixed in advance.
d.A zero total says nothing about the slope. A steep line, a flat line and the wrong line altogether all have residuals adding to zero.
🏷️ Residuals always sum to zero. Judge fit by their squares, r², and the plot.

Question 14

⚖️ What it does NOT mean

Which design supports a causal claim

Ruggiero wants to claim that daily walking improves mood. Of the four studies below, the one whose design supports that claim is:
  • a200 adults who joined a walking group, measured twice
  • bwalking and mood averages for 30 city neighbourhoods
  • c60 adults randomly assigned to a daily walk or no change
  • da survey of 600 adults on their walking and their mood
🔎 What it is really asking

Which design decides the explanatory variable rather than recording it.

🧭 Which type of question this is

What it does NOT mean: what a causal claim requires.

🛠️ The procedure

A causal claim needs the explanatory variable to be assigned, not observed. Random assignment makes the groups alike in everything else, so a difference afterwards has only one place left to come from.

🧮 The working
Take them one at a time and ask what survives each study.

The survey. People chose how much they walk. Cheerful people may walk more, and pain, age or shift work could drive both. Reverse direction and confounding both survive, whatever the size of r.

The walking group measured twice. They volunteered, so they are not like non-joiners to begin with, and everything else that happened over those weeks — the season, the attention, simply getting older — is inside the before-and-after difference. With no comparison group, there is nothing to subtract it against.

The neighbourhood averages. Thirty averages can correlate strongly while the individuals inside them do not, and a neighbourhood is not a person.

The randomised study. Assignment, not choice, decides who walks. The two groups differ only by chance in everything else, so a mood difference afterwards points at the walking. Sixty adults is a modest sample — that is a question of precision, not of the causal arrow.

The habit: ask one question of any causal headline — “who decided the x?”
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Measuring joiners twice has no comparison group, so everything else that happened over the same weeks is mixed into the change — and they chose to join.
b.Averages for 30 neighbourhoods describe neighbourhoods. A group-level correlation need not hold for the individuals inside the groups.
d.A survey records what people already do. The arrow could run the other way, or a third variable could drive both, and the survey cannot tell.
🏷️ Causal claim? Ask who decided the explanatory variable.

Question 15

⚖️ What it does NOT mean

Which rival explanations the data can remove

Hollebeek finds r = +0.52 between weekly volunteering hours and a life-satisfaction score across 300 adults, and writes that volunteering raises life satisfaction. One colleague answers that satisfied people take on more volunteering; another that being retired produces both. Her data can:
  • arule out the first, because r is positive
  • brule out the second, because r is this strong
  • crule out both, because 300 adults is a large sample
  • drule out neither, since nobody was assigned any hours
🔎 What it is really asking

Can the size or sign of a correlation choose between rival explanations?

🧭 Which type of question this is

What it does NOT mean: rival explanations for one correlation.

🛠️ The procedure

A correlation is consistent with the arrow running either way, and with a third variable driving both. Neither the sign nor the size of r chooses between them — only the design can.

🧮 The working
Three stories, one number:

• Volunteering → satisfaction, her own reading.
• Satisfaction → volunteering: the arrow backwards. People who feel good take things on.
• Retirement → both: retired adults have free hours and, on average, different satisfaction. A confounder, with no direct link between the two at all.

All three predict a positive correlation of about this size. r is a single number and cannot separate them.

Nor does the sample help. 300 adults makes r precise, not causal — a larger sample measures the same ambiguous quantity more exactly. Three thousand adults would leave all three stories standing.

What would settle it: assigning volunteering hours, or at the very least measuring retirement and comparing adults who match on it.

The habit: for every causal sentence, write the arrow backwards and name one third variable. If the data cannot rule either out, neither can the sentence.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.A positive r is what the reverse direction predicts too. Satisfied people volunteering more would produce exactly the same sign.
b.Strength is no defence against a confounder. Retirement could produce a strong correlation between two things it separately affects.
c.A large sample removes imprecision, not alternative explanations. All three stories survive 300 adults and would survive 3,000.
🏷️ Size and sign cannot rule out a rival story. Only the design can.

Question 1

📐 Testing a slope

Degrees of freedom for the slope test

Occupational psychologist Lindqvist regresses a staff wellbeing score on monthly supervision hours across 27 clinics. The degrees of freedom for the t test of the slope are:
Regression of wellbeing score on monthly supervision hours · 27 clinics
PredictorCoefficientStd. ErrortP
Constant41.20002.760014.928.000
Supervision hours1.55000.40023.873.001
  • a27
  • b1
  • c25
  • d26
🔎 What it is really asking

One predictor costs two degrees of freedom.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Testing a slope: degrees of freedom.

🛠️ The procedure

df = n − p − 1, where p is the number of predictors. With one predictor that is n − 2, because the line has two things estimated from the data: a slope and an intercept.

🧮 The working
n = 27 clinics, p = 1 predictor.

df = 27 − 1 − 1 = 25

The same 25 runs everything on the right-hand side of this analysis: the t test for the slope, the t test for the constant, any confidence interval for either, and the Residual error row of the ANOVA table — where it is printed for you.

Use the printout as a check. If the error row says 25 and you have written 26, one of you is wrong, and it is not the printout.

Why not n − 1: that is the df for a single mean, where only one quantity is estimated. A line estimates two.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.27 is n itself. Every df rule subtracts something; none of them is just the sample size.
b.1 is the model df, the number of predictors. It is the first of the pair in the F test, not the df for the t test.
d.26 is n − 1, the Total df in the ANOVA table. It is the df for one mean, not for a line.
🏷️ One predictor → n − 2. It is also the Residual error row.

Question 2

📐 Testing a slope

The t statistic for a slope

In Lindqvist’s output the slope is 1.5500 with a standard error of 0.4002. The value of the t statistic for testing H₀: β = 0, to two decimal places, is:
Regression of wellbeing score on monthly supervision hours · 27 clinics
PredictorCoefficientStd. ErrortP
Constant41.20002.760014.928.000
Supervision hours1.55000.40023.873.001
  • a3.87
  • b0.26
  • c1.55
  • d2.06
🔎 What it is really asking

Estimate divided by its own standard error.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Testing a slope: the test statistic.

🛠️ The procedure

t = (b − 0) ⁄ SE(b). It is the same (estimate − null) ⁄ SE shape as every t test you have met; only the estimate has changed.

🧮 The working
t = 1.5500 ⁄ 0.4002 = 3.873, so 3.87 — and the printout confirms it.

The 0 is there because H₀ says the slope is zero: no linear relationship between supervision hours and wellbeing. Any other null value would go in its place.

On 25 df, 3.87 gives a two-sided P of .00069, printed as .001. At α = .05 H₀ is rejected: supervision hours do predict wellbeing.

What t is really measuring: how many standard errors the estimated slope sits away from zero. Nearly four of them — a slope that far out is hard to put down to sampling noise.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.0.26 is 0.4002 ⁄ 1.5500, the division upside down. t is always estimate over standard error.
c.1.55 is the slope itself. Unstandardised, it tells you nothing about significance — a slope of 1.55 with an SE of 4 would be nowhere near significant.
d.2.06 is t* on 25 df, the 5% critical value. That is what you compare 3.87 against.
🏷️ t = b ⁄ SE(b). Estimate on top, every time.

Question 3

📐 Testing a slope

Interpreting a significant slope

Lindqvist’s slope of 1.5500 has P = .001. Using α = .05, the correct interpretation is:
Regression of wellbeing score on monthly supervision hours · 27 clinics
PredictorCoefficientStd. ErrortP
Constant41.20002.760014.928.000
Supervision hours1.55000.40023.873.001
  • asupervision hours explain 1.55% of the variation in wellbeing
  • bwellbeing rises by 1.55 points in 1.55 clinics out of 27
  • cthe correlation between the two variables is 1.55
  • deach extra supervision hour predicts 1.55 more wellbeing points
🔎 What it is really asking

State what the slope means in the study’s own units.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Testing a slope: interpretation.

🛠️ The procedure

A slope is a rate: the predicted change in y for a one-unit increase in x. Say it in the actual units of the study, and say "predicted", not "causes".

🧮 The working
The units: wellbeing points per supervision hour.

So two clinics one hour apart in monthly supervision differ, on average, by 1.55 wellbeing points — and P = .001 says a relationship this strong is unlikely to be sampling noise.

Three things to keep out of that sentence:
• Cause. Clinics were not assigned their supervision hours. Better-run clinics may do more of everything.
• Individual clinics. The slope describes an average rate, not a promise about any one clinic.
• Size of effect. P = .001 says the slope is not zero. Whether 1.55 points is a lot depends on the scale — and r² here is only 37.5%.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.A share of variation explained is r², which is 37.5% here. The slope is a rate in units, not a percentage.
b.A slope says nothing about how many clinics do anything. It is a rate of change, not a count.
c.The correlation is √0.375 = 0.61. A correlation can never exceed 1, so 1.55 could not be one.
🏷️ Slope = predicted change in y per one-unit rise in x. Say the units out loud.

Question 4

📏 An interval for a slope

A confidence interval for a slope

Using t* = 2.0595 on 25 df, the 95% confidence interval for Lindqvist’s slope, to three decimal places, is:
Regression of wellbeing score on monthly supervision hours · 27 clinics
PredictorCoefficientStd. ErrortP
Constant41.20002.760014.928.000
Supervision hours1.55000.40023.873.001
  • a1.510 to 1.590
  • b0.726 to 2.374
  • c1.150 to 1.950
  • d0.750 to 2.350
🔎 What it is really asking

Estimate plus or minus t* times the standard error.

🧭 Which type of question this is

An interval for a slope: computing it.

🛠️ The procedure

b ± t* SE(b), with t* from the t table on the same df as the test — n − 2 = 25 here.

🧮 The working
margin = 2.0595 × 0.4002 = 0.8244

interval = 1.5500 ± 0.8244

  lower: 1.5500 − 0.8244 = 0.726
  upper: 1.5500 + 0.8244 = 2.374

Read it out loud: each extra supervision hour is worth somewhere between 0.73 and 2.37 wellbeing points. That is a wide range — a threefold span — which is what 27 clinics buys you.

And it agrees with the test, as it must. The interval misses zero, and the test rejected H₀: β = 0. A 95% interval and a two-sided test at α = .05 always point the same way about the value zero.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.1.510 to 1.590 is 1.55 ± 0.04, with the standard error divided by 10 somewhere. An interval that tight would need hundreds of clinics.
c.1.150 to 1.950 is 1.55 ± 0.40, using the standard error without multiplying it by t*. That gives roughly a 68% interval, not 95%.
d.0.750 to 2.350 is 1.55 ± 0.80, using t* = 2 flat. Close, but the table value on 25 df is 2.0595 and the question asks for three decimals.
🏷️ b ± t* SE(b), t* on n − 2 df. Not b ± SE.

Question 5

📏 An interval for a slope

Reading a confidence interval for a slope

A different study reports a 95% confidence interval for its slope of −0.40 to 1.85. At the 5% level, the test of H₀: β = 0 for that study:
  • arejects H₀, because the interval is wide
  • bcannot be decided from the interval alone
  • cdoes not reject H₀, because the interval contains 0
  • drejects H₀, because most of the interval is above 0
🔎 What it is really asking

What does an interval containing zero tell you about the test?

🧭 Which type of question this is

An interval for a slope: the link to the test.

🛠️ The procedure

A 95% interval and a two-sided test at α = .05 are two views of one calculation. If the interval contains the null value, the test does not reject it.

🧮 The working
Zero lies inside −0.40 to 1.85. So zero is among the slope values the data are consistent with, and H₀: β = 0 survives. Do not reject.

The interval tells you more than the test does, though. It says the slope could plausibly be anywhere from slightly negative to fairly strongly positive — the study is not evidence of "no relationship", it is simply uninformative about the direction.

That distinction is worth keeping: "we found no significant relationship" and "we found no relationship" are different claims, and an interval this wide supports only the first.

The general rule: look at where the interval sits relative to the null value, not at how much of it lies on one side.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Width does not drive the decision. A wide interval usually means less evidence, not more.
b.The interval decides it completely for a two-sided test at the matching level. That is the whole point of the correspondence.
d."Most of the interval" is not a decision rule. Either the null value is inside the interval or it is not, and here it is.
🏷️ Interval contains 0 → do not reject. Not significant ≠ no relationship.

Question 6

🧱 The regression ANOVA table

Completing the ANOVA table

Three entries have been removed from the ANOVA table for Lindqvist’s regression. The missing MS for residual error, to two decimal places, is:
The same table with three entries removed
SourceSSdfMSF
Regression7501750.00?
Residual error1250??
Total200026
  • a50.00
  • b48.08
  • c1250.00
  • d25.00
🔎 What it is really asking

A mean square is always its own SS over its own df.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The regression ANOVA table: filling a gap.

🛠️ The procedure

MS = SS ⁄ df, row by row. For the error row the df is n − 2, and you can get it from the table itself: 26 − 1 = 25.

🧮 The working
Error df = Total df − Regression df = 26 − 1 = 25.

MS error = 1250 ⁄ 25 = 50.00

And then the rest of the table falls out:
  MS regression = 750 ⁄ 1 = 750.00
  F = 750.00 ⁄ 50.00 = 15.00

Every ANOVA table works the same way, whatever the design: the SS column and the df column both add up down the table, each MS is that row’s SS over that row’s df, and F is a ratio of two mean squares. Learn the shape once.

MS error has a name: it is the estimated variance of the residuals, and its square root is s.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.48.08 is 1250 ⁄ 26, dividing by the Total df. Each row divides by its own df.
c.1250.00 is the SS for that row, before dividing. SS and MS are different columns.
d.25.00 is the df for that row, not a mean square.
🏷️ MS = that row’s SS ⁄ that row’s df. The df column adds up too.

Question 8

🧱 The regression ANOVA table

r-squared from the ANOVA table

Using the sums of squares in Lindqvist’s table, the percentage of the variation in wellbeing explained by supervision hours is:
The analysis-of-variance table for the same regression
SourceSSdfMSFP
Regression7501750.0015.00.001
Residual error12502550.00
Total200026
  • a62.5%
  • b60.0%
  • c61.2%
  • d37.5%
🔎 What it is really asking

The regression SS as a share of the total SS.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The regression ANOVA table: r-squared from the sums of squares.

🛠️ The procedure

r² = SS regression ⁄ SS total. The SS column splits the total variation in y into the part the line accounts for and the part it does not.

🧮 The working
r² = 750 ⁄ 2000 = 0.375, so 37.5%.

Read the split: of the 2000 units of total variation in wellbeing, the line accounts for 750 and leaves 1250 in the residuals.

Both routes agree, as they must. r = √0.375 = 0.6124, and squaring the correlation gives 0.375 back. The ANOVA table and the correlation are telling you the same thing in different notation.

And the honest summary of this analysis: the slope is clearly not zero (P = .001), and the line still leaves 62.5% of the variation in wellbeing unexplained. Significance and explanatory power are separate questions.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.62.5% is 1250 ⁄ 2000, the share left unexplained. Right ratio, wrong row on top.
b.60.0% is 750 ⁄ 1250, regression over error. The denominator must be the total.
c.61.2% is r rather than r², read as a percentage. √0.375 = 0.6124 — squaring is what turns a correlation into a share of variation.
🏷️ r² = SSM ⁄ SST. Denominator is Total, never Error.

Question 9

🅕 The overall F test

Computing the overall F

The value of the F statistic for Lindqvist’s regression, to two decimal places, is:
The same table with three entries removed
SourceSSdfMSF
Regression7501750.00?
Residual error1250??
Total200026
  • a15.00
  • b0.60
  • c4.24
  • d3.87
🔎 What it is really asking

A ratio of two mean squares, not of two sums of squares.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The overall F test: computing it.

🛠️ The procedure

F = MS regression ⁄ MS error. Work out both mean squares first — dividing the sums of squares straight away gives a plausible wrong number that is always on the option list.

🧮 The working
MS regression = 750 ⁄ 1 = 750.00
MS error      = 1250 ⁄ 25 = 50.00

F = 750.00 ⁄ 50.00 = 15.00

The df come as a pair: (1, 25) — the model df, then the error df. On (1, 25) the 5% critical value is 4.2417, so 15.00 is far past it and P = .0007.

Why the mean squares and not the SS: the two sums of squares are built from different numbers of free quantities — one and twenty-five. Dividing each by its own df puts them on the same footing, which is the only way their ratio means anything.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.0.60 is 750 ⁄ 1250, the sums of squares divided directly. It skips both mean squares and is the designed trap here.
c.4.24 is the critical value of F on (1, 25) at α = .05 — what you compare 15.00 against.
d.3.87 is the t statistic for the slope. Its square is F; the two are not the same number.
🏷️ F = MSM ⁄ MSE. Mean squares first, always.

Question 10

🅕 The overall F test

The relationship between t and F

Lindqvist notices that her slope t is 3.873 and her F is 15.00. With one predictor, these two:
The analysis-of-variance table for the same regression
SourceSSdfMSFP
Regression7501750.0015.00.001
Residual error12502550.00
Total200026
  • atest the same hypothesis, but F is the more powerful
  • bcan disagree when the sample is small
  • ctest the same hypothesis, and t² = F
  • dtest different hypotheses, so the P-values differ
🔎 What it is really asking

Are these two tests related, or two separate questions?

🧭 Which type of question this is

The overall F test: its relation to the slope test.

🛠️ The procedure

In a regression with one predictor the overall F test and the t test for the slope are the same test: t² = F, and the two P-values are identical.

🧮 The working
Square the t: 3.873² = 15.00. That is the F.

Both give P = .00069, printed as .001 in both tables.

The critical values match in the same way: t* on 25 df is 2.0595386, and squaring it gives 4.2417, exactly the 5% critical value of F on (1, 25). (The rounded 2.0595 squares to 4.2415 — the identity is exact, the printed decimals are not.)

Both are testing one hypothesis, written two ways: "the slope is zero" and "the model explains nothing".

When they stop being the same: with two or more predictors. Then F asks whether the predictors together explain anything, and each t asks about one predictor with the others already in the model. Two genuinely different questions — which is why both tests are printed.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Neither is more powerful than the other, because they are the same test. They reject together and fail to reject together.
b.The identity is algebra, so sample size cannot break it. t² = F holds in every single-predictor regression.
d.With a single predictor there is only one hypothesis to test. "Slope is zero" and "the model explains nothing" are the same statement.
🏷️ One predictor: t² = F, same P. Two or more: different questions.

Question 11

🅕 The overall F test

What the F test is testing

In a regression of wellbeing on supervision hours, the null hypothesis of the overall F test is best written as:
The analysis-of-variance table for the same regression
SourceSSdfMSFP
Regression7501750.0015.00.001
Residual error12502550.00
Total200026
  • athe sample correlation is zero
  • bthe two variables are not linearly related in the sample
  • cthe residuals have a mean of zero
  • dthe slope of the population line is zero
🔎 What it is really asking

A hypothesis is about the population, and about the right quantity.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The overall F test: the hypothesis.

🛠️ The procedure

Hypotheses are always about population quantities. For a one-predictor regression the F test’s H₀ is β = 0: in the population, the line is flat.

🧮 The working
H₀: β = 0 — supervision hours carry no linear information about wellbeing in the population.

Hₐ: β ≠ 0 — they carry some.

A large F means the model explains far more variation than residual noise alone would produce, which is evidence against a flat line.

Two habits worth building:
• A hypothesis never mentions the sample. The sample slope is 1.55 and the sample correlation is 0.61 — those are measurements, not claims to be tested.
• A hypothesis is a statement someone could be wrong about. "The residuals have mean zero" is forced by the arithmetic of least squares, so there is nothing there to test.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The sample correlation is 0.61, a number you already have. Hypotheses concern the population — "the population correlation is zero" would be fine, and is equivalent to β = 0.
b.A statement about the sample cannot be a null hypothesis. We can see the sample; what is uncertain is the population behind it.
c.Residuals from a least-squares fit have mean exactly zero whenever the model includes an intercept — forced by the arithmetic, so not a testable claim.
🏷️ H₀: β = 0, about the POPULATION line. Never about the sample.

Question 12

🎯 Mean response or one individual

Mean response against one individual

Lindqvist computes, for clinics with 9 supervision hours, both a 95% interval for the mean wellbeing score and a 95% interval for the score of one such clinic. Comparing the two:
Regression of wellbeing score on monthly supervision hours · 27 clinics
PredictorCoefficientStd. ErrortP
Constant41.20002.760014.928.000
Supervision hours1.55000.40023.873.001
  • awhich is wider depends on the value of x
  • bthe interval for one clinic is wider
  • cthe interval for the mean is wider
  • dthey have the same width but different centres
🔎 What it is really asking

Which of the two has more sources of uncertainty in it?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Mean response or one individual: which interval is wider.

🛠️ The procedure

Both intervals share the same centre, ŷ. The interval for one individual is always wider, because it must allow for individual scatter around the line as well as for uncertainty about where the line is.

🧮 The working
Centre, for both: ŷ = 41.2 + 1.55 × 9 = 55.15.

The interval for the mean response carries one source of error: we do not know exactly where the population line sits.

The interval for one clinic carries that, plus a second: even if we knew the line perfectly, individual clinics scatter around it with SD s = 7.07.

More uncertainty, wider interval — always, at every x, by a clear margin.

Match the interval to the question. "What is the average wellbeing of clinics with 9 hours of supervision?" is the mean response. "What will this clinic score?" is the prediction interval, and it is the one that stays honest about how much scatter there is.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The ordering never changes with x. Both intervals widen as you move away from x̄, but the prediction interval stays the wider one throughout.
c.The mean-response interval is the narrower of the two. It is only trying to locate the line, not to catch a single clinic.
d.The widths are different and the centres are the same — exactly the other way round.
🏷️ One individual = wider, always. Same centre, more scatter to cover.

Question 13

🎯 Mean response or one individual

Where a prediction interval is narrowest

Lindqvist’s clinics average 6.0 supervision hours a month. Her 95% interval for the mean wellbeing score is narrowest at:
Regression of wellbeing score on monthly supervision hours · 27 clinics
PredictorCoefficientStd. ErrortP
Constant41.20002.760014.928.000
Supervision hours1.55000.40023.873.001
  • ax = 6.0
  • bx = 0
  • cthe largest x in her data
  • devery x equally
🔎 What it is really asking

Where does the line pivot, and so where is it best pinned down?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Mean response or one individual: how the width changes with x.

🛠️ The procedure

Both intervals are narrowest at x̄ and widen in both directions as x moves away from it. The fitted line pivots about (x̄, ȳ), so that is where its position is known best.

🧮 The working
x̄ = 6.0, so the interval is narrowest at x = 6.0.

Why. Think of the uncertainty in the line as a small amount of wobble in its slope, hinged at the point of means. Right at the hinge, a change of slope barely moves the predicted value. Far out along the lever, the same wobble moves it a lot.

So the band around the line is not a pair of parallel lines — it is bow-tie shaped, pinched at x̄ and flaring out at both ends.

The practical consequence, and the real point of the question: predictions near the middle of your data are the trustworthy ones. Predictions at the edges are much less certain, and predictions outside the range of x — extrapolation — have no interval worth quoting at all.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.x = 0 is six hours below the mean, far out along the lever arm, so the interval there is much wider than at x̄ — and if no clinic received none, it is extrapolation as well.
c.The largest x is at the far end of the lever arm — among the widest points of the band.
d.Equal width at every x would mean the uncertainty band was a pair of parallel lines. It is a bow tie.
🏷️ Narrowest at x̄, flaring both ways. The line pivots at (x̄, ȳ).

Question 14

🖥️ Reading computer output

Finding a number in a printout

In Lindqvist’s coefficient table, the number 2.7600 is:
Regression of wellbeing score on monthly supervision hours · 27 clinics
PredictorCoefficientStd. ErrortP
Constant41.20002.760014.928.000
Supervision hours1.55000.40023.873.001
  • athe predicted wellbeing score at zero hours
  • bthe standard deviation of the residuals
  • cthe standard error of the constant
  • dthe standard error of the slope
🔎 What it is really asking

Read the row label and the column heading before anything else.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading computer output: locating the right cell.

🛠️ The procedure

A coefficient table is read by row and column: the row names the term, the column names the quantity. Find both before you reach for a formula.

🧮 The working
2.7600 sits in the Constant row, Std. Error column. So it is the standard error of the intercept.

The whole table, read properly:
  41.2000 — the intercept: predicted wellbeing at zero supervision hours
  2.7600 — its standard error
  14.928 — 41.2000 ⁄ 2.7600, the t for H₀: α = 0
  1.5500 — the slope: points per supervision hour
  0.4002 — its standard error
  3.873 — 1.5500 ⁄ 0.4002, the t for H₀: β = 0

Which row matters: almost always the slope. The test on the constant asks whether the line passes through the origin, which is rarely a question anyone cares about.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The predicted score at zero hours is 41.2000, the coefficient itself. Same row, wrong column.
b.The standard deviation of the residuals is s = √MSE = 7.07, which lives in the ANOVA table and not here at all.
d.The slope’s standard error is 0.4002, one row down. Same column, wrong row — the commonest misread of this table.
🏷️ Row names the term, column names the quantity. Check both.

Question 15

🖥️ Reading computer output

Reading a P-value from output

The entry .001 in the supervision-hours row of Lindqvist’s output means:
Regression of wellbeing score on monthly supervision hours · 27 clinics
PredictorCoefficientStd. ErrortP
Constant41.20002.760014.928.000
Supervision hours1.55000.40023.873.001
  • athe slope is significant one-sided but not two-sided
  • bthere is a 0.1% chance that H₀ is true
  • cthe slope is .001 away from zero
  • dthe two-sided P-value for that slope is about .001
🔎 What it is really asking

What a printed P-value in a coefficient table is, and what it is not.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading computer output: the P column.

🛠️ The procedure

The P column of a coefficient table gives the two-sided P-value for H₀: that coefficient is zero. Software prints it two-sided by default.

🧮 The working
P ≈ .001 for the slope — the exact value is .00069 — so at α = .05 reject H₀ and conclude that supervision hours predict wellbeing.

It is two-sided: it covers slopes that differ from zero in either direction. For a directional hypothesis you would halve it, after checking the sign of the estimate agrees with your prediction.

What a P-value is not: it is not the probability that H₀ is true. It is the probability of getting a slope at least this far from zero if H₀ were true. The conditioning runs the other way round, and no P-value can be turned into a probability about a hypothesis.

Finally, keep the two columns apart: P tells you whether the slope is distinguishable from zero; the coefficient tells you how big it is. A tiny P does not make 1.55 points large.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Nothing in the output is one-sided. Software prints two-sided P-values for coefficients unless you ask otherwise.
b."A 0.1% chance that H₀ is true" reverses the conditional. P is computed assuming H₀, so it cannot also be a probability about H₀.
c.The distance of the slope from zero is 1.55, in wellbeing points. The P-value is a probability and carries no units at all.
🏷️ P column = two-sided P for “this coefficient is zero”. Not P(H₀ true).
