Question 1

📐 Testing a slope

Recovering a coefficient from its standard error and t

Educational psychologist Kuusela regresses a working-memory score on weekly structured study hours for 50 students. The printer has dropped the coefficient for study hours, but the rest of its row survives. That coefficient, to four decimal places, is:
The same output with one coefficient lost in printing
PredictorCoefficientStd. ErrortP
Constant38.20004.34978.782.000
Structured study hours?0.60004.000.000
  • a6.6667
  • b4.6000
  • c2.4000
  • d0.1500
🔎 What it is really asking

The printout gives you two of the three numbers in one relationship. Find the third.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Testing a slope: running the t relationship backwards.

🛠️ The procedure

The three numbers in a coefficient row are tied together by t = b ⁄ SE(b). Rearranged, b = t × SE(b). Decide which one is missing, then rearrange to put it on its own.

🧮 The working
The surviving numbers in the study-hours row are SE(b) = 0.6000 and t = 4.000.

Start from what you know: t = b ⁄ SE(b).

Multiply both sides by SE(b): b = t × SE(b)

b = 4.000 × 0.6000 = 2.4000 working-memory points per study hour.

Check it the way it was printed: 2.4000 ⁄ 0.6000 = 4.000. ✓

The habit: a coefficient row is one equation with three slots. Write t = b ⁄ SE down first, put in the two numbers you have, and solve for the empty slot — never guess which way round to divide.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.6.6667 is 4.000 ⁄ 0.6000, the division upside down. A coefficient of 6.6667 against an SE of 0.6000 would give t = 11.11, not 4.000.
b.4.6000 is 4.000 + 0.6000. Nothing in a coefficient table is ever added — the relationship between the three numbers is a ratio.
d.0.1500 is 0.6000 ⁄ 4.000, dividing when the rearrangement calls for multiplying. A coefficient of 0.1500 against an SE of 0.6000 would give t = 0.25, not 4.000.
🏷️ A coefficient row is one equation: t = b ⁄ SE. Solve for the empty slot.

Question 2

📐 Testing a slope

Testing a slope at a stated level

Developmental psychologist Brandsma regresses vocabulary score on hours of shared reading for 22 toddlers and obtains a slope of 0.84 with a standard error of 0.35. On 20 degrees of freedom the two-sided critical values are 2.086 at α = .05 and 2.845 at α = .01. Working at α = .01, her conclusion is:
  • aretain H₀: t = 2.40 does not reach 2.845
  • breject H₀: t = 2.40 exceeds 2.086
  • creject H₀: the slope 0.84 is above zero
  • dretain H₀: the slope 0.84 is below 2.845
🔎 What it is really asking

Build the statistic yourself, then compare it with the critical value for the level the question names.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Testing a slope: statistic, then decision at a stated α.

🛠️ The procedure

Two steps, in order. t = b ⁄ SE(b) gives the statistic; then compare |t| with the critical value for the α the question asks about. Two critical values are printed, and only one of them is yours.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — the statistic.

t = 0.84 ⁄ 0.35 = 2.400

Step 2 — the comparison. The question says α = .01, so the critical value is 2.845.

|2.400| < 2.845, so retain H₀. At the 1% level there is not enough evidence that shared reading predicts vocabulary.

The exact two-sided P-value is .026, which makes the whole picture clear: .026 is below .05 but above .01. The same slope is significant at the 5% level and not at the 1% level.

And the decision: α is chosen before the data, not after. Once Brandsma has said 1%, the 2.086 row is not available to her — it belongs to a different question.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.t = 2.40 does exceed 2.086, but 2.086 is the 5% critical value. The question fixes α at .01, where the threshold is 2.845.
c.The sign of the slope is not the test. A positive slope can easily arise by chance; that is exactly what the t statistic is for.
d.Comparing 0.84 with 2.845 compares a slope with a t critical value. The slope is in vocabulary points per hour and the critical value is in standard errors.
🏷️ Compute t, then use the critical value for the α you were given.

Question 3

📐 Testing a slope

Using a slope over more than one unit

Two of Kuusela’s students differ by 2.5 structured study hours a week. The difference between their predicted working-memory scores, to two decimal places, is:
Regression of working-memory score on weekly structured study hours · 50 students
PredictorCoefficientStd. ErrortP
Constant38.20004.34978.782.000
Structured study hours2.40000.60004.000.000
  • a0.96
  • b4.90
  • c2.40
  • d6.00
🔎 What it is really asking

The slope is the change for one hour. The question asks about two and a half.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Testing a slope: scaling a rate to the change the question names.

🛠️ The procedure

A slope is a rate: b points per one unit of x. For a change of c units, the predicted change in y is b × c. Read the stem for c before you reach for a number.

🧮 The working
From the printout, b = 2.4000 points per study hour.

The gap between the two students is c = 2.5 hours.

predicted difference = 2.4000 × 2.5 = 6.00 working-memory points.

Sanity check by walking up in whole hours: 2.4 after one hour, 4.8 after two, and half of 2.4 more for the final half hour — 6.0. ✓

The habit: underline the number of units the question moves x by. A slope question that does not say "one unit" is asking you to multiply, and the slope itself is then a wrong answer sitting in plain sight.

And the wording: "predicted", not "caused". Nobody assigned these students their study hours, so 6.00 points is what the line predicts for two students who happen to differ by 2.5 hours.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.96 is 2.4000 ⁄ 2.5, dividing by the change instead of multiplying by it. That would make a bigger gap in x produce a smaller gap in y.
b.4.90 is 2.4000 + 2.5, adding the slope to the change in x. The two numbers are in different units — points per hour and hours — so they cannot be added.
c.2.40 is the predicted difference for a gap of one hour. The students here are 2.5 hours apart.
🏷️ Change in y = b × change in x. Find the change in x in the stem first.

Question 4

📏 An interval for a slope

Recovering a standard error from a printed interval

A journal article reports Kuusela’s 95% confidence interval for the slope as 1.1936 to 3.6064 on 48 degrees of freedom, with t* = 2.0106, but does not print the standard error. The standard error of the slope, to four decimal places, is:
  • a0.3000
  • b0.6000
  • c1.2064
  • d2.4000
🔎 What it is really asking

Take the interval apart into the pieces it was built from.

🧭 Which type of question this is

An interval for a slope: running the construction backwards.

🛠️ The procedure

An interval is b ± t* SE(b), so its half-width is the margin of error, t* × SE(b). Halve the width to get the margin, then divide the margin by t*.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — the width.  3.6064 − 1.1936 = 2.4128

Step 2 — the margin of error is half of that: 2.4128 ⁄ 2 = 1.2064

Step 3 — strip off t*:  SE(b) = 1.2064 ⁄ 2.0106 = 0.6000

A free check falls out on the way: the centre of the interval is the slope itself, (1.1936 + 3.6064) ⁄ 2 = 2.4000, which matches the coefficient Kuusela reported.

The habit: an interval carries three numbers inside it — the estimate at its centre, the margin as its half-width, and t* as the multiplier. Given any two of those you can recover the third, and published papers very often leave out the one you want.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.3000 halves the margin as well as dividing by t*. The halving has already been done once, when the width became the half-width.
c.1.2064 is the margin of error, the half-width. It is t* × SE(b), so it is one division away from the standard error.
d.2.4000 is the centre of the interval — the slope. Halving the sum of the two endpoints gives the estimate, not its precision.
🏷️ Half the width is t* × SE. Divide that by t* and nothing else.

Question 5

📏 An interval for a slope

A confidence interval at a different level

Using t* = 2.6822 on 48 degrees of freedom, the 99% confidence interval for Kuusela’s slope, to three decimal places, is:
Regression of working-memory score on weekly structured study hours · 50 students
PredictorCoefficientStd. ErrortP
Constant38.20004.34978.782.000
Structured study hours2.40000.60004.000.000
  • a1.800 to 3.000
  • b−0.282 to 5.082
  • c0.791 to 4.009
  • d1.194 to 3.606
🔎 What it is really asking

The same construction as a 95% interval, with the multiplier the stem gives you.

🧭 Which type of question this is

An interval for a slope: computing it at a stated confidence level.

🛠️ The procedure

b ± t* SE(b). Changing the confidence level changes only t* — the estimate and the standard error come straight off the printout and do not move.

🧮 The working
From the table: b = 2.4000 and SE(b) = 0.6000.

margin = 2.6822 × 0.6000 = 1.60932

  lower: 2.4000 − 1.60932 = 0.791
  upper: 2.4000 + 1.60932 = 4.009

Compare the 95% interval on the same data, where t* = 2.0106: 1.194 to 3.606. The 99% interval is the wider of the two.

And the decision: that is the trade every confidence level makes. More confidence that you have captured the true slope costs you precision about where it is. At 99% Kuusela can say the slope is somewhere between 0.79 and 4.01 points per hour — still clear of zero, so the result survives at the 1% level too, but a fivefold span is not a precise answer.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.1.800 to 3.000 is 2.4000 ± 0.6000, the standard error used as the margin with no t* at all. That is roughly a 68% interval.
b.−0.282 to 5.082 is 2.4000 ± 2.6822, using t* itself as the margin. t* has to multiply the standard error, not replace it.
d.1.194 to 3.606 is the 95% interval, built with t* = 2.0106. Right method, wrong multiplier for the level the question names.
🏷️ Only t* changes with the level. Higher confidence → wider interval.

Question 6

🧱 The regression ANOVA table

s when the error row is incomplete

Four entries have been removed from the table for Kuusela’s regression. The estimate s of the standard deviation of the residuals, to two decimal places, is:
The same table with four entries removed
SourceSSdfMSF
Regression10241??
Residual error3072??
Total409649
  • a8.00
  • b64.00
  • c7.92
  • d55.43
🔎 What it is really asking

Three short steps: the error df, then its mean square, then one square root.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The regression ANOVA table: rebuilding the error row.

🛠️ The procedure

Work down the table. The df column adds up, so the error df is the Total df minus the Regression df. Then MSE = SSE ⁄ df, and s = √MSE.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — the error df.  49 − 1 = 48  (which is also n − 2, so n = 50 ✓)

Step 2 — the error mean square.  MSE = 3072 ⁄ 48 = 64.00

Step 3 — the square root.  s = √64.00 = 8.00 working-memory points.

Every one of those steps has a wrong answer waiting on the option list: stopping at step 2 gives 64.00, dividing by the Total df gives 7.92, and taking the root before dividing gives 55.43.

The habit: say out loud which row and which column you are in before every division. "Error row, SS over error df." The table is laid out so that each row is self-contained.

What s is for: the typical vertical distance from a student to the line. On a score whose mean is 55.0, being out by about 8 points is substantial — and that stays true however small the P-value turns out to be.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.64.00 is MSE itself, a variance in points squared. s is its square root, and only s is in the units of the score.
c.7.92 is √(3072 ⁄ 49), dividing by the Total df of 49. The error row divides by its own 48.
d.55.43 is √3072, taking the root of the sum of squares before dividing by anything. The root comes last, not first.
🏷️ Error df from the df column, then SS ⁄ df, then the root. In that order.

Question 7

🧱 The regression ANOVA table

Rebuilding the sums of squares from r-squared

Clinical researcher Marchand reports that his regression explains 36% of the variation in therapy outcome, and that the residual sum of squares is 1600. The regression sum of squares is:
  • a4444
  • b900
  • c576
  • d2500
🔎 What it is really asking

Which share of the total does the 1600 represent? Start there.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The regression ANOVA table: working back from r-squared to a sum of squares.

🛠️ The procedure

r² = SSM ⁄ SST, so the unexplained share is 1 − r² = SSE ⁄ SST. Use the share you were given a number for to find SST first, then subtract.

🧮 The working
r² = .36 means the line explains 36% of the total, so the residuals hold the other 64%.

Step 1 — the total.  SSE is that 64%:  0.64 × SST = 1600, so SST = 1600 ⁄ 0.64 = 2500

Step 2 — the regression row.  SSM = SST − SSE = 2500 − 1600 = 900

Check both ways round: 900 ⁄ 2500 = 0.36 ✓ and 900 + 1600 = 2500 ✓

The habit that makes this easy: the number you are handed decides which percentage you divide by. Marchand gave you the residual SS, so pair it with 1 − r². Pairing 1600 with .36 instead is the designed trap, and it is the one most people fall into.

A shortcut worth knowing: SSM = SSE × r² ⁄ (1 − r²) = 1600 × 0.36 ⁄ 0.64 = 900, the same answer in one line.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.4444 is 1600 ⁄ 0.36, pairing the residual SS with the explained share instead of the unexplained one. Right move, wrong percentage.
c.576 is 0.36 × 1600, applying r² to the residual sum of squares. r² is a share of the total, so it cannot be applied to a part of it.
d.2500 is the total sum of squares. It is the first step of the calculation, not the answer — the regression row is what is left after taking 1600 away.
🏷️ Residual SS pairs with 1 − r². Find SST first, then subtract.

Question 8

🧱 The regression ANOVA table

The correlation from the sums of squares

Using the sums of squares in Kuusela’s table, and given that her slope is positive, the correlation between structured study hours and working-memory score, to three decimal places, is:
The analysis-of-variance table for Kuusela’s regression
SourceSSdfMSFP
Regression102411024.0016.00.000
Residual error30724864.00
Total409649
  • a0.250
  • b0.750
  • c0.866
  • d0.500
🔎 What it is really asking

The table gives you r². The question asks for r, with a sign.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The regression ANOVA table: from the sums of squares to r.

🛠️ The procedure

r² = SSM ⁄ SST, then r = ±√r². The square root has two signs, and the sign of the slope decides which one you keep.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — the share explained.  r² = 1024 ⁄ 4096 = 0.2500

Step 2 — the square root.  √0.2500 = 0.500

Step 3 — the sign.  The slope is +2.4000, so r is +0.500.

Read what each number says. r² = 25% is a share of variation and can never be negative. r = +0.500 is a direction and a strength on a scale from −1 to +1.

The habit: an ANOVA table never shows you a sign. Sums of squares are all positive by construction, so whenever a question turns one of them into a correlation you must go to the coefficient for the direction.

And the honest summary: r = 0.5 sounds respectable, and it still leaves 75% of the variation in working memory unexplained. Squaring is what keeps you honest — half the correlation, a quarter of the variation.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.250 is r², the share of variation explained, reported as though it were the correlation. r is its square root.
b.0.750 is 3072 ⁄ 4096, the share of variation left unexplained. It is 1 − r², not r.
c.0.866 is √(3072 ⁄ 4096), the square root of the unexplained share. The root has to be taken of the regression share.
🏷️ r = √(SSM ⁄ SST), with the slope’s sign. Tables have no signs.

Question 9

🅕 The overall F test

F from r-squared and the sample size

Health psychologist Grabowska regresses daily step count on self-reported motivation for 32 adults and reports that the model explains 20% of the variation. The value of the F statistic, to two decimal places, is:
  • a7.50
  • b0.25
  • c6.00
  • d4.17
🔎 What it is really asking

Turn the shares of variation into mean squares, which means dividing each by its df.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The overall F test: building it out of r-squared.

🛠️ The procedure

Take the total sum of squares to be 1. Then SSM = r², SSE = 1 − r², and F = (r² ⁄ 1) ⁄ ((1 − r²) ⁄ (n − 2)). The two df are what stop you simply dividing the shares.

🧮 The working
With one predictor and n = 32: model df = 1, error df = 32 − 2 = 30.

Let SST = 1, so SSM = 0.20 and SSE = 0.80.

MSM = 0.20 ⁄ 1 = 0.20
MSE = 0.80 ⁄ 30 = 0.026667

F = 0.20 ⁄ 0.026667 = 7.50

Written as one line: F = (0.20 ⁄ 0.80) × 30 = 0.25 × 30 = 7.50.

The habit: the sums of squares can be any numbers in that ratio — 20 and 80, or 1024 and 4096 — because F is a ratio of ratios. All that matters is the share and the df.

And the decision: on (1, 30) the 5% critical value is 4.1709, so 7.50 is past it. Notice what this means in general — the same r² of 20% in a sample of 12 would give F = 2.50 and no significant result at all. Explanatory power and significance are separate things, and n is what connects them.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.0.25 is 0.20 ⁄ 0.80, the two shares divided straight into one another. That is the sums-of-squares ratio with the degrees of freedom left out.
c.6.00 is 0.20 × 30, multiplying the explained share by the error df. The unexplained share has to go underneath first.
d.4.17 is the critical value of F on (1, 30) at α = .05 — the number you compare the statistic with.
🏷️ F = (r² ⁄ (1 − r²)) × (n − 2). The df are what the shares are missing.

Question 10

🅕 The overall F test

Recovering the slope t from F

Kuusela’s analysis-of-variance table is printed below, but the coefficient table has been mislaid. Given that her slope is positive, the t statistic for that slope, to two decimal places, is:
The analysis-of-variance table for Kuusela’s regression
SourceSSdfMSFP
Regression102411024.0016.00.000
Residual error30724864.00
Total409649
  • a16.00
  • b−4.00
  • c4.00
  • d256.00
🔎 What it is really asking

With a single predictor, F and t carry the same information. Which way does the conversion go?

🧭 Which type of question this is

The overall F test: converting F back into t.

🛠️ The procedure

With one predictor, t² = F. So |t| = √F, and the sign of t is the sign of the slope.

🧮 The working
The table gives F = 16.00 on (1, 48) df.

|t| = √16.00 = 4.00

The slope is positive, so t = +4.00.

The df line up as they must: F has (1, 48) and t has 48 — the error df, the second of the F pair.

Why this is worth being able to do. The two tables answer the same question when there is one predictor, so a missing coefficient table is not a dead end. The P-value is the same either way: .000218.

What gets lost in F, and found again in t: the direction. F = 16.00 would be identical for a slope of −2.4000, because squaring throws the sign away. That is why the question has to tell you the slope is positive, and why a directional hypothesis always needs the t row rather than the F.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.16.00 is F itself. With one predictor t and F are different numbers reporting the same result — F is the square of t.
b.−4.00 has the right size and the wrong sign. The square root could go either way, and the positive slope settles it.
d.256.00 is 16.00², squaring F when the relationship calls for the square root. Squaring takes you one step further away from t, not towards it.
🏷️ One predictor: |t| = √F, and the slope’s sign gives t its sign.

Question 11

🅕 The overall F test

A decision at two levels at once

Sleep researcher Dragomir regresses sleep quality on daily screen time for 42 adults. On (1, 40) degrees of freedom the critical values of F are 4.0847 at α = .05 and 7.3141 at α = .01. From the table below, her result is:
Dragomir’s regression of sleep quality on daily screen time · 42 adults
SourceSSdf
Regression4051
Residual error270040
Total310541
  • asignificant at both .05 and .01
  • bsignificant at .01 but not at .05
  • cnot significant at either level
  • dsignificant at .05 but not at .01
🔎 What it is really asking

Finish the table first — you cannot compare anything until you have the statistic.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The overall F test: computing it, then comparing at two levels.

🛠️ The procedure

Build F before you look at the critical values: each MS = that row’s SS ⁄ that row’s df, then F = MSM ⁄ MSE. Then compare the one statistic with both thresholds.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — the mean squares.
  MSM = 405 ⁄ 1 = 405.00
  MSE = 2700 ⁄ 40 = 67.50

Step 2 — the statistic.  F = 405.00 ⁄ 67.50 = 6.00

Step 3 — the comparisons.
  6.00 > 4.0847, so it clears the 5% threshold → significant at .05
  6.00 < 7.3141, so it does not clear the 1% threshold → not significant at .01

The exact P-value confirms the sandwich: P = .019, which sits between .01 and .05.

And the decision: the critical values climb as α falls, because demanding more certainty means demanding more evidence. So a result can only ever be significant at the looser level and not the stricter one — never the other way round. If an option claims .01 but not .05, you can rule it out without computing anything.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Significant at both would need F above 7.3141. Dragomir’s 6.00 falls short of the 1% threshold.
b.Significant at .01 but not at .05 is impossible for any data. The 1% critical value is always the higher hurdle, so clearing it means clearing the 5% one too.
c.Not significant at either level would need F below 4.0847, and 6.00 is above it. Dividing 405 by 2700 instead of using the mean squares is what leads here.
🏷️ Clearing .01 always means clearing .05. The reverse is impossible.

Question 12

🎯 Mean response or one individual

Choosing the right standard error for an interval

For students with 10 structured study hours a week, Kuusela’s software reports a standard error of 2.1260 for the mean score of all such students and 8.2777 for the score of one such student. Using t* = 2.0106, her 95% interval for the score of a single student with 10 hours, to two decimal places, is:
Regression of working-memory score on weekly structured study hours · 50 students
PredictorCoefficientStd. ErrortP
Constant38.20004.34978.782.000
Structured study hours2.40000.60004.000.000
  • a38.36 to 71.64
  • b45.56 to 78.84
  • c57.93 to 66.47
  • d53.92 to 70.48
🔎 What it is really asking

Two standard errors are offered and only one belongs to the question. Pick it, then build the interval.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Mean response or one individual: computing the right interval.

🛠️ The procedure

Both intervals are ŷ ± t* × SE and both share the centre ŷ. The question names the quantity, and that choice picks the SE: one individual takes the larger one, because it has to cover individual scatter as well.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — the centre.  ŷ = 38.2000 + 2.4000 × 10 = 62.20

Step 2 — the standard error. The question asks about one student, so SE = 8.2777.

Step 3 — the margin.  2.0106 × 8.2777 = 16.6431

  lower: 62.20 − 16.6452 = 45.56
  upper: 62.20 + 16.6452 = 78.84

Compare the other interval, built on SE = 2.1260: 57.93 to 66.47, a span of 8.5 points against 33.3. Nearly four times narrower — and it answers a different question.

The habit: find the words "one", "a single", "this student" or "on average", "the mean of all". They are the whole question. Everything after that is the same arithmetic either way.

Why the individual interval is so much wider: locating the line is the easy part with 50 students. Predicting one person also has to allow for how far individuals sit from the line, and that is s = 8.00 points, which no amount of extra data shrinks.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.38.36 to 71.64 is centred on ȳ = 55.0, the overall mean score, instead of on the predicted value 62.20. The centre of any interval here is ŷ.
c.57.93 to 66.47 uses SE = 2.1260, the standard error for the mean score of all students with 10 hours. Right centre, wrong question.
d.53.92 to 70.48 is 62.20 ± 8.2777, the standard error used as the margin with no t* at all. It is roughly a 68% interval.
🏷️ Name the quantity, pick its SE, then ŷ ± t* SE. Same arithmetic either way.

Question 13

🎯 Mean response or one individual

Recognising extrapolation

Kuusela’s 50 students reported between 3 and 11 structured study hours a week. A tutor asks her to predict the working-memory score of a student who studies 20 hours. Kuusela should answer that:
Regression of working-memory score on weekly structured study hours · 50 students
PredictorCoefficientStd. ErrortP
Constant38.20004.34978.782.000
Structured study hours2.40000.60004.000.000
  • a20 hours is outside her data, so the prediction is unsupported
  • bthe prediction is sound, since the slope is significant
  • cthe interval at 20 hours is narrower than at 7 hours
  • dthe prediction is sound, since 50 students is a large sample
🔎 What it is really asking

Compare the x the question asks about with the range of x she actually observed.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Mean response or one individual: the limits of a fitted line.

🛠️ The procedure

A fitted line describes the range of x in the data and nothing beyond it. Predicting outside that range is extrapolation, and no interval around it can be trusted.

🧮 The working
Her x runs from 3 to 11 hours. The request is for 20 hours — nearly double the top of her range, and seven hours of it on no evidence at all.

The arithmetic still runs: ŷ = 38.2000 + 2.4000 × 20 = 86.20. It looks like an answer, and it is not one.

Two separate problems with it.
• The shape. Nothing in her data says the relationship stays straight out there. Study hours very plausibly level off, or turn down once exhaustion sets in, and a straight line cannot know that.
• The width. Even if it did stay straight, intervals are narrowest at x̄ = 7.0 and flare out in both directions. At 20 hours the band would be very wide — the opposite of the reassurance the tutor is after.

Say it to a friend: "the line only knows about students who studied between 3 and 11 hours."
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.A significant slope says the line is not flat within the observed range. It says nothing about what happens beyond it.
c.The interval is narrowest at x̄ = 7.0 and widens in both directions. At 20 hours it would be at its widest, not its narrowest.
d.Fifty students is a decent sample, and sample size cannot supply information about study hours nobody in the sample reported.
🏷️ A line only describes the x-values you observed. Outside them, say so.

Question 14

🖥️ Reading computer output

Matching a question to a cell of the printout

A colleague asks Kuusela whether the population line could plausibly pass through the origin. The number in her output that bears on this question is:
Regression of working-memory score on weekly structured study hours · 50 students
PredictorCoefficientStd. ErrortP
Constant38.20004.34978.782.000
Structured study hours2.40000.60004.000.000
  • a38.2000, the constant itself
  • b4.3497, the constant’s standard error
  • c8.782, the t for the constant
  • d4.000, the t for the slope
🔎 What it is really asking

Translate the words into a hypothesis about a coefficient, then find the cell that tests it.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading computer output: deciding which row and column answer the question.

🛠️ The procedure

Translate first, then read. "Passes through the origin" means the predicted score at x = 0 is zero, which is H₀: the constant is 0. The number that tests a coefficient is the t in that coefficient’s row.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — the translation.  Through the origin ⇒ at x = 0, ŷ = 0 ⇒ the intercept is zero. So H₀: α = 0, and it is the Constant row that matters.

Step 2 — the column. An estimate says how big something is; a t says whether it is distinguishable from zero. The question is a test, so the column is t.

Step 3 — read the cell.  Constant row, t column: 8.782, with P = .000.

So the answer to the colleague is no: 8.782 is far from zero, the intercept of 38.2000 is clearly not zero, and the line does not pass through the origin.

The habit: every printout question is two decisions, not one. Which row — which coefficient is the question about? Which column — is it asking how big, how precise, or whether it differs from zero? Pick the row first; it is the step people skip.

Worth adding: a test on the constant is usually of no interest, because x = 0 is often meaningless. Here it would mean a student doing no structured study at all, which is at least imaginable — but it is still outside her 3-to-11-hour range.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.38.2000 is the constant itself — it tells you where the line crosses the axis, not whether that crossing differs from zero by more than sampling noise.
b.4.3497 is the constant’s standard error. It measures precision; on its own it tests nothing, and it is the number the 8.782 was built from.
d.4.000 is the t for the slope, which tests whether the line is flat. Flat and through-the-origin are different questions about different coefficients.
🏷️ Translate the words into H₀ first. Then pick the row, then the column.

Question 15

🖥️ Reading computer output

Turning a printed P-value one-sided

Kuusela predicted before collecting her data that more structured study would go with higher working-memory scores. Her output prints .000 in the P column of the study-hours row. The P-value for her directional prediction is:
Regression of working-memory score on weekly structured study hours · 50 students
PredictorCoefficientStd. ErrortP
Constant38.20004.34978.782.000
Structured study hours2.40000.60004.000.000
  • athe printed value itself, already one-sided
  • btwice the printed value, since one tail is smaller
  • cnot obtainable from the printed output
  • dhalf the printed value, since the slope is positive
🔎 What it is really asking

The output gives one kind of P-value. Her hypothesis asks for another.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading computer output: two-sided output and a one-sided hypothesis.

🛠️ The procedure

Software prints two-sided P-values for coefficients. For a one-sided hypothesis, check the sign of the estimate first; if it points the way you predicted, the one-sided P is half the printed one.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — what is printed.  The P column is two-sided: it covers slopes that differ from zero in either direction. The exact value is .000218, shown as .000.

Step 2 — the sign check.  Kuusela predicted a positive slope and the estimate is +2.4000. The data point the way she predicted. ✓

Step 3 — halve it.  one-sided P = .000218 ⁄ 2 = .000109

Why halving works. The two-sided P is the area in both tails beyond |t| = 4.00. The t distribution is symmetric, so each tail holds exactly half. A one-sided hypothesis only claims one of those tails.

Step 2 is the one people skip, and it is the one that matters. If the slope had come out at −2.4000 while she predicted positive, the printed P would still be .000218 — and her one-sided P would be 1 − .000109, almost 1. Halving a two-sided P without looking at the sign can turn a result that flatly contradicts your prediction into apparent strong support for it.

And the honesty rule: the prediction has to be made before the data, as hers was. Choosing the direction after seeing the sign is not a one-sided test, it is just halving your P-value.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Coefficient tables are two-sided by default. Treating the printed value as already one-sided keeps the whole area from both tails and overstates nothing, but it is not the directional P-value she wants.
b.Doubling goes the wrong way. The printed value already covers two tails; a one-sided hypothesis claims one of them, so the number gets smaller, not larger.
c.It is obtainable, in one step, once the sign of the estimate has been checked against the prediction. The symmetry of the t distribution is what makes it work.
🏷️ Printed P is two-sided. Check the sign agrees, then halve it.

Question 1

📐 Testing a slope

Auditing a sentence written about a slope

Organisational psychologist Rombouts regresses a team engagement score on the hours of training each of 51 work teams receives a month, and writes: "b = 1.4000, SE 0.4000, t(49) = 3.50, P = .001, so training accounts for 1.4% of the variation in engagement." The fault in that sentence is:
Regression of a team engagement score on monthly training hours · 51 teams
PredictorCoefficientStd. ErrortP
Constant28.20004.87305.787.000
Training hours1.40000.40003.500.001
  • athe standard error should not be quoted
  • bthe P-value should be given exactly
  • cthe slope is read as a share of variation
  • dthe degrees of freedom should read 50
🔎 What it is really asking

Is every number in the sentence doing the job its own column does?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Testing a slope: checking a written claim against the printout.

🛠️ The procedure

Each column answers one question and cannot be borrowed for another. A coefficient is a rate in the units of the study. A share of variation is r², and it lives in the other table. Nothing in a coefficient row is a percentage.

🧮 The working
Read the slope properly first: 1.4000 engagement points for each extra training hour a month. Points per hour — a rate, with units.

Now the claim. The share of variation explained is r² = SSM ⁄ SST = 441 ⁄ 2205 = 0.20, so 20%, not 1.4%. The 1.4 was simply lifted out of the coefficient column and given a per-cent sign.

Everything else in her sentence is sound: 51 − 2 = 49 df, 1.4000 ⁄ 0.4000 = 3.50, and P = .001 follows from a t of 3.50 on 49 df.

The habit: before you believe a sentence about regression output, ask which column each number came out of and whether the words round it match that column. A slope answers "how much per unit"; only r² answers "how much of the variation".

Say it to a friend: "1.4 points per hour, and a fifth of the variation — two different numbers from two different tables."
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Printing the standard error beside the coefficient is good practice, not a fault — it is what lets a reader judge how precise the 1.4000 is.
b.P = .001 is the ordinary way of reporting a P-value this small. The exact figure is .0010, and nothing in her sentence would change if she gave it.
d.The df are right. One predictor costs two degrees of freedom, so 51 − 2 = 49. The 50 she might have written is the Total row, which no t test uses.
🏷️ Coefficient = points per unit. r² = share of variation. Never swap them.

Question 2

📐 Testing a slope

When a slope’s P-value cannot be trusted

Developmental psychologist Mielke has 120 reading scores paired with 120 practice-hour totals, and her slope comes out with P = .003. The 120 rows come from 30 children measured on four occasions each. The P-value cannot be trusted because:
  • athe 120 rows are not independent of one another
  • bthe practice hours are not Normally distributed
  • c120 rows are too few for a slope to be tested
  • dthe slope should have been tested one-sided
🔎 What it is really asking

Which requirement does measuring the same child four times break?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Testing a slope: the condition that sample size cannot rescue.

🛠️ The procedure

Every P-value for a slope is built on independent observations. Four scores from one child are more alike than four scores from four children, so the software has been told there is more information in the data than there really is.

🧮 The working
Count what she really has: 30 children, not 120 independent cases.

A child who reads well in March reads well in June. Those four rows move together, so they do not each contribute a fresh piece of evidence — but the formula for SE(b) divides by a quantity built from all 120 rows, so it reports a standard error far too small.

A standard error that is too small makes t too big and P too small. The .003 is not a conservative estimate of the evidence; it is an overstatement of it, and there is no way to tell from the printout alone.

Why this one is special. Normality matters less as the sample grows, and unequal spread can be worked around. Independence cannot be repaired by collecting more data — more rows from the same 30 children make the overstatement worse, not better. Repeated measurements need a method that knows the rows are clustered.

The habit: before trusting any P-value, count the people, not the rows. If one person contributes several rows, stop and say so.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.The predictor is not required to be Normal at all. Normality is a condition on the scatter about the line, and it is the most forgiving of the conditions.
c.120 rows would be a comfortable sample for a single predictor. The trouble is not how many rows there are but how few independent people they came from.
d.A one-sided test would halve the P-value and make the overstatement worse. Direction is not what is wrong here.
🏷️ Count people, not rows. Independence is the condition more data cannot fix.

Question 3

📐 Testing a slope

Which design produced the printed degrees of freedom

Memory researcher Seppälä reports a slope tested on 28 degrees of freedom. The design that produced them is:
  • a28 participants and one predictor
  • b30 participants and two predictors
  • c32 participants and two predictors
  • d30 participants and one predictor
🔎 What it is really asking

Run the df rule backwards over four candidate designs.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Testing a slope: recovering the design from the degrees of freedom.

🛠️ The procedure

df = n − p − 1, where p is the number of predictors. Try each candidate in that formula rather than looking for 28 somewhere in the design.

🧮 The working
Take the four designs in turn:

  30 cases, 1 predictor: 30 − 1 − 1 = 28 ✓
  28 cases, 1 predictor: 28 − 1 − 1 = 26
  30 cases, 2 predictors: 30 − 2 − 1 = 27
  32 cases, 2 predictors: 32 − 2 − 1 = 29

Only the first gives 28.

What the subtraction is paying for. Each coefficient the line estimates — one per predictor, plus the intercept — uses up one degree of freedom. One predictor means two coefficients, so n − 2; two predictors mean three, so n − 3.

The habit: a question that hands you a df and asks about the design is the same rule read from right to left. Write the rule down, put the candidates into it, and do not try to spot the answer in the stem.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.28 participants with one predictor would leave 26 degrees of freedom. The printed df is never the sample size — something has always been taken off it.
b.30 participants with two predictors gives 27. A second predictor costs one more degree of freedom, because a third coefficient has to be estimated.
c.32 participants with two predictors gives 29. Close, but the rule subtracts three here, not two.
🏷️ df = n − predictors − 1. Put each candidate design into the rule.

Question 4

📏 An interval for a slope

Matching a written verdict to an interval

A reviewer writes of Nijhuis’s one-predictor study: "the slope is clearly above zero, and yet the plausible values run from trivially small to very large." The 95% interval she reported for her slope must have been:
  • a−2.60 to −0.10
  • b0.10 to 2.90
  • c−0.20 to 2.60
  • d1.30 to 1.50
🔎 What it is really asking

Two separate facts in one sentence: significance, and width. Find the interval with both.

🧭 Which type of question this is

An interval for a slope: reading a verdict back into an interval.

🛠️ The procedure

An interval carries two pieces of news. Where it sits relative to zero settles the test; how wide it is settles how much you have learnt. Check the two separately.

🧮 The working
Take the reviewer’s two statements one at a time.

"Clearly above zero" — the whole interval must lie above 0. That rules out −0.20 to 2.60 (it straddles zero, so the slope is not significant) and −2.60 to −0.10 (entirely below zero, so the slope is significant in the other direction).

"Trivially small to very large" — the surviving interval has to be wide. 1.30 to 1.50 is a tight range: that study pinned its slope down very precisely, which is the opposite of what he describes.

So it is 0.10 to 2.90: all positive, and a twenty-nine-fold span from one end to the other.

The lesson worth carrying: "significant" and "precise" are different achievements. A study can clear zero and still leave you almost ignorant about the size of the effect — which is exactly why journals ask for intervals and not only P-values.

Say it to a friend: "where it sits tells you the verdict, how wide it is tells you how much you know."
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.−2.60 to −0.10 lies entirely below zero. It is a significant negative slope, and the reviewer describes one above zero.
c.−0.20 to 2.60 contains zero, so that study did not reject H₀: β = 0 and could not be described as clearly above zero.
d.1.30 to 1.50 is significant but narrow. It pins the slope down to within a fifth of a point, which is a precise result rather than an uninformative one.
🏷️ Position settles the test; width settles how much you have learnt.

Question 5

📏 An interval for a slope

A test statistic recovered from a printed interval

Health psychologist Laukkanen publishes only a 95% confidence interval for her slope, 0.60 to 3.00, on 38 degrees of freedom, where t* = 2.0244. The t statistic for her slope, to two decimal places, is:
  • a0.89
  • b2.02
  • c3.04
  • d1.50
🔎 What it is really asking

The interval hides the estimate and the standard error. Get both, then divide.

🧭 Which type of question this is

An interval for a slope: working back through it to the test.

🛠️ The procedure

An interval is b ± t* SE(b), so its centre is b and its half-width is t* SE(b). Recover SE(b) from the half-width, then t = b ⁄ SE(b). The standard error is an input here, not the answer.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — the estimate. The centre of the interval is the slope:
  b = (0.60 + 3.00) ⁄ 2 = 1.80

Step 2 — the standard error. The half-width is t* × SE(b):
  half-width = (3.00 − 0.60) ⁄ 2 = 1.20
  SE(b) = 1.20 ⁄ 2.0244 = 0.5928

Step 3 — the test statistic.
  t = 1.80 ⁄ 0.5928 = 3.04

A check on all three steps at once: t = t* × (centre ⁄ half-width) = 2.0244 × 1.5 = 3.0366. The same 3.04, and it shows what the arithmetic is really doing — asking how many half-widths the centre sits above zero.

And it agrees with the verdict, as it must. The interval misses zero, and 3.04 is past t* = 2.0244. An interval and a two-sided test at the matching level never disagree.

The habit: when a question gives you an interval, write its centre and its half-width in the margin straight away. Almost every question of this kind is one of those two numbers, or something one step beyond them.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.89 is 1.80 ⁄ 2.0244, the centre divided by the multiplier. t* is not a standard error — it is the number the standard error was multiplied by.
b.2.02 is t* itself, the 5% threshold on 38 df. It is what the answer must be compared with, not the answer.
d.1.50 is 1.80 ⁄ 1.20, the centre over the half-width. That is the ratio the shortcut uses, but it still has to be multiplied by t* to become a t statistic.
🏷️ Interval → centre is b, half-width ⁄ t* is SE(b). Then t = b ⁄ SE(b).

Question 6

🧱 The regression ANOVA table

Which sums of squares fit a stated conclusion

Clinical researcher Ostendorf reports that his fitted line accounts for exactly half the variation in his outcome. The pair of sums of squares that matches his report is:
  • aregression 600, residual 600
  • bregression 600, residual 1800
  • cregression 300, residual 1200
  • dregression 1200, residual 1800
🔎 What it is really asking

Which split of the total gives a half? Mind what the denominator is.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The regression ANOVA table: reading the sums of squares as a split.

🛠️ The procedure

r² = SSM ⁄ SST, and SST = SSM + SSE. So "half the variation" means the regression row and the residual row are equal — not that one is half the other.

🧮 The working
Work out the share each candidate gives. The total is always the two added together:

  600 and 600:   600 ⁄ 1200 = 0.50 ✓
  600 and 1800:  600 ⁄ 2400 = 0.25
  300 and 1200:  300 ⁄ 1500 = 0.20
  1200 and 1800: 1200 ⁄ 3000 = 0.40

Only the first gives a half.

Where this goes wrong for most people. "Half" feels as though it should mean SSM is half of SSE, which is the 600-and-1200 pattern and gives a third. The share is always measured against the total, and the total is a number you have to form yourself — no row of the table prints it until you add.

A picture for it: the total variation in y is one cake. The regression row is the slice the line explains and the residual row is the slice left on the plate. Equal slices means half the cake.

The habit: add the two sums of squares before you divide anything. Half the wrong answers in this topic are a correct division by the wrong denominator.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.600 and 1800 make a total of 2400, so the line explains 600 ⁄ 2400 = a quarter. This is the pair where SSM is a third of SSE, which is not the same thing.
c.300 and 1200 make 1500, so the share is 300 ⁄ 1500 = a fifth. The regression row being a quarter of the residual row is not a share of the total.
d.1200 and 1800 make 3000, giving two fifths. It is the closest of the three to a half, and still not one — add before dividing.
🏷️ Share = SSM ⁄ (SSM + SSE). Equal rows means exactly half.

Question 7

🧱 The regression ANOVA table

Whose reading of an ANOVA table survives

Two colleagues read Rombouts’s table below. One says the training hours explain most of the variation in engagement, since F is significant. The other says they explain about a fifth of it. The reading that survives is:
The analysis-of-variance table for the same regression
SourceSSdfMSF
Regression4411441.0012.25
Residual error17644936.00
Total220550
  • athe second: 441 of the 1764 residual
  • bthe second: 441 of the 2205 total
  • cthe first: F = 12.25 is a large F
  • dthe first: a small P means most of it
🔎 What it is really asking

Does a significant F say how much the line explains?

🧭 Which type of question this is

The regression ANOVA table: significance against explanatory power.

🛠️ The procedure

The F column answers whether the slope is distinguishable from zero. The SS column answers how much of the variation the line accounts for: SSM ⁄ SST. They are different questions and the table prints both.

🧮 The working
The share, from the SS column:

  441 ⁄ 2205 = 0.20, so 20% — about a fifth, as the second colleague says.

The first colleague has read a significant F as though it measured size. It does not. F = 12.25 compares the variation the line explains with the variation left over, each divided by its own degrees of freedom — 441 ⁄ 1 against 1764 ⁄ 49. The 49 in that second division is what carries the sample size, and it is why a modest share can still be strongly significant.

Both sentences are true at once, and the honest write-up contains both: the slope is almost certainly not zero, and four fifths of the differences in engagement between these 51 teams have nothing to do with training hours.

The habit: when a reader asks "how much", go to the SS column. When they ask "is it real", go to the F or the P. A single column cannot answer both.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Dividing by the residual row gives 441 ⁄ 1764 = 0.25, which is not a share of anything. The denominator of a share is the Total row.
c.A large F says the line explains more than noise would, not that it explains most of the variation. With 49 residual degrees of freedom a fifth of the variation is plenty to produce F = 12.25.
d.A small P-value responds to the sample size as well as to the strength of the relationship. It is not a measure of how much is explained, at any size.
🏷️ F says whether. SSM ⁄ SST says how much. Report both.

Question 8

🧱 The regression ANOVA table

What rescaling the outcome does to the table

Rombouts’s engagement score runs from 0 to 10. Suppose she had recorded every score on a 0-to-100 scale instead, by multiplying each one by 10, and run the same regression. In the new table:
The analysis-of-variance table for the same regression
SourceSSdfMSF
Regression4411441.0012.25
Residual error17644936.00
Total220550
  • athe SS column changes, the MS column does not
  • bthe SS, MS and F columns all change
  • cnone of the three columns changes at all
  • dthe SS and MS columns change, F does not
🔎 What it is really asking

Which entries of the table carry the units of y, and which are ratios?

🧭 Which type of question this is

The regression ANOVA table: what a change of units touches.

🛠️ The procedure

Every sum of squares is in squared units of y, so multiplying y by 10 multiplies each of them by 10² = 100. The mean squares follow, since each is a SS over an unchanged df. F is a ratio of two mean squares, so the 100s cancel and it is unchanged.

🧮 The working
Follow the columns one at a time.

SS: every deviation in y is ten times bigger, and each is squared, so
  SSM 441 → 44 100,  SSE 1764 → 176 400,  SST 2205 → 220 500.

df: 1, 49 and 50. Degrees of freedom come from the design — 51 teams, one predictor — and the scale of y has nothing to do with them.

MS: each is its row’s SS over its own df, so each is multiplied by 100 too: MSM 44 100, MSE 3600.

F: 44 100 ⁄ 3600 = 12.25. Exactly what it was.

r² is unchanged as well — 44 100 ⁄ 220 500 = 0.20 — and so is the P-value. The slope and its standard error are each ten times bigger, and their ratio, t = 3.50, is untouched.

The habit, and it is a general one: a change of units can never change the evidence. Anything that is a ratio of two quantities in the same units — F, t, r², a P-value — comes out the same. Anything carrying units — a slope, a standard error, a sum of squares — moves with the scale. If a unit conversion moves your P-value, you have made an arithmetic mistake.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The mean squares cannot sit still while the sums of squares move, because each mean square is simply its row’s SS divided by a degrees of freedom that has not changed.
b.F is a ratio of two quantities that were both multiplied by 100, so the factor cancels. Rescaling the outcome never strengthens or weakens the evidence.
c.The sums of squares are in squared units of y, so they must change — the line is now predicting scores ten times larger, and their spread is a hundred times larger in squared terms.
🏷️ Units move the SS and MS. Ratios — F, t, r², P — never move.

Question 9

🅕 The overall F test

Recovering an F from a two-level verdict

Sleep researcher Bardin writes only that her overall F test on (1, 30) degrees of freedom was significant at the 5% level but not at the 1% level. On (1, 30) the critical values are 4.17 and 7.56. Her F could have been:
  • a6.40
  • b3.90
  • c8.20
  • d0.26
🔎 What it is really asking

Her sentence puts the F between two printed thresholds. Which candidate sits there?

🧭 Which type of question this is

The overall F test: reading a verdict back into a statistic.

🛠️ The procedure

"Significant at 5%" means F is above the 5% critical value. "Not at 1%" means it is below the 1% one. Together they trap F between the two numbers.

🧮 The working
Her sentence says: 4.17 < F < 7.56.

Test the candidates:
  6.40 — above 4.17, below 7.56 ✓
  3.90 — below 4.17, so it would not have been significant at all
  8.20 — above 7.56, so it would have been significant at 1% as well
  0.26 — nowhere near either threshold

So 6.40, whose exact P-value is .017 — between .01 and .05, as the sentence requires.

Why the thresholds run that way round. A smaller α is a stricter test, so its critical value is larger: 7.56 at 1% against 4.17 at 5%. An F that clears the stricter bar clears the looser one automatically, which is why "significant at 1% but not at 5%" is a sentence nobody can ever write.

The habit: translate each clause of a verdict into an inequality before you look at the options. Two clauses give you two inequalities, and the answer is whatever satisfies both.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.3.90 is below the 5% critical value of 4.17, so that study would have reported no significant result at either level.
c.8.20 is past the 1% critical value of 7.56, so it would have been significant at both levels and the second half of her sentence would be false.
d.0.26 is below 1, so the residual mean square exceeds the regression mean square. That is as far from significant as an F can get.
🏷️ A stricter α has a LARGER critical value. Turn each clause into an inequality.

Question 10

🅕 The overall F test

What a larger sample does to F

Suppose Rombouts had studied 101 teams rather than 51, with the same slope of 1.4000, the same residual spread s = 6.00, and training hours just as widely spread as before. Her F, to two decimal places, would be about:
The analysis-of-variance table for the same regression
SourceSSdfMSF
Regression4411441.0012.25
Residual error17644936.00
Total220550
  • a6.13
  • b150.06
  • c24.50
  • d12.25
🔎 What it is really asking

Which ingredient of F does doubling the sample change, and in which direction?

🧭 Which type of question this is

The overall F test: how the sample size feeds into it.

🛠️ The procedure

With one predictor F = t² and t = b ⁄ SE(b), where SE(b) = s ⁄ √Sxx. Doubling the number of teams at the same spread of x roughly doubles Sxx, which divides SE(b) by √2, multiplies t by √2, and so doubles F.

🧮 The working
Nothing about the relationship itself has changed: the slope is still 1.4000 and the scatter about the line is still s = 6.00. What has changed is how much x-information the sample carries.

Sxx is a total of squared distances of the x-values from x̄, so with twice as many teams spread the same way it roughly doubles: 225 → 450.

  SE(b) = 6.00 ⁄ √450 = 0.2828  (it was 0.4000)
  t = 1.4000 ⁄ 0.2828 = 4.9497  (it was 3.5000)
  F = 4.9497² = 24.50  (it was 12.25)

Exactly double, because t went up by a factor of √2 and F squares it.

The lesson underneath. A bigger sample does not make an effect bigger — the slope is where it was. It makes the effect easier to see, by shrinking the standard error. That is why P-values cannot be read as measures of size: r² here is still 0.20 in both studies.

The habit: when a question changes the design, find the one ingredient that moves and follow it through the chain SE → t → F. Do not start the calculation again from the sums of squares.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.6.13 is half of 12.25. A larger sample shrinks the standard error, which pushes t and F up, never down.
b.150.06 is 12.25², squaring the F. Squaring is what turns t into F; doing it a second time has no meaning.
d.12.25 is the F she actually has. More data with the same slope and the same scatter cannot leave the evidence where it was — that is the whole reason for collecting it.
🏷️ More data shrinks SE(b). t rises by √2, F doubles, the slope does not move.

Question 11

🅕 The overall F test

A sum of squares recovered from F

Educational psychologist Bogaerts regresses exam marks on lecture attendance for 32 students. Her printout gives an error mean square of 25.00 on 30 degrees of freedom and F = 8.00. Her regression sum of squares, as a whole number, is:
  • a750
  • b625
  • c0.32
  • d200
🔎 What it is really asking

F is a ratio of mean squares. Undo the ratio, then undo the division by df.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The overall F test: running it backwards to a sum of squares.

🛠️ The procedure

F = MSM ⁄ MSE, so MSM = F × MSE. Then MSM = SSM ⁄ df, and with one predictor that df is 1, so SSM = MSM. The mean square is a step on the way, not the answer.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — undo the ratio.
  MSM = 8.00 × 25.00 = 200.00

Step 2 — undo the division by the model df.
  SSM = MSM × 1 = 200

Walk the table forwards to check it, filling in what else is now known:
  SSE = MSE × 30 = 25.00 × 30 = 750
  SST = 200 + 750 = 950, on 31 df
  F = (200 ⁄ 1) ⁄ (750 ⁄ 30) = 200 ⁄ 25 = 8.00 ✓

(And r² = 200 ⁄ 950 = 0.21 — another strongly significant regression explaining about a fifth of the variation.)

Why the model df being 1 is a gift. It makes the regression mean square and the regression sum of squares the same number, so the second step costs nothing. With two predictors it would not: MSM would have to be multiplied by 2.

The habit: an ANOVA table is a chain of multiplications and divisions. Enter it wherever the question lets you in, and undo the steps in the reverse of the order they were done.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.750 is 25.00 × 30, the residual sum of squares. Right move, wrong row — that is the variation the line does not explain.
b.625 is 25.00², squaring the mean square. Nothing in an ANOVA table is ever squared; the columns are joined by multiplying and dividing.
c.0.32 is 8.00 ⁄ 25.00, dividing where the rearrangement calls for multiplying. If MSM were 0.32 the F would be 0.0128, not 8.00.
🏷️ MSM = F × MSE. With one predictor, SSM is the same number as MSM.

Question 12

🎯 Mean response or one individual

Building an interval for a mean response

For teams receiving 18 training hours a month, Rombouts’s software reports a standard error of 2.5428 for the mean engagement score, with t* = 2.0096. The 95% interval for the mean engagement of such teams, to two decimal places, is:
Regression of a team engagement score on monthly training hours · 51 teams
PredictorCoefficientStd. ErrortP
Constant28.20004.87305.787.000
Training hours1.40000.40003.500.001
  • a39.89 to 50.11
  • b48.29 to 58.51
  • c50.86 to 55.94
  • d51.39 to 55.41
🔎 What it is really asking

Find the centre from the fitted line first, then add and subtract t* × SE.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Mean response or one individual: computing the interval.

🛠️ The procedure

ŷ ± t* × SE. The centre is not given to you: build it from the coefficient table with ŷ = constant + slope × x. The predicted value is an input here, not the answer.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — the centre, from the printed coefficients.
  ŷ = 28.2000 + 1.4000 × 18 = 28.2000 + 25.2000 = 53.40

Step 2 — the margin.
  2.0096 × 2.5428 = 5.11

Step 3 — the interval.
  lower: 53.40 − 5.11 = 48.29
  upper: 53.40 + 5.11 = 58.51

Read it out loud: teams training 18 hours a month average somewhere between 48.3 and 58.5 engagement points. Not a single team — the average of all such teams.

Why this x is a sensible one to ask about. Her teams average 12 hours, and 18 is six hours out from that. The interval is narrowest at x̄ and widens either side, so a prediction at 18 is still well supported; one at 40 hours would be extrapolation and no interval would be worth quoting.

The habit: every interval of this kind is centre ± multiplier × standard error. Write those three slots down, fill them in, and the arithmetic cannot go astray — the slot people leave empty is the centre.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.39.89 to 50.11 is the right margin around the wrong centre — it is built on the mean engagement of all 51 teams, 45.00, instead of on the value the line predicts at 18 hours.
c.50.86 to 55.94 is 53.40 ± 2.5428, the standard error used as the margin with no multiplier. That is roughly a 68% interval, not a 95% one.
d.51.39 to 55.41 is 53.40 ± 2.0096, using t* itself as the margin. t* has to multiply the standard error, never stand in for it.
🏷️ ŷ ± t* × SE. Build the centre from the coefficients first.

Question 13

🎯 Mean response or one individual

Spotting a misread interval

Told that the 95% interval for the mean engagement of teams training 18 hours a month is 48.29 to 58.51, a head of department concludes: "so almost every team training 18 hours scores between 48 and 59." Her mistake is that the interval:
  • alocates an average, not single teams
  • bwas computed at the wrong value of x
  • cis too narrow to carry 95% confidence
  • dshould have been centred on 45.00
🔎 What it is really asking

Whose uncertainty does this interval describe — the line’s, or a team’s?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Mean response or one individual: what each interval is about.

🛠️ The procedure

An interval for the mean response says where the average of all teams at that x lies. Covering most individual teams needs the wider prediction interval, which allows for the scatter of teams about the line as well.

🧮 The working
Both intervals sit on the same centre, ŷ = 53.40. What differs is what they are trying to catch.

  mean of all such teams: 53.40 ± 5.11 → 48.29 to 58.51
  a single such team: 53.40 ± 13.10 → 40.30 to 66.50

The head of department is asking about individual teams, so the honest range is the second — two and a half times wider.

Where the extra width comes from. The first interval allows only for not knowing exactly where the population line sits. The second allows for that and for the fact that teams scatter about the line with s = 6.00 engagement points. Even with the line known perfectly, individual teams would still differ.

And the practical sting: collecting more teams would shrink the first interval towards nothing, and would barely touch the second. Individual scatter is a fact about teams, not a shortage of data.

The habit: underline "almost every", "a single", "this one" against "on average", "the mean of all". That one choice decides which interval you quote, and the arithmetic is otherwise identical.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.The value of x is the right one — 18 hours is what she asked about, and 53.40 is what the line predicts there.
c.The interval is not too narrow for its own job. It carries 95% confidence about the mean; it is simply being read as though it were about individuals.
d.45.00 is the mean engagement of all 51 teams, and no interval at x = 18 should be centred there. The centre is the fitted value, 53.40.
🏷️ Mean-response interval = where the average sits. Individuals need the wider one.

Question 14

🖥️ Reading computer output

What can be read off without computing anything

Of the four quantities below, the one Rombouts can read straight off the printed row, with no arithmetic at all, is:
Regression of a team engagement score on monthly training hours · 51 teams
PredictorCoefficientStd. ErrortP
Constant28.20004.87305.787.000
Training hours1.40000.40003.500.001
  • athe 95% interval for the slope
  • bthe predicted score at 18 hours
  • cthe standard error of the slope
  • dthe share of variation explained
🔎 What it is really asking

Which of these is a printed cell, and which have to be built?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading computer output: printed cells against computed quantities.

🛠️ The procedure

A coefficient table prints four things per term: the estimate, its standard error, its t and its P. Everything else about the regression — shares, intervals, predictions — has to be built from those, or from the other table.

🧮 The working
Take them one at a time.

  SE of the slope — printed, in the Std. Error column of the training-hours row: 0.4000. Read and done.
  Share of variation — r², which needs the sums of squares from the other table: 441 ⁄ 2205 = 0.20.
  95% interval — needs a t* from the t table and then b ± t* SE(b).
  Predicted score at 18 hours — needs 28.2000 + 1.4000 × 18 = 53.40.

Only the first is sitting in a cell.

Why the distinction is worth having. Under exam pressure the expensive mistake is doing arithmetic that was never needed, or hunting for a cell that was never printed. Knowing the shape of the table tells you instantly which of the two situations you are in.

The habit: picture the coefficient table as four columns — how big, how precise, how many standard errors from zero, how surprising. If the question asks for something that is not one of those four, you have work to do.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.An interval needs a multiplier from the t table on 49 df, and then two arithmetical steps. The table supplies its ingredients, not the interval itself.
b.A predicted score has to be built by putting x = 18 into the fitted line. The table gives the two coefficients the prediction is made from.
d.The share of variation is r², and nothing in a coefficient table is a share. It comes from the sums of squares in the analysis-of-variance table.
🏷️ A coefficient row prints estimate, SE, t and P. Everything else you build.

Question 15

🖥️ Reading computer output

The question a printout cannot answer

Four questions are put to Rombouts about her 51 teams. The one her output cannot answer at all is:
The analysis-of-variance table for the same regression
SourceSSdfMSF
Regression4411441.0012.25
Residual error17644936.00
Total220550
  • ahow much of the variation is explained
  • bhow precisely the rate is pinned down
  • cis the rate distinguishable from zero
  • dwould more training raise engagement
🔎 What it is really asking

Which question is about cause, and which three are about the numbers in front of her?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading computer output: the limits of what regression output can say.

🛠️ The procedure

Regression output describes an association in data already collected. Whether changing x would change y is a question about cause, and it is settled by how the study was designed, not by any cell of the printout.

🧮 The working
Three of the four are answered by the printout:

  How much of the variation — r² = 441 ⁄ 2205 = 0.20, from the SS column.
  How precisely — SE(b) = 0.4000, and the interval 0.60 to 2.20 that follows from it.
  Distinguishable from zero — t = 3.50, P = .001, so yes.

The fourth is not. Her 51 teams chose how much training to take, and the teams that take more may differ in other ways: better-resourced, better-led, under less pressure. Any of those could raise engagement and training hours together.

So "teams with more training score higher, at 1.4 points an hour" is supported. "Give a team more training and its engagement will rise" is not, however small the P-value.

What would license the causal claim: assigning the training hours — randomly, by the researcher. Nothing in the arithmetic can substitute for that, and no column of the printout records whether it happened.

Say it to a friend: "the output tells me how these teams differ, not what would happen if I changed one of them."
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The share of variation is exactly what the SS column is for: 441 of the 2205 total, a fifth of it.
b.How precisely the rate is pinned down is the standard error, 0.4000, which is printed beside the slope for precisely this purpose.
c.Whether the rate is distinguishable from zero is what the t of 3.50 and the P of .001 answer — and the F of 12.25 answers the same question again.
🏷️ Output gives association, precision and share. Cause comes from the design.

Question 1

🔢 Degrees of freedom

Degrees of freedom for the F test

Health psychologist Reyes compares four relaxation methods, with 12 participants in each, on an end-of-study stress score. The degrees of freedom for her F test are:
End-of-study stress scores under four methods · 48 participants
Relaxation methodnmean stress scoreSD
Breathing1225.54.1
Progressive muscle1228.55.0
Guided imagery1231.55.6
Control (waiting list)1234.55.2
All 484830.0
  • a(3, 47)
  • b(4, 44)
  • c(3, 44)
  • d(4, 48)
🔎 What it is really asking

A pair of numbers: groups minus one, then total minus groups.

🧭 Which type of question this is

One-way ANOVA: degrees of freedom.

🛠️ The procedure

df = (k − 1, N − k), where k is the number of groups and N the total number of observations. F always needs two df, and the order matters.

🧮 The working
k = 4 methods, and N = 4 × 12 = 48 participants.

Numerator (between groups): k − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3
Denominator (within groups): N − k = 48 − 4 = 44

So (3, 44), and they check out against the table: 3 + 44 = 47, which is the Total df, N − 1.

Why it matters: the critical value depends on both. On (3, 44) the 5% cut-off is 2.8165. Write (4, 48) by mistake and you would compare against 2.5652 — a different, easier threshold.

Say it to a friend: "one less than the number of groups, then the number of people minus the number of groups."
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.(3, 47) pairs the correct numerator with the Total df. The denominator is N − k = 44, and 3 + 44 must equal 47.
b.(4, 44) forgets the − 1 on the numerator. Four groups give three degrees of freedom between them.
d.(4, 48) is k and N with no subtraction at all. Every df rule subtracts something.
🏷️ (k − 1, N − k). The two must add to N − 1.

Question 2

🔢 Degrees of freedom

Recovering the design from the df

A one-way ANOVA table reports df of 4 between groups and 55 within groups. The study had:
  • a5 groups and 60 observations
  • b4 groups and 55 observations
  • c5 groups and 55 observations
  • d4 groups and 59 observations
🔎 What it is really asking

Run the two df rules backwards.

🧭 Which type of question this is

One-way ANOVA: reading the design out of the df.

🛠️ The procedure

Invert the rules: k = (k − 1) + 1 and N = (N − k) + k.

🧮 The working
k − 1 = 4, so k = 5 groups.

N − k = 55, so N = 55 + 5 = 60 observations.

Check: 4 + 55 = 59 = N − 1. ✓

Why this is worth being able to do. An exam printout often gives you the df and not the design, and then asks a question that needs k — how many pairwise comparisons there are, or what the hypotheses look like. The df are the design, written in code.

Here, five groups: H₀ sets five means equal, and there would be 10 possible pairwise comparisons.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.4 groups and 55 observations reads both df as the quantities themselves, with no adding back.
c.5 groups with 55 observations gets k right but takes the error df to be N. N is 55 + 5 = 60.
d.4 groups and 59 observations reads the numerator df as k and the total df as N. Both are one step out.
🏷️ k = numerator df + 1. N = denominator df + k.

Question 3

🔢 Degrees of freedom

What each df counts

In Reyes’s analysis the 44 degrees of freedom within groups come from:
The one-way ANOVA table for the four methods
SourceSSdfMSF
Between groups5403180.007.20
Within groups11004425.00
Total164047
  • athe 44 participants who were not in the control group
  • bthe 48 participants minus the four who set each group’s own mean
  • cthe number of pairwise comparisons available
  • d11 degrees of freedom in each of the four groups
🔎 What it is really asking

Where does the error df physically come from?

🧭 Which type of question this is

One-way ANOVA: what the within-groups df counts.

🛠️ The procedure

The within-groups df is the sum over groups of each group’s own n − 1. That is why it can also be written N − k.

🧮 The working
Each group of 12 contributes 12 − 1 = 11 df to the estimate of spread, because one df is used up by that group’s own mean.

Four groups: 11 + 11 + 11 + 11 = 44. The same number as 48 − 4, by exactly this route.

What it is for. MSW = 1100 ⁄ 44 = 25.00 pools the four groups’ spreads into one estimate of the common variance — which is why the equal-spread condition has to hold for the pooling to make sense. Its square root, 5.00, is the pooled SD.

The payoff of pooling: 44 df instead of the 11 you would have from one group alone. More df means a lower critical value and a more sensitive test.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Nothing about the control group is special — all four groups contribute equally, 11 df each.
b.No participant is removed. N − k = 44 subtracts four means — one degree of freedom spent per group — and all 48 people still contribute to the estimate.
c.There are 6 pairwise comparisons among four groups, which is a separate matter entirely from degrees of freedom.
🏷️ Within-groups df = Σ(nᵢ − 1) = N − k. One df per group mean is spent.

Question 4

🧱 The ANOVA table

Completing the ANOVA table

Four entries have been removed from Reyes’s ANOVA table. The missing MS between groups, to two decimal places, is:
The same table with four entries removed
SourceSSdfMSF
Between groups540???
Within groups1100?25.00
Total164047
  • a11.49
  • b180.00
  • c135.00
  • d540.00
🔎 What it is really asking

That row’s SS over that row’s df.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The ANOVA table: filling a gap.

🛠️ The procedure

MS = SS ⁄ df, row by row. Get the df column straight first — it adds up down the table just as the SS column does.

🧮 The working
Between-groups df = Total df − Within df. And Within df = 44, since 1100 ⁄ 25.00 = 44 from the row that is printed.

So between-groups df = 47 − 44 = 3, which is also k − 1.

MS between = 540 ⁄ 3 = 180.00

And the table completes itself: F = 180.00 ⁄ 25.00 = 7.20.

Two free checks every time. The SS column adds: 540 + 1100 = 1640. ✓ The df column adds: 3 + 44 = 47. ✓ If either fails, something was copied wrong before you ever reached a mean square.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.11.49 is 540 ⁄ 47, dividing by the Total df. Each row divides by its own.
c.135.00 is 540 ⁄ 4, dividing by k instead of k − 1. The subtraction is what degrees of freedom are.
d.540.00 is the SS for that row, before any division. SS and MS are different columns.
🏷️ MS = row SS ⁄ row df. Both the SS and the df columns add up — check them.

Question 5

🧱 The ANOVA table

Computing F from the mean squares

From Reyes’s completed table, the value of the F statistic, to two decimal places, is:
The one-way ANOVA table for the four methods
SourceSSdfMSF
Between groups5403180.007.20
Within groups11004425.00
Total164047
  • a2.82
  • b0.14
  • c7.20
  • d0.49
🔎 What it is really asking

The ratio of the two mean squares, in the right order.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The ANOVA table: the F ratio.

🛠️ The procedure

F = MS between ⁄ MS within. Between on top — F asks how big the differences between groups are relative to the noise inside them.

🧮 The working
MS between = 540 ⁄ 3 = 180.00
MS within  = 1100 ⁄ 44 = 25.00

F = 180.00 ⁄ 25.00 = 7.20

What 7.20 means. The spread between the four method means is 7.2 times larger than the spread you would expect from individual variation alone. If all four methods were identical, F would hover around 1.

The decision: on (3, 44) the 5% critical value is 2.8165 and the 1% value is 4.2606. 7.20 clears both; P = .0005. The four methods do not all produce the same mean stress score.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.2.82 is the critical value on (3, 44) at α = .05. It is the threshold, not the statistic.
b.0.14 is 25.00 ⁄ 180.00, the ratio inverted. Between groups always goes on top.
d.0.49 is 540 ⁄ 1100, the sums of squares divided directly. The mean squares come first — this is the single most common error in the whole topic.
🏷️ F = MSB ⁄ MSW. Mean squares first, between on top.

Question 6

🧱 The ANOVA table

The decision from the critical value

Reyes obtains F = 7.20 on (3, 44) df. The critical value at α = .05 is 2.8165. Her decision is to:
The one-way ANOVA table for the four methods
SourceSSdfMSF
Between groups5403180.007.20
Within groups11004425.00
Total164047
  • areject H₀, since 7.20 exceeds 2.8165
  • bretain H₀, since 7.20 exceeds 2.8165
  • creject H₀, since 7.20 is more than twice 2.8165
  • dreject H₀ only if the group SDs are equal
🔎 What it is really asking

Compare statistic with critical value, and get the direction right.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The ANOVA table: making the decision.

🛠️ The procedure

For F, large values are the evidence. If the statistic is bigger than the critical value, reject H₀. There is no lower tail to worry about.

🧮 The working
7.20 > 2.8165, so reject H₀ at the 5% level. The exact P-value is .0005.

Conclusion in words: the four methods do not all produce the same mean stress score.

Why F has only one tail. F is a ratio of two variance estimates, so it cannot be negative, and anything that pushes the group means apart pushes F up. An F near zero would mean the group means were unusually close together, which is not evidence of a difference.

What the rejection does not say: not which methods differ, and not that all four differ from each other. For that you need follow-up comparisons.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Retaining H₀ gets the direction backwards. Exceeding the critical value is exactly what rejection means.
c."More than twice" is not a rule. Exceeding the critical value at all is enough; by how much is not part of the decision.
d.The equal-spread condition should be checked before running the test, not used as an extra hurdle after it. Here the SDs run 4.1 to 5.6 and the condition is comfortably met.
🏷️ F large → reject. One tail only; F cannot be negative.

Question 7

🧱 The ANOVA table

The share of variation between groups

Using Reyes’s sums of squares, the proportion of the total variation in stress scores that lies between the four methods, to three decimal places, is:
The one-way ANOVA table for the four methods
SourceSSdfMSF
Between groups5403180.007.20
Within groups11004425.00
Total164047
  • a0.146
  • b0.329
  • c0.671
  • d0.491
🔎 What it is really asking

One sum of squares as a share of the total.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The ANOVA table: the sums of squares as a split.

🛠️ The procedure

The total variation splits in two: SST = SSB + SSW. The share attributable to the grouping is SSB ⁄ SST.

🧮 The working
SSB ⁄ SST = 540 ⁄ 1640 = 0.329, so about 33%.

Check the split: 540 + 1100 = 1640. ✓ The remaining 1100 ⁄ 1640 = 0.671 is variation within methods — differences between people given the same method.

What this adds to the F test. F = 7.20 with P = .0005 says the method differences are real. This 33% says how much of the story they are: two thirds of the variation in stress scores has nothing to do with which method anyone received.

Significance and size are separate questions, and an ANOVA table answers both — the F column for one, the SS column for the other.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.146 is 240 ⁄ 1640 — a miscopied numerator. Read the Between groups row: 540.
c.0.671 is 1100 ⁄ 1640, the share within groups. Right ratio, wrong row on top.
d.0.491 is 540 ⁄ 1100, between over within. The denominator has to be the Total.
🏷️ SSB ⁄ SST. Denominator Total, never Within.
