Question 8

✅ The equal-spread condition

Checking the equal-spread condition

Educational researcher Hughes compares exam marks under three teaching conditions, with SDs of 2.1, 4.8 and 6.4. On the usual rule of thumb, the equal-spread condition is:
Exam marks under three teaching conditions · Hughes’s study
Teaching conditionnmeanSD
Lecture only2060.02.1
Lecture plus seminar2062.04.8
Flipped classroom2063.56.4
All 606061.8
  • amet, since all three SDs are below 10
  • bmet, since the three group sizes are equal
  • cnot met, since the three SDs are not identical
  • dnot met, since 6.4 is more than twice 2.1
🔎 What it is really asking

Apply the ratio rule to the largest and smallest SD.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conditions: the equal-spread rule of thumb.

🛠️ The procedure

Compare the largest SD with the smallest. The usual guideline is that the ratio should be no more than about 2. ANOVA pools the groups’ spreads into one number, and pooling needs them to be comparable.

🧮 The working
largest ⁄ smallest = 6.4 ⁄ 2.1 = 3.05

That is well over 2, so the condition is not met and the F test here is not trustworthy.

Compare Reyes’s study, where the SDs run 4.1 to 5.6: 5.6 ⁄ 4.1 = 1.37, comfortably inside the rule.

Why pooling cares. MSW is one shared estimate of how much people vary within a condition. If one condition really does spread three times as widely as another, there is no single "within-condition spread" to estimate, and the F ratio is comparing against a figure that describes nobody.

What to do: report the problem, consider a transformation, or use a test that does not assume equal variances. Do not simply run the F test and hope.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The absolute size of the SDs is irrelevant — the rule is about their ratio. SDs of 21, 48 and 64 would fail in exactly the same way.
b.Equal group sizes make ANOVA more robust, but they do not repair a 3-to-1 spread ratio, and they are a separate matter from the condition itself.
c.Identical SDs are never required or expected. Some variation between them is normal; the rule of thumb is what makes "some" precise.
🏷️ Largest SD ⁄ smallest SD ≤ about 2. It is a ratio, not a size.

Question 9

✅ The equal-spread condition

The conditions as a set

Before trusting her F test, Reyes should check that:
End-of-study stress scores under four methods · 48 participants
Relaxation methodnmean stress scoreSD
Breathing1225.54.1
Progressive muscle1228.55.0
Guided imagery1231.55.6
Control (waiting list)1234.55.2
All 484830.0
  • athe groups are independent, roughly Normal, and similar in spread
  • bthe four group means are approximately equal
  • cthe four groups contain the same number of participants
  • dthe stress scores are measured on a ratio scale
🔎 What it is really asking

Which conditions does a one-way ANOVA actually require?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conditions: the full set.

🛠️ The procedure

Three conditions: independent samples, each population roughly Normal (less critical as n grows), and similar spreads. Equal group sizes are a convenience, not a condition.

🧮 The working
Run them on Reyes’s study:
• Independence. Different people in each method, assigned at random. ✓
• Normality. With 12 per group this matters, but F is fairly forgiving unless the data are strongly skewed or have clear outliers. Look at the distributions.
• Equal spread. SDs 4.1, 5.0, 5.6, 5.2 — a ratio of 1.37. ✓

What is emphatically not a condition: that the means be equal. That is the null hypothesis — the thing being tested. A condition you check beforehand can never be the claim under test.

And equal n: helpful, because equal group sizes make the test more robust to unequal spreads. But unbalanced designs are analysed the same way.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Equal means is H₀. If you had to assume it, there would be nothing left to test.
c.Equal group sizes make the test more robust but are not required. Reyes happens to have 12 in each; she could have had 10, 12, 15 and 11.
d.An interval scale is enough for means and variances to be meaningful. A true zero point is not needed.
🏷️ Independent, roughly Normal, similar spreads. Equal means is the hypothesis.

Question 10

⚖️ Hypotheses and conclusions

Writing the hypotheses

For Reyes’s four relaxation methods, the hypotheses tested by the F test are:
End-of-study stress scores under four methods · 48 participants
Relaxation methodnmean stress scoreSD
Breathing1225.54.1
Progressive muscle1228.55.0
Guided imagery1231.55.6
Control (waiting list)1234.55.2
All 484830.0
  • aH₀: the control mean is highest; Hₐ: it is not
  • bH₀: the four sample means are equal; Hₐ: they are not
  • cH₀: all four means are equal; Hₐ: not all four are equal
  • dH₀: all four means are equal; Hₐ: all four means differ
🔎 What it is really asking

Both hypotheses, and in particular the exact wording of Hₐ.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Hypotheses: writing them for ANOVA.

🛠️ The procedure

H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ = μ₄. Hₐ: not all of the means are equal — which is satisfied the moment one mean differs from the others.

🧮 The working
H₀ is a single statement that all four population means coincide.

Hₐ is its negation, and the negation of "all equal" is "not all equal" — not "all different". One method standing apart while the other three sit together already makes H₀ false.

Two traps in one question.
• "All differ" is too strong. It is a much narrower claim than the negation of H₀, and rejecting H₀ never establishes it.
• μ, not x̄. Hypotheses are about population means. The four sample means are 25.5, 28.5, 31.5 and 34.5 — plainly not equal, and no hypothesis is needed to tell us so.

Also note what Hₐ is not: directional. There is no one-sided ANOVA — F squares the differences and loses the direction.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Naming the control group as highest makes H₀ directional and specific. ANOVA’s H₀ is always the plain equality of all the means.
b.Sample means are known quantities, not hypotheses. We can see they differ; the question is about the populations behind them.
d."All four means differ" is far stronger than the negation of H₀. H₀ is false as soon as a single mean is out of line.
🏷️ H₀: all μ equal. Hₐ: NOT all equal. Population means, never x̄.

Question 11

⚖️ Hypotheses and conclusions

What a small P-value does and does not say

Reyes’s F test gives P = .0005. She may conclude that:
End-of-study stress scores under four methods · 48 participants
Relaxation methodnmean stress scoreSD
Breathing1225.54.1
Progressive muscle1228.55.0
Guided imagery1231.55.6
Control (waiting list)1234.55.2
All 484830.0
  • aevery method differs from every other method
  • bguided imagery is better than breathing
  • cthe control group has the highest true mean
  • dthe four methods do not all produce the same mean
🔎 What it is really asking

How far does a significant F let you go?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Hypotheses and conclusions: the reach of a significant F.

🛠️ The procedure

A significant F rejects "all the means are equal". It says somewhere among the groups there is a difference. It does not say where, how many, or in which direction.

🧮 The working
Rejecting H₀ licenses exactly one sentence: the four methods do not all produce the same mean stress score.

Her sample means are 25.5, 28.5, 31.5 and 34.5, and the control is highest — but that ordering is a feature of this sample. The F test never looked at individual pairs, so it cannot certify any of them.

What comes next, properly. Follow-up comparisons designed for the job — Tukey’s procedure, or planned contrasts chosen before the data were seen — each with the multiple-testing problem accounted for. Only then may you name a pair.

The discipline: an omnibus test earns you an omnibus conclusion. Anything more specific needs its own test.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a."Every method differs from every other" is Hₐ read as "all differ". Rejecting "all equal" does not establish it.
b.Naming a pair requires a test on that pair. F pooled all four methods into one number.
c.The control mean is highest in the sample. Turning that into a claim about true means needs a comparison the F test has not made.
🏷️ Significant F = at least one differs. Not which, not how many.

Question 12

⚖️ Hypotheses and conclusions

Wording a non-significant result

Hughes’s three teaching conditions give F = 2.70 on (2, 57) df, P = .076. At α = .05 the correct write-up is:
Exam marks under three teaching conditions · Hughes’s study
Teaching conditionnmeanSD
Lecture only2060.02.1
Lecture plus seminar2062.04.8
Flipped classroom2063.56.4
All 606061.8
  • athe test should be repeated with more participants
  • bthere is not enough evidence that the means differ
  • cthe three teaching conditions have equal means
  • dthe means differ, but only slightly
🔎 What it is really asking

How to report a failure to reject, honestly.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Hypotheses and conclusions: failing to reject.

🛠️ The procedure

P > α means fail to reject H₀. That is a statement about the evidence, not about the world. You never conclude that H₀ is true.

🧮 The working
P = .076 is above .05, so H₀ is not rejected. The critical value on (2, 57) is 3.1588, and 2.70 does not reach it.

The honest sentence: these data do not provide enough evidence that the three conditions differ in mean exam mark.

Why not "they are equal". The sample means are 60.0, 62.0 and 63.5 — a 3.5-mark spread, and the flipped classroom came out ahead. The test says a gap this size could plausibly arise by chance with 20 participants per condition; it does not say the gap is zero. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

Worth adding here: her SD ratio is 6.4 ⁄ 2.1 = 3.05, so the equal-spread condition fails too. This P-value was not reliable in the first place, and that belongs in the write-up alongside it.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.More participants might well change the result, but that is a plan for a future study, not a conclusion from this one.
c.Concluding equality asserts H₀. A test can fail to reject a hypothesis; it can never confirm one.
d."Differ but only slightly" claims a difference the test did not find, and sneaks in a judgement about size that a P-value cannot make.
🏷️ P > α → not enough evidence. Never “the means are equal”.

Question 13

🔀 Why not many t tests

Why not many t tests

Reyes could have compared her four methods with a t test on every pair instead of one F test. With all six tests run at α = .05, the chance of at least one false positive if all four methods were truly identical is closest to:
End-of-study stress scores under four methods · 48 participants
Relaxation methodnmean stress scoreSD
Breathing1225.54.1
Progressive muscle1228.55.0
Guided imagery1231.55.6
Control (waiting list)1234.55.2
All 484830.0
  • a26%
  • b5%
  • c30%
  • d50%
🔎 What it is really asking

Combine the error rates of six independent tests.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Why not many t tests: the multiplicity problem.

🛠️ The procedure

Each test holds α = .05 individually. Across several tests the chance that at least one goes wrong is 1 − (1 − α)ᵏ, where k is the number of tests.

🧮 The working
Four groups give 4 × 3 ⁄ 2 = 6 pairs.

P(no false positive in one test) = 0.95
P(none in six) = 0.95⁶ = 0.735
P(at least one) = 1 − 0.735 = 0.265, about 26%.

(That calculation treats the six tests as independent. They are not quite — each group appears in three of them — so 26% is the standard textbook figure rather than an exact family-wise rate. The point it makes is not affected.)

So a researcher comparing four identical methods pair by pair has better than a one in four chance of announcing a difference that is not there — while believing the error rate is 5%.

And it gets worse quickly: five groups give 10 tests and a 40% chance. That is the reason ANOVA exists — one test, one α, one decision about the whole family of means.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.5% is the error rate of a single test. The problem is precisely that it does not survive being repeated.
c.30% comes from 6 × 0.05 = 0.30, adding the rates. Adding gives an upper bound; the multiplicative calculation gives 26%.
d.50% is the figure for about 14 tests. Six pairs give 26%.
🏷️ 1 − 0.95ᵏ. Six pairs → 26%, not 5%.

Question 14

🔀 Why not many t tests

What ANOVA buys you

Compared with running every pairwise t test, the advantage of a single one-way ANOVA is that it:
End-of-study stress scores under four methods · 48 participants
Relaxation methodnmean stress scoreSD
Breathing1225.54.1
Progressive muscle1228.55.0
Guided imagery1231.55.6
Control (waiting list)1234.55.2
All 484830.0
  • aidentifies exactly which pairs of means differ from each other
  • bis unaffected by the number of groups
  • cholds the overall error rate at α for the whole family
  • dneeds fewer assumptions about the data
🔎 What it is really asking

What problem does the single F test actually solve?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Why not many t tests: what ANOVA fixes.

🛠️ The procedure

ANOVA answers the whole question in one test, so the 5% risk is spent once rather than once per pair. That is its purpose.

🧮 The working
One hypothesis, one test, one α. The chance of wrongly announcing "the methods are not all the same" stays at 5% whether there are three groups or ten.

It achieves this by pooling: MSW combines all four groups’ spreads into a single error estimate on 44 df, instead of a separate two-group estimate on 22 df for each pair. More df, one test, controlled error rate.

Be clear about what it does not buy. ANOVA will not tell you which methods differ. That is the trade: you get a protected overall test, and locating the difference is a separate step with its own correction.

The conditions are no weaker, either — independence, approximate Normality and equal spreads, the same list a pooled t test needs, now across all four groups at once.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Identifying pairs is exactly what ANOVA cannot do — it is why follow-up comparisons exist.
b.The number of groups changes the df and the critical value considerably. What stays fixed is the error rate, not the test itself.
d.The assumptions are the same ones a pooled two-sample t test makes, applied to all four groups. Nothing is relaxed.
🏷️ One test, one α, for the whole family. It won’t say which pair.

Question 15

🔀 Why not many t tests

One-way ANOVA against the two-sample t test

A researcher compares just two groups and runs a one-way ANOVA. Her result, compared with a pooled two-sample t test on the same data, will be:
  • adifferent, since ANOVA uses a different error term
  • bthe same P-value only if the groups are equal in size
  • cthe same statistic but on different degrees of freedom
  • dthe same, with F equal to t²
🔎 What it is really asking

With two groups, are these two tests related or merely similar?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Why not many t tests: the two-group case.

🛠️ The procedure

With k = 2, one-way ANOVA is the pooled two-sample t test: F = t², and the two-sided P-values are identical.

🧮 The working
The df line up: ANOVA has (1, N − 2) and the t test has N − 2.

The error terms line up: MSW with two groups is exactly the pooled variance s²_p the t test uses.

And the statistics line up: F = t². A t of 2.35 gives an F of 5.52, with the same P-value either way.

So why have both? Because the t test keeps a direction — it can be one-sided and it comes with a confidence interval for the difference between the two means. ANOVA earns its place from three groups upwards, where there is no single difference to put an interval around.

The family resemblance: this is the same relationship you met between χ² and z on a 2 × 2 table, and between F and t for a regression slope. Squaring a two-sided test statistic is a recurring move.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.MSW with two groups is the pooled variance, the same error term the t test uses. Nothing differs.
b.The identity holds for unequal group sizes too, as long as the t test is the pooled version rather than Welch’s.
c.The df correspond exactly: (1, N − 2) against N − 2. Nothing is lost or gained.
🏷️ Two groups: F = t², same P. ANOVA earns its keep from three groups up.

Question 1

🔢 Degrees of freedom

Degrees of freedom with unequal group sizes

Developmental psychologist Terlouw compares five reading-support programmes on an end-of-year fluency score. The programmes were given to 10, 15, 20, 15 and 15 children. The degrees of freedom for her F test are:
  • a(4, 74)
  • b(5, 70)
  • c(4, 70)
  • d(5, 75)
🔎 What it is really asking

The two df rules still apply — but you have to build N yourself first.

🧭 Which type of question this is

One-way ANOVA: degrees of freedom from an unbalanced design.

🛠️ The procedure

df = (k − 1, N − k). Nothing changes when the groups are unequal: k is still the number of groups and N is still the total number of children, so add the group sizes up before you subtract anything.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — the total.  N = 10 + 15 + 20 + 15 + 15 = 75

Step 2 — the two df.
  numerator (between groups): k − 1 = 5 − 1 = 4
  denominator (within groups): N − k = 75 − 5 = 70

So (4, 70).

Check it for free: the two must add to N − 1, and 4 + 70 = 74 = 75 − 1. ✓ That single addition catches almost every slip in this question.

The habit: unequal groups are the normal case in real research, and they change nothing about the df. Write N = Σnᵢ at the top of your working and the rest is the same rule you already know.

Why it matters: on (4, 70) the 5% critical value is 2.5027. Write (5, 75) instead and you would be reading an entirely different row of the table.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.(4, 74) pairs the right numerator with the Total df. The two df must add to 74, so 74 cannot itself be the second one.
b.(5, 70) forgets the − 1 on the numerator. Five programmes give four degrees of freedom between them, because the grand mean is fixed.
d.(5, 75) is k and N with no subtraction at all. Every degrees-of-freedom rule takes something away.
🏷️ Add the group sizes to get N, then (k − 1, N − k). They sum to N − 1.

Question 2

🔢 Degrees of freedom

From the df to the number of comparisons

A one-way ANOVA table reports 6 degrees of freedom between groups and 63 within groups. The number of different pairs of groups that could be compared in this study is:
  • a21
  • b15
  • c42
  • d7
🔎 What it is really asking

Two steps: recover how many groups there were, then count the pairs.

🧭 Which type of question this is

One-way ANOVA: reading the design out of the df, then using it.

🛠️ The procedure

First invert the df rules: k = (between df) + 1. Then count pairs with k(k − 1) ⁄ 2 — the ⁄ 2 is there because comparing A with B is the same comparison as B with A.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — the number of groups.  k − 1 = 6, so k = 7.

(And N, if you want it: N − k = 63, so N = 63 + 7 = 70. Check: 6 + 63 = 69 = N − 1 ✓)

Step 2 — the pairs.  7 × 6 ⁄ 2 = 42 ⁄ 2 = 21

Count a small case by hand to see why the ⁄ 2 belongs there. With three groups there are AB, AC and BC — three pairs, and 3 × 2 ⁄ 2 = 3. ✓

Why this is worth being able to do. An exam printout very often gives you the df and not the design. The df are the design, written in code — and once you have k you can get the hypotheses, the number of comparisons, and the critical value.

And the warning the 21 carries: twenty-one t tests at α = .05 would give about a two-in-three chance of at least one false positive — 1 − 0.95²¹ = .66. That is the reason this study ran one F test instead.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.15 is the number of pairs among 6 groups, which comes from reading the between-groups df as k itself rather than as k − 1.
c.42 is 7 × 6, the number of ordered pairs. It counts A against B and B against A as two different comparisons.
d.7 is the number of groups, not the number of comparisons between them. Seven groups generate far more than seven pairs.
🏷️ k = between df + 1. Then pairs = k(k − 1) ⁄ 2.

Question 3

🔢 Degrees of freedom

How the df would change with a different design

Suppose Terlouw had recruited 20 children for every one of her five programmes instead of the numbers she actually used. Her within-groups degrees of freedom would then be:
End-of-year reading fluency under five programmes · 75 children
Reading-support programmenmean fluencySD
Control (usual lessons)1044.05.3
Phonics tutoring1548.05.8
Paired reading2050.06.0
Audio-assisted reading1552.06.2
Reading club1554.06.4
All 757550.0
  • a99
  • b100
  • c80
  • d95
🔎 What it is really asking

Rebuild N for the new design, then apply the within-groups rule to it.

🧭 Which type of question this is

One-way ANOVA: applying the df rule to a changed design.

🛠️ The procedure

Within-groups df = N − k. Recompute N for the design the question describes, keep k the same, and subtract.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — the new total.  N = 5 × 20 = 100 children.

Step 2 — the within-groups df.  N − k = 100 − 5 = 95

Check: between-groups df is still 4, because there are still five programmes, and 4 + 95 = 99 = N − 1. ✓

Compare the study she actually ran: 75 − 5 = 70. Adding 25 children buys 25 more degrees of freedom for the error term, and nothing at all for the numerator.

The habit: k counts groups and N counts observations. The two move independently — recruiting more children never changes the between-groups df, and adding a programme changes both.

Why anyone would care: the 5% critical value falls from 2.5027 on (4, 70) to 2.4675 on (4, 95). A bigger error df means a lower hurdle and a more sensitive test — a small gain here, but it is always in that direction.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.99 is N − 1, the Total df for the new design. The within-groups row subtracts k, not 1.
b.100 is N itself. Every df rule subtracts something; none of them is just a count of observations.
c.80 is 100 − 20, taking away one group’s size instead of the number of groups. N − k subtracts five means, one per programme.
🏷️ N − k: k counts groups, N counts observations. Rebuild N first.

Question 4

🧱 The ANOVA table

Rebuilding F from a nearly empty table

Four entries have been removed from Terlouw’s ANOVA table. Remembering that she compared five programmes, the missing value of F, to two decimal places, is:
The same table with four entries removed
SourceSSdfMSF
Between groups720???
Within groups2520??
Total324074
  • a0.20
  • b5.00
  • c0.29
  • d2.50
🔎 What it is really asking

The df column has to be rebuilt before any mean square can be worked out.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The ANOVA table: completing it from the SS column alone.

🛠️ The procedure

Work in order: df, then MS = SS ⁄ df row by row, then F = MSB ⁄ MSW. Five groups give k − 1 = 4 between, and the df column adds down to the Total.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — the df.
  between groups: k − 1 = 5 − 1 = 4
  within groups: 74 − 4 = 70

Step 2 — the mean squares.
  MSB = 720 ⁄ 4 = 180.00
  MSW = 2520 ⁄ 70 = 36.00

Step 3 — the ratio.  F = 180.00 ⁄ 36.00 = 5.00

Two free checks on the way: the SS column adds (720 + 2520 = 3240 ✓) and the df column adds (4 + 70 = 74 ✓).

What 5.00 means. The spread between the five programme means is five times larger than the spread you would expect from children differing from one another inside a programme. If all five programmes worked identically, F would hover around 1.

And the decision: on (4, 70) the critical values are 2.5027 at 5% and 3.5996 at 1%. F = 5.00 clears both, and P = .0013.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.20 is 36.00 ⁄ 180.00, the ratio inverted. Between groups always goes on top — F asks how large the group differences are relative to the noise.
c.0.29 is 720 ⁄ 2520, the two sums of squares divided straight into one another. Skipping the mean squares is the single most common error in this topic.
d.2.50 is the critical value on (4, 70) at α = .05. It is the hurdle, not the statistic that has to clear it.
🏷️ df first, then MS = SS ⁄ df, then F = MSB ⁄ MSW. Never SSB ⁄ SSW.

Question 5

🧱 The ANOVA table

Recovering a sum of squares from F

Educational researcher Bergström compares four reading schemes with 20 schoolchildren in each. Her printout keeps the within-groups mean square and the F ratio; the sums of squares, the degrees of freedom and the between-groups mean square are all missing. The between-groups sum of squares is:
Bergström’s ANOVA table · four groups of 20 schoolchildren
SourceSSdfMSF
Between groups???3.75
Within groups??48.00
Total?79
  • a720
  • b3648
  • c540
  • d180
🔎 What it is really asking

Climb the table backwards: F gives you a mean square, and a mean square gives you a sum of squares.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The ANOVA table: running MS = SS ⁄ df backwards.

🛠️ The procedure

Reverse the two relationships. F = MSB ⁄ MSW gives MSB = F × MSW; then MS = SS ⁄ df gives SS = MS × df. Use each row’s own df.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — the df.  k = 4 and N = 4 × 20 = 80, so between df = 3 and within df = 80 − 4 = 76.  (The printed Total df of 79 confirms it: 3 + 76 = 79 ✓)

Step 2 — the between-groups mean square.  MSB = F × MSW = 3.75 × 48.00 = 180.00

Step 3 — the sum of squares.  SSB = MSB × df = 180.00 × 3 = 540

The rest of the table falls out if you want it: SSW = 48.00 × 76 = 3648, and SST = 540 + 3648 = 4188.

The habit: an ANOVA table is a chain — SS → MS → F going down, and F → MS → SS coming back up. Write the chain out and you can enter it at whichever link the question hands you.

And the warning: step 3 is where the df must be the between-groups 3. Reaching for 4, or for the 76 next door, is what every wrong option here is built from.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.720 is 180.00 × 4, multiplying by k instead of by the 3 degrees of freedom between groups. The subtraction is what degrees of freedom are.
b.3648 is the within-groups sum of squares, 48.00 × 76. Right arithmetic, wrong row of the table.
d.180 is MS between groups — the answer to step 2, one multiplication short of a sum of squares.
🏷️ Going up the table: MS = F × MSW, then SS = MS × that row’s df.

Question 6

🧱 The ANOVA table

The pooled standard deviation from the table

From Terlouw’s table, the pooled estimate of the standard deviation of fluency scores within a programme, to two decimal places, is:
The same table with the within-groups mean square removed
SourceSSdfMSF
Between groups7204180.005.00
Within groups252070?
Total324074
  • a6.00
  • b36.00
  • c50.20
  • d13.42
🔎 What it is really asking

The within-groups row holds a variance. The question asks for a standard deviation.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The ANOVA table: the pooled SD from the within-groups row.

🛠️ The procedure

Two steps. MSW = SSW ⁄ df is the pooled variance; the pooled standard deviation is √MSW. Both come from the within-groups row and nowhere else.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — the mean square.  MSW = 2520 ⁄ 70 = 36.00

(Or read it off the F: MSW = MSB ⁄ F = 180.00 ⁄ 5.00 = 36.00. Either route, same number.)

Step 2 — the square root.  pooled SD = √36.00 = 6.00 fluency points.

Compare it with the five printed SDs: 5.3, 5.8, 6.0, 6.2, 6.4. The pooled value of 6.00 sits among them, as it must — it is the square root of a weighted average of their squares, with the larger groups counting for more.

What the pooled SD is for. It is the one estimate of how much children vary inside a programme, and it is what F measures the differences between programmes against. This is also why the equal-spread condition matters: if the five spreads were wildly different there would be no single within-programme spread to pool, and 6.00 would describe nobody.

Mind the units: 36.00 is in fluency points squared, which nobody can picture. 6.00 is in points.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.36.00 is MSW itself — the pooled variance, in squared units. The standard deviation is its square root.
c.50.20 is √2520, taking the root of the sum of squares before dividing by the df. The division comes first.
d.13.42 is √180.00, the root of the between-groups mean square. That describes how far apart the programme means are, not the spread inside a programme.
🏷️ Pooled SD = √MSW, from the within row. Divide first, then take the root.

Question 7

🧱 The ANOVA table

The share of variation from F and the df

Social psychologist Lemoine compares three persuasion strategies with 10 participants in each and obtains F = 8.00. The proportion of the total variation in attitude change that lies between the three strategies, to three decimal places, is:
  • a0.628
  • b0.372
  • c0.593
  • d0.889
🔎 What it is really asking

You are given a ratio of mean squares and asked for a ratio of sums of squares. The df are what stand between them.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The ANOVA table: rebuilding the SS split from F.

🛠️ The procedure

Let MSW = 1 unit. Then MSB = F units, so SSB = F × dfB and SSW = 1 × dfW in the same units. The share is then SSB ⁄ (SSB + SSW).

🧮 The working
Step 1 — the df.  k = 3 and N = 30, so dfB = 2 and dfW = 30 − 3 = 27.

Step 2 — the sums of squares, in units of MSW.
  SSB = F × dfB = 8.00 × 2 = 16
  SSW = 1 × dfW = 27
  SST = 16 + 27 = 43

Step 3 — the share.  16 ⁄ 43 = 0.372, about 37%.

It does not matter that you never learn the real sums of squares. If MSW were 5 the two sums of squares would be 80 and 135, and 80 ⁄ 215 is still 0.372. A ratio of ratios does not care about the scale.

The habit: set the awkward quantity to 1 and work in units of it. It turns a question that looks under-specified into two multiplications.

And what the two numbers say together: F = 8.00 on (2, 27) gives P = .002, so the strategies really do differ. The 37% says how much of the story they are — nearly two thirds of the variation in attitude change has nothing to do with which strategy anyone received. Significance and size are separate questions.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.628 is 27 ⁄ 43, the share of variation left within the strategies. Right denominator, wrong row on top.
c.0.593 is 16 ⁄ 27, between over within. The denominator of a share of the total has to be the total.
d.0.889 is 8 ⁄ (8 + 1), treating F itself as the ratio of the two sums of squares. That leaves the degrees of freedom out, and they are exactly what separate a mean square from a sum of squares.
🏷️ SSB = F × dfB and SSW = dfW, in units of MSW. Then SSB ⁄ SST.

Question 8

✅ The equal-spread condition

The equal-spread rule when variances are printed

Clinical psychologist Scalise compares three therapy formats with 18 clients in each. Her output reports the group variances as 12.25, 20.25 and 42.25. On the usual rule of thumb, the equal-spread condition is:
End-of-therapy distress scores under three formats · 54 clients
Therapy formatnmean distress scorevariance
Online self-help1831.012.25
Group therapy1827.520.25
Individual therapy1825.042.25
  • anot met: 42.25 ⁄ 12.25 = 3.45, which is over 2
  • bnot met: the three variances are nowhere near equal
  • cmet: all three groups contain 18 clients
  • dmet: the SDs are 3.5, 4.5 and 6.5, a ratio of 1.86
🔎 What it is really asking

Check what the printed column actually contains before you apply the rule to it.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conditions: the ratio rule applied to the right quantity.

🛠️ The procedure

The rule of thumb compares the largest and smallest standard deviation and asks for a ratio no bigger than about 2. A variance is an SD squared, so take square roots first — otherwise you are testing a squared ratio against an unsquared limit.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — convert. √12.25 = 3.5, √20.25 = 4.5, √42.25 = 6.5.

Step 2 — the ratio.  largest ⁄ smallest = 6.5 ⁄ 3.5 = 1.86

1.86 is under 2, so the condition is met and the F test can go ahead.

Look at how close this was to going the other way. Applying the rule to the variances gives 42.25 ⁄ 12.25 = 3.45, which looks like a clear failure. It is not a failure at all — it is the square of 1.86, because squaring both numbers squares their ratio. Testing 3.45 against a limit of 2 compares the wrong quantity with the wrong threshold.

The habit: read the column heading. SPSS output will give you variances, SDs, or standard errors depending on what was asked for, and the rule is written in SDs. If you prefer to work in variances, square the limit too: a ratio of 4 is the equivalent cut-off.

Say it to a friend: "the rule is about SDs, so if the table gives variances, root them first."
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.42.25 ⁄ 12.25 = 3.45 is the ratio of the variances, and it is the square of the SD ratio. Compared against the right limit for variances — about 4 — it passes as well.
b.Identical variances are never required or expected. Some difference between them is normal in any sample, and the ratio rule is what makes "some" precise.
c.Equal group sizes do make the test more robust to unequal spreads, but they are a separate matter and cannot settle the condition on their own.
🏷️ The rule is on SDs. Given variances, take roots first — or square the limit.

Question 9

✅ The equal-spread condition

Spotting a violation of independence

Consumer psychologist Pavlenko asks each of 30 volunteers to use all three relaxation apps, one app per week, and then compares the three mean ratings with a one-way ANOVA. The objection to this analysis is that:
  • athe three sets of ratings are not independent
  • bthe sample of 30 is too small for three groups
  • cthe three group means will be too close together
  • dthe ratings are not on an interval scale
🔎 What it is really asking

Where do the three sets of scores come from — different people, or the same ones?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conditions: independence and the one-way design.

🛠️ The procedure

One-way ANOVA needs independent samples: a different, unrelated set of people in each group. When every participant appears in every condition, the scores are linked person by person and that condition fails.

🧮 The working
Count what Pavlenko actually has: 30 people, each rating three apps, so 90 ratings — but only 30 independent sources of information.

A volunteer who rates everything generously will sit above average in all three conditions. Those three ratings move together, so they are not three independent observations.

What the test would get wrong. A one-way ANOVA would claim N − k = 90 − 3 = 87 within-groups degrees of freedom, as though 90 unrelated people had been measured. The error term would be inflated by the differences between volunteers — differences that have nothing to do with which app is better — and the test would be less sensitive than it should be while reporting df it has not earned.

What to do instead: this is a repeated-measures (within-subjects) design, and it needs a repeated-measures ANOVA, which separates the person-to-person differences out of the error term. Done properly, the design is actually an advantage — each volunteer is their own comparison.

The habit: before anything else, ask "is this the same people measured several times, or different people in each group?" It decides which test you are allowed to use.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Thirty volunteers is a perfectly workable sample. The problem is the structure of the data, not its size.
c.How close the means turn out to be is the result, not a condition. A condition is something you check before the data can be trusted.
d.Ratings are routinely treated as interval for means and variances, and in any case that objection would apply equally to a between-subjects version of the same study.
🏷️ Same people in every condition → not independent → repeated measures.

Question 10

⚖️ Hypotheses and conclusions

What the null hypothesis does and does not state

For Terlouw’s five reading-support programmes, the null hypothesis of the F test states that:
End-of-year reading fluency under five programmes · 75 children
Reading-support programmenmean fluencySD
Control (usual lessons)1044.05.3
Phonics tutoring1548.05.8
Paired reading2050.06.0
Audio-assisted reading1552.06.2
Reading club1554.06.4
All 757550.0
  • athe five population means are all 50.0
  • bat least two population means differ
  • cthe five population means are all equal
  • dthe five sample means are all equal
🔎 What it is really asking

Three traps in one: population or sample, equal or equal to something, and H₀ or Hₐ.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Hypotheses: reading H₀ precisely.

🛠️ The procedure

H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ = μ₄ = μ₅. It is about population means, it says they coincide without saying at what value, and it is the claim being tested rather than its negation.

🧮 The working
H₀ is one statement: whatever the true mean fluency under each programme is, it is the same under all five.

Three things it is not.
• Not about the sample. Her sample means are 44.0, 48.0, 50.0, 52.0 and 54.0 — visibly unequal, and no hypothesis is needed to tell us so. The question is whether the populations behind them coincide.
• Not a value. The grand mean of 50.0 is printed in the table, and H₀ says nothing about it. "All equal" leaves the common value completely free; a hypothesis that also fixed it at 50.0 would be a different and much stronger claim.
• Not the negation. "At least two differ" is Hₐ, the alternative.

The habit: write μ, not x̄, every time. If a sentence about hypotheses contains a number you read off the printout, it has almost certainly gone wrong.

And note what Hₐ is not: directional. There is no one-sided ANOVA — F squares the differences and loses the direction.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.H₀ says the five means coincide; it never says at what value. The 50.0 in the table is the grand mean of this sample, not part of the hypothesis.
b."At least two differ" is Hₐ, the alternative hypothesis. It is what rejecting H₀ would leave you with.
d.The sample means are known quantities, 44.0 through 54.0. A hypothesis is a claim about the populations we cannot see.
🏷️ H₀: all five μ equal — population means, and no value named.

Question 11

⚖️ Hypotheses and conclusions

What a P-value is a probability of

A one-way ANOVA on four groups gives P = .002, and the researcher writes: "there is a 0.2% chance that the four means are equal." This is wrong because:
  • aP = .002 is too large to reject H₀ anyway
  • bthe four sample means are obviously unequal
  • cP should be doubled for a two-sided test
  • dP is computed assuming the means are equal
🔎 What it is really asking

Which way round does the conditional probability run?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Hypotheses and conclusions: what a P-value measures.

🛠️ The procedure

A P-value is P(data at least this extreme | H₀ is true). It is computed starting from H₀, so it can never also be a probability about H₀.

🧮 The working
Unpack what the software did. It assumed the four population means were equal, worked out the distribution of F under that assumption, and found that only 0.2% of that distribution lies above the F it observed.

So .002 answers: "if the means really were equal, how often would data look this extreme?"  Rarely.

The researcher’s sentence answers a different question: "given these data, how likely is it that the means are equal?"  That is the conditional the other way round, and nothing in the calculation points that way.

Why the two cannot be swapped. Think of a different pair: the chance of a positive test given a rare disease is high, while the chance of the disease given a positive test may be low. Same two events, opposite conditionals, completely different numbers.

What she may write instead: "if the four programmes had identical means, data this extreme would arise about twice in a thousand studies, so we reject the hypothesis that they are identical." Longer, and true.

Say it to a friend: "P assumes H₀ and judges the data — it never judges H₀."
✗ Why the others are wrong
a..002 is comfortably below any usual α, so H₀ is rejected. The decision is right; it is the sentence explaining it that is wrong.
b.The sample means being unequal is not the issue — they always are. The claim at fault is about the population means, and about what a probability can attach to.
c.The F test has no sides to choose between. F is one-tailed by construction and software prints the only P-value there is.
🏷️ P assumes H₀ and judges the data. It is never P(H₀ is true).

Question 12

⚖️ Hypotheses and conclusions

Reporting an F below 1

Memory researcher Zielinska compares four revision techniques and obtains F = 0.86 on (3, 76) degrees of freedom, where the critical value at α = .05 is 2.7249. Her write-up should say that:
  • athe four means differ, since F is positive
  • bthese data give no evidence of a difference
  • cthe four techniques have equal mean marks
  • dsomething is wrong, as F cannot fall below 1
🔎 What it is really asking

An F this small — is it a result, a non-result, or a mistake?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Hypotheses and conclusions: failing to reject, with F below 1.

🛠️ The procedure

F below the critical value means fail to reject H₀, and the honest report is about the evidence, never about the world. An F under 1 is perfectly ordinary and is not a sign of an error.

🧮 The working
0.86 < 2.7249, so H₀ is not rejected. The exact P-value is .466 — nowhere near significant.

The honest sentence: these data do not provide evidence that the four revision techniques differ in mean mark.

Why F below 1 is nothing to worry about. F = MSB ⁄ MSW, and when H₀ is true both mean squares estimate the same variance. Two estimates of the same quantity land either side of each other, so under H₀ an F below 1 is entirely ordinary — on her (3, 76) degrees of freedom it happens about 60% of the time. All it says is that the four group means sat a little closer together than chance alone would typically put them.

And why not "the means are equal". Failing to reject is not confirming. The four sample means will differ by something; the test says a difference that size is unremarkable, not that the true difference is zero. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

The habit: small F → report the lack of evidence. Large F → report that not all the means are equal. Neither direction ever licenses the word "proved".
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.F is a ratio of two variance estimates, so it is positive for every possible data set. Being positive carries no information at all.
c.Concluding equality asserts H₀. A test can fail to reject a hypothesis; it can never confirm one.
d.F below 1 is entirely possible and in fact common when H₀ is true. It means the between-groups mean square came out smaller than the within-groups one.
🏷️ F < 1 is ordinary, not an error. Report no evidence, not equality.

Question 13

🔀 Why not many t tests

How fast the error rate grows with k

Social researcher Jankowiak compares six groups by running a t test on every pair, each at α = .05. If all six populations were in fact identical, the chance of getting at least one significant result is closest to:
  • a54%
  • b75%
  • c26%
  • d5%
🔎 What it is really asking

Count the tests first, then combine their error rates.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Why not many t tests: the error rate across a family of tests.

🛠️ The procedure

Count the pairs, m = k(k − 1) ⁄ 2, then use 1 − (1 − α)ᵐ for the chance that at least one of them goes wrong.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — the number of tests.  6 × 5 ⁄ 2 = 15 pairs.

Step 2 — the family-wise rate.
  P(one test does not misfire) = 0.95
  P(none of the fifteen misfires) = 0.95¹⁵ = 0.463
  P(at least one misfires) = 1 − 0.463 = 0.537, about 54%

So Jankowiak, comparing six identical populations, is more likely than not to announce at least one difference that is not there — while believing his error rate is 5%.

(The fifteen tests are not quite independent, since each group appears in five of them, so 54% is the standard textbook figure rather than an exact rate. The point it makes is unaffected.)

Watch how fast it climbs: four groups give 6 tests and 26%; five groups give 10 and 40%; six groups give 15 and 54%. The number of pairs grows faster than the number of groups, which is what drives it.

That is the reason ANOVA exists — one test, one α, one decision about the whole family of means.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.75% is 15 × 0.05, adding the fifteen error rates together. Adding gives an upper bound only, and with 20 or more tests it would pass 100%.
c.26% is the figure for four groups, which give six pairs rather than fifteen. Counting the pairs is the step that was missed.
d.5% is the error rate of a single test. The whole problem is that it does not survive being repeated fifteen times.
🏷️ Pairs m = k(k − 1) ⁄ 2, then 1 − 0.95ᵐ. Six groups → 15 pairs → 54%.

Question 14

🔀 Why not many t tests

What pooling buys in degrees of freedom

Terlouw’s within-groups mean square pools all five programmes and rests on 70 degrees of freedom. If instead she ran a single pooled t test comparing only the control group with the paired-reading group, that test would have:
End-of-year reading fluency under five programmes · 75 children
Reading-support programmenmean fluencySD
Control (usual lessons)1044.05.3
Phonics tutoring1548.05.8
Paired reading2050.06.0
Audio-assisted reading1552.06.2
Reading club1554.06.4
All 757550.0
  • a30 df
  • b74 df
  • c28 df
  • d70 df
🔎 What it is really asking

A two-sample t test uses only the two groups in it. How many children is that?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Why not many t tests: the degrees of freedom a pooled error term earns.

🛠️ The procedure

A pooled two-sample t test has n₁ + n₂ − 2 degrees of freedom — one lost per group mean. Only the two groups being compared contribute.

🧮 The working
The control group has 10 children and the paired-reading group has 20.

df = 10 + 20 − 2 = 28

Compare that with the ANOVA’s 70. The F test’s error term pools all five programmes, so every child in the study helps estimate the within-programme spread, even the ones in programmes this particular comparison is not about.

Why more df is better. The 5% critical value for a two-sided t on 28 df is 2.048; on 70 df it is 1.994. More degrees of freedom means a lower hurdle and a more sensitive test — the same observed difference is easier to detect.

So ANOVA buys two things at once: one α spent on the whole family instead of one per pair, and a sharper estimate of the error. And the price: the pooling is only honest if the five spreads really are similar, which is exactly why the equal-spread condition has to be checked.

What it still will not do: tell you which programmes differ. That needs a follow-up comparison with its own correction.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.30 df is 10 + 20 with no subtraction. Each of the two group means costs one degree of freedom.
b.74 df is the Total df for the whole study, N − 1. It belongs to the grand mean, not to a comparison of two programmes.
d.70 df is the ANOVA’s pooled error df, which draws on all 75 children. A two-sample t test on two of the groups cannot claim it.
🏷️ Pooled two-sample t: n₁ + n₂ − 2. ANOVA pools all k groups instead.

Question 15

🔀 Why not many t tests

Converting a two-group F into t

Sports psychologist Ritsema compares two warm-up routines with a one-way ANOVA and obtains F = 6.25 on (1, 48) degrees of freedom. The magnitude of the pooled two-sample t statistic on the same data, to two decimal places, is:
  • a6.25
  • b39.06
  • c1.58
  • d2.50
🔎 What it is really asking

With two groups these are the same test. Which way round does the conversion go?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Why not many t tests: the two-group case, computed.

🛠️ The procedure

With k = 2, one-way ANOVA is the pooled two-sample t test: F = t². So |t| = √F.

🧮 The working
|t| = √6.25 = 2.50

The degrees of freedom line up as they must: F has (1, 48) and t has 48 — the second number of the F pair. With N = 50 participants that is N − 2, exactly what a two-sample t test would use.

The error terms line up too: with two groups, MSW is the pooled variance s²p that the t test uses. Nothing differs but the notation.

What is lost going to F, and found going back: the sign. F = 6.25 would be identical whichever routine came out ahead, because squaring throws the direction away. That is why the question can only ask for the magnitude of t — the printout cannot tell you whether it is +2.50 or −2.50 without the group means.

So why have both tests? Because t keeps the direction, can be made one-sided, and comes with a confidence interval for the difference between the two means. ANOVA earns its place from three groups upwards, where there is no single difference to put an interval around.

The family resemblance: the same squaring relationship links χ² to z on a 2 × 2 table, and F to t for a regression slope.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.6.25 is F itself. With two groups t and F report the same result as two different numbers, one the square of the other.
b.39.06 is 6.25², squaring F when the relationship calls for the square root. That moves one step further from t, not towards it.
c.1.58 is √2.50, the square root taken twice. One root turns F into |t|; a second one leaves a number that tests nothing.
🏷️ Two groups: |t| = √F on the error df. Squaring loses the sign.

Question 1

🔢 Degrees of freedom

The degrees of freedom after a group is added

Educational psychologist Sommerfeldt compares four ways of giving exam feedback, with 16 students in each, and her F test runs on (3, 60) degrees of freedom. A reviewer asks her to add a fifth format, keeping 16 students in each group. The pair of degrees of freedom becomes:
Revision effort after four kinds of exam feedback · 64 students
Exam-feedback formatnmean revision-effort scoreSD
Grade only1644.07.1
Written comments1647.07.8
Recorded voice note1653.08.2
One-to-one meeting1656.08.8
All 646450.0
  • a(5, 75)
  • b(4, 60)
  • c(4, 75)
  • d(4, 76)
🔎 What it is really asking

Both numbers move, because adding a group adds people as well.

🧭 Which type of question this is

One-way ANOVA: how the design drives the two degrees of freedom.

🛠️ The procedure

(k − 1, N − k). Recruiting a fifth group of 16 changes both k and N, so work out the new k and the new N first and only then apply the rules.

🧮 The working
New design: k = 5 formats, N = 5 × 16 = 80 students.

  between groups: k − 1 = 5 − 1 = 4
  within groups: N − k = 80 − 5 = 75

So (4, 75), and the free check works: 4 + 75 = 79 = N − 1.

What she has actually bought. The error df has gone up from 60 to 75, because 16 more students are contributing 15 more degrees of freedom to the pooled estimate of spread. More error df means a lower critical value and a more sensitive test — the 5% threshold falls from 2.76 on (3, 60) to 2.49 on (4, 75).

Contrast that with splitting the same students more finely. If she had kept 64 students and divided them into five groups instead of four, the pair would be (4, 59): numerator up, denominator down. Adding groups costs error df; adding people pays for them.

The habit: read whether the new group brings its own participants. That one detail decides whether N moves with k.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.(5, 75) forgets the − 1 on the first number. Five formats leave four degrees of freedom between them, because the grand mean is fixed.
b.(4, 60) leaves the error df where it was. The 16 extra students contribute 15 fresh degrees of freedom to the within-groups estimate.
d.(4, 76) applies N − k with the old k of 4. The group count in that subtraction has to be the new one, 5, because five means are now being estimated.
🏷️ New group with its own people: k and N both rise. The pair still sums to N − 1.

Question 2

🔢 Degrees of freedom

The group size recovered from the degrees of freedom

Kalmijn’s one-way ANOVA table prints a Total df of 59 and a between-groups df of 3, and his groups were equal in size. The number of participants in each group, as a whole number, is:
  • a15
  • b20
  • c14
  • d30
🔎 What it is really asking

Get k and N out of the df first, then divide one by the other.

🧭 Which type of question this is

One-way ANOVA: reading the design out of the degrees of freedom.

🛠️ The procedure

Total df = N − 1 and between-groups df = k − 1. Add one to each, then the group size is N ⁄ k. Three steps, and the df are the only input.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — the number of groups.  k − 1 = 3, so k = 4.

Step 2 — the number of participants.  N − 1 = 59, so N = 60.

Step 3 — the group size.  60 ⁄ 4 = 15 in each.

Check it from the other end: the within-groups df must be N − k = 60 − 4 = 56, and that is also 4 × (15 − 1) = 56 — each group of 15 spending one degree of freedom on its own mean. ✓

Why this is worth being able to do. A printout hands you degrees of freedom and not the design, and the next question often needs k or n — for the number of pairwise comparisons, for the hypotheses, or to judge whether the groups are large enough for the Normality condition to be forgiving. The df are the design, written in code.

The habit: write "+1 on the between row, +1 on the Total row" in the margin. Never divide until both have been added back.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.20 is 60 ⁄ 3, dividing the sample size by the between-groups df instead of by the number of groups. The 3 has to become 4 before it is used as a divisor.
c.14 is the number of degrees of freedom each group contributes, 15 − 1. It is one short of the group size, because one df per group is spent on that group’s mean.
d.30 would be right if the table had come from two groups. The between-groups df of 3 says there were four.
🏷️ k = between df + 1, N = Total df + 1, then divide. Add back before dividing.

Question 3

🔢 Degrees of freedom

Whose reading of the degrees of freedom survives

Neuhaus and Abramczyk are handed a one-way ANOVA table showing 2 degrees of freedom between groups and 87 within groups. Neuhaus says the study had 90 participants; Abramczyk says 89. The one who is right is:
  • aAbramczyk, since the two df add to N
  • bNeuhaus, since 87 is N and k is 3
  • cAbramczyk, since 87 + 2 counts people
  • dNeuhaus, since the two df add to N − 1
🔎 What it is really asking

Do the two printed df add to the number of people, or to one less?

🧭 Which type of question this is

One-way ANOVA: what the two degrees of freedom add up to.

🛠️ The procedure

(k − 1) + (N − k) = N − 1, always. The two printed df add to the Total df, which is one less than the number of observations.

🧮 The working
Add them: 2 + 87 = 89. That is the Total df, so N = 89 + 1 = 90. Neuhaus is right.

The same answer by the other route: k − 1 = 2, so k = 3 groups; and N − k = 87, so N = 87 + 3 = 90. ✓ The two routes always agree, and running both is the cheapest check in the topic.

Where Abramczyk’s 89 comes from. He added the two df and stopped. The sum is the Total df, N − 1, and every df in the table has had something taken off it — the table never prints a plain count of people anywhere.

Say it to a friend: "the two numbers add to one less than the number of people, because the grand mean has already been spent."
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Adding the two df gives 89, which is the Total df, not N. One degree of freedom has gone on the grand mean before the table even starts.
b.87 is not N. It is N − k, the within-groups df, so it is three short of the sample size — one short for each of the three group means.
c.87 + 2 is a sum of two degrees of freedom, not a count of people. It lands on the Total df of 89, which is one below N.
🏷️ The two df add to N − 1. k = first + 1, and N = second + k.

Question 4

🧱 The ANOVA table

What doubling each group does to F

Suppose Sommerfeldt had tested 32 students in each format rather than 16, with the same four group means and the same spread of scores inside each format. Her F, to two decimal places, would be:
The one-way ANOVA table for the four feedback formats
SourceSSdfMSF
Between groups14403480.007.50
Within groups38406064.00
Total528063
  • a30.00
  • b15.00
  • c7.50
  • d3.75
🔎 What it is really asking

Which row of the table does doubling every group size change?

🧭 Which type of question this is

The ANOVA table: how group size feeds into F.

🛠️ The procedure

SSB = Σ nᵢ(x̄ᵢ − x̄)², so doubling every group size doubles SSB while the df between groups stays at k − 1 — and that doubles MSB. The within-groups mean square estimates the spread inside a format, which has not changed, so MSW stays put and F doubles.

🧮 The working
The numerator, which moves:
  the four means are still 6, 3, 3 and 6 points from the grand mean, so the squared deviations still add to 90
  SSB = 32 × 90 = 2880  (it was 16 × 90 = 1440)
  MSB = 2880 ⁄ 3 = 960.00  (it was 480.00)

The denominator, which does not:
  MSW is an estimate of how much students vary within a format, and nothing in the stem has changed that. It stays at 64.00 — now resting on 128 − 4 = 124 degrees of freedom instead of 60.

F = 960.00 ⁄ 64.00 = 15.00, twice the 7.50 she has.

The lesson underneath. The four formats are no further apart than before — the means are identical. A bigger sample has not made the effect bigger; it has made it easier to detect, because each group mean is now pinned down more precisely. The share of variation between groups is unchanged at 2880 ⁄ (2880 + 7936) = 0.27.

The habit: when a question changes the design, decide first whether the quantity that moved sits on the top of F or the bottom, and whether anything in the df column moves with it.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.30.00 quadruples F. SSB is multiplied by the factor the group sizes grew by — two — and not by its square.
c.7.50 is the F she has. Doubling every group size makes each mean more reliable, so the same differences between the means now count as stronger evidence.
d.3.75 halves F. Halving would need the group differences to shrink or the within-format spread to grow, and neither has happened.
🏷️ SSB carries nᵢ, so doubling every group doubles SSB, MSB and F. MSW stays.

Question 5

🧱 The ANOVA table

Recovering an F from a two-level verdict

Social psychologist Lindeboom reports only that her F test on three groups of 10 was significant at the 5% level but not at the 1% level. The critical values on (2, 27) degrees of freedom are 3.35 and 5.49. Her F could have been:
  • a6.20
  • b0.75
  • c4.10
  • d2.90
🔎 What it is really asking

Her sentence traps F between the two printed thresholds.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The ANOVA table: reading a verdict back into a statistic.

🛠️ The procedure

"Significant at 5%" puts F above the 5% critical value. "Not at 1%" puts it below the 1% one. Two clauses, two inequalities, and the answer satisfies both.

🧮 The working
Her df: k − 1 = 2 and N − k = 30 − 3 = 27, which is the (2, 27) the critical values are quoted on. ✓

Her sentence says: 3.35 < F < 5.49.

  4.10 — above 3.35, below 5.49 ✓
  2.90 — below 3.35, so not significant at either level
  6.20 — above 5.49, so significant at 1% too
  0.75 — below 1, nowhere near

So 4.10, whose exact P-value is .028: between .01 and .05, exactly as the sentence requires.

Why the stricter level has the bigger critical value. Demanding 1% evidence means demanding more, so the bar is higher: 5.49 against 3.35. Which is why "significant at 1% but not at 5%" is a sentence that can never be written — clearing the higher bar clears the lower one automatically.

The habit: turn each clause of a stated verdict into an inequality before you look at the options. The answer is whatever lives in the gap.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.6.20 is past the 1% critical value of 5.49, so it would have been significant at both levels and her second clause would be false.
b.0.75 is below 1, meaning the group means are closer together than ordinary within-group variation would predict. That is as far from significant as F gets.
d.2.90 is below the 5% critical value of 3.35, so that study would have reported no significant difference at all and her first clause would be false.
🏷️ Stricter α → bigger critical value. Two clauses give two inequalities.

Question 6

🧱 The ANOVA table

Finding the mistake in a reported F

Cognitive psychologist Mazurek’s table shows a between-groups sum of squares of 600 on 4 degrees of freedom and a within-groups sum of squares of 1800 on 45. He reports F = 0.33. His mistake is that he:
  • adivided the two sums of squares
  • bdivided the two mean squares upside down
  • cused the Total df in the denominator
  • dforgot to take a square root at the end
🔎 What it is really asking

Where does 0.33 come from, and which step of the F ratio is missing?

🧭 Which type of question this is

The ANOVA table: diagnosing a wrong F.

🛠️ The procedure

F = MSB ⁄ MSW, and each mean square is its own row’s SS over that row’s df. Dividing the sums of squares straight away skips both divisions at once, and it is the commonest error in the topic.

🧮 The working
Where his number came from: 600 ⁄ 1800 = 0.333. The sums of squares, divided directly.

What he should have done:
  MSB = 600 ⁄ 4 = 150.00
  MSW = 1800 ⁄ 45 = 40.00
  F = 150.00 ⁄ 40.00 = 3.75

Not a small slip: 0.33 says the group means are closer together than chance would predict, and 3.75 says they are well apart. One is on the wrong side of every critical value in the table.

Why the mean squares and not the sums of squares. The two sums of squares are built from different numbers of free quantities — four and forty-five. Dividing each by its own df puts them on the same footing, which is the only way their ratio means anything. SSB is a total over 5 group means; SSW is a total over 50 people.

A free check he skipped: an F far below 1 should always make you suspicious. Under H₀ the mean squares are both estimating the same variance, so F sits near 1 and drifting far below it usually means an arithmetical slip rather than unusually similar groups.

The habit: write the df column down beside the SS column and do the two divisions before you even think about the ratio.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Inverting the mean squares would have given 40.00 ⁄ 150.00 = 0.267, not 0.333. His figure is the sums of squares divided, not the mean squares.
c.The Total df is 49, and 600 ⁄ 49 = 12.24, which is not what he reports either. Each row divides by its own df, never by the Total.
d.Nothing in the F ratio is ever square-rooted. A square root turns the within-groups mean square into the pooled standard deviation, which is a different quantity.
🏷️ Two divisions before the ratio: SS ⁄ df on each row, then MSB ⁄ MSW.

Question 7

🧱 The ANOVA table

Whose reading of the table survives

Two colleagues read Sommerfeldt’s table below. One says the four feedback formats explain nearly all the variation in revision effort, since F is significant. The other says they explain a little over a quarter of it. The reading that survives is:
The one-way ANOVA table for the four feedback formats
SourceSSdfMSF
Between groups14403480.007.50
Within groups38406064.00
Total528063
  • athe first: a small P means nearly all
  • bthe second: 1440 of the 5280 total
  • cthe first: F = 7.50 is a large F
  • dthe second: 1440 of the 3840 within
🔎 What it is really asking

Does a significant F say how much the grouping explains?

🧭 Which type of question this is

The ANOVA table: significance against the size of the effect.

🛠️ The procedure

The F column answers whether the means differ. The SS column answers how much of the variation the grouping accounts for: SSB ⁄ SST, with the Total row underneath. Two questions, two columns.

🧮 The working
The share, from the SS column:

  1440 ⁄ 5280 = 0.273, so about 27% — a little over a quarter, as the second colleague says.

The first colleague has read a significant F as a measure of size. It is not one. F = 7.50 compares 1440 ⁄ 3 with 3840 ⁄ 60, and that 60 in the second division is what carries the sample size into the statistic. A modest share of variation over 64 students is easily enough to clear the 5% critical value of 2.76.

Both sentences belong in the write-up, and they say different things: the four formats do not all produce the same mean effort, and nearly three quarters of the differences in effort between these students have nothing to do with which format they got.

The habit: "is it real?" is the F column. "How much?" is the SS column. If a sentence answers one question with the other column’s number, it is wrong however confident it sounds.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.A P-value responds to sample size as well as to how far apart the means are, so it cannot measure how much is explained. The same share in 640 students would give a far smaller P.
c.A large F says the means are further apart than within-group noise would explain, not that the grouping explains most of the variation. With 60 error degrees of freedom a quarter is plenty for F = 7.50.
d.1440 ⁄ 3840 = 0.375 divides by the within-groups row. A share of the total needs the Total row, 5280, underneath it.
🏷️ SSB ⁄ SST is how much. F and P are whether. Denominator is always Total.

Question 8

🧱 The ANOVA table

What rescaling the outcome does to the table

Sommerfeldt’s revision-effort score runs from 0 to 100. Suppose she had recorded every score divided by 10, on a 0-to-10 scale, and run the same analysis. In the new table:
The one-way ANOVA table for the four feedback formats
SourceSSdfMSF
Between groups14403480.007.50
Within groups38406064.00
Total528063
  • athe F column changes, the SS column does not
  • bthe SS, MS and F columns all change
  • cnone of the four columns changes at all
  • dthe SS and MS columns change, F does not
🔎 What it is really asking

Which entries carry the units of the outcome, and which are ratios?

🧭 Which type of question this is

The ANOVA table: what a change of units touches.

🛠️ The procedure

Every sum of squares is in squared units of the outcome, so dividing every score by 10 divides each of them by 10² = 100. The mean squares follow, since each is a SS over an unchanged df. F is a ratio of two mean squares, so the hundredths cancel and it does not move.

🧮 The working
Column by column:

SS: every deviation is a tenth of what it was, and each is squared, so each sum of squares is divided by 100:
  SSB 1440 → 14.40,  SSW 3840 → 38.40,  SST 5280 → 52.80.

df: 3, 60 and 63. Degrees of freedom come from the design — four formats, 64 students — and the scale of the outcome has nothing to do with them.

MS: each is its row’s SS over its own df, so each is divided by 100 as well: MSB 4.80, MSW 0.64.

F: 4.80 ⁄ 0.64 = 7.50. Exactly what it was.

The P-value is unchanged too, and so is the share of variation between groups: 14.40 ⁄ 52.80 = 0.273, as before.

The habit, and it is a general one: a change of units can never change the evidence. Anything that is a ratio of two quantities in the same units — F, a P-value, a share of variation — comes out the same. Anything carrying units — a mean, a standard deviation, a sum of squares — moves with the scale.

Say it to a friend: "measuring in tenths does not make the groups more alike."
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.F is a ratio of two mean squares that were both divided by 100, so the factor cancels out of it. Changing the units of a score cannot weaken or strengthen the evidence about the means.
b.The sums of squares must change, because they are totals of squared deviations in the units of the outcome. Dividing every score by 10 divides each of them by 100.
c.The SS and MS columns do change. Only the df column and the F column survive a change of units untouched.
🏷️ Units move the SS and MS columns. F, P and the share of variation never move.

Question 9

✅ The equal-spread condition

Which study breaks the equal-spread guideline

Peyrard reviews four studies, each comparing three equally sized groups, and notes down their group standard deviations. On the usual guideline, the study whose spreads are clearly too unequal to pool is the one with:
  • a3.0, 4.2 and 9.5
  • b6.0, 7.1 and 8.4
  • c12.0, 15.0 and 20.0
  • d0.8, 1.1 and 1.4
🔎 What it is really asking

Apply the same test to all four: largest over smallest.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conditions: the equal-spread guideline as a ratio.

🛠️ The procedure

Compare the largest standard deviation with the smallest. The usual guideline is that the ratio should be no more than about 2. It is a guideline, not a sharp rule, and it is about the ratio and never the size.

🧮 The working
One division each:

  3.0, 4.2, 9.5:      9.5 ⁄ 3.0 = 3.17  ✗ well over 2
  6.0, 7.1, 8.4:      8.4 ⁄ 6.0 = 1.40  ✓
  12.0, 15.0, 20.0:  20.0 ⁄ 12.0 = 1.67  ✓
  0.8, 1.1, 1.4:      1.4 ⁄ 0.8 = 1.75  ✓

Only the first is clearly outside the guideline.

The trap in the list. The third study has the biggest standard deviations by far and the fourth has the smallest, and neither fact matters at all. Multiply every SD in a study by 1000 and the ratio is untouched — which is the point, because the ratio is what pooling cares about.

Why pooling cares. MSW is one shared estimate of how much people vary inside a group. If one group genuinely spreads three times as widely as another, there is no single "within-group spread" to estimate, and F is comparing the group differences against a figure that describes nobody.

The habit: find the largest and the smallest, divide, compare with 2. Ignore the middle values and ignore the units entirely.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.6.0, 7.1 and 8.4 give a ratio of 1.40, comfortably inside the guideline. Three standard deviations are never expected to be identical.
c.12.0, 15.0 and 20.0 are the largest spreads in the list and give a ratio of only 1.67. The absolute size of a standard deviation has nothing to do with the guideline.
d.0.8, 1.1 and 1.4 give 1.75 — the closest of the three to the guideline and still inside it. Small numbers can have a large ratio, and these do not.
🏷️ Largest SD ⁄ smallest SD, against about 2. A ratio, never a size.

Question 10

✅ The equal-spread condition

Choosing the analysis a design actually allows

Perception researcher Lindell measures the same 24 adults under three lighting conditions, then treats the 72 scores as 72 independent observations in a one-way ANOVA. What she needs instead is:
  • athree paired comparisons, each at α = .05
  • ba one-way ANOVA with 23 degrees of freedom
  • can analysis built for repeated measures
  • da one-way ANOVA on the 24 adults’ means
🔎 What it is really asking

The same people appear in all three conditions. Which analysis is designed for that?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conditions: matching the analysis to the design.

🛠️ The procedure

A one-way ANOVA requires the groups to be made of different, independent people. When every participant appears in every condition, the design is repeated measures, and it needs a method that knows which score belongs to which person.

🧮 The working
What is wrong with her analysis: an adult who responds strongly in dim light responds strongly in bright light too. Her three sets of 24 scores are linked person by person, so they carry less independent information than 72 unrelated scores would — and the within-groups mean square, computed as though they were unrelated, is inflated by exactly the stable between-person differences a repeated-measures analysis would set aside.

A method for repeated measures removes those person differences from the error term first. That is usually a gain in sensitivity, not a loss: the same data often give a larger F once each adult acts as their own control.

Why independence is the serious condition. Normality softens as the groups grow and unequal spread can be worked around, but no sample size repairs a broken independence — collecting 72 adults measured three times each would make the problem bigger, not smaller.

The habit: count the people and ask how many scores each one gave. One score each means a one-way ANOVA is on the table; several scores each means it is not.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Three paired comparisons each at α = .05 would respect the pairing but spend the 5% three times over, carrying a family-wise error rate of about 14%.
b.Changing the degrees of freedom does not change what the method assumes. The error term itself is built the wrong way, and no df will fix it.
d.Averaging each adult’s three scores throws away the very comparison she wants. Collapsing the conditions into one number per person leaves nothing to compare.
🏷️ One score per person → one-way ANOVA. Several each → repeated measures.

Question 11

✅ The equal-spread condition

Which printed figure settles the equal-spread check

Clinical psychologist Timmerman compares four therapy programmes with 20 clients in each, and his output prints a pooled within-groups standard deviation of 6.00. The one further figure he needs before he can judge the equal-spread condition is:
  • athe within-groups degrees of freedom
  • bthe four programme mean scores
  • cthe total number of clients tested
  • deach programme’s own standard deviation
🔎 What it is really asking

The guideline compares two numbers. Does the printout give them?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Conditions: what the equal-spread check is computed from.

🛠️ The procedure

The guideline compares the largest group standard deviation with the smallest. That needs the groups taken separately; a single pooled figure has already averaged them together and cannot be undone.

🧮 The working
What the pooled 6.00 is: one number summarising how much clients vary inside a programme, averaged across all four. It is the square root of MSW, and it is exactly what the F test needs — but it is the thing the condition is supposed to validate, so it cannot also be the evidence for it.

Four very different groups and four nearly identical ones can give the same pooled 6.00:
  SDs 5.8, 5.9, 6.1, 6.2 → pooled 6.00, ratio 1.07, comfortably fine
  SDs 2.5, 4.5, 6.0, 9.0 → pooled 5.99, ratio 3.60, clearly not fine

He cannot tell which situation he is in without the four separate standard deviations.

Why the other figures cannot help. The within-groups df and the client total describe the size of the study; the four means describe where the groups sit. The condition is about the spread inside each group, and only a per-group measure of spread speaks to it.

The habit: before answering a conditions question, ask what two numbers the guideline actually compares — then look for those, and not for something that sounds related.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The within-groups df, 80 − 4 = 76, says how much data the pooled estimate rests on. It says nothing about whether the four spreads were alike enough to pool.
b.The four means say where the groups sit, which is what the F test is about. The condition concerns the spread inside each group, not the gaps between them.
c.The client total of 80 is already known from the design, and sample size is not what the guideline compares. Equal group sizes help but cannot settle it.
🏷️ The guideline needs the group SDs separately. A pooled SD has lost them.

Question 12

⚖️ Hypotheses and conclusions

Recovering the result from the way it was written up

Memory researcher Vuorinen’s write-up ends: "these data do not show that the four conditions differ in mean recall." Her F ran on (3, 60) degrees of freedom, where the 5% critical value is 2.76. The result behind that sentence is:
  • aF = 7.50, P < .001
  • bF = 1.90, P = .139
  • cF = 2.90, P = .042
  • dF = 3.10, P = .033
🔎 What it is really asking

Which pair of numbers would make a researcher write that particular sentence?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Hypotheses and conclusions: reading a statistic back out of a conclusion.

🛠️ The procedure

"Do not show" is the wording of a failure to reject H₀. That means P > .05 and, equivalently, F below the critical value. Check both halves of each candidate; they must agree.

🧮 The working
Her sentence says H₀ survived, so look for F < 2.76 and P > .05 together.

  F = 1.90, P = .139 — below 2.76, above .05 ✓
  F = 2.90, P = .042 — past the critical value, P under .05: she would have rejected
  F = 3.10, P = .033 — the same, more clearly so
  F = 7.50, P < .001 — a strongly significant result, nothing like her sentence

So F = 1.90, P = .139.

Notice what her sentence does not say. Not "the four conditions have the same mean recall". Failing to reject H₀ is a statement about the evidence, never about the world — with F = 1.90 the four means are a little apart, and a gap that size is the kind of thing a study of this size produces by chance. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

The free check in every question of this kind: F and P must tell the same story. F above the critical value always comes with P below α. If a printed pair disagrees, one of the two has been misread.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.F = 7.50 with P < .001 is strong evidence against equal means — the sort of result that gets a write-up saying the conditions clearly differ.
c.F = 2.90 is past the 5% critical value of 2.76 and its P of .042 is below .05. That researcher would have reported a difference, not a failure to find one.
d.F = 3.10 with P = .033 is significant at the 5% level. Her sentence would then be the opposite of what her own numbers showed.
🏷️ “Do not show” means F below the critical value AND P above α. Both, or neither.

Question 13

⚖️ Hypotheses and conclusions

Counting the faults in a written pair of hypotheses

Social psychologist Rutgers writes his hypotheses for a four-group study as "H₀: x̄₁ = x̄₂ = x̄₃ = x̄₄ against Hₐ: μ₁ ≠ μ₂ ≠ μ₃ ≠ μ₄". His pair contains:
  • atwo faults, one in each hypothesis
  • bone fault, in the null hypothesis only
  • cone fault, in the alternative only
  • dno fault: that is the standard pair
🔎 What it is really asking

Check each hypothesis separately — the symbol used, and the claim made.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Hypotheses: auditing a written pair.

🛠️ The procedure

Two things to check in each line. Hypotheses are about population means, so they are written with μ and never x̄. And Hₐ is the negation of H₀, so it reads "not all of the means are equal" — not a chain of ≠ signs.

🧮 The working
H₀: x̄₁ = x̄₂ = x̄₃ = x̄₄. Fault one. The sample means are quantities he has already measured; he can see whether they are equal, so there is nothing there to test. It should be μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ = μ₄.

Hₐ: μ₁ ≠ μ₂ ≠ μ₃ ≠ μ₄. Fault two. That chain claims all four population means differ from one another, which is far stronger than the negation of H₀. H₀ is false the moment one mean stands apart from the rest, so Hₐ is "not all four are equal" — a sentence, not a chain.

Two faults, one in each line.

Why the second fault matters in practice. If Hₐ really were "all four differ", then rejecting H₀ would license saying every format differs from every other — which is exactly the overclaim that follow-up comparisons exist to prevent.

The habit: read a hypothesis twice. Once for the symbol: μ, never x̄. Once for the strength: the alternative is the plain negation, nothing more.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Both lines are wrong, not just the null. A chain of ≠ signs claims much more than the negation of "all equal" and is never how Hₐ is written.
c.Both lines are wrong, not just the alternative. Writing x̄ in a hypothesis makes a claim about numbers already measured, which no test can be about.
d.Neither line is standard. The standard pair is μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ = μ₄ against "not all four population means are equal".
🏷️ μ never x̄, and Hₐ is “not all equal” — never a chain of ≠ signs.
