Question 14

⚖️ Hypotheses and conclusions

The hypotheses after a condition is dropped

Sommerfeldt decides her grade-only condition was poorly implemented and re-runs the analysis on the remaining three formats. Her null hypothesis now:
Revision effort after four kinds of exam feedback · 64 students
Exam-feedback formatnmean revision-effort scoreSD
Grade only1644.07.1
Written comments1647.07.8
Recorded voice note1653.08.2
One-to-one meeting1656.08.8
All 646450.0
  • asets the three sample means equal
  • bbecomes directional, with fewer groups
  • csets three population means equal
  • dis unchanged, since it names no value
🔎 What it is really asking

What exactly does H₀ list, and does dropping a group change the list?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Hypotheses: what H₀ is a statement about.

🛠️ The procedure

H₀ for a one-way ANOVA sets the population means of the groups in the analysis equal to one another. Change which groups are in the analysis and you change the hypothesis, because the list of means is shorter.

🧮 The working
Before: H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ = μ₄ — the four formats all produce the same mean revision effort.

After: H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ — three formats, three means, a different and weaker claim. A world in which grade-only feedback differs from the rest but the other three agree makes the first H₀ false and the second true.

Everything downstream moves with it: k = 3, so the between-groups df falls to 2; N = 48, so the within-groups df falls to 45; and the pair becomes (2, 45).

A word of caution about dropping it at all. Deciding which conditions to analyse after seeing the results is how a 5% error rate quietly becomes something much larger. If grade-only was poorly implemented, that is a judgement that should rest on how the study ran, not on which condition came out awkwardly.

The habit: write H₀ out in full, with one μ for each group you are actually analysing. The number of μ symbols is the number of groups, every time.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.A hypothesis is never about sample means. Her three sample means are quantities she has measured and can simply look at.
b.Dropping a group does not put a direction into the hypothesis. Hₐ is still "not all of them are equal", with no order claimed among the means.
d.It is not unchanged. H₀ names no value, which is true, but it does list one population mean per group — and there is now one fewer of them.
🏷️ One μ per group in the analysis. Drop a group and H₀ gets shorter.

Question 15

⚖️ Hypotheses and conclusions

The question the F test is not built to answer

Sommerfeldt’s F test puts a single claim on trial. Of the four questions below, the one it is not built to answer is:
Revision effort after four kinds of exam feedback · 64 students
Exam-feedback formatnmean revision-effort scoreSD
Grade only1644.07.1
Written comments1647.07.8
Recorded voice note1653.08.2
One-to-one meeting1656.08.8
All 646450.0
  • awhether all four population means coincide
  • bwhether format accounts for any variation
  • cwhether the means differ somewhere
  • dwhich two formats differ from each other
🔎 What it is really asking

Three of these are one hypothesis in different words. Which is the odd one out?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Hypotheses: the single claim an F test tests.

🛠️ The procedure

One hypothesis, written several ways: H₀: all the population means are equal, which is the same as saying the grouping accounts for no variation. Naming a pair is a different question, and needs its own comparison.

🧮 The working
The three that are the same question:

  "do all four population means coincide?" — H₀ itself
  "does format account for any variation?" — the same claim read off the SS column
  "do the means differ somewhere?" — Hₐ, the negation of H₀

Reject H₀ and all three are answered at once, because they were one question all along.

Which two formats differ is not among them. F pools all four formats into a single number: it would come out at 7.50 whichever format carried the difference, and it never looked at a pair. Her sample means run 44.0, 47.0, 53.0 and 56.0, and that ordering is a feature of this sample until a comparison designed for pairs has examined it.

What answers it properly: a follow-up procedure that accounts for how many pairs are being looked at, or a comparison planned before the data were collected. Either gives a named pair, a direction and an interval for the size of the difference — three things F cannot give.

The discipline: an omnibus test earns an omnibus conclusion.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Whether the four population means coincide is H₀ word for word. That is precisely what the F test puts on trial.
b.Whether format accounts for any variation is the same hypothesis in the language of the sums of squares. If no mean differed, the between-groups row would be noise alone.
c.Whether the means differ somewhere is Hₐ. A significant F answers it — and "somewhere" is as specific as the answer gets.
🏷️ F tests one claim: all means equal. Naming a pair is a separate test.

Question 16

🔀 Why not many t tests

Recovering the design from a family-wise error rate

Statistics tutor Panagopoulos tells his class that a researcher who ran a t test on every pair of his equally sized groups at α = .05 faced about a 40% chance of at least one false positive if all the means were in fact equal. That researcher had:
  • a10 groups
  • b5 groups
  • c4 groups
  • d8 groups
🔎 What it is really asking

Work back from the rate to the number of tests, and from the tests to the groups.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Why not many t tests: from the error rate back to the design.

🛠️ The procedure

The family-wise rate is 1 − (1 − α)ᵐ, where m is the number of pairs, not the number of groups. So find the m that gives 40%, then the k with m = k(k − 1) ⁄ 2 pairs.

🧮 The working
Step 1 — how many tests give 40%?
  1 − 0.95ᵐ = 0.40, so 0.95ᵐ = 0.60, and m = 10.
  (Check: 0.95¹⁰ = 0.599, so the rate is 1 − 0.599 = 0.401.)

Step 2 — how many groups give 10 pairs?
  k(k − 1) ⁄ 2 = 10 → 5 × 4 ⁄ 2 = 10 ✓, so k = 5 groups.

The step everyone skips: the exponent counts the pairs, never the groups. Five groups raise 0.95 to the tenth power, not the fifth — and 1 − 0.95⁵ would be only 23%, a badly wrong answer that comes from putting k where m belongs.

Watch how steeply it climbs: 3 groups give 3 pairs and 14%; 4 give 6 and 26%; 5 give 10 and 40%. The number of pairs grows roughly like k², which is what drives the rate up so quickly.

(The pairwise tests are not quite independent, since each group appears in several of them, so these are the standard textbook figures rather than exact rates. The point they make is unaffected.)

That is the reason ANOVA exists — one test, one α, one decision about the whole family of means.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.10 groups make 45 pairs and a rate of about 90%. The 10 in this question is the number of tests, which is where that answer comes from.
c.4 groups make 4 × 3 ⁄ 2 = 6 pairs, and 1 − 0.95⁶ = 26%. That is the figure for a four-group study, not 40%.
d.8 groups make 28 pairs, and 1 − 0.95²⁸ = 76%. Far past 40% — by eight groups the practice is hopeless.
🏷️ 1 − 0.95ᵐ with m = pairs = k(k − 1) ⁄ 2. Ten pairs → five groups → 40%.

Question 17

🔀 Why not many t tests

How the number of comparisons grows

Sommerfeldt’s four formats can be compared in six different pairs. If she adds a fifth format, the number of pairs available becomes, as a whole number:
Revision effort after four kinds of exam feedback · 64 students
Exam-feedback formatnmean revision-effort scoreSD
Grade only1644.07.1
Written comments1647.07.8
Recorded voice note1653.08.2
One-to-one meeting1656.08.8
All 646450.0
  • a7
  • b20
  • c10
  • d8
🔎 What it is really asking

Count the pairs for the new design, rather than adjusting the old count.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Why not many t tests: counting the comparisons a design offers.

🛠️ The procedure

m = k(k − 1) ⁄ 2. Each of the k groups can be paired with the other k − 1, and dividing by 2 stops every pair being counted from both ends.

🧮 The working
With k = 5: 5 × 4 ⁄ 2 = 10 pairs.

List them if it helps — call the formats A to E: AB, AC, AD, AE, BC, BD, BE, CD, CE, DE. Ten.

Why it jumps by four and not by one. The new format E has to be compared with each of the four formats already there, so it brings four new pairs, not one. Add a sixth and it would bring five more, taking the count to 15.

And the cost of those four extra tests. Run them all at α = .05 and the chance of at least one false positive, with every mean truly equal, climbs from 1 − 0.95⁶ = 26% to 1 − 0.95¹⁰ = 40%. Adding one condition to the design adds half as much again to the risk.

The habit: when a design changes, recount the pairs from scratch with k(k − 1) ⁄ 2. Adjusting the previous count in your head is where the wrong answers in this question come from.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.7 adds a single pair for the single new format. The new format has to be compared with all four of the others, which is four new pairs.
b.20 is 5 × 4, counting every pair twice — once from each end. The division by 2 is what stops AB and BA being treated as two comparisons.
d.8 doubles the number of groups instead of counting pairs. Pairing is not a matter of two per group — each group pairs with every other one.
🏷️ m = k(k − 1) ⁄ 2. A new group brings k − 1 new pairs, not one.

Question 18

🔀 Why not many t tests

When a comparison may be made without an F test

A colleague of Sommerfeldt’s, Siersma, had predicted before any data were collected that a one-to-one meeting would produce more revision effort than written comments, and wants to test only those two formats, skipping the overall F test. That is:
  • alegitimate: a comparison fixed in advance keeps its 5%
  • bwrong: the overall F test must always be run first
  • cwrong: two groups cannot be compared inside a design of four
  • dlegitimate only if the overall F test turns out significant
🔎 What it is really asking

Is it the number of tests that protects α, or the fact that the data did not choose them?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Why not many t tests: what the 5% actually belongs to.

🛠️ The procedure

α = .05 belongs to a comparison chosen before the data. A single planned comparison, named in advance, carries exactly its stated error rate — with or without an omnibus F test in front of it. What spends α is searching.

🧮 The working
What Siersma is doing: one comparison, fixed before a single score existed. He is not choosing it because it looked promising, and he is not quietly passing over the other five pairs. His 5% is intact.

Contrast the practice that is not legitimate: looking at the four means, noticing that one-to-one and written comments are furthest apart, and testing that pair at α = .05. Same arithmetic, but the data chose the comparison, so the test is really about the largest of six gaps and its true error rate is far above 5%.

So what is the F test for? For the case where you have no prediction and want to ask the whole question at once — one protected test of "are these all the same?", followed by a procedure that pays for however many pairs you then go on to inspect. It is the right tool for exploring, not a toll gate every comparison must pass through.

Say it to a friend: "if I named the comparison before I saw the data, my 5% is mine. If the data named it, the data has already spent it."
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.A planned comparison does not need an omnibus test in front of it. The F test is what you run when you have no specific prediction to make.
c.Comparing two of the four groups is perfectly ordinary — follow-up comparisons do exactly that. What matters is whether the pair was chosen in advance.
d.Making the comparison conditional on the F test being significant would change its error rate, and it is not what protects a planned comparison in the first place.
🏷️ α belongs to a comparison named before the data. Searching is what spends it.

Question 1

🧩 Reading the design

Reading the design

Educational psychologist Varga gives each of 60 participants one of two kinds of feedback (written or video) on one of three task difficulties (easy, moderate or hard), with the same number of participants in every condition, and measures motivation afterwards. Her design is:
  • aa one-way design with six conditions
  • ba 3 × 2 factorial with 6 participants per cell
  • ca 2 × 3 factorial with 10 participants per cell
  • da 2 × 3 factorial with 20 participants per cell
🔎 What it is really asking

Count the factors, their levels, and the people per cell.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading the design: factors, levels and cells.

🛠️ The procedure

Name the factors and count their levels. The number of cells is the levels multiplied together, and n per cell is N divided by the number of cells.

🧮 The working
Two factors: feedback type with 2 levels, task difficulty with 3. So a 2 × 3 factorial.

Cells: 2 × 3 = 6.

Participants per cell: 60 ⁄ 6 = 10.

Why it is not a one-way design with six conditions. The arithmetic would be the same, but the analysis would throw away the structure. A factorial design lets her ask three questions from one dataset — does feedback type matter, does difficulty matter, and does the effect of feedback depend on difficulty — and the third of those is invisible to a one-way analysis.

Get this right first. Every degrees-of-freedom figure in the table follows from 2, 3 and 10.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Treating it as one factor with six conditions loses the interaction — the question the design was built to answer.
b.3 × 2 and 2 × 3 describe the same design, but 6 per cell is wrong: that would be 36 participants.
d.20 per cell would need 120 participants. 60 ⁄ 6 = 10.
🏷️ Factors × levels = cells. n per cell = N ⁄ cells.

🔎 What it is really asking

Count the rows of the table that get an F.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading the design: what the analysis delivers.

🛠️ The procedure

A two-factor ANOVA tests three things: the main effect of A, the main effect of B, and the A × B interaction. Each gets its own F, and all three share the same error term.

🧮 The working
Look down the table: three rows carry an F, and the Error and Total rows do not.

• Feedback type: F = 160.00 ⁄ 20.00 = 8.00
• Task difficulty: F = 90.00 ⁄ 20.00 = 4.50
• Interaction: F = 50.00 ⁄ 20.00 = 2.50

Every one of them divides by the same MS error of 20.00. That shared denominator is what makes a factorial design efficient: one pool of 54 error df serves all three tests.

Which to read first: the interaction. If it is significant, the two main effects have to be described with care, because the effect of each factor then depends on the level of the other.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Two would be the two main effects, leaving out the interaction — the one effect a factorial design exists to find.
c.Six is the number of cells. Cells are conditions, not hypotheses.
d.One F is what a one-way ANOVA gives you. The second factor and the interaction add two more.
🏷️ Three F tests: A, B, A × B. All over the same MS error.

🔎 What it is really asking

Multiply the two main-effect df together.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Degrees of freedom: the interaction row.

🛠️ The procedure

df for A × B = (a − 1)(b − 1) — the two main-effect df multiplied. It is the same shape as the chi-square rule for a two-way table.

🧮 The working
a = 2 feedback types, b = 3 difficulties.

df A = 2 − 1 = 1
df B = 3 − 1 = 2
df A × B = 1 × 2 = 2

Check the whole column, which must add to N − 1 = 59:
  1 + 2 + 2 + 54 = 59 ✓

And the error df: N − ab = 60 − 6 = 54, exactly as printed.

Use that addition every time. It catches a wrong interaction df instantly, because the four rows will not reach N − 1.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.3 is a + b − 2 = 1 + 2, adding the main-effect df instead of multiplying them.
b.5 is the number of cells minus one, 6 − 1. That is the df you would have if you treated the six cells as one factor — and it is exactly 1 + 2 + 2, the three effects added together.
c.6 is the number of cells. No df rule is a plain count of cells.
🏷️ df A × B = (a − 1)(b − 1). Multiply, never add.

Degrees of freedom for the error term

In Varga’s 2 × 3 study of 60 participants, the degrees of freedom for the error row are:
The same table with the error degrees of freedom removed
SourceSSdfMSF
Feedback type (A)1601160.008.00
Task difficulty (B)180290.004.50
A × B interaction100250.002.50
Error1080??
Total152059
  • a50
  • b54
  • c59
  • d57
🔎 What it is really asking

Total observations minus the number of cells.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Degrees of freedom: the error row.

🛠️ The procedure

df error = N − ab, the total number of observations minus the number of cells. Equivalently, each cell contributes n − 1.

🧮 The working
N = 60, and there are ab = 2 × 3 = 6 cells.

df error = 60 − 6 = 54

By the other route: each of the 6 cells of 10 contributes 10 − 1 = 9 df, and 6 × 9 = 54. Same number, and it shows where the df come from — one is spent on each cell mean.

What it buys: MS error = 1080 ⁄ 54 = 20.00, the single estimate of within-cell variance that all three F tests divide by. Its square root, 4.47, is the typical distance from a participant to their own cell mean.

And the df drive the critical values: on (1, 54) the 5% cut-off is 4.0195, and on (2, 54) it is 3.1682.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.50 would be N − 10, subtracting the cell size. It is the number of cells that is subtracted, not n.
c.59 is the Total df, N − 1. The error row is what is left after the three effects are taken out: 59 − 1 − 2 − 2 = 54.
d.57 would be N − 3, subtracting the number of effects rather than the number of cells.
🏷️ df error = N − ab. Also Σ(n − 1) over the cells.

Question 5

🔢 Degrees of freedom

Recovering a design from the df

A two-factor ANOVA table shows df of 2 for factor A, 3 for factor B and 6 for the interaction. Factor A and factor B have:
  • a3 and 3 levels
  • b2 and 6 levels
  • c3 and 4 levels
  • d2 and 3 levels
🔎 What it is really asking

Add one to each main-effect df, then check the product.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Degrees of freedom: reading the design out of the table.

🛠️ The procedure

Invert the rules: a = df A + 1 and b = df B + 1. Then confirm against the interaction, which must equal df A × df B.

🧮 The working
a = 2 + 1 = 3 levels of A.
b = 3 + 1 = 4 levels of B.

Check the interaction: 2 × 3 = 6. ✓ Matches the printed df, so the reading is consistent.

So this is a 3 × 4 design with 12 cells.

Why the check matters. The interaction df is the thing that pins the reading down. If you had guessed 3 and 3 levels, the interaction df would have to be 2 × 2 = 4, not 6 — and the table would have told you at once that you were wrong.

Exam habit: the df column is the design in code. Decode it before you touch a mean square.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.3 and 3 levels would give an interaction df of 2 × 2 = 4. The table says 6.
b.2 and 6 levels would give an interaction df of 1 × 5 = 5, and A’s df would be 1.
d.2 and 3 levels reads the main-effect df as the numbers of levels, skipping the "+ 1" on each. Its interaction would be 1 × 2 = 2.
🏷️ a = df A + 1, b = df B + 1. Confirm with df A × df B.

🧱 Completing the table

Completing the table

Five entries are missing from Varga’s table. The SS for error is:
The same table with five entries removed
SourceSSdfMSF
Feedback type (A)160???
Task difficulty (B)180290.004.50
A × B interaction100?50.002.50
Error?5420.00
Total152059
  • a1080
  • b1420
  • c440
  • d1520
🔎 What it is really asking

The SS column adds down to the Total.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Completing the table: a missing sum of squares.

🛠️ The procedure

SS total = SS A + SS B + SS A×B + SS error. The SS column adds up, so any one missing entry is the total minus the rest. The df column adds up the same way.

🧮 The working
SS error = 1520 − (160 + 180 + 100) = 1520 − 440 = 1080

Confirm it against the MS that is printed: 1080 ⁄ 54 = 20.00. ✓ Two independent routes to the same number, which is as good as a check ever gets.

The rest of the table then completes itself:
  df A = 1, so MS A = 160 ⁄ 1 = 160.00 and F = 160.00 ⁄ 20.00 = 8.00
  df A × B = 2, as (2 − 1)(3 − 1)

The one-line summary of every ANOVA table: the SS column adds, the df column adds, each MS is that row’s SS over its own df, and every F divides by MS error.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.1420 is 1520 − 100, subtracting the interaction only. All three effects come out of the total.
c.440 is the sum of the three effect SS — what you subtract, not the answer.
d.1520 is the Total SS. The error row is only the part of it that none of the effects explains.
🏷️ SS column adds to Total. Check any MS you fill in against its printed F.

🔎 What it is really asking

That effect’s mean square over the error mean square.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Completing the table: an F statistic.

🛠️ The procedure

F = MS effect ⁄ MS error. Every F in the table has the same denominator, MS error.

🧮 The working
MS A = 160 ⁄ 1 = 160.00
MS error = 1080 ⁄ 54 = 20.00

F = 160.00 ⁄ 20.00 = 8.00

The decision: on (1, 54) df the 5% critical value is 4.0195. 8.00 clears it, and P = .0066. Written and video feedback do not produce the same mean motivation.

Note the df pair: (df of the effect, df of the error) — here (1, 54). The interaction, with 2 df, is tested on (2, 54) against 3.1682 instead.

And the other two results, for context: difficulty F = 4.50 (P = .016) is also significant; the interaction F = 2.50 (P = .092) is not.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.1.78 is 160 ⁄ 90, dividing by another effect’s mean square. The denominator is always MS error.
c.0.15 is 160 ⁄ 1080, the sums of squares divided directly. Mean squares first, always.
d.2.96 is 160 ⁄ 54, dividing the effect SS by the error df. Two different rows have been mixed together.
🏷️ F = MS effect ⁄ MS error. Same denominator for all three.

Deciding on three effects at once

Varga’s three F statistics are 8.00 on (1, 54), 4.50 on (2, 54) and 2.50 on (2, 54). The critical values at α = .05 are 4.0195 on (1, 54) and 3.1682 on (2, 54). Her conclusion is:
Two-factor ANOVA · motivation score · 10 participants per cell
SourceSSdfMSF
Feedback type (A)1601160.008.00
Task difficulty (B)180290.004.50
A × B interaction100250.002.50
Error10805420.00
Total152059

  • cthe interaction is significant, so the main effects cannot be read

🔎 What it is really asking

Three separate comparisons, each against its own critical value.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Completing the table: reading all three results.

🛠️ The procedure

Compare each F with the critical value on its own df pair. Interaction and main effects are separate decisions.

🧮 The working
• Feedback type: 8.00 against 4.0195 on (1, 54) → significant, P = .0066.
• Task difficulty: 4.50 against 3.1682 on (2, 54) → significant, P = .0156.
• Interaction: 2.50 against 3.1682 on (2, 54) → not significant, P = .0915.

Why this is the comfortable case. With no significant interaction, the effect of feedback type is much the same at every difficulty level, so the two main effects can be described on their own: the two kinds of feedback differ, and motivation changes with difficulty, and those two statements do not interfere with each other. (Which kind of feedback is higher needs the cell means, which this table does not give — F squares the difference and loses its sign.)

Watch the df pair. 2.50 and 4.50 share the same df here, but if you compared the interaction against 4.0195 by mistake you would reach the same verdict for the wrong reason — and on other tables that slip changes the answer.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The interaction’s 2.50 falls short of 3.1682. P = .092, which is not significant at the 5% level.
b.Task difficulty’s 4.50 clears its own critical value of 3.1682 comfortably. Both main effects are significant, not just one.
c.The interaction is not significant here — and even when it is, the main effects are still reported, just interpreted with care rather than discarded.
🏷️ Each F against its own df pair. Three separate decisions.

Question 9

📈 Interaction plots

Reading an interaction plot

Clinical researcher Serrano compares two therapies delivered in group or individual sessions, 12 participants per cell, and plots the four cell means. The plot shows:
Serrano’s interaction plot: the two therapies cross over
  • aan interaction, since the lines cross
  • ba main effect of therapy, since the lines are far apart
  • cno effects at all, since the row and column means are equal
  • da main effect of format, since one format is higher
🔎 What it is really asking

What does the shape of the lines tell you?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Interaction plots: reading the shape.

🛠️ The procedure

Parallel lines → no interaction. Lines that converge, diverge or cross → an interaction: the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other.

🧮 The working
Read the four cell means behind the plot:

Therapy A: 70.0 in group sessions, 58.0 individually — group is 12 points better.
Therapy B: 58.0 in group sessions, 70.0 individually — group is 12 points worse.

The effect of format reverses completely depending on the therapy. That is an interaction, and the crossing lines are what it looks like.

Now the striking part. Both row means are 64.0 and both column means are 64.0. So there is no main effect of therapy and no main effect of format — SS A and SS B are exactly zero — while the interaction is enormous. Her output gives SS error 1584 on 44 df, so MS error = 36.00 and F = 1728 ⁄ 36.00 = 48.00, P < .0001.

The lesson: a factor with no main effect can still matter enormously. Looking only at the margins here would have you report that neither therapy nor format makes any difference, when in fact the right pairing is worth 12 points.
Mean outcome score · 12 participants per cell · Serrano’s study
Group sessionsIndividual sessionsRow mean
Therapy A70.058.064.0
Therapy B58.070.064.0
Column mean64.064.064.0
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.The lines are not far apart on average — each therapy is higher in one format and lower in the other. Both row means are 64.0, so there is no therapy main effect at all.
c.The equal margins do mean both main effects are zero, but "no effects at all" misses the interaction, which is the largest thing in this dataset.
d.Neither format is higher overall: both column means are 64.0. One format is better for one therapy and worse for the other.
🏷️ Crossing lines = interaction. Zero main effects do not mean nothing is happening.

Question 10

📈 Interaction plots

What parallel lines mean

In an interaction plot for a different study, the two lines are clearly separated and exactly parallel. This indicates:
  • ano effects of any kind
  • bthat the two factors are measured on the same scale
  • ca main effect of the line factor and no interaction
  • dan interaction with no main effects
🔎 What it is really asking

Separation and slope are telling you about two different things.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Interaction plots: parallel lines.

🛠️ The procedure

Vertical separation between the lines shows a main effect of the line factor. Parallelism shows no interaction. The common slope shows a main effect of the x-axis factor.

🧮 The working
Take the three readings off the plot one at a time:

• Are the lines apart? Yes — so the factor shown by the lines has a main effect. One level sits above the other at every x.
• Are they parallel? Yes — so no interaction. Moving along the x-axis changes both lines by the same amount, which is precisely what "the effect of one factor does not depend on the other" means.
• Do they slope? A common non-zero slope would mean a main effect of the x-axis factor too.

Compare Serrano’s plot, which is the mirror image of this one: lines crossing, margins identical — all interaction, no main effects.

Three questions, three answers, in that order. Apart? Parallel? Sloping?
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Clear separation is a main effect. "No effects of any kind" would need the two lines lying flat on top of each other.
b.Both lines are the same response variable on the same vertical axis. Scales are not what the plot is about.
d.An interaction is exactly what parallel lines rule out. Crossing or converging lines would show one.
🏷️ Apart = main effect of the line factor. Parallel = no interaction.

Question 11

📈 Interaction plots

What a significant interaction does to the main effects

Serrano’s interaction is significant (F = 48.00, P < .0001). How should she report the two main effects?
Mean outcome score · 12 participants per cell · Serrano’s study
Group sessionsIndividual sessionsRow mean
Therapy A70.058.064.0
Therapy B58.070.064.0
Column mean64.064.064.0
  • areport them as usual, since they are tested separately
  • bconclude that neither therapy nor format has any effect
  • cdrop the interaction and re-run the analysis without it
  • ddescribe each factor separately for each level of the other
🔎 What it is really asking

What a significant interaction changes about the write-up.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Interaction plots: reporting when the interaction is significant.

🛠️ The procedure

When the interaction is significant, a main effect averaged over the other factor can be misleading. The honest report describes the effect of each factor separately at each level of the other — these are the simple effects.

🧮 The working
Her margins say the main effects are zero. Her cells say something quite different:

• For Therapy A: group sessions beat individual by 12.0 points.
• For Therapy B: individual sessions beat group by 12.0 points.

Average those two and you get zero — which is all a main effect can ever report, and it describes nobody in the study.

So the write-up is: "the better format depends on the therapy" followed by the two simple effects. Not "format had no effect", which is true of the average and false of every participant.

The general rule: read the interaction first. If it is significant, main effects are described within the levels of the other factor, not instead of them.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Reporting "no effect of format" because the margins are equal is exactly the error this question is about. The margins average away a 12-point effect in each direction.
b.Neither factor is without effect. Each matters a great deal — but only in combination with the other.
c.Dropping a significant interaction discards the main finding of the study. The interaction is the result here.
🏷️ Significant interaction → report simple effects, not averaged main effects.

Question 12

▦ Cell means and margins

Computing a marginal mean

In Serrano’s design the marginal mean for group sessions, across both therapies, is:
Mean outcome score · 12 participants per cell · Serrano’s study
Group sessionsIndividual sessionsRow mean
Therapy A70.058.064.0
Therapy B58.070.064.0
Column mean64.064.064.0
  • a12.0
  • b64.0
  • c70.0
  • d58.0
🔎 What it is really asking

Average the cells in that column — equal cell sizes, so a plain average.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Cell means and margins: computing one.

🛠️ The procedure

A marginal mean averages across the other factor. With equal n in every cell it is the plain average of that row’s or column’s cell means.

🧮 The working
The group-sessions column holds 70.0 (Therapy A) and 58.0 (Therapy B).

(70.0 + 58.0) ⁄ 2 = 64.0

The individual-sessions column: (58.0 + 70.0) ⁄ 2 = 64.0 as well. Identical — which is why SS for format is exactly zero and its F is zero.

And this is the trap the whole theme is built around. A marginal mean of 64.0 in both columns makes format look irrelevant. The cells say group sessions are worth +12 for Therapy A and −12 for Therapy B. The margin is an average of two real and opposite effects, and it reports neither.

Read the cells before you trust the margins. The margins are the main effects; the cells are what happened.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.12.0 is the size of the simple effect of format within each therapy, not a mean.
c.70.0 is one cell — Therapy A in group sessions. A margin averages across the other factor.
d.58.0 is the other cell in that column, Therapy B in group sessions.
🏷️ Marginal mean = average across the other factor. Equal n → plain average.

Question 13

▦ Cell means and margins

From cell means to a main effect

In a 2 × 2 study the four cell means are 50, 56, 60 and 66, arranged so that each row mean is 53 and 63 and each column mean is 55 and 61. The design shows:
  • aboth main effects, and no interaction
  • ban interaction, since all four cell means differ
  • ca main effect of the row factor only
  • dno main effects, since all four cells differ
🔎 What it is really asking

Do the differences stay constant across the other factor?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Cell means and margins: diagnosing the effects.

🛠️ The procedure

Check whether the effect of one factor is the same size at each level of the other. Same size → no interaction, whatever the main effects do.

🧮 The working
The cells, laid out: row 1 is 50 and 56; row 2 is 60 and 66.

• Effect of the column factor in row 1: 56 − 50 = +6.
• Effect of the column factor in row 2: 66 − 60 = +6.

Identical, so no interaction — and plotted, these would be two exactly parallel lines.

The margins carry the rest: rows 53 against 63 is a 10-point row effect; columns 55 against 61 is a 6-point column effect. Both main effects are real.

The point worth taking away: four different cell means do not imply an interaction. Additive main effects alone produce four different cells — 50, +6, +10, and +16 for both together. An interaction is not "the cells differ"; it is "the differences differ".
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.All four cell means differing is not an interaction. Two additive main effects produce four distinct cells on their own.
c.The column factor has a main effect too: 55 against 61, a 6-point gap that shows up identically in both rows.
d.Both main effects are present and sizeable. Different cells are not a sign that the margins are flat.
🏷️ Interaction = the differences differ. Not just “the cells differ”.

⚖️ What it does NOT mean

What a factorial result does not mean

Varga found a significant main effect of feedback type (F = 8.00, P = .007) and a non-significant interaction (F = 2.50, P = .092). She may conclude that:
Two-factor ANOVA · motivation score · 10 participants per cell
SourceSSdfMSF
Feedback type (A)1601160.008.00
Task difficulty (B)180290.004.50
A × B interaction100250.002.50
Error10805420.00
Total152059
  • athe interaction is absent, so difficulty has no effect
  • bvideo feedback causes higher motivation in all participants
  • cfeedback type matters at much the same rate across all three difficulties
  • dfeedback type matters only at one of the three difficulties
🔎 What it is really asking

What does a non-significant interaction license alongside a significant main effect?

🧭 Which type of question this is

What it does NOT mean: reading main effects and interaction together.

🛠️ The procedure

A non-significant interaction means the data give no evidence that the effect of one factor changes across the levels of the other. The main effect can then be described as a single, roughly constant effect.

🧮 The working
Interaction P = .092 — no evidence that the feedback effect differs by difficulty. So the gap between written and video feedback is, as far as these data show, about the same at every difficulty level.

That is what makes the main effect interpretable on its own, and it is the right reading.

Three things to keep out of the conclusion:
• "Only at one level" would require a significant interaction, which she does not have.
• "Difficulty has no effect" is contradicted by her own table: difficulty F = 4.50, P = .016.
• "In all participants" over-reads a difference in means. Individual participants vary — the within-cell SD is 4.47 — so plenty of people given written feedback scored above plenty given video.

And a last caution: P = .092 is not proof of no interaction. It is a failure to detect one, and with 10 per cell that is not the same thing.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Difficulty is significant in its own right, F = 4.50 with P = .016. A non-significant interaction says nothing against a main effect.
b."All participants" turns a difference in group means into a claim about every individual — and with no cell means given, even the direction is unestablished.
d."Only at one difficulty" is a claim about an interaction, and her interaction is not significant.
🏷️ Non-significant interaction = no evidence the effect changes. Not proof it doesn’t.

Question 15

⚖️ What it does NOT mean

Why a factorial design is worth running

Serrano could have run two separate one-way studies, one on therapy and one on format. Running them as a single 2 × 2 factorial instead gave her:
Mean outcome score · 12 participants per cell · Serrano’s study
Group sessionsIndividual sessionsRow mean
Therapy A70.058.064.0
Therapy B58.070.064.0
Column mean64.064.064.0
  • aa smaller error term, since the factors are combined
  • ba one-sided test of each factor
  • cprotection against unequal cell sizes
  • dthe interaction, which neither separate study could find
🔎 What it is really asking

What can a factorial design answer that two separate studies cannot?

🧭 Which type of question this is

What it does NOT mean: the value of the design.

🛠️ The procedure

Two separate one-way studies can each estimate a main effect. Only a factorial design can ask whether the factors depend on each other, because only there does every combination occur.

🧮 The working
Her two separate studies would have reported, correctly, that therapy makes no difference and format makes no difference. Both main effects are exactly zero.

Both conclusions would have been badly wrong about what is happening — the pairing is worth 12 points in either direction, F = 48.00, P < .0001.

The interaction is only visible because all four combinations were run. A study on format alone never separates Therapy A from Therapy B, so the +12 and the −12 land in the same average and cancel.

The second, quieter advantage: she answered three questions with 48 participants instead of two questions with two separate samples. Factorial designs are more economical as well as more informative.

The headline: run the factors together and you can ask whether they talk to each other.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Against two separate one-way studies, each holding the other factor constant, the error is the same within-cell variance. The interaction is what only the factorial design can give her.
b.F tests have one tail and no direction, factorial or not. Squaring loses the sign.
c.Unequal cell sizes are a complication for a factorial design rather than something it protects you from.
🏷️ Only a factorial design can find an interaction. Separate studies cannot.

Question 1

🧩 Reading the design

Reading a design out of a described study

Developmental psychologist Vanhoutte recruits 96 children. She crosses four age bands (6, 8, 10 and 12 years) with two instruction formats (a demonstration or written steps), filling every combination with the same number of children, and scores each child on a construction task. Her design is:
  • aa 2 × 4 factorial with 8 per cell
  • ba one-way design with eight conditions
  • ca 4 × 2 factorial with 12 per cell
  • da 4 × 2 factorial with 24 per cell
🔎 What it is really asking

Two things at once: the shape of the crossing, and how many children sit in one combination.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading the design: factors, levels and cells.

🛠️ The procedure

Count the levels of each factor and multiply them for the number of cells. Then n per cell = N ⁄ cells. Do the two steps in that order — the cell size cannot be found before the cells have been counted.

🧮 The working
Step one, the shape. Age band has 4 levels, instruction format has 2. So a 4 × 2 factorial, and 4 × 2 = 8 cells.

Step two, the cell size. 96 ⁄ 8 = 12 children per cell.

Sanity check in the other direction: 8 cells × 12 children = 96 ✓

The habit: never divide N by a number of levels. 96 ⁄ 4 = 24 and 96 ⁄ 2 = 48 are both real quantities — children per age band and children per format — and neither of them is the cell size. Divide by the product.

Everything downstream rests on 4, 2 and 12: df A = 3, df B = 1, df A × B = 3, df error = 96 − 8 = 88.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.2 × 4 and 4 × 2 describe the same crossing, but 8 per cell comes to 64 children, not 96.
b.Eight conditions treated as one factor throws the structure away, and with it the interaction — the only question a factorial design adds.
d.24 per cell across eight cells would need 192 children. She has 96, so 96 ⁄ 8 = 12.
🏷️ Cells = levels multiplied. n per cell = N ⁄ cells. Two steps, that order.

Question 2

🧩 Reading the design

What the output will contain

Vanhoutte runs her 4 × 2 study and asks for the full output. The number of cell means it reports and the number of F tests it carries out are:
  • aeight cell means and three F tests
  • beight cell means and eight F tests
  • csix cell means and three F tests
  • deight cell means and two F tests
🔎 What it is really asking

Two counts that come from two different rules — cells from the design, F tests from the analysis.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading the design: what the analysis delivers.

🛠️ The procedure

Cell means = a × b, one per combination. F tests = 3 in any two-factor ANOVA: A, B and A × B. The two counts are unrelated, and a bigger design does not buy more F tests.

🧮 The working
Cell means: 4 age bands × 2 formats = 8. One mean for 6-year-olds given a demonstration, one for 6-year-olds given written steps, and so on.

F tests: 3, whatever the size of the design.
  • age band (main effect)
  • instruction format (main effect)
  • age band × instruction format (interaction)

A 2 × 2 gives three F tests on four cells; a 5 × 6 gives three F tests on thirty cells. The count of effects is fixed by having two factors, not by how many levels they have.

And the decision: all three F tests divide by the same MS error, so one pool of 88 error degrees of freedom serves the lot. That shared denominator is why a factorial design is economical.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Eight F tests would be one per cell. Cells are conditions to be compared, not hypotheses to be tested.
c.Six cell means belongs to a 3 × 2 design. Four age bands crossed with two formats make 4 × 2 = 8.
d.Two F tests leaves out the interaction — the one effect neither factor can show on its own.
🏷️ Cell means = a × b. F tests = 3, always, in a two-factor ANOVA.

Question 3

🔢 Degrees of freedom

Recovering the error df from a part-filled df column

Health psychologist Dalgaard crosses four coping styles with three kinds of stressor and measures reported strain. Part of her output survives below. The degrees of freedom for the error row are:
Dalgaard’s output: the df column, with two entries removed
Sourcedf
Coping style (A)3
Stressor type (B)2
A × B interaction?
Error?
Total71
  • a66
  • b59
  • c68
  • d60
🔎 What it is really asking

Fill the interaction row first, then let the column add to the total.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Degrees of freedom: completing the column.

🛠️ The procedure

The df column adds to the Total. So fill in every other row first: df A × B = (a − 1)(b − 1), and then df error = Total − A − B − A × B.

🧮 The working
The interaction row is the one you have to supply before anything else works:

df A × B = 3 × 2 = 6

Now the column adds:
  df error = 71 − 3 − 2 − 6 = 60

Check it the other way round. Total df = N − 1 = 71, so N = 72 observations, and there are ab = 4 × 3 = 12 cells:
  df error = N − ab = 72 − 12 = 60 ✓

Two independent routes to 60, which is as good as a check ever gets. As a bonus the design has fallen out of the df column: 72 ⁄ 12 = 6 participants per cell.

The habit: the interaction row is the one people forget. Write it in before you subtract anything.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.66 is 71 − 3 − 2, which forgets that the interaction row takes degrees of freedom too.
b.59 is 71 − 12, subtracting the twelve cells from the Total df instead of from the 72 observations.
c.68 is 72 − 4, the error df of a one-way ANOVA on four coping-style groups. There is a second factor in this design.
🏷️ Supply the interaction df first. Then the column adds to the Total.

Question 4

🔢 Degrees of freedom

Recovering the cell size from the df column

Cognitive psychologist Eichler crosses three study strategies with two session timings and records words recalled. Only the degrees-of-freedom column of her output survives. The number of participants in each cell is:
All that survives of Eichler’s output: the df column
Sourcedf
Study strategy (A)2
Session timing (B)1
A × B interaction2
Error42
Total47
  • a24
  • b8
  • c7
  • d6
🔎 What it is really asking

Decode the design from the df, then work out how many people the error df implies.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Degrees of freedom: reading the design out of the table.

🛠️ The procedure

Three steps. a = df A + 1 and b = df B + 1 give the cells. N = Total df + 1 (or df error + ab). Then n = N ⁄ ab.

🧮 The working
Step one — the design:
  a = 2 + 1 = 3 strategies, b = 1 + 1 = 2 timings, so ab = 6 cells.
  Check against the interaction row: 2 × 1 = 2 ✓

Step two — the sample size:
  N = Total df + 1 = 47 + 1 = 48
  Or from the error row: N = df error + ab = 42 + 6 = 48 ✓

Step three — the cell size:
  n = 48 ⁄ 6 = 8 participants per cell

And the slow route, which shows what the error df is: each of the 6 cells contributes n − 1 df, so 6(n − 1) = 42, n − 1 = 7, n = 8.

The habit: a df column is the design written in code. Decode a, b, N and n in that order, and only then start on the mean squares.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.24 is 48 ⁄ 2, the participants at each level of session timing — three cells’ worth of people, not one cell’s.
c.7 is 42 ⁄ 6, the n − 1 that each of the six cells contributes. Add the one back to get the cell size.
d.6 is the number of cells, 3 × 2. It is what you divide by, not the answer.
🏷️ a = df A + 1, b = df B + 1, N = Total df + 1, then n = N ⁄ ab.

Question 5

🔢 Degrees of freedom

The df pair for an interaction F

Communication researcher Lindhout crosses three message framings with four source types and tests 5 participants in every combination. The pair of degrees of freedom against which she judges the interaction F is:
  • a2 and 48
  • b11 and 48
  • c6 and 48
  • d6 and 59
🔎 What it is really asking

Which two numbers an F is looked up on — and which row each of them comes from.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Degrees of freedom: choosing the df pair for a test.

🛠️ The procedure

Every F is read on (df of the effect, df of the error). For the interaction that is (a − 1)(b − 1) on top and N − ab underneath.

🧮 The working
The design first: a = 3, b = 4, so ab = 12 cells and N = 12 × 5 = 60.

Numerator — the interaction df:
  (3 − 1)(4 − 1) = 2 × 3 = 6

Denominator — the error df:
  N − ab = 60 − 12 = 48

So the interaction F is judged on (6, 48), where the 5% critical value is 2.2946.

Check the whole column: 2 + 3 + 6 + 48 = 59 = N − 1 ✓

And the decision: her three F tests use three different numerators — 2 for framing, 3 for source, 6 for the interaction — and all three share the same denominator of 48. Reading an F on the wrong pair moves the goalposts without telling you.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.2 and 48 uses factor A’s 2 df as the numerator. The interaction’s own df is (3 − 1)(4 − 1) = 6.
b.11 and 48 uses ab − 1 = 11, the df you would have if the twelve cells were treated as one factor.
d.6 and 59 pairs the interaction df with the Total df. The second number of a pair is always the error df.
🏷️ F is read on (effect df, error df). Interaction df = (a − 1)(b − 1).

Question 6

🧱 Completing the table

Completing a table before an F can be computed

The F column of Eichler’s table has been lost, along with two mean squares and one sum of squares. The F statistic for the main effect of study strategy, to two decimal places, is:
Eichler’s table with the error SS, two mean squares and every F removed
SourceSSdfMSF
Study strategy (A)2882??
Session timing (B)48148.00?
A × B interaction32216.00?
Error?42?
Total87247
  • a12.00
  • b0.57
  • c3.43
  • d6.00
🔎 What it is really asking

The F you want needs a denominator that is not printed. Build it first.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Completing the table: an F that needs two earlier steps.

🛠️ The procedure

Work in the order the table is built: the SS column adds to the Total, then each MS = SS ⁄ df for its own row, then F = MS effect ⁄ MS error.

🧮 The working
Step one — the missing sum of squares, from the column:
  SS error = 872 − (288 + 48 + 32) = 872 − 368 = 504

Step two — the two mean squares:
  MS error = 504 ⁄ 42 = 12.00
  MS strategy = 288 ⁄ 2 = 144.00

Step three — the F:
  F = 144.00 ⁄ 12.00 = 12.00

Check the printed rows against that MS error: 48.00 ⁄ 12.00 = 4.00 for timing and 16.00 ⁄ 12.00 = 1.33 for the interaction. Both are ordinary-looking F values, so the 12.00 underneath is believable.

And the decision: on (2, 42) the 5% critical value is 3.2199. 12.00 is far past it, P = .0001, so the three strategies do not all produce the same mean recall.

The habit: in a gapped table, never reach straight for the cell you were asked about. Fill the column, then the mean squares, then the F.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.0.57 is 288 ⁄ 504, the two sums of squares divided directly. Each has to become a mean square first.
c.3.43 is 144 ⁄ 42, the effect’s mean square over the error df rather than over the error mean square.
d.6.00 is 288 ⁄ 48, dividing by another effect’s sum of squares. The denominator of every F in the table is MS error.
🏷️ Column adds → mean squares → F. In that order, every time.

Question 7

🧱 Completing the table

Recovering a sum of squares from an F

Psychotherapy researcher Lombardi crosses two delivery modes with four session lengths, 7 clients per cell, and measures therapeutic alliance. Three entries are missing from her output. The sum of squares for session length is:
Lombardi’s table with session length’s SS and MS, and the SS total, removed
SourceSSdfMSF
Delivery mode (A)1501150.007.50
Session length (B)?3?4.50
A × B interaction180360.003.00
Error9604820.00
Total?55
  • a13.5
  • b270
  • c90
  • d1800
🔎 What it is really asking

Run the usual chain backwards: from the F that is printed to the SS that is not.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Completing the table: working backwards from a printed F.

🛠️ The procedure

Forwards the chain is SS → MS → F. Backwards it is MS = F × MS error, then SS = MS × df. Two multiplications, in that order.

🧮 The working
Step one — the mean square, from the F and the error mean square:
  MS B = 4.50 × 20.00 = 90.00

Step two — the sum of squares, from the mean square and its own df:
  SS B = 90.00 × 3 = 270

Now the table is closed, so check it adds up:
  SS total = 150 + 270 + 180 + 960 = 1560
  df total = 1 + 3 + 3 + 48 = 55 = N − 1 = 56 − 1 ✓

And the decision: on (3, 48) the 5% critical value is 2.7981, so session length’s 4.50 is significant (P = .007). So are delivery mode, 7.50 on (1, 48) against 4.0427, and the interaction, 3.00 on (3, 48), P = .040.

The habit: whichever cell is missing, the four relationships never change — the SS column adds, the df column adds, MS = SS ⁄ df, F = MS ⁄ MS error. Pick whichever one has only one unknown left in it.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.13.5 is 4.50 × 3, multiplying F straight by the df and leaving MS error out of the chain altogether.
c.90 is the mean square for session length, one step short of the answer. SS = MS × df.
d.1800 is 90 × 20, multiplying the mean square by MS error instead of by its own 3 degrees of freedom.
🏷️ Backwards: MS = F × MS error, then SS = MS × df.

Question 8

🧱 Completing the table

Three decisions on two different critical values

Eichler’s three F statistics are 12.00 on (2, 42), 4.00 on (1, 42) and 1.33 on (2, 42). The critical values at α = .05 are 3.2199 on (2, 42) and 4.0727 on (1, 42). Her conclusion is:
Two-factor ANOVA · words recalled · 8 participants per cell
SourceSSdfMSF
Study strategy (A)2882144.0012.00
Session timing (B)48148.004.00
A × B interaction32216.001.33
Error5044212.00
Total87247
  • aboth main effects are significant, not the interaction
  • bthe strategy and interaction effects are significant
  • call three of the effects are significant
  • donly the strategy main effect is significant
🔎 What it is really asking

Three comparisons, and two of them use a different critical value from the third.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Completing the table: reading all three results.

🛠️ The procedure

Match each F to the critical value on its own df pair. Two critical values are given here because the three effects do not all have the same numerator df.

🧮 The working
• Study strategy: 12.00 against 3.2199 on (2, 42) → significant, P = .0001.
• Session timing: 4.00 against 4.0727 on (1, 42) → not significant, P = .052.
• Interaction: 1.33 against 3.2199 on (2, 42) → not significant, P = .275.

So one of the three clears its bar.

Look hard at the middle line. Timing has 1 df, not 2, so its critical value is 4.0727 and its F of 4.00 falls just short. Compare it against 3.2199 by mistake — the other critical value on the page — and you would call it significant. One slip in reading the df, one wrong conclusion.

And the honest write-up of a P of .052: not significant at the 5% level, and nowhere near proof that timing does nothing. It is a near miss with 8 per cell.

The habit: write the df pair beside every F before you look anything up.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Session timing’s 4.00 is judged on (1, 42) against 4.0727 and falls just short, P = .052. Matched to 3.2199 by mistake it would look significant.
b.The interaction’s 1.33 is far below its critical value of 3.2199, with P = .275. Nothing in the table makes it significant.
c.Timing misses its own critical value and so does the interaction. Only one of the three effects clears the bar.
🏷️ Write the df pair next to each F first. Then look up each one separately.

Question 9

📈 Interaction plots

Reading three effects off one plot

Developmental psychologist Lauridsen measures task-switching accuracy in monolingual and bilingual nine-year-olds at three levels of task load, 12 children per cell, and plots the six cell means. The plot shows:
Lauridsen’s plot of the six cell means · 12 children per cell
  • aan interaction and both main effects
  • ban interaction but no main effects
  • ctwo main effects and no interaction
  • da main effect of task load only
🔎 What it is really asking

A plot carries three separate pieces of information. Read all three before choosing.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Interaction plots: reading the shape.

🛠️ The procedure

Three questions, in this order. Are the lines apart? → main effect of the line factor. Do they slope? → main effect of the x-axis factor. Are they parallel? → no interaction; converging, diverging or crossing → interaction.

🧮 The working
Apart? Yes. The bilingual line sits above the monolingual line at every load, so there is a main effect of language group — row means 84.0 against 76.0.

Sloping? Yes, both lines fall as load rises. Column means 88.0, 81.0, 71.0 — a main effect of task load.

Parallel? No. The gap between the lines is 2 points at low load, 6 at medium and 16 at high load. Diverging lines are an interaction.

All three, then. Her output gives F = 24.00 on (1, 66) for group, F = 36.50 on (2, 66) for load, and F = 6.50 on (2, 66) for the interaction, P = .003 — every one of them past its critical value.

The habit: an interaction does not have to cross. "The effect of one factor depends on the level of the other" is exactly what a widening gap says: load costs the monolingual children 24 points and the bilingual children 10.

And note what is safe to say here. Because you are reading means and not an F, you may name the direction: the bilingual line is the higher one. An F on its own would never license that.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Both main effects are there: one line sits above the other throughout, and both lines fall as the load rises.
c.Parallel lines would mean no interaction. These start 2 points apart and finish 16 apart.
d.Task load is not the only effect. The bilingual line is above the monolingual line at every one of the three loads.
🏷️ Apart? Sloping? Parallel? Three readings, three different effects.

Question 10

📈 Interaction plots

Telling a main effect from an interaction on a plot

Motivation researcher Kirchner plots mean persistence for two reward schedules across three practice sessions, 10 children per cell. The plot shows:
Kirchner’s plot of the six cell means · 10 children per cell
  • aa main effect of session only
  • bno effects of any kind
  • cboth main effects and no interaction
  • dan interaction and both main effects
🔎 What it is really asking

The lines are apart and sloping. Does either of those make an interaction?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Interaction plots: parallel lines that slope.

🛠️ The procedure

Separation and slope are both main effects. Only a change in the gap is an interaction. A plot can be dramatic and still have no interaction at all.

🧮 The working
Measure the gap at each session, which is the only reading that answers the interaction question:

  Session 1: 48 − 40 = 8
  Session 2: 54 − 46 = 8
  Session 3: 60 − 52 = 8

Identical, so the lines are exactly parallel and SS for the interaction is exactly zero — its F is 0.00.

The two main effects are both large. Row means 54.0 against 46.0 gives F = 30.00 on (1, 54) for reward schedule; column means 44.0, 50.0, 56.0 gives F = 22.50 on (2, 54) for session.

Hold this plot next to Lauridsen’s. Both have two separated, sloping lines. The only difference is whether the gap stays put — 8, 8, 8 here against 2, 6, 16 there — and that one difference is the whole interaction question.

The habit: do not judge an interaction by eye from how steep or how far apart the lines are. Subtract the two lines at each x and look at those numbers.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Session is not the only effect. The variable-reward line sits 8 points above the fixed-reward line throughout.
b.Neither line is flat and the two are clearly apart, so both main effects are present and sizeable.
d.An interaction would need the gap between the lines to change. It is 8 points at every one of the three sessions.
🏷️ Subtract the lines at each x. Constant gap = no interaction, however steep.

Question 11

📈 Interaction plots

Finding a missing main effect on a plot

Decision researcher Novotný trains participants in a deliberate or an intuitive strategy and tests them under three levels of time pressure, 8 participants per cell. Her plot shows that there is no main effect of:
Novotný’s plot of the six cell means · 8 participants per cell
  • astrategy, since the two lines end up level
  • btime pressure, since neither line is flat
  • cstrategy, since the lines cross in the middle
  • dtime pressure, since its three averages match
🔎 What it is really asking

A main effect lives in the margins. Which margins does this plot leave flat?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Interaction plots: locating a zero main effect.

🛠️ The procedure

The main effect of the x-axis factor is the average of the lines at each x, not the slope of either line. Average the points vertically at each x and see whether those averages move.

🧮 The working
Average the two lines at each level of pressure:

  No pressure: (84 + 56) ⁄ 2 = 70
  Moderate:    (74 + 66) ⁄ 2 = 70
  High:        (64 + 76) ⁄ 2 = 70

The three marginal means are identical, so SS for time pressure is exactly zero and its F is 0.00.

The other margin is not flat. Row means are 74.0 for the deliberate strategy and 66.0 for the intuitive one — a real main effect, F = 24.00 on (1, 42).

And the crossing is the interaction: F = 50.00 on (2, 42), the largest thing in the study. Pressure costs the deliberate group 20 points and gains the intuitive group 20.

The trap in plain words: both lines are steep, so pressure obviously matters — yet its main effect is zero, because the two slopes are mirror images and the average of them is flat. A main effect is an average, and averages hide opposites.

The habit: for the x-axis factor, look at the midpoint between the lines, not at the lines.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Strategy does have a main effect: the deliberate line averages 74.0 and the intuitive line 66.0.
b.Neither line being flat is exactly why you must average them. Each pressure level averages to 70.
c.Crossing lines are the interaction, not a missing main effect. The two strategy means are 74.0 and 66.0.
🏷️ x-axis main effect = the midpoint between the lines at each x.

One column of the table, averaged — so decide which direction you are averaging in.

Cell means and margins: computing one.

🛠️ The procedure

A marginal mean averages across the other factor. With equal n in every cell it is the plain average of that row’s or that column’s cell means.

🧮 The working
The high-load column holds 63.0 (monolingual) and 79.0 (bilingual).

(63.0 + 79.0) ⁄ 2 = 71.0

The equal cell size of 12 is what makes a plain average right. With unequal cells you would have to weight each cell by its own n.

Do the other two columns while you are here, because the set of them is the main effect of load:
  Low load:    (87.0 + 89.0) ⁄ 2 = 88.0
  Medium load: (78.0 + 84.0) ⁄ 2 = 81.0
  High load:   71.0

Check: those three average to (88.0 + 81.0 + 71.0) ⁄ 3 = 80.0, and so do the two row means, (76.0 + 84.0) ⁄ 2 = 80.0. Both margins must land on the same grand mean ✓

The habit: the stem names the factor you are averaging over — "across both language groups". Find that factor in the table and collapse it.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.63.0 is a single cell, monolingual children at high load. A margin needs both groups in it.
c.80.0 is the grand mean of all 72 children. A marginal mean averages over one factor only, not both.
d.76.0 is the monolingual row mean. Right kind of average, wrong direction through the table.
🏷️ Marginal mean = average across the other factor. Equal n → plain average.

Question 13

▦ Cell means and margins

Recovering a cell mean from a margin

Educational researcher Ackermann crosses two note-taking methods with two lecture paces, 15 students per cell, and scores comprehension. One cell mean is missing from her table. Its value, to one decimal place, is:
Mean comprehension score · 15 students per cell · grand mean 39.5
Slow paceFast paceRow mean
Longhand notes?38.041.0
Laptop notes42.034.038.0
  • a44.0
  • b38.0
  • c41.0
  • d42.0
🔎 What it is really asking

A row mean is an equation with one unknown in it. Solve it.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Cell means and margins: working backwards from a margin.

🛠️ The procedure

With equal cell sizes, row mean = (cell₁ + cell₂) ⁄ 2. Rearranged, the missing cell = 2 × row mean − the other cell.

🧮 The working
The longhand row has one known cell, 38.0, and a row mean of 41.0:

  (x + 38.0) ⁄ 2 = 41.0
  x + 38.0 = 82.0
  x = 44.0

Now check it against a margin the row mean did not use. All four cells must average to the grand mean of 39.5:
  (44.0 + 38.0 + 42.0 + 34.0) ⁄ 4 = 158 ⁄ 4 = 39.5 ✓

With the table complete, the column means come out at 43.0 for a slow pace and 36.0 for a fast one, so both factors have margins that move.

The sanity check worth internalising: a row mean always sits between its two cells. 41.0 lies 3 above 38.0, so the missing cell must lie 3 above 41.0. If your answer is on the same side of the row mean as the cell you were given, you have made an arithmetic slip.

The habit: treat every printed margin as an equation, not as decoration.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.38.0 is the other cell in that row, longhand notes at a fast pace. The row mean lies between the two cells.
c.41.0 is the row mean itself. The missing cell has to sit as far above it as 38.0 sits below it.
d.42.0 is the cell below it in the same column, laptop notes at a slow pace — right column, wrong row.
🏷️ Missing cell = 2 × row mean − the other cell. Then check the grand mean.

Question 14

⚖️ What it does NOT mean

Reporting a factor whose main effect is zero

Novotný’s interaction is significant (F = 50.00, P < .0001) while the main effect of time pressure is not (F = 0.00). What she may report about time pressure is:
Novotný’s plot of the six cell means · 8 participants per cell
  • aits effect is too small to be worth reporting
  • bits effect cannot be read while F equals zero
  • cit matters, but oppositely in the two strategies
  • dit has no effect on decision accuracy at all
🔎 What it is really asking

A main effect of zero and a huge interaction. Which of them describes the participants?

🧭 Which type of question this is

What it does NOT mean: a zero main effect alongside an interaction.

🛠️ The procedure

A main effect is an average over the other factor. When the interaction is significant, that average can describe nobody in the study, and the honest report is the simple effects — the effect of the factor at each level of the other.

🧮 The working
What the margins say: 70, 70, 70. Time pressure makes no difference on average, and F = 0.00 is the arithmetic of that.

What the cells say:
  • Deliberate strategy: 84 → 74 → 64. Pressure costs 20 points.
  • Intuitive strategy: 56 → 66 → 76. Pressure gains 20 points.

Average +20 and −20 and you get 0. That zero is a true statement about the average and a false statement about every participant in the study.

So the write-up is: "the effect of time pressure reverses between the two strategies", followed by the two simple effects. Not "time pressure had no effect".

And the decision: read the interaction first, always. If it is significant, describe each factor within the levels of the other instead of averaging over them.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Too small is not the issue. Each simple effect is 20 points — they are large, and they cancel in the average.
b.An F of exactly zero is perfectly readable. It says the three marginal means are identical, which they are, at 70 apiece.
d."No effect at all" is what the flat margin says and what the cells flatly contradict: 20 points down for one strategy, 20 up for the other.
🏷️ Zero main effect ≠ no effect. Check the cells before you believe a margin.

Question 15

⚖️ What it does NOT mean

What a table of F values licenses

Eichler has her output in front of her but no cell means. It gives F = 12.00 for study strategy (P = .0001), F = 4.00 for session timing (P = .052) and F = 1.33 for the interaction (P = .275). She may conclude that:
Two-factor ANOVA · words recalled · 8 participants per cell
SourceSSdfMSF
Study strategy (A)2882144.0012.00
Session timing (B)48148.004.00
A × B interaction32216.001.33
Error5044212.00
Total87247
  • aself-testing produced the highest mean recall score
  • bsession timing made no difference to recall at all
  • cstrategy matters at one session timing but not both
  • dthe three strategies do not all give the same mean
🔎 What it is really asking

Three P-values, and only one of them supports a sentence. Which sentence?

🧭 Which type of question this is

What it does NOT mean: the reach of a significant F.

🛠️ The procedure

A significant F says the means for that factor are not all equal. It carries no direction, no named pair and no pattern — squaring the deviations throws all of that away. A non-significant F is a failure to detect, not a finding of no effect.

🧮 The working
Strategy: P = .0001, so reject H₀. H₀ was "the three strategy means are equal", so the conclusion is that they are not all equal. Stop there.

Three sentences the output cannot support:
• Which strategy is best. F = 12.00 would be identical if the three means were in the reverse order. With no cell means on the page, direction is simply not available.
• That timing does nothing. P = .052 is a near miss at 8 per cell. "We did not detect a difference" and "there is no difference" are different claims, and only the first is hers.
• That strategy works at one timing only. That is a claim about the interaction, and its P of .275 gives no evidence for it.

Say it to a friend: "the strategies are not all the same; I cannot yet say which is best, and timing came close without getting there."

And the habit: before writing a conclusion, ask what would have to be on the page to support it — a cell mean, a pairwise test, an interaction. If it is not there, the sentence does not go in.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Naming a highest strategy needs the cell means. An F squares the deviations and keeps no direction at all.
b.Timing’s P of .052 is a failure to reach significance, not evidence that timing makes no difference.
c."At one timing but not both" is a claim about the interaction, whose F of 1.33 gives P = .275.
🏷️ Significant F = not all equal. Nothing about which, how much or which way.

Question 1

🧩 Reading the design

Why the crossing is worth keeping

Consumer psychologist Marrero shows each of 80 shoppers one of four label designs on a shelf laid out in one of two ways, and times how long they take to choose. Her colleague Boersma calls the study one factor with eight conditions; Marrero calls it a 4 × 2 crossing. Marrero wants to know whether the best label depends on the layout. The description that can answer her is:
  • aMarrero’s — eight conditions would need eight F tests
  • bneither — the question needs a third factor in the design
  • cMarrero’s — only a crossing separates the interaction
  • dBoersma’s — eight conditions cover every combination
🔎 What it is really asking

Which way of describing the same 80 shoppers keeps her question alive?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading the design: what the crossing adds.

🛠️ The procedure

Both descriptions contain the same eight groups of shoppers. Only the crossed one records which label and which layout each group had, so only it can ask whether the two depend on each other.

🧮 The working
The eight groups are the same either way: 4 × 2 = 8 cells, and 80 ⁄ 8 = 10 shoppers in each.

What differs is what the analysis is allowed to ask.

One factor, eight conditions. A single F statistic on ab − 1 = 7 df. It can say "these eight groups are not all alike" and nothing more. It cannot separate the label effect from the layout effect, because a single factor has no idea that condition 3 and condition 7 share a label.

Crossed, 4 × 2. Three F tests, on 3 df for label, 1 df for layout and 3 df for the interaction, all sharing an error row of 80 − 8 = 72 df. Those same 7 df, spent in three named pieces instead of one anonymous lump — and the third piece is her question.

The habit: "does A depend on B" is only answerable if the analysis knows which A and which B every participant had. Keep the crossing in the description and it does.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Eight conditions treated as one factor give one F test, not eight. The number of F tests is not what separates the two descriptions — the crossing is.
b.No third factor is needed. "Does the best label depend on the layout" is a question about two factors, and a 4 × 2 crossing already contains it in full.
d.Boersma’s eight conditions hold the same eighty shoppers, but one factor gives one F statistic on 7 degrees of freedom, with nothing in it that distinguishes a label effect from a layout effect.
🏷️ One factor with ab conditions, or a crossing: only the crossing has an interaction.

Question 2

🧩 Reading the design

What happens when a factor is dropped

Health psychologist Abendroth crosses three relaxation scripts with two room temperatures, 11 adults in every combination, and scores reported calm. A reviewer tells her to drop room temperature and analyse the three scripts on their own. The effect on her analysis is that:
  • athe temperature variation moves into the error term
  • bthe script sums of squares are recomputed from scratch
  • cthe F statistic for script is left exactly as it was
  • dthe interaction is tested on fewer degrees of freedom
🔎 What it is really asking

If a factor is taken out of the analysis, where does the variation it held go?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Reading the design: what a factor is doing in the table.

🛠️ The procedure

A one-way analysis has only two places to put variation: the factor it keeps, and error. Everything the dropped factor and the interaction were explaining is therefore pooled into error.

🧮 The working
Her crossed table has four rows: script 2 df, temperature 1 df, the interaction 2 df, and error 66 − 6 = 60 df.

Drop temperature and two rows are left: script on 2 df, and error on 66 − 3 = 63 df. Three more error degrees of freedom — and the error sum of squares is now SS temperature + SS interaction + SS error, because nothing else is left to hold them.

With equal cell sizes the script sum of squares is the same number in both analyses. So the numerator of her F stands still while the denominator takes on extra variation, and her F for script falls — unless temperature and the interaction were explaining almost nothing, in which case it barely moves.

And the interaction is simply gone. There is no second factor left for script to interact with, so the question the design was built to answer is no longer on the table.

The habit: variation does not vanish when a row is removed. Find out which row inherits it.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.With equal cell sizes the script sum of squares comes out identical in the two analyses. It is the error row that is rebuilt, not the script row.
c.The F for script almost always falls. Its numerator does not move, and the error mean square underneath it has taken on the variation temperature and the interaction used to hold.
d.The interaction is not tested at all once a factor is dropped — there is no second factor left to interact with. Losing that test is the whole cost of the advice.
🏷️ Drop a factor and its variation joins the error. Nothing disappears.

Question 3

🔢 Degrees of freedom

Choosing a design from a printed df column

Educational psychologist Elzinga reports the degrees-of-freedom column below and nothing else. The design behind it is:
All that survives of Elzinga’s output: the degrees-of-freedom column
Sourcedf
Factor A2
Factor B2
A × B interaction4
Error63
Total71
  • a3 × 3 with 7 participants per cell
  • b2 × 5 with 8 participants per cell
  • c4 × 2 with 9 participants per cell
  • d3 × 3 with 8 participants per cell
🔎 What it is really asking

Four candidate designs, and the winner has to match every row, not one.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Degrees of freedom: reading the design out of the table.

🛠️ The procedure

Five rules, all at once. a = df A + 1, b = df B + 1, df A × B = df A × df B, df error = N − ab and Total = N − 1. Test a candidate against the lot before you accept it.

🧮 The working
Build each candidate’s whole column and compare:

  3 × 3, n = 8: A 2, B 2, A × B 4, N = 72, error 72 − 9 = 63, total 71 ✓ every row
  3 × 3, n = 7: A 2, B 2, A × B 4 — the first three rows exactly right, then N = 63 gives error 63 − 9 = 54 and total 62 ✗
  2 × 5, n = 8: interaction 1 × 4 = 4, which matches — but A would be 1 and B 4, and the error row 80 − 10 = 70 ✗
  4 × 2, n = 9: N = 72, so the total of 71 matches — but A 3, B 1, interaction 3 and error 72 − 8 = 64 ✗

Look at how the three losers fail. One matches the effect rows and misses the error row. One matches the interaction and misses the main effects. One matches the Total and misses everything else. Each is right about a different single row.

The habit: a df column is the design written in code, and a candidate has to decode all of it. Stopping at the first row that agrees is how these items are lost.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.3 × 3 with 7 per cell matches the first three rows exactly and then fails: 63 participants over 9 cells leave 63 − 9 = 54 error degrees of freedom, not 63.
b.2 × 5 with 8 per cell does give the printed interaction df of 1 × 4 = 4, and the wrong main effects with it — df A would be 1 and df B 4, not 2 and 2.
c.4 × 2 with 9 per cell lands on the printed Total of 71, because it also has 72 participants. Its main-effect df are 3 and 1 and its interaction df is 3.
🏷️ A candidate design has to satisfy every row of the df column at once.

Question 4

🔢 Degrees of freedom

What adding a level does to the column

Cognitive psychologist Fiorelli has run a 2 × 3 design with 10 participants per cell. She now adds a fourth level to the second factor, still filling every combination with 10. Her interaction and error degrees of freedom become:
  • a7 and 72
  • b3 and 72
  • c2 and 72
  • d3 and 54
🔎 What it is really asking

Recompute both numbers for the enlarged design — neither survives untouched.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Degrees of freedom: how the column responds to a bigger design.

🛠️ The procedure

df A × B = (a − 1)(b − 1) and df error = N − ab. A new level changes b, which changes the number of cells, which changes N as well — so both figures move.

🧮 The working
Before: 2 × 3 = 6 cells and N = 60. Interaction (2 − 1)(3 − 1) = 2, error 60 − 6 = 54.

After: 2 × 4 = 8 cells, and 8 × 10 = 80 participants.
  Interaction: (2 − 1)(4 − 1) = 1 × 3 = 3
  Error: 80 − 8 = 72

Check the whole column: 1 + 3 + 3 + 72 = 79 = N − 1 = 80 − 1 ✓

What the new level cost her. Twenty more participants, and in exchange one more interaction degree of freedom and eighteen more error degrees of freedom. The extra error df lower the bar slightly; the extra interaction df raise it, because a wider interaction is being asked to show itself.

The habit: when the design changes, recompute the column from a, b and n. Never patch one row of an old column and leave the rest.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.7 and 72 uses ab − 1 = 8 − 1, the df the eight cells would have as a single factor. That is the three effects added together, not the interaction.
c.2 and 72 keeps the old interaction df. Adding a level takes df B from 2 to 3, and the interaction is df A multiplied by that.
d.3 and 54 keeps the old error df. Twenty more participants arrive with the two new cells, so the error row grows from 54 to 72.
🏷️ Add a level and the cells, N, the interaction df and the error df all move.
