Question 5

🔢 Degrees of freedom

Recovering the number of cells

Clinical psychologist Guzmán’s output has lost its three effect rows in printing. From what survives, the number of cells in her design, as a whole number, is:
Guzmán’s output with the three effect rows lost in printing
Sourcedf
Factor A?
Factor B?
A × B interaction?
Error60
Total71
  • a13
  • b72
  • c12
  • d11
🔎 What it is really asking

Two degrees of freedom, with the number of cells sitting in the gap between them.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Degrees of freedom: recovering the design from two rows.

🛠️ The procedure

Total df = N − 1 hands you N. Then df error = N − ab rearranges to ab = N − df error. Two subtractions, in that order.

🧮 The working
Step one — the number of observations:
  N = Total df + 1 = 71 + 1 = 72

Step two — the number of cells:
  ab = N − df error = 72 − 60 = 12

Check it from the other side. The three effect rows must share 71 − 60 = 11 df, and the three effects of any design always add to ab − 1. With ab = 12 that is 11 ✓

And the design falls out as a bonus: 12 cells of 72 ⁄ 12 = 6 participants each. (Which 12 cells is not recoverable — 3 × 4, 4 × 3, 2 × 6 and 6 × 2 all have twelve, and only the main-effect df would tell them apart.)

The habit: the error row and the Total row between them hold the number of cells. It is the single most useful thing to read off a half-printed table.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.13 adds one where the rule subtracts. The "+ 1" belongs to N = Total df + 1, and it has already been spent getting to 72.
b.72 is N, the number of observations. Dividing it by the 12 cells gives the 6 participants who sit in each one.
d.11 is Total df minus error df, which is the three effect rows added together. That always comes to ab − 1, one short of the number of cells.
🏷️ ab = N − df error, and N = Total df + 1.

Question 6

🧱 Completing the table

Finding the entry that does not follow

Sport psychologist Halkias’s output is printed below. Exactly one entry in it does not follow from the others. It is:
Halkias’s output as printed · free-throw accuracy · 5 players per cell
SourceSSdfMSF
Warm-up (A)120260.004.00
Crowd noise (B)90330.002.00
A × B interaction180630.003.00
Error7204815.00
Total111059
  • athe F for the interaction
  • bthe MS for the interaction
  • cthe MS for the error row
  • dthe SS for the Total row
🔎 What it is really asking

Which single number cannot be rebuilt from the numbers around it?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Completing the table: checking a printed table for consistency.

🛠️ The procedure

Four rules hold in every table, and each one is a one-line check. The SS column adds, the df column adds, each MS = SS ⁄ df for its own row, and every F = MS ⁄ MS error. Run them in that order.

🧮 The working
The SS column: 120 + 90 + 180 + 720 = 1110 ✓ as printed.

The df column: 2 + 3 + 6 + 48 = 59 ✓ as printed. And the design behind it is 3 × 4 with 5 per cell: a = 3, b = 4, 12 cells, N = 60, error 60 − 12 = 48 ✓

The mean squares, row by row:
  120 ⁄ 2 = 60.00 ✓    90 ⁄ 3 = 30.00 ✓    180 ⁄ 6 = 30.00 ✓    720 ⁄ 48 = 15.00 ✓

The F values:
  60.00 ⁄ 15.00 = 4.00 ✓
  30.00 ⁄ 15.00 = 2.00 ✓
  30.00 ⁄ 15.00 = 2.00 — and the table prints 3.00 ✗

Why it cannot be any of the others. The 15.00 underneath is confirmed twice over by the two F values that do check out. The interaction mean square of 30.00 is forced by its own SS and df, and raising it to 45.00 to justify an F of 3.00 would put 270 in the SS column and stop the column adding. The Total SS is exactly the four rows above it. Only the F is free to be wrong.

And it matters: on (6, 48) the 5% critical value is 2.2946. The printed 3.00 clears it and the real 2.00 (P = .084) does not, so the misprint changes the verdict on the interaction.

The habit: four checks, one line each, before you believe a printed table.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.The interaction mean square is 180 ⁄ 6 = 30.00, exactly as printed. Changing it to fit an F of 3.00 would need a sum of squares of 270, and the SS column would stop adding to 1110.
c.The error mean square is 720 ⁄ 48 = 15.00, and the two F values that do work — 4.00 and 2.00 — both divide by it correctly. It is the best-confirmed number on the page.
d.The Total sum of squares is exactly 120 + 90 + 180 + 720 = 1110. The column adds, so the total is not the entry at fault.
🏷️ SS adds, df adds, MS = SS ⁄ df, F = MS ⁄ MS error. Four checks, one line each.

Question 7

🧱 Completing the table

Recovering the error mean square from an F

Educational psychologist Rautio crosses three marking schemes with two feedback timings, 9 students per cell. Her error row has been lost apart from its degrees of freedom. The error mean square, to two decimal places, is:
Rautio’s table with the error row, two F values and the SS total removed
SourceSSdfMSF
Marking scheme (A)3602180.0011.25
Feedback timing (B)96196.00?
A × B interaction160280.00?
Error?48?
Total?53
  • a7.50
  • b16.00
  • c32.00
  • d3.75
🔎 What it is really asking

An F that is printed can be run backwards to the denominator underneath it.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Completing the table: working backwards from a printed F.

🛠️ The procedure

Forwards, F = MS effect ⁄ MS error. Rearranged, MS error = MS effect ⁄ F. Use the one row where both the mean square and the F are printed.

🧮 The working
The marking-scheme row is the only row with both: MS = 180.00 and F = 11.25.

MS error = 180.00 ⁄ 11.25 = 16.00

Now the table closes, and every closure is a check:
  SS error = 16.00 × 48 = 768, so SS total = 360 + 96 + 160 + 768 = 1384
  F for timing = 96.00 ⁄ 16.00 = 6.00
  F for the interaction = 80.00 ⁄ 16.00 = 5.00
Both come out as ordinary-looking F values, which is a sign the 16.00 is the right denominator rather than a slip.

The df agree too: 2 + 1 + 2 + 48 = 53 = N − 1 = 54 − 1 ✓

And the decision: on (2, 48) the 5% critical value is 3.1907, so 11.25 is far past it, P = .0001. The three marking schemes do not all produce the same mean.

The habit: before running anything backwards, look along the rows for one that has two of the three quantities printed. That is the row that will give you the third.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.7.50 is 360 ⁄ 48, the effect’s sum of squares over the error df. That mixes two rows together and leaves the printed F out of the calculation altogether.
c.32.00 is 360 ⁄ 11.25, running the F backwards from the sum of squares instead of the mean square. An F is a ratio of mean squares at both ends.
d.3.75 is 180 ⁄ 48, the effect mean square over the error df. Degrees of freedom turn a sum of squares into a mean square; they are never the denominator of an F.
🏷️ MS error = MS effect ⁄ F. Pick the row where both are printed.

Question 8

🧱 Completing the table

Matching a table to a written conclusion

Social psychologist Kaltenbach’s discussion reads: "Neither the reward nor the task mattered on its own, but the right pairing of the two mattered a great deal." The pattern of sums of squares behind that sentence is:
  • alarge for both main effects, near-zero for the interaction
  • blarge in all three of the effect rows of her table
  • cnear-zero in all three of the effect rows of her table
  • dnear-zero for both main effects, large for the interaction
🔎 What it is really asking

Translate a sentence of prose into the three effect rows of a table.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Completing the table: reading a table off a conclusion.

🛠️ The procedure

Each clause maps onto one row. "Not on its own" is a main effect near zero. "The right pairing" is the interaction, and it has to be the large row.

🧮 The working
Take the sentence in pieces.

"Neither the reward ... mattered on its own" — a main effect is what a factor does averaged over the other one. If that is nothing, the reward margins barely move, so SS for reward is near zero.

"nor the task ... on its own" — the same again for the task margins.

"the right pairing ... mattered a great deal" — the cells sit a long way from what two flat margins would predict, and that distance is exactly what the interaction sum of squares measures. It has to be large.

So two near-empty effect rows and one big one — and a plot of the cells with lines that cross, since crossing is what flat margins plus a real pairing look like.

What her sentence cannot be telling you, and what a reader should ask for next: which pairing is the right one. That is in the cell means, not in any sum of squares, because squaring throws the direction away.

The habit: read a results sentence clause by clause and put each clause in a row. If two clauses land in the same row, one of them is not about this table.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Two large main effects with no interaction is the additive case — each factor shifts the scores on its own, which is the exact opposite of "neither mattered on its own".
b.All three rows large would mean both factors matter in their own right and depend on each other. Her first clause rules out the first half of that.
c.All three rows near zero describes a study in which nothing happened at all. Her last clause says that something mattered a great deal.
🏷️ “On its own” = a main effect. “The right pairing” = the interaction.

Question 9

📈 Interaction plots

Predicting the shape of a plot

Developmental psychologist Nordby measures reading fluency in two age groups at three print sizes, 10 children per cell. Plotted with print size along the bottom and one line per age group, her cell means would appear as:
Mean reading fluency · 10 children per cell · Nordby’s study
Large printMedium printSmall printRow mean
Nine-year-olds88.080.072.080.0
Seven-year-olds64.068.072.068.0
  • atwo lines converging until they meet at the right
  • btwo parallel lines, both sloping downwards
  • ctwo lines crossing between the middle and the right
  • dtwo lines diverging as they move to the right
🔎 What it is really asking

Turn six printed means into the shape a plot of them would have.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Interaction plots: from the cell means to the picture.

🛠️ The procedure

Subtract the two lines at each x and read the sequence of gaps. A constant gap is parallel, a shrinking gap is converging, a gap that passes through zero and out the other side is crossing, and a growing gap is diverging.

🧮 The working
The gap between the two age groups at each print size:

  Large print:  88.0 − 64.0 = 24
  Medium print: 80.0 − 68.0 = 12
  Small print:  72.0 − 72.0 = 0

The gap shrinks steadily to nothing and stops there. The lines meet at the right-hand edge and do not come out the other side, so they converge rather than cross.

Read the margins while you are here. Row means 80.0 and 68.0, so a main effect of age group. Column means 76.0, 74.0 and 72.0 — a very weak one of print size. With a within-cell SD of 6.0 her output gives F = 60.00 on (1, 54) for group, F = 2.22 on (2, 54) for print size with P = .118, and F = 20.00 on (2, 54) for the interaction.

The surprise worth keeping. Both lines slope hard, and print size is still the weakest thing in the study. The nine-year-olds fall 16 points across the three sizes and the seven-year-olds rise 8, so the column means — the average of the two — barely move. A main effect is an average, and averages hide opposites.

The habit: gaps first for the shape, margins second for the main effects. Two readings, two different questions.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Parallel lines would need the same gap at every print size. These gaps are 24, 12 and 0, which is the one thing parallel rules out.
c.Crossing needs the gap to pass through zero and come out the other side, so that the lines swap over. Here it reaches zero at the last print size and the lines stop.
d.Diverging is the gap growing from left to right. This gap shrinks, from 24 points down to none at all.
🏷️ Subtract the lines at each x. The sequence of gaps names the shape.

Question 10

📈 Interaction plots

Checking a sentence against the figure

Motivation researcher Radulescu plots mean effort for two instruction styles across three practice sessions, 12 participants per cell. Her results section says the gap between the two styles widens as practice goes on. Set against the plot, what is wrong is:
Radulescu’s plot of the six cell means · 12 per cell
  • athe sentence — the gap narrows instead of widening
  • bthe plot — parallel lines cannot carry a main effect
  • cthe sentence — the gap is 14 points at every session
  • dthe plot — a widening gap is drawn as crossing lines
🔎 What it is really asking

The figure and the sentence disagree. Which is wrong, and what gives it away?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Interaction plots: a write-up tested against the figure.

🛠️ The procedure

A claim about a widening gap is a claim about an interaction. There is only one way to test it: subtract the two lines at each x and look at the differences.

🧮 The working
The gaps, session by session:

  Session 1: 60.0 − 46.0 = 14
  Session 2: 68.0 − 54.0 = 14
  Session 3: 76.0 − 62.0 = 14

The same every time. The lines are exactly parallel, the interaction sum of squares is exactly zero, and its F is 0.00. Her sentence describes something that is not in her figure.

The plot is fine, and there are two real effects in it. Row means 68.0 and 54.0, so a main effect of style. Column means 53.0, 61.0 and 69.0, so a main effect of session. Both lines climb 16 points from the first session to the last, and they climb together.

What probably happened. Both lines rise steeply, so "the effect grows with practice" feels right. It describes the scores growing, not the gap growing. Those are two different sentences and only one of them is about an interaction.

Say it to a friend: "both got better by the same amount — the distance between them never changed."

The habit: never judge a gap by eye from two rising lines. Subtract them at each x and read the three numbers.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The gap does not narrow either. It is 14 points at the first session, 14 at the second and 14 at the third — unchanged in both directions.
b.Parallel lines carry main effects perfectly well. These two sit 14 points apart throughout, which is a main effect of style, and both slope, which is one of session.
d.The plot is drawn from her own cell means and matches them exactly. Crossing is only one of the shapes an interaction can take, and a widening gap would not need it.
🏷️ A “widening gap” is a claim about the interaction. Subtract the lines to test it.

Question 11

📈 Interaction plots

Where in the plot the interaction lives

Memory researcher Sjöberg plots words recalled under two rehearsal methods across three test sessions, 9 participants per cell. If she were to analyse only the first two sessions, the effect on her interaction would be that:
Sjöberg’s plot of the six cell means · 9 per cell
  • athe interaction is unchanged by the loss
  • bthe interaction doubles in size
  • cboth main effects vanish instead
  • dthe interaction vanishes from the output
🔎 What it is really asking

Which levels is the change in the gap happening between?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Interaction plots: what dropping a level does.

🛠️ The procedure

An interaction is a change in the gap between the lines. Read the gap at every level and you can see which levels the change happens between — and therefore which levels are carrying the interaction.

🧮 The working
The gaps, session by session:

  Session 1: 60.0 − 52.0 = 8
  Session 2: 66.0 − 58.0 = 8
  Session 3: 72.0 − 46.0 = 26

Identical at the first two sessions, then a jump. All of the change in the gap happens between session 2 and session 3, so all of the interaction is carried by the third session.

Keep only sessions 1 and 2 and the lines are 8 points apart at both — exactly parallel. SS for the interaction becomes exactly zero and its F is 0.00.

The main effects survive the cut. On the two kept sessions the row means are 63.0 and 55.0 and the column means 56.0 and 62.0, giving SS 576 for method and SS 324 for session. Both are still there.

For contrast, the full three-session analysis gives SS 2646 for method, SS 324 for session and SS 972 for the interaction. With a within-cell SD of 6.0 that is F = 13.50 on (2, 48) for the interaction, P = .00002 — and it all comes from one level.

The habit: an interaction is not spread evenly across the levels. Read the gaps one at a time and the plot tells you which level is doing the work.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Unchanged is the one thing it cannot be. The change in the gap happens entirely between the second session and the third, and the third is the level being removed.
b.Nothing doubles. Dropping the level that carries the whole change in the gap leaves a constant gap of 8 points, which is no interaction at all.
c.Both main effects survive on the two kept sessions. The methods still differ by 8 points throughout, and the two sessions still differ, 56.0 against 62.0.
🏷️ Read the gaps level by level. An interaction can live in one level only.

Question 12

▦ Cell means and margins

Working backwards from both margins

Occupational psychologist Holmgren reports the margins of her 2 × 2 study but not the four cell means. Reading across the top row and then the bottom row, the set of cell means below that is consistent with her margins is:
Holmgren’s margins only · job satisfaction · 15 employees per cell
Flexible hoursFixed hoursRow mean
Open-plan office??70.0
Private office??58.0
Column mean68.060.064.0
  • a74.0, 62.0, 66.0, 54.0
  • b74.0, 66.0, 62.0, 54.0
  • c70.0, 70.0, 58.0, 58.0
  • d68.0, 60.0, 68.0, 60.0
🔎 What it is really asking

Four candidate tables, each of which has to reproduce both margins, not one.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Cell means and margins: working backwards from the margins.

🛠️ The procedure

With equal cell sizes every margin is the plain average of the cells it covers. So check a candidate twice: average its two rows, then average its two columns.

🧮 The working
Her margins: rows 70.0 and 58.0, columns 68.0 and 60.0, grand mean 64.0.

Test 74.0, 66.0, 62.0, 54.0:
  rows    (74.0 + 66.0) ⁄ 2 = 70.0 ✓    (62.0 + 54.0) ⁄ 2 = 58.0 ✓
  columns (74.0 + 62.0) ⁄ 2 = 68.0 ✓    (66.0 + 54.0) ⁄ 2 = 60.0 ✓

All four margins reproduced, so this is the set among the four.

Now the part worth keeping, because it is the whole theme in one line. The margins of a 2 × 2 do not pin the cells down. Try 76.0, 64.0, 60.0, 56.0: its rows are 70.0 and 58.0 and its columns 68.0 and 60.0 — the same margins, a different table. One degree of freedom is always left over, and that degree of freedom is the interaction.

The set above happens to be the additive one: every cell is the grand mean plus its row deviation plus its column deviation (74.0 = 64.0 + 6.0 + 4.0), so its interaction is exactly zero. The 76.0 version has the same main effects and a real interaction.

So a results section that prints only margins has not told you what happened. It has given you the two main effects and nothing at all about whether the factors depend on each other.

The habit: check a candidate against every margin, and never assume the margins were enough.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.74.0, 62.0, 66.0, 54.0 has the four right numbers in the wrong places. Its rows average to 68.0 and 60.0 and its columns to 70.0 and 58.0 — the two margins swapped.
c.70.0, 70.0, 58.0, 58.0 reproduces the two row means and then fails on the columns: both column averages come out at 64.0 rather than 68.0 and 60.0.
d.68.0, 60.0, 68.0, 60.0 reproduces the two column means and fails on the rows: both row averages come out at 64.0 rather than 70.0 and 58.0.
🏷️ Equal n: every margin is a plain average. Check the rows AND the columns.

Question 13

▦ Cell means and margins

A margin when the cells are unequal

Clinical psychologist Urbanek crosses two session formats with two client age bands, but her cells are not equally filled. The mean distress score of all 25 clients who received the brief format, to one decimal place, is:
Mean distress score at discharge · Urbanek’s four cells, unequally filled
Brief formatExtended format
Under 4060.0 (n = 20)66.0 (n = 18)
40 and over80.0 (n = 5)74.0 (n = 7)
  • a64.0
  • b70.0
  • c60.0
  • d80.0
🔎 What it is really asking

The mean of a named group of 25 people — so each of the 25 counts once.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Cell means and margins: unequal cell sizes.

🛠️ The procedure

A margin is the mean of the people in it, so each cell is weighted by its own n: (n₁m₁ + n₂m₂) ⁄ (n₁ + n₂). The plain average of the two cell means is right only when the two cells are the same size.

🧮 The working
The brief-format column holds 20 clients averaging 60.0 and 5 clients averaging 80.0.

  (20 × 60.0) + (5 × 80.0) = 1200 + 400 = 1600
  1600 ⁄ 25 = 64.0

The 20 pull four times as hard as the 5, so the answer sits close to 60.0 rather than halfway between the two cells.

Now look at what the plain average would have done. (60.0 + 80.0) ⁄ 2 = 70.0 for the brief format — and (66.0 + 74.0) ⁄ 2 = 70.0 for the extended format as well. Unweighted, the two formats look identical. Weighted, they are 64.0 and (18 × 66.0 + 7 × 74.0) ⁄ 25 = 68.2, a gap of 4.2 points. The unweighted average has hidden the whole main effect.

Why equal cells are worth designing for. When every cell holds the same n the two kinds of margin agree, and a main effect means one unambiguous thing. The moment the cells are unequal they part company, and a reader has to be told which margin is being reported.

The habit: count the people in the group the stem names. If the counts differ, weight before you average.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.70.0 is the plain average of 60.0 and 80.0, which would be right only if the two cells held the same number of clients. One holds 20 and the other holds 5.
c.60.0 is the younger clients’ own cell mean. It is close to the answer because that cell is four times the size of the other, but it leaves five clients out entirely.
d.80.0 is the older clients’ cell mean — five people out of the twenty-five. Treating their cell as equal in weight to the other is exactly what produces the 70.0.
🏷️ Unequal cells → weight each cell mean by its own n before averaging.

Question 14

⚖️ What it does NOT mean

The claim an F cannot support

Health psychologist Vranesic’s results section reads: "The interaction was not significant, F(2, 54) = 1.80, p = .18. The main effect of script was significant, F(1, 54) = 9.00, p = .004, so the structured script produced higher mean adherence than the open script." The part her figures cannot support is:
  • asharing one error term across the two tests
  • breporting both effects from the same data set
  • cnaming which script produced the higher mean
  • dcalling the interaction non-significant at .18
🔎 What it is really asking

Three of the four things she does are ordinary. One needs a number she has not printed.

🧭 Which type of question this is

What it does NOT mean: direction and the F statistic.

🛠️ The procedure

An F statistic has no sign — the deviations are squared before they are summed. A significant F says the means are not all equal, and nothing about which is larger. Direction lives in the cell means, which are nowhere in her paragraph.

🧮 The working
Her F of 9.00 on (1, 54) does clear the 5% critical value of 4.0195, and P = .004. So the two scripts do not produce the same mean adherence. That much is hers.

Which script is higher is a separate statement, and the identical F of 9.00 would have come out of the two means the other way round. Nothing in a squared quantity remembers which way it pointed.

The repair is one line: print the means. "Adherence was higher under the structured script (M = 62.4) than the open script (M = 55.1), F(1, 54) = 9.00, p = .004." The means now carry the direction and the F does its own job, which is to say the gap is bigger than chance would produce.

The three things she gets right:
• P = .18 is above .05, and 1.80 on (2, 54) falls short of 3.1682 — a correctly reported non-significant interaction.
• Both tests divide by the same error mean square. That is how a factorial table works, and it is why 54 is the second df in both pairs.
• Two effects out of one data set is the point of the design, not a flaw in it.

Say it to a friend: "the F says they differ; only the means say which way."
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.All three F tests in a factorial table share the same error mean square, which is why 54 appears as the second degree of freedom in both of her pairs.
b.Testing two effects on one data set is what a factorial design is for. It is more economical than running two separate studies, not a problem with the write-up.
d.An interaction F of 1.80 on (2, 54) falls short of its 3.1682 critical value, and P = .18. Calling that non-significant at the 5% level is correct reporting.
🏷️ An F never names a direction. Print the means or do not claim one.

Question 15

⚖️ What it does NOT mean

What a non-significant interaction permits

A 2 × 3 study by Wierzbicki returns an interaction F of 2.10 on (2, 54), P = .13. He writes that the study has shown the two factors do not interact. His supervisor Ylönen says he has only failed to find an interaction. The reading that survives is:
  • aWierzbicki’s — P = .13 establishes additivity
  • bYlönen’s — the interaction F was built wrongly
  • cneither — the main effects settle the question
  • dYlönen’s — a null result is not proof of absence
🔎 What it is really asking

What does a P-value above .05 entitle you to say, and what does it not?

🧭 Which type of question this is

What it does NOT mean: a non-significant interaction.

🛠️ The procedure

A test can reject H₀ or fail to reject it. Failing to reject is not accepting: the data are compatible with no interaction, and also with a small or moderate one that this study was too small to see.

🧮 The working
His F of 2.10 on (2, 54) is below the 5% critical value of 3.1682, so H₀ — "the effect of one factor is the same at every level of the other" — is not rejected. P = .13.

What that permits. He may report the interaction as non-significant, and he may describe each main effect as a single averaged figure rather than level by level.

What it does not permit. "The two factors do not interact." His error df of 54 in a 2 × 3 design means N = 60, so 10 participants per cell — and with 10 per cell a real interaction of moderate size would quite often return a P of .13. His result does not tell "there is no interaction" apart from "there is one I could not detect".

The asymmetry in one line: a small P is evidence of an effect; a large P is an absence of evidence, which is not evidence of absence.

What would let him say more. An interval around the size of the interaction. If it is narrow and sits close to zero, he can fairly say an interaction of any practical size has been ruled out. A P-value of .13 on its own cannot do that, because it mixes the size of the effect and the size of the study into one number.

Say it to a friend: "I did not find one" — never "there is not one".
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.P = .13 is a failure to reject, not a demonstration of additivity. A test that cannot find an effect has not shown that the effect is absent.
b.There is nothing wrong with the F. 2.10 on (2, 54) is a perfectly ordinary interaction F; the disagreement is about what may be said after it, not how it was computed.
c.The main effects answer a different question altogether. Whether the two factors depend on each other is not settled by how large either of them is on its own.
🏷️ Not significant = not detected. Never “there is no effect”.

Question 1

🔁 Splitting the variation

Recognising a repeated-measures design

Addiction researcher Brennan measures a craving score in 16 participants at baseline, four weeks and eight weeks. The appropriate analysis is:
  • athree separate paired t tests
  • ba two-factor ANOVA with participant as a second factor of interest
  • ca repeated-measures ANOVA on 16 participants
  • da one-way ANOVA on 48 independent observations
🔎 What it is really asking

Are the 48 scores independent of one another?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Splitting the variation: identifying the design.

🛠️ The procedure

If the same people are measured more than once, the observations are not independent and the analysis must take the pairing into account. That is a repeated-measures ANOVA.

🧮 The working
There are 48 scores but only 16 people. A participant who craves heavily at baseline is likely to crave heavily at four weeks too — their three scores are tied together.

A one-way ANOVA would treat all 48 as independent, which is simply false, and would bundle the differences between people into the error term, where they inflate it enormously.

What repeated measures does instead: it pulls the between-person variation out first and sets it aside, leaving a much smaller error term built only from within-person inconsistency. For Brennan this is the difference between F = 10.00 and F = 2.50 on exactly the same three means.

The tell in an exam stem: "the same participants", "each participant", "before and after", "at three time points". Count the people and count the scores — if the scores outnumber the people, the design is repeated.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Three paired t tests would compare the time points two at a time, which raises the error rate across the family — the same problem ANOVA exists to solve.
b.Participant is handled as a blocking term, not as a second factor of interest. There is only one observation per participant per time point, so no interaction with participant can be separated from error.
d.A one-way ANOVA assumes 48 independent observations. There are 16 people, so the assumption fails and the error term is wrong.
🏷️ Scores outnumber people → repeated measures. Pull the person variation out.

Question 2

🔁 Splitting the variation

Where the variation goes

In Brennan’s table, the total variation of 1200 is split into which parts?
Repeated-measures ANOVA · craving score at three time points · 16 participants
SourceSSdfMSF
Between subjects90015
Condition120260.0010.00
Error (condition × subject)180306.00
Total120047
  • abetween subjects 900, condition 120 and error 180
  • bcondition 120 and error 1080
  • cbetween subjects 900 and within-subjects error 300
  • dcondition 120, time 900 and error 180
🔎 What it is really asking

Name the three boxes the total splits into.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Splitting the variation: the three-way split.

🛠️ The procedure

A repeated-measures ANOVA splits the total twice: first into between subjects and within subjects, then the within-subjects part into condition and error.

🧮 The working
Total 1200 splits as:

  Between subjects: 900 — people differ from each other. Set aside, and by convention not tested.
  Within subjects: 300 — how each person’s own scores move across the three time points. This splits again:
    Condition: 120 — movement shared by everybody, the effect being tested.
    Error: 180 — movement that differs from person to person.

Check: 900 + 120 + 180 = 1200 ✓ and 120 + 180 = 300 ✓

Read the proportions. 900 ⁄ 1200 = 75% of all the variation is simply that people differ. In an independent-groups design that 900 would sit in the error term. Here it is removed before the test, and the condition effect is judged against the 180 instead.

That removal is the entire point of the design.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Condition 120 with error 1080 is what you get if the between-subject variation is left in the error term — which is exactly the independent-groups analysis, and gives F = 2.50 instead of 10.00.
c.Between subjects 900 and error 300 stops one split too early. The 300 of within-person variation has to be divided into the condition effect and what is left.
d.Condition and time are the same factor here, counted twice. There is one within-subjects factor with three levels.
🏷️ Total → between subjects + within subjects; within → condition + error.

Question 3

🔁 Splitting the variation

What the person term is for

The between-subjects row of Brennan’s table has no F statistic. The reason is that:
Repeated-measures ANOVA · craving score at three time points · 16 participants
SourceSSdfMSF
Between subjects90015
Condition120260.0010.00
Error (condition × subject)180306.00
Total120047
  • aits mean square cannot be computed from the numbers in the table
  • bit has too few degrees of freedom to test
  • cit is already included in the condition row
  • dthe differences between participants are not what she is testing
🔎 What it is really asking

Why is the biggest row in the table not tested?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Splitting the variation: the role of the person term.

🛠️ The procedure

The between-subjects term is there to be removed, not tested. Isolating it is what shrinks the error term; nobody doubts that different people have different baseline craving.

🧮 The working
Its mean square is perfectly computable — 900 ⁄ 15 = 60.00 — and it would be large. That is not the obstacle.

The obstacle is that the question has no interest. Of course participants differ from one another; that is true of every sample ever collected. There is no hypothesis worth testing there.

Its value is structural. By giving the person differences a row of their own, they are kept out of the error term. Error falls from 1080 to 180, and the test of condition becomes far more sensitive.

The analogy worth carrying: it is a blocking variable. You are not studying the blocks — you are stopping them from adding noise to the comparison you do care about.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.It can be computed: 900 ⁄ 15 = 60.00. Many packages print it. Computability is not the issue.
b.15 degrees of freedom is plenty — more than the condition row’s 2. The number is not the problem.
c.It is kept strictly separate from the condition row. Mixing the two is precisely what the design is built to prevent.
🏷️ The person term is removed, not tested. That is what shrinks the error.

Question 4

🔢 Degrees of freedom

Degrees of freedom for the condition effect

The degrees of freedom for Brennan’s condition effect are:
The same table with five entries removed
SourceSSdfMSF
Between subjects900?
Condition120???
Error (condition × subject)?306.00
Total120047

  • b2
  • c3

🔎 What it is really asking

Count the measurement occasions, minus one.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Degrees of freedom: the condition row.

🛠️ The procedure

df condition = k − 1, where k is the number of times each person was measured. The number of participants does not come into it.

🧮 The working
k = 3 time points (baseline, four weeks, eight weeks).

df = 3 − 1 = 2

This is the same k − 1 rule as a one-way ANOVA — what changes in a repeated-measures design is the error df, not this one.

The full column, and it must add to 47:
  Between subjects: n − 1 = 15
  Condition: k − 1 = 2
  Error: (n − 1)(k − 1) = 15 × 2 = 30
  Total: nk − 1 = 48 − 1 = 47
  Check: 15 + 2 + 30 = 47 ✓
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.47 is the Total df, nk − 1.
c.3 is k, the number of time points, with no subtraction.
d.15 is n − 1, the between-subjects df. That row counts people; this one counts occasions.
🏷️ df condition = k − 1, occasions only. Never n.

Question 5

🔢 Degrees of freedom

Degrees of freedom for the error term

For Brennan’s 16 participants measured at 3 time points, the degrees of freedom for the error term are:
The same table with the error degrees of freedom removed
SourceSSdfMSF
Between subjects90015
Condition120260.0010.00
Error (condition × subject)180??
Total120047
  • a32
  • b15
  • c30
  • d45
🔎 What it is really asking

The two other df, multiplied.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Degrees of freedom: the error row.

🛠️ The procedure

df error = (n − 1)(k − 1) — the between-subjects df multiplied by the condition df. The error term is the condition × subject interaction, so its df multiply like any interaction’s.

🧮 The working
n = 16 participants, k = 3 occasions.

df error = (16 − 1)(3 − 1) = 15 × 2 = 30

MS error = 180 ⁄ 30 = 6.00, and that is the denominator of the F test: 60.00 ⁄ 6.00 = 10.00 on (2, 30).

Compare the independent-groups design. Three separate groups of 16 would give 48 − 3 = 45 error df — more df, which on its own helps. But its error mean square would be 24.00 instead of 6.00, because the person differences would still be in it. The repeated design trades a few degrees of freedom for a four-times-smaller error, and that is a trade worth making.

The multiplication is the signature of an interaction df, which is exactly what this term is.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.32 would be 48 − 16, subtracting the number of participants from the number of observations. The rule multiplies.
b.15 is n − 1, the between-subjects df on its own. The error df is that times k − 1.
d.45 is N − k, the error df of an independent-groups one-way ANOVA on 48 observations. It would be right if 48 different people had been measured once each.
🏷️ df error = (n − 1)(k − 1). It is an interaction df, so multiply.

Question 6

🔢 Degrees of freedom

Recovering the design from the df

A repeated-measures table shows 3 df for the condition effect and 36 for the error. The study had:
  • a13 participants measured 4 times
  • b12 participants measured 4 times
  • c13 participants measured 3 times
  • d36 participants measured 4 times
🔎 What it is really asking

Invert both rules, then check the product.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Degrees of freedom: reading the design out of the table.

🛠️ The procedure

k = df condition + 1, then n − 1 = df error ⁄ df condition, so n = that + 1.

🧮 The working
k − 1 = 3, so k = 4 occasions.

df error = (n − 1)(k − 1) = (n − 1) × 3 = 36, so n − 1 = 12 and n = 13 participants.

Check the whole column: between subjects 12, condition 3, error 36 — total 51, and nk − 1 = 13 × 4 − 1 = 51 ✓

Why bother. The df are the only place an exam printout states the design. Once you can read 13 people measured 4 times off a df column, questions about hypotheses, about sphericity, and about how many comparisons there are all become answerable.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.12 participants would give (12 − 1) × 3 = 33 error df, not 36. The 12 is n − 1, and n is one more.
c.3 occasions would make the condition df 2, not 3.
d.36 is the error df itself, not a number of participants.
🏷️ k = df condition + 1; n = df error ⁄ df condition + 1. Then check nk − 1.

🔎 What it is really asking

MS condition over MS error — and note which error.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The table: the F ratio.

🛠️ The procedure

F = MS condition ⁄ MS error, where the error is the condition × subject term — not the between-subjects row.

🧮 The working
MS condition = 120 ⁄ 2 = 60.00
MS error = 180 ⁄ 30 = 6.00

F = 60.00 ⁄ 6.00 = 10.00 on (2, 30) df.

The decision: the 5% critical value on (2, 30) is 3.3158. 10.00 is far past it, and P = .0005. Craving scores change across the three time points.

Which denominator, and why it matters so much. Divide by the between-subjects MS of 60.00 instead and F would be 1.00 — a complete non-result. The right error term is the one built from within-person inconsistency, because that is the only noise standing between the condition means and the conclusion.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.67 is 120 ⁄ 180, the sums of squares divided directly. Mean squares first.
b.2.50 is the F you get if the person variation is left in the error term — the independent-groups analysis of the same means. It is not significant, and it is the number this design exists to avoid.
c.3.32 is the critical value on (2, 30) at α = .05, not the statistic.
🏷️ F = MS condition ⁄ MS (condition × subject). Not the person row.

The condition SS as a share of the within-person total, not of everything.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The table: reading the sums of squares as shares.

The within-subjects variation is SS condition + SS error. The share explained by the condition is SS condition ⁄ (SS condition + SS error).

🧮 The working
Within-person total = 120 + 180 = 300.

In words: of all the movement in a person’s own craving score across the eight weeks, about 40% follows the common pattern that everyone shares, and 60% is each individual going their own way.

Why the denominator is 300 and not 1200. Of the 1200 total, 900 is simply that different people have different craving levels — that was removed before any test, and it has nothing to do with change over time. Including it would understate the effect badly: 120 ⁄ 1200 = 10%.

Match the denominator to the question. "Within participants" names the pool to divide by.

b.0.10 is 120 ⁄ 1200, dividing by the overall total. That answers a different question, and it folds in the person differences the design removed.
c.0.67 is 120 ⁄ 180, the condition SS over the error SS. The denominator has to be the within-person total of 300.
d.0.75 is 900 ⁄ 1200, the share of the total that is between-subject variation. Big, and not what was asked.

Question 10

🔧 Sphericity and the correction

What sphericity requires

The sphericity condition for Brennan’s repeated-measures ANOVA requires that:
Repeated-measures ANOVA · craving score at three time points · 16 participants
SourceSSdfMSF
Between subjects90015
Condition120260.0010.00
Error (condition × subject)180306.00
Total120047
  • athe 16 participants are a random sample
  • bthe three conditions are measured in a randomly counterbalanced order
  • cthe differences between each pair of conditions have equal variances
  • dthe craving scores at each time point have equal means
🔎 What it is really asking

Equal variances — but of what, exactly?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Sphericity: what the condition says.

🛠️ The procedure

Sphericity is the requirement that the variances of the differences between every pair of conditions are equal. It is the repeated-measures counterpart of the equal-spread condition.

🧮 The working
With three time points there are three pairwise differences: baseline − 4 weeks, baseline − 8 weeks, and 4 weeks − 8 weeks. Sphericity asks that these three sets of differences have equal variances.

Why it can fail in exactly this kind of study. Measurements taken close together in time usually agree more closely than measurements eight weeks apart, so the variance of the baseline − 8 week difference tends to be the largest of the three. Time-series designs break sphericity routinely.

What failure does: it makes the F test too liberal — the real P-value is larger than the one printed, so you reject H₀ more often than the stated 5%. That is why a correction exists.

With only two conditions there is just one difference, so sphericity cannot fail and no correction is ever needed.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Random sampling matters for generalising to a population, but it is not what sphericity is about.
b.Counterbalancing the order is good practice against carry-over effects. It is a design matter, not the sphericity condition.
d.Equal means across the time points is H₀ — the thing being tested. A condition checked beforehand can never be the hypothesis.
🏷️ Sphericity = equal variances of the pairwise DIFFERENCES.

Question 11

🔧 Sphericity and the correction

Applying the Greenhouse-Geisser correction

Brennan’s output reports ε = 0.80. The Greenhouse-Geisser corrected degrees of freedom for the condition effect are:
Repeated-measures ANOVA · craving score at three time points · 16 participants
SourceSSdfMSF
Between subjects90015
Condition120260.0010.00
Error (condition × subject)180306.00
Total120047
  • a2.0 and 30.0
  • b2.5 and 37.5
  • c1.6 and 30.0
  • d1.6 and 24.0
🔎 What it is really asking

Multiply both df by epsilon.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Sphericity: the correction.

🛠️ The procedure

Greenhouse-Geisser multiplies both degrees of freedom by ε. The F statistic itself is unchanged; only the df it is judged against move.

🧮 The working
Original df: 2 and 30.

Corrected: 2 × 0.80 = 1.6 and 30 × 0.80 = 24.0

Fractional df are entirely normal here — software interpolates in the F distribution.

What it does to the verdict. F stays at 10.00. The critical value rises from 3.3158 to 3.6542, and P rises from .0005 to .0013. Still comfortably significant — Brennan’s conclusion survives the correction, which is the best possible outcome of applying one.

Why the df shrink rather than the F. Fewer effective degrees of freedom means a higher bar, which compensates for the test being too liberal when sphericity fails. ε = 1 means perfect sphericity and no change at all; the further ε falls below 1, the bigger the penalty.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.2.0 and 30.0 are the uncorrected df. Applying the correction has to change them.
b.2.5 and 37.5 are the df divided by 0.80. The correction multiplies, so the df must get smaller, never larger.
c.1.6 and 30.0 corrects only the numerator. Both df are multiplied by ε.
🏷️ GG: multiply BOTH df by ε. F unchanged, the bar goes up.

Question 12

🔧 Sphericity and the correction

When a correction changes nothing that matters

After the Greenhouse-Geisser correction Brennan’s P-value moves from .0005 to .0013. She should report:
  • aneither, since sphericity was violated
  • bthe corrected test, which is still significant at 5%
  • cthe uncorrected test, since the correction changed little
  • dboth, and treat the result as inconclusive
🔎 What it is really asking

Which P-value belongs in the write-up when both are available?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Sphericity: what to report.

🛠️ The procedure

If sphericity is in doubt, report a corrected test and say which one — Greenhouse-Geisser when ε is well below 1, Huynh-Feldt when ε is high (conventionally above about .75). A result that survives a correction is the stronger result.

🧮 The working
P = .0013 is still far below .05, so the conclusion is unchanged: craving scores differ across the three time points.

Report the corrected figures — F = 10.00 on 1.6 and 24.0 df, P = .001 — and say that Greenhouse-Geisser was applied. That one sentence tells a reader the result is not an artefact of a violated condition.

Which correction, strictly: at ε = 0.80 many texts would prefer Huynh-Feldt, because Greenhouse-Geisser is conservative when ε is this high. Either way the choice is between corrections, not between correcting and not.

Why not the uncorrected one. "The correction changed little" is a judgement you can only make after looking at both, and choosing the more favourable of two P-values is not a defensible procedure even when the difference is small.

When it does matter: a correction can push a P-value from .04 to .07. Deciding in advance to report the corrected test is what stops that decision being made for you by the number itself.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.A violated condition is what the correction is for. It is a reason to correct, not a reason to abandon the analysis.
c.Choosing the uncorrected test because it is more favourable is the problem, not the solution — however small the difference turns out to be.
d."Inconclusive" misreads two P-values that agree. Both are well under .05; they point the same way.
🏷️ Sphericity in doubt → report the corrected test, and say you did.

Question 13

💪 What the pairing buys you

What the pairing buys you

Brennan’s three means, analysed as three independent groups of 16 instead, would give F = 2.50, P = .093. The reason the repeated-measures analysis gives F = 10.00 is that:
The same three means, analysed two ways
Analysed as…error SSerror dfMS errorFP
16 participants measured 3 times180306.0010.00.0005
3 independent groups of 1610804524.002.50.0934
  • athe person differences are removed from the error term
  • bthe repeated analysis has more degrees of freedom
  • cthe condition means are further apart when people are paired
  • drepeated measures uses a one-sided test
🔎 What it is really asking

Which part of the F ratio changed, and why?

🧭 Which type of question this is

What the pairing buys you: the mechanism.

🛠️ The procedure

Pairing does not change the condition means. It changes the error term: the variation between people is pulled out into its own row instead of sitting in the denominator.

🧮 The working
The numerator is identical in both analyses: MS condition = 60.00. The means are the means.

The denominator is not:
  Repeated measures: MS error = 180 ⁄ 30 = 6.00
  Independent groups: MS error = 1080 ⁄ 45 = 24.00

The 1080 is 900 + 180 — the person differences plus the within-person error, lumped together. Four times the error, so a quarter of the F: 2.50 against 10.00.

And the verdicts differ. P = .093 against P = .0005. Same three means, same 48 scores, opposite conclusions — the difference is entirely in what counts as noise.

The trade, stated plainly: you give up 15 error degrees of freedom (30 instead of 45) and you take out 900 units of variation. Almost always worth it.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.It has fewer degrees of freedom — 30 against 45. The gain comes in spite of that, not because of it.
c.The condition means are unchanged by how you analyse them. MS condition is 60.00 either way.
d.Every F test is one-tailed and non-directional. Nothing about sidedness differs between the two analyses.
🏷️ Pairing shrinks the DENOMINATOR. The means never move.

Question 14

💪 What the pairing buys you

The cost of a repeated-measures design

Alongside its gain in sensitivity, a repeated-measures design brings which specific risk?
  • aa loss of random assignment to the study
  • ba larger error term than independent groups
  • ccarry-over effects from one condition to the next
  • dunequal numbers of observations per condition
🔎 What it is really asking

What can go wrong precisely because the same people are measured twice?

🧭 Which type of question this is

What the pairing buys you: the cost side.

🛠️ The procedure

Measuring the same people repeatedly invites order and carry-over effects: practice, fatigue, boredom, or simply remembering the first measurement. The usual protection is counterbalancing the order.

🧮 The working
In Brennan’s design the three measurements are at fixed times, so order cannot be counterbalanced — but the risk is still there in other forms. Participants may become practised at the craving questionnaire, or may answer later rounds in the light of what they said the first time.

In designs where conditions can be ordered freely — three versions of a task, say — the fix is to vary the order across participants so that any practice or fatigue effect is spread evenly over the conditions instead of loading onto one.

The other costs, for completeness: fewer error degrees of freedom (30 against 45 here), the sphericity condition to worry about, and dropout — a participant who misses one session loses all their data from the analysis.

The balance: a four-times-smaller error term usually outweighs all of it, which is why the design is so widely used.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Random assignment is unaffected; in many repeated designs it is the order that is randomised, which is random assignment doing exactly its job.
b.The error term is smaller, not larger — 6.00 against 24.00 here. That is the whole reason for the design.
d.Each participant is measured once in every condition, so the numbers per condition are automatically equal — that is a feature of the design, not a risk.
🏷️ The cost is order and carry-over effects. Counterbalance where you can.

Question 15

💪 What the pairing buys you

Writing the conclusion

Brennan’s corrected test gives F = 10.00, P = .001 across baseline, four weeks and eight weeks. Her conclusion is that:
Repeated-measures ANOVA · craving score at three time points · 16 participants
SourceSSdfMSF
Between subjects90015
Condition120260.0010.00
Error (condition × subject)180306.00
Total120047
  • acraving fell steadily from baseline to eight weeks
  • bthe treatment caused craving to fall
  • ccraving at eight weeks was lower than at baseline
  • dmean craving changed across the three time points
🔎 What it is really asking

What does a significant omnibus F over three occasions establish?

🧭 Which type of question this is

What the pairing buys you: the reach of the conclusion.

🛠️ The procedure

A repeated-measures F is an omnibus test, exactly like a one-way F: it says the means are not all equal. It does not say which occasions differ, in what direction, or why.

🧮 The working
Rejecting H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ licenses one sentence: mean craving is not the same at all three time points.

Three readings it does not license:
• A direction or a pattern. The omnibus F squares the deviations from the grand mean, so the pattern is not in it — a score that fell and rebounded can give exactly the same F as a steady decline.
• A specific pair. Baseline against eight weeks needs its own comparison, with the multiplicity allowed for.
• Cause. There is no control group here. Eight weeks of anything — regression to the mean, seasonality, simply being in a study — could move craving scores. A single-arm repeated design is observational about cause, however neat the statistics.

What would license a causal claim: a control group measured on the same schedule, so that change over time and change due to treatment can be told apart.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.A steady fall is a pattern claim. The F test cannot distinguish a decline from a dip and a rebound.
b.Causation needs a comparison group. With one arm, the passage of time and the treatment are completely entangled.
c.Naming baseline against eight weeks requires a planned or corrected pairwise comparison, which the omnibus F has not performed.
🏷️ Significant F = not all equal. No direction, no pair, no cause.

Question 1

🔁 Splitting the variation

Counting the data set before choosing the analysis

Consumer psychologist Vermeulen asks each of 24 participants to rate all four advertisements she has prepared, in an order that differs from one person to the next. Her data set, and the analysis it calls for, are:
  • a24 ratings, repeated measures on 24 people
  • b96 ratings, a two-factor ANOVA on 24 people
  • c96 ratings, repeated measures on 24 people
  • d96 ratings, a one-way ANOVA on 96 people
🔎 What it is really asking

Two counts and one decision: how many scores, how many people, and whether the scores are independent.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Splitting the variation: identifying the design.

🛠️ The procedure

Count the scores (people × occasions) and the people separately. If the scores outnumber the people, the observations are not independent and the design is repeated measures.

🧮 The working
Scores: 24 people × 4 advertisements = 96 ratings.

People: 24. Each of them appears in the data set four times.

So the 96 ratings are not 96 independent observations. A participant who rates generously will tend to rate all four advertisements generously, and those four ratings move together.

Why the varied order matters. Counterbalancing is the giveaway that she knows the design is repeated: it is there to stop practice, fatigue or boredom from loading onto whichever advertisement happened to come last.

And what the analysis will do with it: pull the 24 participants’ overall generosity into a between-subjects row of its own, then test the four advertisements against what is left — the within-person inconsistency.

The habit: count the scores, count the people, divide. The answer is the number of occasions.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.24 ratings would be one per person. Each of the 24 rated all four advertisements, which is 96 ratings in total.
b.A two-factor ANOVA needs two factors of interest. There is one — advertisement — with participant as a blocking term.
d.A one-way ANOVA would treat the 96 ratings as coming from 96 independent people. There are 24, each counted four times.
🏷️ Scores ÷ people = occasions. Scores > people → repeated measures.

Question 2

🔁 Splitting the variation

Which row is the error term

Sport psychologist Kallio measures a concentration score in 12 athletes under each of four pre-performance routines. The row of her table that the F test uses as its noise is:
Repeated-measures ANOVA · concentration score · 12 athletes, 4 routines
SourceSSdfMSF
Between athletes180011163.64
Routine270390.009.00
Error (routine × athlete)3303310.00
Total240047
  • athe routine × athlete term
  • bthe between-athletes term
  • cthe two of them added together
  • dthe whole within-athlete portion
🔎 What it is really asking

Four quantities in one table. Which one sits underneath the F?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Splitting the variation: the three-way split.

🛠️ The procedure

The total splits twice: first into between athletes and within athletes, then the within part into routine and routine × athlete. The last of those four is the error term, and the only one that goes under an F.

🧮 The working
Read the table as the two splits that built it:

  Total 2400
   ├─ Between athletes 1800 — athletes differ from each other. Removed, not tested.
   └─ Within athletes 600 — how one athlete’s own score moves across the four routines. This splits again:
        ├─ Routine 270 — the movement everybody shares. The effect being tested.
        └─ Routine × athlete 330 — the movement that differs from athlete to athlete. The error term.

Check: 1800 + 270 + 330 = 2400 ✓ and 270 + 330 = 600 ✓

So F = MS routine ⁄ MS error = 90.00 ⁄ 10.00 = 9.00 on (3, 33) df.

Why noise cannot be the 600. The within-athlete total still has the routine effect inside it. An error term has to be the part that is left over once the effect is taken out, or you would be dividing a quantity by itself.

The habit: the error row is always the interaction between the effect and the participants. In a table, it is the row with a × in its name.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.The between-athletes term is removed before the test, not used as noise. That removal is the whole point of the design.
c.Adding the two together gives 2130 — the error term an independent-groups analysis would use. Pooling them undoes the design.
d.The within-athlete total of 600 still contains the routine effect being tested. Noise cannot include the signal.
🏷️ Error = the condition × participant row. Not the person row, not the two pooled.

Question 3

🔁 Splitting the variation

What happens to the person variation in the other design

Of Kallio’s total variation of 2400, the between-athletes row holds 1800. Had she instead tested four separate groups of 12 athletes, that 1800 would:
Repeated-measures ANOVA · concentration score · 12 athletes, 4 routines
SourceSSdfMSF
Between athletes180011163.64
Routine270390.009.00
Error (routine × athlete)3303310.00
Total240047
  • astill be removed before the test
  • bbe added to the routine term
  • ccancel out of the analysis
  • dbe pooled into the error term
🔎 What it is really asking

The same variation exists either way. The question is which row it lands in.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Splitting the variation: the role of the person term.

🛠️ The procedure

Only a design in which each person is measured more than once can separate the person variation from the error. With one score per person there is nothing to compare a person with, so their variation stays in the error term.

🧮 The working
Kallio’s design measures each athlete four times, so it can ask "how far is this athlete from the average athlete?" — and give the answer its own row of 1800.

Four separate groups give each athlete one score. That score differs from the group mean for two reasons at once — the athlete is unusual, and the occasion was unusual — and nothing in the data can tell the two apart. Both go into error:

  error SS = 1800 + 330 = 2130 on 48 − 4 = 44 df
  MS error = 2130 ⁄ 44 = 48.41, against 10.00 in her actual table
  F = 90.00 ⁄ 48.41 = 1.86, against 9.00

Same four routine means, same 48 scores, F down by a factor of nearly five.

And the decision flips: the critical value on (3, 44) is 2.8165, so 1.86 is not significant (P = .150), while 9.00 on (3, 33) clears 2.8916 easily (P = .0002).

The habit: ask "what else could this deviation be?" The repeated design can answer it. The independent design cannot, and pays for it in the denominator.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Only a repeated-measures design can remove it, because only there is each athlete measured more than once.
b.It never joins the effect being tested. Differences between athletes say nothing about which routine works.
c.Nothing cancels — the variation is in the data either way. All that changes is which row of the table it lands in.
🏷️ One score per person → the person variation is stuck in the error.

Question 4

🔢 Degrees of freedom

The df pair for a repeated-measures F

Kallio measured 12 athletes under 4 routines. The pair of degrees of freedom against which her routine F is judged is:
  • a11 and 33
  • b3 and 33
  • c3 and 44
  • d3 and 47
🔎 What it is really asking

Two numbers from two different rules, and only one of them involves the athletes.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Degrees of freedom: choosing the df pair for a test.

🛠️ The procedure

An F is read on (df of the effect, df of the error). Here that is k − 1 on top and (n − 1)(k − 1) underneath.

🧮 The working
Numerator — the routine df:
  k − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3

Denominator — the error df, which is an interaction df and therefore multiplies:
  (n − 1)(k − 1) = (12 − 1)(4 − 1) = 11 × 3 = 33

Check the whole column: between athletes 11, routine 3, error 33 — and 11 + 3 + 33 = 47 = nk − 1 = 48 − 1 ✓

And the decision: on (3, 33) the 5% critical value is 2.8916. Her F of 9.00 is far past it, P = .0002.

What the 33 is made of. Each athlete supplies three within-person differences, and there are eleven athletes’ worth of freedom in how those differences vary from person to person. That is why it multiplies rather than adds.

The habit: write the pair as (effect, error) before you look anything up, and never let the Total df into it.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.11 and 33 uses the between-athletes df as the numerator. That row is never tested at all.
c.3 and 44 is the df pair of an independent-groups ANOVA on 48 scores, where the error df is N − k = 44.
d.3 and 47 pairs the effect df with the Total df. The second number of the pair is always the error df.
🏷️ (k − 1, (n − 1)(k − 1)). The error df multiplies, because it is an interaction.

Question 5

🔢 Degrees of freedom

Recovering the design from two df

A repeated-measures table shows 4 degrees of freedom for the condition effect and 72 for the error. Educational researcher Westergaard’s study therefore had:
  • a19 participants measured 4 times
  • b73 participants measured 5 times
  • c19 participants measured 5 times
  • d18 participants measured 5 times
🔎 What it is really asking

Invert the two df rules, in the right order, then check the total.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Degrees of freedom: reading the design out of the table.

🛠️ The procedure

k = df condition + 1. Then, because df error = (n − 1)(k − 1), n − 1 = df error ⁄ df condition, so n = that + 1. Occasions first, people second — the second step needs the first.

🧮 The working
Step one — the occasions:
  k − 1 = 4, so k = 5 measurements per participant.

Step two — the people:
  (n − 1) × 4 = 72, so n − 1 = 18 and n = 19 participants.

Step three — the check that catches every slip:
  between subjects 18 + condition 4 + error 72 = 94
  nk − 1 = 19 × 5 − 1 = 94 ✓

So 19 people, 5 occasions, 95 individual scores.

Why the two "+ 1"s are the whole question. Both rules subtract one, so both inversions add one, and both are easy to drop. The total-df check is the only thing that will tell you if you dropped one.

The habit: never report a recovered design without adding the three df and comparing them with nk − 1.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.4 occasions would make the condition df 3, not 4. Add one to the condition df to get k.
b.73 comes from 72 + 1, treating the error df as if it counted participants. It counts their inconsistency.
d.18 participants would give (18 − 1) × 4 = 68 error degrees of freedom, not 72. The 18 is n − 1.
🏷️ k = df condition + 1, then n = df error ⁄ df condition + 1. Check against nk − 1.

Question 6

🔢 Degrees of freedom

How many scores the data file holds

Clinical researcher Meijboom’s repeated-measures output shows 2 degrees of freedom for the condition effect and 38 for the error. The number of individual scores in her data file is:
  • a60
  • b41
  • c57
  • d20
🔎 What it is really asking

Not the number of people and not a degrees-of-freedom figure — the number of rows of data.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Degrees of freedom: from the df column to the size of the data set.

🛠️ The procedure

Recover k and n first, then the scores are simply n × k. Equivalently, scores = Total df + 1, once the between-subjects row has been put back.

🧮 The working
Step one — the occasions: k = 2 + 1 = 3.

Step two — the people: (n − 1) × 2 = 38, so n − 1 = 19 and n = 20.

Step three — the scores: 20 × 3 = 60.

Check by the other route. The three df must add to the Total:
  between subjects 19 + condition 2 + error 38 = 59
  and scores = Total df + 1 = 59 + 1 = 60 ✓

Watch the row that is not printed. The output shows two df figures, but the table has three rows. Forget the between-subjects 19 and the total comes out 19 short every time.

Keep the two counts apart: 20 people, 60 scores. "n" in a repeated-measures design means participants, and the data file is longer than n.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.41 is 38 + 2 + 1, which adds the two printed df and forgets the between-subjects row entirely.
c.57 is 19 × 3, using n − 1 in place of n. The 19 is one fewer than the number of people.
d.20 is the number of participants. Each of them supplies three scores, not one.
🏷️ Recover k and n, then scores = n × k. Remember the unprinted person row.

Question 7

🧱 The table

Completing a table to reach the F

The mean squares and the F have been removed from Kallio’s table. Her F statistic for the routine effect, to two decimal places, is:
Kallio’s table with the routine mean square, the error mean square and the F removed
SourceSSdfMSF
Between athletes180011163.64
Routine2703??
Error (routine × athlete)33033?
Total240047
  • a0.55
  • b9.00
  • c0.82
  • d2.73
🔎 What it is really asking

Two mean squares have to be built before the division can happen.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The table: the F ratio.

🛠️ The procedure

MS = SS ⁄ df for each row, then F = MS condition ⁄ MS error, where the error is the condition × subject row.

🧮 The working
Step one — the numerator:
  MS routine = 270 ⁄ 3 = 90.00

Step two — the denominator:
  MS error = 330 ⁄ 33 = 10.00

Step three — the ratio:
  F = 90.00 ⁄ 10.00 = 9.00 on (3, 33) df

And the decision: the 5% critical value on (3, 33) is 2.8916. 9.00 is well past it and P = .0002, so mean concentration is not the same under all four routines.

The denominator is the whole exam question. The between-athletes mean square of 163.64 is printed right there, and it is the biggest number in the table — which is exactly why it is tempting. Divide by it and F becomes 0.55, a complete non-result. The right error term is built from within-athlete inconsistency, because that is the only noise standing between the four routine means and the conclusion.

The habit: find the row with a × in its name. That is your denominator.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.0.55 is 90 ⁄ 163.64, dividing by the between-athletes mean square. That row is never the denominator.
c.0.82 is 270 ⁄ 330, the two sums of squares divided directly. Each has to become a mean square first.
d.2.73 is 90 ⁄ 33, the routine mean square over the error df instead of over the error mean square.
🏷️ F = MS condition ⁄ MS (condition × subject). The biggest MS is not the denominator.

Question 8

🧱 The table

Recovering the person row from the total

The between-athletes sum of squares has been removed from Kallio’s table. Its value is:
Kallio’s table with the between-athletes SS and mean square removed
SourceSSdfMSF
Between athletes?11
Routine270390.009.00
Error (routine × athlete)3303310.00
Total240047
  • a2130
  • b600
  • c1470
  • d1800
🔎 What it is really asking

The column adds to the Total, so the missing row is the total minus everything else.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The table: filling a gap.

🛠️ The procedure

SS total = SS between subjects + SS condition + SS error. Any one missing entry is the Total minus the other two — both of them, not just one.

🧮 The working
SS between athletes = 2400 − 270 − 330 = 2400 − 600 = 1800

Check it against the mean square the design implies:
  1800 ⁄ 11 = 163.64, a sensible figure for the row — and far bigger than the error mean square of 10.00, which is the normal state of affairs.

Read what the 1800 means: 1800 ⁄ 2400 = 75% of all the variation in the data is simply that some athletes concentrate better than others. In an independent-groups design that three-quarters would be sitting in the error term.

And the habit: when one entry is missing from a column that adds up, subtract every other entry. The commonest slip is to subtract one row, notice the answer looks plausible, and stop.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.2130 is 2400 − 270, which subtracts the routine row and leaves the error row in. Both have to come out.
b.600 is 270 + 330, the within-athlete total. It is what you subtract from 2400, not the answer.
c.1470 is 2400 − 600 − 330, subtracting the error row twice: once inside the 600 and once again on its own.
🏷️ Missing SS = Total − every other row. Then check it against its own MS.

A share of the within-person variation

Of the variation that occurs within Kallio’s athletes, the proportion attributable to the routine, to two decimal places, is:

SourceSSdfMSF
Between athletes180011163.64

Error (routine × athlete)?33?
Total240047

🔎 What it is really asking

The denominator is named in the stem — and it is not printed in the table.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The table: reading the sums of squares as shares.

🛠️ The procedure

The within-person variation is SS condition + SS error, which is also SS total − SS between subjects. The share is SS condition ⁄ (within-person total).

🧮 The working
Step one — build the denominator, which the gapped table does not give you directly:
  within-athlete total = 2400 − 1800 = 600
  (and so the missing error SS is 600 − 270 = 330, if you want it)

Step two — the share:
  270 ⁄ 600 = 0.45, so 45%

In words: of all the movement in one athlete’s own concentration score across the four routines, about 45% follows the pattern everybody shares, and 55% is each athlete going their own way.

Why the denominator is 600 and not 2400. Of the 2400, a full 1800 is simply that different athletes concentrate differently. That was removed before any test and has nothing to do with routines. Leave it in and the effect looks four times smaller: 270 ⁄ 2400 = 0.11.

The habit: the stem names the pool. "Within athletes" means build the within-athlete total first, then divide.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.0.11 is 270 ⁄ 2400, dividing by the overall total. That folds the athlete differences back in after the design removed them.
c.0.82 is 270 ⁄ 330, the routine SS over the error SS. The denominator has to be the within-athlete total of 600.
d.0.75 is 1800 ⁄ 2400, the share of everything that is differences between athletes. Large, and not what was asked.
🏷️ Match the denominator to the words in the stem, then build it before dividing.

Question 10

🔧 Sphericity and the correction

What would violate sphericity

Kallio’s four routines produce six pairwise differences. Sphericity would be violated if:
Repeated-measures ANOVA · concentration score · 12 athletes, 4 routines
SourceSSdfMSF
Between athletes180011163.64
Routine270390.009.00
Error (routine × athlete)3303310.00
Total240047
  • athe four routines differ in their spread
  • bthe 12 athletes differ widely from each other
  • cthose six differences vary in spread
  • dthe four routines differ in their means
🔎 What it is really asking

Equal variances — of the conditions, or of the differences between them?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Sphericity: what the condition says.

🛠️ The procedure

Sphericity requires the variances of the differences between every pair of conditions to be equal. Not the variances of the conditions themselves — the variances of the subtractions.

🧮 The working
With four routines there are 4 × 3 ⁄ 2 = six pairs: A−B, A−C, A−D, B−C, B−D and C−D. Work out each athlete’s six difference scores, then the variance of each set of twelve. Sphericity asks that those six variances be equal.

Why the distinction is not pedantry. Two conditions can have quite different spreads and still give difference scores of equal variance, because var(X − Y) = var(X) + var(Y) − 2cov(X, Y). It is the covariances that decide, and they do not appear in the condition variances at all.

When it fails in practice: whenever some pairs of conditions are more closely related than others — adjacent time points, or two routines that resemble each other. Those pairs produce small, consistent differences and the distant pairs produce large ones.

What failure costs: the F test becomes too liberal — the true P-value is bigger than the printed one — which is what a correction is for. With only two conditions there is one difference, so sphericity cannot fail at all.

Say it to a friend: "subtract every pair, then check the spreads match."
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Unequal spread in the conditions themselves is not the rule. The covariances between them decide whether the differences match.
b.Athletes differing from one another is pulled into its own row. It is the reason for the design, not a violation of it.
d.Differing means is the hypothesis under test. A condition you check beforehand can never be the hypothesis itself.
🏷️ Sphericity = equal variances of the pairwise DIFFERENCES. Not of the conditions.

Question 11

🔧 Sphericity and the correction

Corrected degrees of freedom

Kallio’s output reports ε = 0.70. Her Greenhouse-Geisser corrected degrees of freedom for the routine effect, each to one decimal place, are:
Repeated-measures ANOVA · concentration score · 12 athletes, 4 routines
SourceSSdfMSF
Between athletes180011163.64
Routine270390.009.00
Error (routine × athlete)3303310.00
Total240047
  • a3.0 and 33.0
  • b2.1 and 33.0
  • c4.3 and 47.1
  • d2.1 and 23.1
🔎 What it is really asking

Which df move, and in which direction.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Sphericity: the correction.

🛠️ The procedure

Greenhouse-Geisser multiplies both degrees of freedom by ε. The F statistic itself does not change — only the distribution it is judged against.

🧮 The working
Uncorrected df: 3 and 33.

  3 × 0.70 = 2.1
  33 × 0.70 = 23.1

Fractional degrees of freedom are completely normal here; software interpolates in the F distribution.

What it does to the verdict. F stays at 9.00. The 5% critical value rises from 2.8916 to 3.3684, and P rises from .0002 to .0011. Still comfortably significant, so her conclusion survives the correction — the best possible outcome of applying one.

Why the df shrink rather than the F. Fewer effective degrees of freedom means a higher bar, which compensates for a test that is too liberal when sphericity fails. ε = 1 is perfect sphericity and changes nothing; the further ε falls below 1, the bigger the penalty.

The habit: ε is at most 1, so the corrected df must come out smaller. If yours got bigger, you divided.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.3.0 and 33.0 are the uncorrected df. Applying a correction has to move them.
b.2.1 and 33.0 corrects the numerator only. Both degrees of freedom are multiplied by ε.
c.4.3 and 47.1 divide by 0.70 instead of multiplying. A correction makes the df smaller, never larger.
🏷️ Multiply BOTH df by ε. F unchanged, critical value up.

Question 12

🔧 Sphericity and the correction

When the correction changes the verdict

Memory researcher Lundgren tests 15 participants under four conditions and obtains F = 3.20 with an uncorrected P = .033. Her output reports ε = 0.55, and on the corrected degrees of freedom the same F gives P = .068. She should report:
  • athe uncorrected test, since ε is below 0.75
  • bthe corrected test, which is not significant
  • cthe uncorrected test, which is significant
  • dboth, and call the result inconclusive
🔎 What it is really asking

Two P-values on opposite sides of .05. Which one is the result?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Sphericity: what to report.

🛠️ The procedure

When sphericity is in doubt, the corrected test is the result. Decide that before seeing which P-value is friendlier — choosing the more favourable of two P-values is not a defensible procedure.

🧮 The working
Her corrected degrees of freedom:
  3 × 0.55 = 1.65 and 42 × 0.55 = 23.1

The critical value rises from 2.8270 on (3, 42) to 3.6355 on (1.65, 23.1). Her F of 3.20 cleared the first bar and does not clear the second, which is why P moves from .033 to .068.

So the write-up is: F = 3.20 on 1.65 and 23.1 df, P = .068, Greenhouse-Geisser applied — not significant at the 5% level.

Compare Kallio, where ε was 0.70 and P went from .0002 to .0011. There the correction changed nothing that mattered. Here it changes the verdict. The procedure is the same in both cases, and that is exactly the point: it cannot be chosen after looking.

And an honest word about .068: it is not evidence that the four conditions are identical. It is a failure to detect a difference with 15 participants and a badly non-spherical covariance structure.

The habit: decide the analysis from the design and the conditions, never from the P-values it produces.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.ε below .75 is the usual reason to prefer Greenhouse-Geisser to Huynh-Feldt — a choice between corrections, not against correcting.
c.Choosing the uncorrected test because it is the significant one is picking the more favourable of two P-values.
d."Inconclusive" is not a reading of two P-values that disagree. The corrected one is the one that applies.
🏷️ Corrected test is the result — decided before you see the P-values.
