Question 13

💪 What the pairing buys you

Recomputing the F without the pairing

Had Kallio tested four independent groups of 12 athletes instead, with exactly the same four routine means, her F statistic, to two decimal places, would have been:
Repeated-measures ANOVA · concentration score · 12 athletes, 4 routines
SourceSSdfMSF
Between athletes180011163.64
Routine270390.009.00
Error (routine × athlete)3303310.00
Total240047
  • a1.86
  • b9.00
  • c2.03
  • d12.00
🔎 What it is really asking

Rebuild the denominator for the other design. The numerator does not move.

🧭 Which type of question this is

What the pairing buys you: the mechanism.

🛠️ The procedure

Without pairing, the person variation has nowhere to go but the error term. Pooled error SS = SS between subjects + SS error, on N − k degrees of freedom. The condition mean square is unchanged.

🧮 The working
Numerator, unchanged, because the means are the means:
  MS routine = 270 ⁄ 3 = 90.00

Denominator, rebuilt:
  pooled error SS = 1800 + 330 = 2130
  df = N − k = 48 − 4 = 44
  MS error = 2130 ⁄ 44 = 48.41

The F:
  90.00 ⁄ 48.41 = 1.86 on (3, 44) df

And the verdicts differ. The critical value on (3, 44) is 2.8165, so 1.86 gives P = .150 — nothing. Her actual test gave 9.00 with P = .0002. Same 48 scores, same four means, opposite conclusions, and the only difference is what counts as noise.

The trade, stated plainly: she gives up 11 error degrees of freedom, 33 instead of 44, and takes 1800 units of variation out of the denominator. Almost always worth it.

The habit: when a question asks what the other design would have given, change only the denominator.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.9.00 is her actual repeated-measures F. The independent analysis has a different error term underneath it.
c.2.03 is 90 ⁄ (2130 ⁄ 48), dividing the pooled error SS by N instead of by N − k = 44.
d.12.00 is 90 ⁄ (330 ⁄ 44), keeping the small repeated-measures error SS but putting it on the independent design’s df.
🏷️ Pairing changes the DENOMINATOR only. Pool the person row and recount the df.

Question 14

💪 What the pairing buys you

What the lost degrees of freedom buy

Kallio’s design leaves her with 33 error degrees of freedom where four independent groups would have had 44. What she receives in exchange is:
Repeated-measures ANOVA · concentration score · 12 athletes, 4 routines
SourceSSdfMSF
Between athletes180011163.64
Routine270390.009.00
Error (routine × athlete)3303310.00
Total240047
  • aeleven extra error degrees of freedom
  • bprotection against carry-over effects
  • can error mean square 4.8 times smaller
  • da routine mean square 4.8 times larger
🔎 What it is really asking

Something was given up. Name what came back for it.

🧭 Which type of question this is

What the pairing buys you: the trade.

🛠️ The procedure

A repeated-measures design trades degrees of freedom for a smaller error mean square. Fewer df raise the critical value a little; a much smaller denominator raises the F a lot.

🧮 The working
What she gives up: 11 error degrees of freedom. The critical value rises from 2.8165 on (3, 44) to 2.8916 on (3, 33) — a penalty, and a tiny one.

What she gets:
  MS error, independent groups: 2130 ⁄ 44 = 48.41
  MS error, repeated measures:  330 ⁄ 33 = 10.00
  48.41 ⁄ 10.00 = 4.84 times smaller

And so F rises from 1.86 to 9.00 while the numerator never moves.

Why the trade is nearly always worth taking. Degrees of freedom affect the bar by a few per cent. The error mean square divides straight into the F. A design that costs you a little of the first to win a lot of the second is a good design.

And what it costs besides df: the sphericity condition to worry about, dropout that removes a participant’s whole row, and order or carry-over effects — which is why conditions are counterbalanced wherever they can be.

The habit: when you see fewer df in the repeated analysis, look at the mean square before concluding anything was lost.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.She gives up eleven error degrees of freedom, 33 against 44. The gain comes in spite of that, not because of it.
b.Carry-over is a risk the repeated design adds, not a protection it offers. Counterbalancing is the defence against it.
d.The routine mean square is 90.00 in both analyses. Pairing never moves the condition means.
🏷️ A few df traded for a much smaller MS error. That is the whole bargain.

Question 15

💪 What the pairing buys you

Writing the conclusion from an omnibus F

Kallio’s routine effect is significant (F = 9.00, P = .0002) across her four pre-performance routines. Her output contains no comparisons between individual routines. She may conclude that:
Repeated-measures ANOVA · concentration score · 12 athletes, 4 routines
SourceSSdfMSF
Between athletes180011163.64
Routine270390.009.00
Error (routine × athlete)3303310.00
Total240047
  • aevery athlete concentrated best under the same routine
  • bconcentration rose steadily from routine 1 to routine 4
  • cthe fourth routine beat the first on concentration
  • dmean concentration differs across the four routines
🔎 What it is really asking

One sentence is licensed by a significant omnibus F. Which one?

🧭 Which type of question this is

What the pairing buys you: the reach of the conclusion.

🛠️ The procedure

A repeated-measures F is an omnibus test: it says the condition means are not all equal. It names no pair, no direction, no pattern, and says nothing about any individual participant.

🧮 The working
Rejecting H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ = μ₄ licenses exactly one sentence: mean concentration is not the same under all four routines.

Three readings it does not license:
• A pattern. The F squares the deviations from the grand mean, so a steady rise and a rise-then-fall can give the identical F of 9.00.
• A specific pair. Routine 4 against routine 1 needs its own comparison, with the six possible pairs allowed for.
• An individual. "Every athlete" turns a statement about four means into a statement about twelve people. The error row of 330 is precisely the evidence that athletes do not all move together.

What would license more: planned or corrected pairwise comparisons for the pairs she cares about, and the four cell means printed beside them so the direction is visible.

One thing she can say that a single-arm time study could not: because every athlete performed every routine in a counterbalanced order, the comparison between routines is a within-person experimental contrast, not a before-and-after. Order effects are spread across the routines rather than confounded with them.

Say it to a friend: "the routines are not all the same — I do not yet know which is best."
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.A group mean says nothing about every individual. Athletes vary around their own cell mean, which is what the error row measures.
b.A steady rise is a pattern claim. The omnibus F cannot tell a rise from a dip followed by a rebound.
c.Naming two routines needs a pairwise comparison with the six pairs allowed for, which she has not run.
🏷️ Omnibus F = not all equal. No pair, no direction, no individual.

Question 1

🔁 Splitting the variation

Spotting the design among four candidates

Occupational psychologist Achterberg wants to compare three rota designs on nurses’ reported fatigue, and is offered four ways of collecting the data. The one whose scores would not be independent of one another is:
  • a45 nurses rated a new rota and 45 rated the old
  • b30 nurses each rated one rota design on one day
  • c30 nurses each rated all three rota designs
  • d90 nurses each rated one of three rota designs
🔎 What it is really asking

Count the scores and the people in each study. Which one has more scores than people?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Splitting the variation: identifying the design.

🛠️ The procedure

Observations stop being independent when the same person contributes more than one score. Divide the scores by the people: the answer is the number of occasions, and anything above one means the scores arrive in sets.

🧮 The working
Take them one at a time:

  30 nurses × 3 designs = 90 scores from 30 people → 3 occasions each
  90 nurses × 1 design  = 90 scores from 90 people → 1 each
  45 + 45 nurses × 1    = 90 scores from 90 people → 1 each
  30 nurses × 1 design  = 30 scores from 30 people → 1 each

Only the first has more scores than people. A nurse who reports high fatigue on one rota will tend to report high fatigue on the others, so her three scores move together and cannot be treated as three unrelated observations.

And look at what follows from that. The first design would pull the nurses’ own fatigue levels into a row of their own on 30 − 1 = 29 df, leaving a condition row on 3 − 1 = 2 df and an error row on 29 × 2 = 58 df. Treated instead as 90 independent scores, the same comparison would be read on 2 and 87 df — with all the differences between nurses still in the denominator.

The tell in an exam stem: "each ... all three" against "each ... one of three". Those two phrases decide the entire analysis, and they look almost the same on the page.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Two groups of 45 is still one score per nurse. Splitting people into groups never links their scores to each other; measuring the same person twice does.
b.Thirty nurses rating one design on one day give 30 scores from 30 people. Fewer scores than the others, and still exactly one each.
d.Ninety nurses rating one design each give 90 scores from 90 people. Three groups of different nurses, one score apiece, are independent observations.
🏷️ Scores ÷ people = occasions. More than one occasion → the scores come in sets.

Question 2

🔁 Splitting the variation

Matching a split to a reported share

Sleep researcher Bexell reports a total variation of 4000 and says that three-quarters of it was set aside before the condition effect was tested. The split of her table consistent with that is:
  • abetween 3000, condition 400, error 600
  • bbetween 1000, condition 600, error 2400
  • cbetween 2000, condition 1000, error 1000
  • dbetween 3000, condition 600, error 600
🔎 What it is really asking

Which row holds the three-quarters — and does the column still add to 4000?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Splitting the variation: the three-way split.

🛠️ The procedure

The row that is set aside is between participants; the two rows that remain are the condition effect and the error. So a candidate has to put three-quarters of the total in the person row and have all three rows add to the total.

🧮 The working
Three-quarters of 4000 is 3000, and that has to sit in the between-participants row — the one the design removes rather than tests.

Now test every candidate on both counts:

  3000 + 400 + 600 = 4000 ✓ and 3000 ⁄ 4000 = 0.75 ✓
  1000 + 600 + 2400 = 4000 ✓ but 1000 ⁄ 4000 = 0.25 ✗
  2000 + 1000 + 1000 = 4000 ✓ but 2000 ⁄ 4000 = 0.50 ✗
  3000 + 600 + 600 = 4200 ✗ — it never reaches the total at all

Read what the winner says. Within a participant there are 400 + 600 = 1000 units of movement across the conditions, and 400 of those — two-fifths — follow the pattern everybody shares. The other 3000 is simply that some people sleep worse than others, and it is out of the denominator before anything is tested.

The habit: a share question carries two checks, not one. Does the column add, and is the numerator the row the words actually name?
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.Between 1000 out of 4000 is a quarter, not three-quarters. This column does add up, which is exactly why the share has to be checked as well.
c.Between 2000 out of 4000 is a half. Half the variation removed is a perfectly possible table — it is simply not the one her sentence describes.
d.These three rows come to 4200, so they cannot be a split of 4000 whatever their shares. The three rows of the table always add to the total.
🏷️ Two checks on a split: does the column add, and whose share is it?

Question 3

🔁 Splitting the variation

What the error row actually measures

Reading the error row of a repeated-measures table, Carreira says it measures how precisely the instrument records each score. Dietl says it measures the extent to which people do not all change in the same way. The reading that survives is:
  • aCarreira’s — it is the precision of the measure
  • bDietl’s — it is how far people differ overall
  • cneither — it is the size of the condition effect
  • dDietl’s — it is people changing differently
🔎 What it is really asking

What is being added up in that row?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Splitting the variation: the role of the error term.

🛠️ The procedure

The error row is the condition × participant term. It is built from each person’s own pattern across the conditions, and it measures how far those patterns disagree with one another.

🧮 The working
Picture two participants in a three-condition study. One gains 4 points from the first condition to the second; so does the other. Their patterns agree, and they contribute nothing at all to the error row.

Now suppose the first gains 4 and the second loses 6. The condition row knows only the average movement; the disagreement between the two patterns is what the error row collects.

So the error row is inconsistency of change, person by person — and it is the right yardstick for the condition effect, because the condition effect is itself a claim about a pattern of change that everybody shares.

Why measurement precision is not the answer. Imprecision does land in that row, along with everything else unexplained — but so does a participant who genuinely responds the other way round, and that is not noise in the instrument. The row has a name, and the name is the interaction between the conditions and the people.

And why it is not the differences between people. Those have a row of their own, directly above it. One participant scoring 20 points higher than another at every condition adds nothing to the error row, because a constant gap is not a difference in pattern.

The habit: find the row with a × in its name, then read the × as "depends on".
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Measurement imprecision does end up in that row, and so does a participant who really responds differently from the rest. The row is named for the interaction, not for the instrument.
b.How far people differ overall is the between-participants row, which sits above the error row and is removed before any test. A constant gap between two people never enters the error term.
c.The size of the condition effect is the condition row. The error row is what is left once that shared pattern has been taken out, which is precisely why it can serve as the denominator.
🏷️ The error row is condition × participant: how much people’s patterns disagree.

Question 4

🔢 Degrees of freedom

What more participants do to the column

Clinical researcher Ekdahl has tested 20 patients under three treatments, and now recruits five more patients, each tested under all three. Her condition and error degrees of freedom become:
  • a2 and 50
  • b2 and 48
  • c2 and 38
  • d3 and 48
🔎 What it is really asking

One of the two numbers moves when more people arrive, and one does not.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Degrees of freedom: how the column responds to more participants.

🛠️ The procedure

df condition = k − 1 counts occasions only. df error = (n − 1)(k − 1) counts both, so a change in n is felt by the error row and nowhere else.

🧮 The working
Before: n = 20, k = 3. Condition df 3 − 1 = 2, error df (20 − 1)(3 − 1) = 19 × 2 = 38.

After: n = 25, k = 3.
  Condition: k − 1 = 3 − 1 = 2 — unchanged, because the number of treatments has not moved.
  Error: (25 − 1)(3 − 1) = 24 × 2 = 48

Check the whole column: between patients 24, condition 2, error 48 →
  24 + 2 + 48 = 74 = nk − 1 = 75 − 1 ✓

What the five extra patients bought her. Ten more error degrees of freedom, two per patient, and nothing at all in the numerator. More error df lower the bar a little: on (2, 38) the 5% critical value is 3.2448 and on (2, 48) it is 3.1907.

The habit: write (n − 1)(k − 1) out in full before you reach for the numbers in the stem. Both brackets subtract one, and both are easy to drop.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.2 and 50 is 25 × 2, using n in place of n − 1. The person row spends one degree of freedom, and the error row inherits that subtraction.
c.2 and 38 is the study she started with, 19 × 2. The five new patients each add two error degrees of freedom, so that row has to grow.
d.3 and 48 uses k rather than k − 1 for the condition row. Three treatments carry two degrees of freedom, because one of the three is spent on the grand mean.
🏷️ df condition = k − 1 only. df error = (n − 1)(k − 1), so it moves with n.

Question 5

🔢 Degrees of freedom

Choosing a design from two printed df

Cognitive researcher Mendoza’s output survives only as the two rows below. The design behind them is:
All that reached the page of Mendoza’s output
Sourcedf
Between participants?
Condition?
Error (condition × participant)60
Total79
  • a13 participants, 6 conditions
  • b20 participants, 4 conditions
  • c16 participants, 5 conditions
  • d21 participants, 4 conditions
🔎 What it is really asking

Four candidates, and each has to satisfy both printed rows at once.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Degrees of freedom: reading the design out of the table.

🛠️ The procedure

Two rules to satisfy together: df error = (n − 1)(k − 1) and Total df = nk − 1. A candidate that matches one and misses the other is wrong.

🧮 The working
Check all four on both rows:

  16 × 5: error 15 × 4 = 60 ✓   total 80 − 1 = 79 ✓
  21 × 4: error 20 × 3 = 60 ✓   total 84 − 1 = 83 ✗
  13 × 6: error 12 × 5 = 60 ✓   total 78 − 1 = 77 ✗
  20 × 4: error 19 × 3 = 57 ✗   total 80 − 1 = 79 ✓

Only 16 participants measured 5 times satisfies both, so the two missing rows are 15 and 4 — and 15 + 4 + 60 = 79 ✓

Why one printed df is never enough. Sixty factorises several ways — 15 × 4, 20 × 3, 12 × 5 — so three different designs here produce an error row of exactly 60. The Total row is what chooses between them. The fourth candidate is the same trap from the other side: it matches the Total and misses the error row.

The habit: when a question prints two numbers, test your candidate against both before you stop reading.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.13 participants measured 6 times also give 12 × 5 = 60 error degrees of freedom, and their 78 scores leave a Total of 77.
b.20 participants measured 4 times give the printed Total of 79, because 80 scores leave 79. Their error row is 19 × 3 = 57, not 60.
d.21 participants measured 4 times do give 20 × 3 = 60 error degrees of freedom, and then their 84 scores leave a Total of 83 rather than 79.
🏷️ Two printed df, two checks. Factorising one of them is only half the job.

Question 6

🔢 Degrees of freedom

Recovering the number of occasions

Memory researcher Hvidberg’s output prints the two rows below. The number of occasions on which each participant was measured, as a whole number, is:
Hvidberg’s output with the condition row and the total removed
Sourcedf
Between participants14
Condition?
Error (condition × participant)70
Total?
  • a6
  • b5
  • c15
  • d70
🔎 What it is really asking

Divide one printed df by the other, then remember which rule subtracted one.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Degrees of freedom: reading the design out of the table.

🛠️ The procedure

The person row is n − 1 and the error row is (n − 1)(k − 1), so the error row is the person row multiplied by k − 1. Divide, then add the one back: k = df error ⁄ df person + 1.

🧮 The working
df error ⁄ df person = 70 ⁄ 14 = 5, and that 5 is k − 1, not k.

So k = 5 + 1 = 6 occasions, and n = 14 + 1 = 15 participants, for 90 scores in all.

Check the whole column: 14 + (6 − 1) + 70 = 14 + 5 + 70 = 89 = nk − 1 = 90 − 1 ✓

What the division is doing. Each participant supplies k − 1 = 5 within-person differences, and there are 14 participants’ worth of freedom in how those differences vary from person to person. The error row is those two counts multiplied together, so dividing it by one of them hands back the other.

The habit: every rule here subtracts one somewhere, so running one backwards means putting that one back. The total-df check is what tells you whether you did.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.5 is 70 ⁄ 14, which is k − 1 rather than k. The subtraction built into every degrees-of-freedom rule has to be undone when the rule is run backwards.
c.15 is the number of participants, 14 + 1. That is the other count in this table, and it comes out of the person row rather than out of the division.
d.70 is the error row itself. It is built from both counts multiplied together, so it cannot be either of them on its own.
🏷️ df error ⁄ df person = k − 1. Add one back for the number of occasions.

Question 7

🧱 The table

A sum of squares recovered from an F

Sport psychologist Järvinen measures grip strength in 13 athletes under four warm-up protocols. Several entries are missing below. The sum of squares for protocol, as a whole number, is:
Järvinen’s table with the protocol sum of squares, two mean squares and the total removed
SourceSSdfMSF
Between athletes156012130.00
Protocol?3?7.00
Error (protocol × athlete)18036?
Total?51
  • a175
  • b105
  • c35
  • d21
🔎 What it is really asking

From a printed F back to a sum of squares — two multiplications, in the right order.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The table: working backwards from a printed F.

🛠️ The procedure

Forwards the chain is SS → MS → F. Backwards it is MS = F × MS error, then SS = MS × that row’s own df. Build the error mean square first, because the F is defined against it.

🧮 The working
Step one — the error mean square:
  MS error = 180 ⁄ 36 = 5.00

Step two — the protocol mean square, from the F:
  MS protocol = 7.00 × 5.00 = 35.00

Step three — the sum of squares, from its own df:
  SS protocol = 35.00 × 3 = 105

Now the table closes, so check it. SS total = 1560 + 105 + 180 = 1845, and the df 12 + 3 + 36 = 51 = nk − 1 = 52 − 1 ✓ The printed person mean square agrees too: 1560 ⁄ 12 = 130.00.

And the decision: on (3, 36) the 5% critical value is 2.8663, so 7.00 clears it comfortably and P = .0008. Mean grip strength is not the same under all four protocols.

The habit: going backwards, undo the steps in the order they were done. MS error first, because the F was formed against it; the row’s own df last, because that is what the mean square was divided by.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.175 is 35.00 × 5.00, multiplying the mean square by MS error instead of by the row’s own 3 degrees of freedom. MS error belongs one step earlier.
c.35 is the protocol mean square, one multiplication short of the answer. A mean square is a sum of squares that has already been divided by its own df.
d.21 is 7.00 × 3, multiplying the F straight by the degrees of freedom and leaving the error mean square out of the chain altogether.
🏷️ Backwards: MS = F × MS error, then SS = MS × its own df.

Question 8

🧱 The table

Building the denominator from a reported summary

Educational psychologist Kolarik measures concentration in 15 pupils under three classroom layouts and reports the five figures below. The error mean square her test needs, to two decimal places, is:
Concentration under three classroom layouts · everything Kolarik reports
What Kolarik reportsValue
Pupils in the study15
Classroom layouts, each pupil in all of them3
Total sum of squares2500
Share of it lying between pupils80%
Sum of squares for layout150
  • a83.93
  • b25.00
  • c5.36
  • d12.50
🔎 What it is really asking

The denominator of the test, from a summary that is not laid out as a table.

🧭 Which type of question this is

The table: rebuilding a row that was never printed.

🛠️ The procedure

Rebuild the row before dividing. Between = the stated share × total, then SS error = total − between − condition, and df error = (n − 1)(k − 1). Only then MS error = SS error ⁄ df error.

🧮 The working
Step one — the three sums of squares:
  between pupils = 0.80 × 2500 = 2000
  layout = 150, as reported
  error = 2500 − 2000 − 150 = 350

Step two — the degrees of freedom, from 15 pupils and 3 layouts:
  person 15 − 1 = 14, layout 3 − 1 = 2, error 14 × 2 = 28
  check 14 + 2 + 28 = 44 = nk − 1 = 45 − 1 ✓

Step three — the mean square:
  MS error = 350 ⁄ 28 = 12.50

The step that does the damage if you skip it. The 2000 has to come out before the error row is built. Leave it in and the denominator becomes 2350 ⁄ 28 = 83.93 — nearly seven times too big, and the whole advantage of the design thrown away in a subtraction that was never done.

And the payoff, now that you have it. MS layout = 150 ⁄ 2 = 75.00, so the test comes out at 75.00 ⁄ 12.50 = 6.00 on (2, 28) df, against a 5% critical value of 3.3404 and with P = .007. Built on the 83.93 instead it would have been 0.89, and nothing at all.

The habit: a reported percentage is a row of the table in disguise. Turn it into a sum of squares, build the whole column, and only then start dividing.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.83.93 is 2350 ⁄ 28 — the error row built without taking the 2000 of between-pupil variation out of it first. That is the independent-groups denominator, and avoiding it is the entire point of the design.
b.25.00 is 350 ⁄ 14, the right sum of squares over the person row’s degrees of freedom. Every mean square uses its own row’s df, and the error row has 28.
c.5.36 is 150 ⁄ 28, the layout sum of squares over the error degrees of freedom. Two different rows have been mixed together.
🏷️ Turn a reported share into a sum of squares, build the column, then divide.

Question 9

🧱 The table

Finding the entry that does not follow

Clinical researcher Lampinen’s output is printed below. Exactly one entry in it does not follow from the others. It is:
Lampinen’s output as printed · symptom score · 15 patients, 4 conditions
SourceSSdfMSF
Between patients210014140.00
Condition240380.008.00
Error (condition × patient)4204210.00
Total276059
  • athe person row’s mean square
  • bthe error row’s mean square
  • cthe condition row’s F
  • dthe Total sum of squares
🔎 What it is really asking

Which single number cannot be rebuilt from the numbers around it?

🧭 Which type of question this is

The table: checking a printed table for consistency.

🛠️ The procedure

Four rules hold in every repeated-measures table. The SS column adds, the df column adds to nk − 1, each MS = SS ⁄ df for its own row, and F = MS condition ⁄ MS error.

🧮 The working
The columns first.
  SS: 2100 + 240 + 420 = 2760 ✓ as printed.
  df: 14 + 3 + 42 = 59 ✓ as printed — and the design behind that is 15 patients measured 4 times, since 15 − 1 = 14, 4 − 1 = 3 and 14 × 3 = 42.

Then each row’s own mean square.
  person:    2100 ⁄ 14 = 150.00 — the table prints 140.00 ✗
  condition:  240 ⁄ 3 = 80.00 ✓
  error:      420 ⁄ 42 = 10.00 ✓

And the F. 80.00 ⁄ 10.00 = 8.00 ✓ as printed, P = .0002 on (3, 42) against a critical value of 2.8270.

Where the 140.00 comes from. 2100 ⁄ 15 — divided by the number of patients instead of by the row’s own 14 degrees of freedom, which are printed right beside it. It is the commonest slip in the table, and it sits on the one row that never gets an F, so nothing downstream catches it.

Why none of the others can be the fault. The error mean square of 10.00 is confirmed twice — once by 420 ⁄ 42 and once by the F that divides by it. The F follows from two mean squares that both check out. The Total is exactly the three rows added.

The habit: run MS = SS ⁄ df down every row, the untested one included.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.The error mean square is 420 ⁄ 42 = 10.00, and the printed F of 8.00 divides by it correctly. Two independent checks land on that number.
c.The condition F is 80.00 ⁄ 10.00 = 8.00, exactly as printed, and both of those mean squares come straight from their own rows.
d.The Total sum of squares is 2100 + 240 + 420 = 2760, as printed. The SS column adds, so the total is not the entry at fault.
🏷️ Run MS = SS ⁄ df down every row — the untested one included.

Question 10

🔧 Sphericity and the correction

Sphericity with only two conditions

Comparing two relaxation conditions in the same participants, Nyholm says the sphericity condition cannot fail when there are only two conditions. Pellegrini says two variances still have to match. The reading that survives is:
  • aNyholm’s — a correction is applied in any case
  • bneither — the condition needs three conditions
  • cNyholm’s — one difference cannot be unequal
  • dPellegrini’s — the two conditions must match
🔎 What it is really asking

How many sets of differences are there when there are only two conditions?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Sphericity: what the condition says.

🛠️ The procedure

Sphericity is about the variances of the differences between pairs of conditions. With k conditions there are k(k − 1) ⁄ 2 pairs, so with k = 2 there is exactly one — and one variance cannot be unequal to anything.

🧮 The working
k = 2 gives 2 × 1 ⁄ 2 = 1 pair, so there is a single set of difference scores: each participant’s second score minus their first. Its variance is whatever it is. There is nothing for it to differ from, so the condition holds by construction, ε = 1, and multiplying both df by 1 changes nothing.

Where Pellegrini goes wrong. Two conditions do have two variances of their own, and they may be wildly different — sphericity never asks about them. It asks about the spread of the subtractions, and var(X − Y) = var(X) + var(Y) − 2cov(X, Y) shows why the two questions come apart: the covariance decides, and it appears in neither condition variance.

And as k grows. Three conditions give 3 pairs, four give 6, five give 10. More pairs means more variances that all have to agree, and more chance that they do not — which is why time-series designs with several occasions break the condition routinely.

Say it to a friend: "two conditions, one subtraction, nothing to compare it to."
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Nyholm reaches the right conclusion, and not for that reason. There is nothing to correct here: ε is 1, and multiplying both degrees of freedom by 1 leaves them exactly where they were.
b.Three conditions are not a minimum for the condition to exist. It simply cannot be violated below three, because below three there is only one difference to look at.
d.Two conditions do have two variances, and sphericity is not about them. It is about the spread of the difference scores, and with two conditions there is only one set of those.
🏷️ k conditions → k(k − 1) ⁄ 2 pairs. With two, sphericity cannot fail.

Question 11

🔧 Sphericity and the correction

Undoing a correction to find the design

Developmental researcher Stegeman’s output prints corrected degrees of freedom of 2.40 and 48.00 for her condition effect, alongside ε = 0.80. Her design was:
  • a20 participants, 4 conditions
  • b21 participants, 3 conditions
  • c16 participants, 5 conditions
  • d21 participants, 4 conditions
🔎 What it is really asking

Undo the correction first, then read the design off the restored degrees of freedom.

🧭 Which type of question this is

Sphericity: the correction, worked back to the design.

🛠️ The procedure

The correction multiplies both df by ε, so dividing by ε restores them. Then k = df condition + 1, and since df error = (n − 1)(k − 1), n − 1 = df error ⁄ df condition.

🧮 The working
Step one — undo the correction:
  2.40 ⁄ 0.80 = 3   and   48.00 ⁄ 0.80 = 60

Step two — read the design off those:
  k = 3 + 1 = 4 conditions
  (n − 1) × 3 = 60, so n − 1 = 20 and n = 21 participants

Check the column: 20 + 3 + 60 = 83 = nk − 1 = 84 − 1 ✓

Why both printed figures are needed. 16 participants in 5 conditions have df of 4 and 60, which correct to 3.20 and 48.00 — the same denominator and the wrong numerator. 20 participants in 4 conditions have df of 3 and 57, which correct to 2.40 and 45.60 — the same numerator and the wrong denominator. Each near miss matches one of the two printed numbers.

A free check on any ε. It is at most 1, so corrected df are always smaller than the originals and restoring them means dividing. And the restored figures have to come out as whole numbers, which tells you at once whether you divided by the right ε.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.20 participants in 4 conditions have degrees of freedom of 3 and 57, which correct to 2.40 and 45.60. The numerator matches the printout and the denominator does not.
b.21 participants in 3 conditions have degrees of freedom of 2 and 40, which correct to 1.60 and 32.00. Neither of the printed figures comes out of that design.
c.16 participants in 5 conditions have degrees of freedom of 4 and 60, which correct to 3.20 and 48.00. The denominator matches the printout and the numerator does not.
🏷️ Divide both corrected df by ε to restore them, then read off the design.

Question 12

🔧 Sphericity and the correction

What a correction does not touch

Memory researcher Tronstad’s results section reads: "Sphericity was violated (ε = 0.75), so a correction was applied. The degrees of freedom became 2.25 and 33.75, and the F statistic rose from 4.80 to 5.60." The error in that sentence is:
  • athe corrected pair of df is the wrong pair
  • ba correction never changes the F itself
  • cthe corrected df should have risen, not fallen
  • dan ε of 0.75 rules out applying a correction
🔎 What it is really asking

Of the quantities a correction touches, which one is it not allowed to move?

🧭 Which type of question this is

Sphericity: what the correction does and does not do.

🛠️ The procedure

A correction rescales the degrees of freedom and nothing else. The F statistic is built from two mean squares and is unchanged; what moves is the distribution it is judged against, and therefore the critical value and the P-value.

🧮 The working
Her degrees of freedom are right. Her study has 16 participants in 4 conditions, so uncorrected the df are 3 and (16 − 1)(4 − 1) = 45, and

  3 × 0.75 = 2.25   and   45 × 0.75 = 33.75 ✓

Her F is not. 4.80 came out of MS condition ⁄ MS error, and the correction touches neither mean square. It stays at 4.80.

What moves instead is the bar. The 5% critical value rises from 2.8115 on (3, 45) to 3.1557 on (2.25, 33.75), and P rises from .006 to .012. Still significant, so her conclusion survives — but it survives a harder test than the uncorrected one, which is the entire purpose of correcting.

Why the penalty goes on the df rather than on the F. When the pairwise differences do not have equal variances, the F statistic is still a reasonable measure of the condition effect; it is the reference distribution that is wrong. Shrinking the df picks a reference distribution with a fatter upper tail, which raises the bar by about the right amount.

The habit: after a correction, three things have moved — the df, the critical value and the P-value — and one has not.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.The pair is right: 3 × 0.75 = 2.25 and 45 × 0.75 = 33.75, and the 45 is (16 − 1)(4 − 1) for her 16 participants in four conditions.
c.The corrected df must fall, because ε is at most 1 and both df are multiplied by it. Her 2.25 and 33.75 are smaller than 3 and 45, exactly as they should be.
d.An ε of 0.75 is well below 1, so a correction is called for. Which of the available corrections to prefer is a matter of convention that texts disagree about; applying none is not what the ε supports.
🏷️ A correction moves the df, the bar and the P-value. Never the F.

Question 13

💪 What the pairing buys you

The error df the other design would have had

Sport psychologist Zaragoza tested 13 rowers under four stroke rates, which leaves her error row on 36 degrees of freedom. Analysed instead as four independent groups of 13 rowers, the error degrees of freedom would be:
  • a48
  • b36
  • c51
  • d39
🔎 What it is really asking

A different design counts error df by a different rule. Which rule, and on what?

🧭 Which type of question this is

What the pairing buys you: the degrees of freedom either way.

🛠️ The procedure

Repeated measures: df error = (n − 1)(k − 1). Independent groups: df error = N − k, where N is the number of scores. The two rules do not resemble one another at all.

🧮 The working
Her 13 rowers × 4 stroke rates give N = 52 scores.

  Repeated measures:  (13 − 1)(4 − 1) = 12 × 3 = 36
  Independent groups: N − k = 52 − 4 = 48

So the independent analysis has twelve more error degrees of freedom — and that is the one respect in which it is better off.

Where the twelve went. They are spent on the 13 rowers’ own levels, twelve degrees of freedom’s worth, which the repeated design lifts out of the error row and puts in a row of its own. The independent design never gets to do that: each of its rowers supplies one score, and one score cannot be compared with the same rower.

And why the trade is worth taking anyway. Degrees of freedom move the bar by a few per cent — the 5% critical value is 2.8663 on (3, 36) against 2.7981 on (3, 48). The error mean square divides straight into the F, and it is usually several times smaller once the rower differences are out of it. A small penalty on the bar, a large gain in the ratio.

The habit: fewer degrees of freedom in the repeated analysis is expected. Look at the mean square before concluding that anything was lost.
✗ Why the others are wrong
b.36 is her actual error row, (13 − 1)(4 − 1). The independent analysis counts its error df as scores minus conditions, which is a different rule and a different number.
c.51 is the Total df, nk − 1 = 52 − 1. That is what all the rows add to in either design, so it cannot be the error row of one of them.
d.39 is 52 − 13, subtracting the rowers from the scores. The independent rule subtracts the number of conditions, and there are four of those.
🏷️ Repeated: (n − 1)(k − 1). Independent: N − k. Different rules, different numbers.

Question 14

💪 What the pairing buys you

When the design cannot be used at all

Educational psychologist Zorzi is asked to advise on four proposals, each of which would measure the same people under every condition in an order that varies from one participant to the next. The proposal that varying the order cannot rescue is:
  • atiming a reaction task at three caffeine doses
  • brecording mood on four afternoons of one week
  • cteaching two problem-solving methods to the same pupils
  • drating four poster designs in a varied order
🔎 What it is really asking

Which conditions leave a permanent mark on the participant?

🧭 Which type of question this is

What the pairing buys you: the cost side.

🛠️ The procedure

Measuring the same people repeatedly invites carry-over — practice, fatigue, or simply remembering. Varying the order spreads a reversible carry-over evenly over the conditions. It can do nothing when a condition changes the participant permanently.

🧮 The working
Teaching is irreversible. A pupil who has been taught the first method cannot be returned to not knowing it, so when the second method is taught its score comes from a different pupil from the one who met the first. Reversing the order for half the class does not undo that — it simply gives half the class a contaminated score on one method and half a contaminated score on the other.

The other three leave nothing behind that varying the order cannot even out:
• Poster ratings: a participant may tire across the four, and the ordering spreads that tiredness evenly over the designs.
• Caffeine doses: the drug clears, so with a long enough gap each dose starts from the same baseline, and the varied order evens out practice on the task.
• Four afternoons: the occasions are the conditions, so there is no order to choose — and the change across the week is the thing being studied.

What to do with the teaching study instead. Different pupils in each condition, which turns a within-person comparison into a between-groups one and pays for it in the error term. That is the honest price, and it is the right price when the alternative is a confound you cannot remove.

The habit: before choosing a repeated design, ask whether a participant can be put back as they were.
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.Caffeine wears off, so with a long enough gap each dose starts from the same baseline. Practice on the reaction task is exactly what the varied order evens out.
b.Four afternoons of one week are occasions rather than treatments, so there is no order to vary — and the change across the week is the thing being measured.
d.Rating four poster designs leaves nothing permanent behind. A participant may tire over the four, and varying the order spreads that evenly across the designs.
🏷️ Counterbalancing evens out reversible carry-over. It cannot undo learning.

Question 15

💪 What the pairing buys you

The sentence an omnibus F cannot carry

Clinical researcher Osmani’s results section reads: "Reaction time differed across the four testing sessions, F(3, 45) = 7.20, p < .001, and performance was worst in the fourth session." Her output contains no comparisons between individual sessions. The part she may not write is:
  • acalling p below .001 a significant result
  • breading the F on 3 and 45 degrees of freedom
  • csaying reaction time differed across sessions
  • dnaming the fourth session as the worst
🔎 What it is really asking

One of her four claims needs a comparison she has not run. Which?

🧭 Which type of question this is

What the pairing buys you: the reach of the conclusion.

🛠️ The procedure

A repeated-measures F is an omnibus test: it says the condition means are not all equal. Naming one condition is a different question, and it needs its own comparisons with the number of them paid for.

🧮 The working
Her F of 7.20 on (3, 45) clears the 5% critical value of 2.8115 comfortably, and P = .0005. H₀ was μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ = μ₄, so what she has is exactly this: mean reaction time is not the same at all four sessions.

Naming the fourth session as the worst goes beyond that twice over. The F squares the deviations from the grand mean, so it keeps no direction at all; and it sums over all four sessions at once, so it points at no single one of them.

What she would need. Comparisons between individual sessions — and with four conditions there are 4 × 3 ⁄ 2 = 6 pairs, so running all six at 5% apiece would produce a false positive far more often than 5% of the time. Either plan the comparisons in advance or adjust their threshold, and print the four means beside them so the direction is visible.

The three things that are fine in her sentence. The df pair of 3 and 45 is right for 16 participants measured four times: k − 1 = 3 and (16 − 1)(4 − 1) = 45. A P below .001 is significant at any conventional level. And "differed across sessions" is precisely what the omnibus test licenses.

Say it to a friend: "the four sessions are not all the same — I cannot yet say which is worst."
✗ Why the others are wrong
a.A P-value below .001 is significant at any conventional level, and reporting it that way rather than as an exact figure is ordinary practice.
b.The pair 3 and 45 is correct for 16 participants measured four times: the condition row is k − 1 = 3 and the error row is 15 × 3 = 45.
c."Differed across sessions" is exactly the sentence a significant omnibus F supports. It is the one claim in her results section that needs nothing further.
🏷️ Omnibus F = not all equal. Naming a condition needs its own comparisons.
